column16: The CoA has three main goals in addressing climate change related issues, these include: 1) 100% clean energy for all Atlantans by 2035. 2) Fresh, affordable food within ½ accessible mile for 100% of Atlantans by 2030. 3) 59% reduction in GHG emissions by 2030 and net zero by 2050. Additionally, the City intervenes in the Georgia Public Service Commission's Integrated Resource Plan (IRP) and Rate Case process with the Georgia Coalition of Local Governments, this is essential for the City to advocate for a clean energy future and give 2.1M residents a voice for shaping energy policy and resource decisions. State energy policy is essential to meet greenhouse gas reduction and clean energy goals. Lastly, the CoA collaborates with local governments across the state and region through the Southeast Sustainability Directors Network (SSDN).

column18:
Environmental justice and equity are key components that are embedded into CoA climate initiatives, and the definition of our office includes science-based analysis informed by the community. The City of Atlanta has a Climate Resilience Advisory Board, which includes diverse local stakeholders to serve in prioritizing strategies, contributing analytical and research support, and supporting community engagement to aid the City in analyzing and selecting key initiatives. The board has four working groups that include: 1) Clean Energy Funding 2) Community and Partner Engagement 3) Decarbonize Atlanta Buildings 4) Transformative Multimodal Transportation 5) Urban Agriculture and Food Systems. 

The City has been developing Climate Resilient ATL, which will be the city's first community-led and data driven, Climate Resilience Action Plan. This is to shape a climate resilient City Built for the Future. CoA has a goal to reach 2,500 Atlanta residents to gather feedback through the Community Feedback Survey and through community visioning sessions. These community visioning events include a kick-off meeting, quadrant-based workshops, a high energy burden roundtable, festival tabling, and a wrap-up meeting. The strategies, policies, and incentives that will be included in the plan will be informed and driven by these community engagement efforts.
column19:
For developing climate resilience actions in the newly established plan will include equitable and inclusive distribution of climate action, we know the effects of climate change are impacted unequally across the city and the City has a role in providing programs that target the most vulnerable. For example, the City piloted a WeatheRISE ATL, which is a program for weatherizing homes and aiding in meeting our reduction of energy burden goal. This program invested $2,400,000 to comprehend certain areas of energy-burdened neighborhoods due to lighting, HVAC, insulation, and age of buildings to help provide upgrades in the highest energy-burdened neighborhoods which are approximately 200 homes to date. The benefits of this program include the preservation of naturally occurring affordable housing, a decrease in carbon emissions, improved health outcomes, job training opportunities, and contractor business development. The partners who are moving this work forward are Sustainable Georgia Futures, PAHL, and Greenlink Analytics (https://www.100atl.com/weatherise-atl). 

Another example is the Commercial Property Assessed Clean Energy program (“C-PACE”) provides city of Atlanta property owners with an innovative financing tool to make needed structural repairs and upgrades to their properties to save energy and water use. Invest Atlanta has authorized the issuance of $500M+ in bonds for the program. Commercial property owners can choose from hundreds of eligible building improvements, ranging from windows and doors to roofing, to solar panel arrays, and HVAC units. The program benefits include: 100% project financing from $5,000 to $20MM+, eligibility based primarily on property equity, financing approvals within as little as 3 days, up to 20 years, fully amortized terms with fixed rates, up to 100% CLTV, no prepayment penalties for partial or full prepayments, no payments for up to 12 or more months, no capital outlays, no guarantors, and no financial covenants. This payment structure flows through a property's solid waste bill (so this program is not associated with a person, but with a property, making it more equitable and does not rely on credit score/traditional financing mechanisms).

Additionally, Atlanta was a selected City in March 2024 for the Bloomberg American Sustainable Cities initiative to drive progress on climate mitigation and promote equitable outcomes. The Bloomberg Philanthropies Innovation Team (I-Team) sits within the Office of Policy, in an effort to tackle climate change and racial wealth gaps. Lastly, a Climate Risk and Vulnerability Assessment study is being conducted in collaboration with local scientific experts to analyze and map climate perils facing Atlanta and the most vulnerable areas facing the load of environmental impact and this will inform actions and priority areas of focus, especially in regard to adaptation.

The four strategic axes on which the Barcelona Climate Emergency Action Plan is based are as follows:- Mitigation- Adaptation- Climate Justice- Promotion of Citizen Action. This is still valid in the new Climate Plan.

Therefore, the plan places the most vulnerable people at the center of climate policies, understanding vulnerable people as those who, either because of their socioeconomic situation or because of their condition, health or age, suffer more directly from the effects of climate change. climate. 

Thus, among the objectives of the plan for 2030 are the following:- 0 people in a situation of energy poverty- 100% of the population within a 5-minute walk of a climate shelter- 10,000 homes/year refurbished- Improve the thermal comfort of schools.

Among the action lines there are also the following ones: 

C1. Implementing the Neighborhood Plan 2025-2028
Description: The draft of the new Neighbourhood Plan 2025-2028 includes actions to adapt
public spaces and facilities in the city to the climate and social realities of neighbourhoods
(with particular emphasis on boosting the city's green infrastructure, shaded areas and social
and environmental services and improving connectivity) and to promote projects with social
return that support access to clean energy while leading to a lower and more efficient use of
energy, particularly in the most vulnerable households, thus helping achieve the decarbonisation
and emission reduction targets and mitigate the effects of energy poverty.
● Improving connectivity and pedestrian accessibility within neighbourhoods to enable
local residents to access facilities and services more easily with their usual daily travel.
● When drafting projects, ensuring they reflect the necessary studies (e.g. in relation to
shade or the reflectance of materials) and a checklist of criteria to ensure premium urban
planning standards from an environmental and climate adaptation point of view and in
relation to the achievement of the desired goals of increasing greenery, creating shade,
depaving, generating energy and sustainable drainage systems, among others.
● Promoting energy collection projects with social return that give local residents
better access to clean, local and renewable energy, with particular focus on the most
vulnerable households.


C2. Ensuring people's health and well-being in connection with climate change:
● Designing a health and climate change strategy to deliver more on the City Council's
undertakings in a cross-cutting way.
● Improving access to healthcare for those who are more vulnerable to the effects of
climate change and adapting the health system to this new reality.
● Ensuring that there are alternative energy supply systems and resources in place in case
there is a fault with the healthcare system.
● Monitoring and checking for pests to prevent the transmission of vector-borne diseases
and applying public health protocols for cases of arbovirus-transmitted infections in the
population.
● Taking account of climate considerations in mental health programmes, providing more
resources and working collaboratively with the community in relation to these matters.
● Designing the strategy against the feminisation of poverty and job insecurity and
addressing the issue of caregiving, all this while taking the climate emergency into

The actions identified in our most recent (July 25) Net Zero Action Plan have number of co benefits and opportunities. The Clean Air Zone, implemented in 2021 has not only seen a reduction in vehicle emissions and particulates in the city centre which reduce the city wide emissions, but also brings health benefits as the air quality improves and the number of journeys taken by other means (walking, cycling) increases.   Since the Clean Air Zone began operation in 2021, the percentage of the most polluting vehicles entering the city has dropped - from just over 15% in June 2021 to 4.5% in August 2024. 

The climate actions identified in the transport plan look to increase and improve the provision of cycling lanes and walking routes, providing more attractive alternatives to private vehicle use and thereby leading to reduced carbon emissions. This will also have the co-benefit of reducing traffic congestion and improving the health of those who take advantage of walking and cycling routes. Similarly, reallocating road space to cyclists and public transport, and reducing parking availability frees up more space for development and promotes health benefits through air quality improvements. The BTP monitoring strategy has been developed to measure progress in achieving the aims and objectives of the Birmingham Transport Plan. To better understand the greenhouse gas emissions from transport, an indicator for traffic flows in the city has been developed, using over 700 real time traffic sensors that have been strategically placed around the city. This data shows there were 3.69 billion vehicle miles travelled by motorised modes of travel in Birmingham during 2023. This represents an increase of 3.4% on 2022. Using the average UK vehicle emissions for 2023, we have estimated that 680,000 tCO2e were emitted by transport in Birmingham in 2023 . Over the next year this monitoring will be developed to increase our confidence in the data to create a more reliable local estimate of carbon emissions arising from transport.


Birmingham District Heat Network is a centralised heat network which supplies major buildings in the city centre with efficient heating, cooling and power. The scheme provides affordable heating, saving the council money whilst producing less emissions than building-level heating system alternatives. The network also provides future opportunity to decarbonise multiple buildings at once as the gas-fired systems are converted to a decarbonised source. This opportunity is currently being explored. 

EV charging points introduced across the city seek to reduce carbon emissions but similarly have co-benefits of improving air quality, noise pollution, and also providing infrastructure to support uptake of Electric vehicles among residents and businesses. We have also commenced with a pilot for lamppost charging which helps make EV accessible to those who live in dense terraced housing with no off street parking and therefore space to install private chargers. The trial rollout includes 560 lamppost chargers (5kw-7kw) which are being delivered using £1m of Off Street Residential Charge Point scheme funding and is working with its delivery partner Ubitricity to install the chargers. An additional £14m of funding has been allocated through the Local EV infrastructure scheme to the region and the Council plan to make use of this funding to expand this network over the coming years. Our Birmingham Hydrogen Bus scheme has included the purchase of 20 hydrogen buses and we are looking to scale up to 100+ vehicles. The co-benefits relate to the Tyseley energy park where the buses are refuelled which is a site at the forefront of research and delivery of low carbon and zero carbon transport fuels and energy generation. The demand for hydrogen created by the hydrogen buses will help increase the scaling of the energy park and could make alternatives more accessible for other businesses. 

Retrofitting, SHDF, ECO4 and whole house retrofit pilots: all these schemes seek to improve the energy efficiency and decarbonise council and privately owned homes but deliver co-benefits for residents. In the immediate term, better insulated homes reduce the heating bill for residents, improving affordability of heat. Risk of damp and mould is reduced improving indoor air quality and benefiting occupiers health. Affordable warmth also helps reduce the likelihood of excess winter deaths. Quality homes also decrease the budgetary demands which buildings with shorter lifespans or buildings which will need to be retrofitted create. Thus the investment into buildings of a higher standard can be a more sustainable use of council funds. column16: Chicago's climate action plan goes far beyond reducing emissions—it's designed to unlock a wide range of benefits that improve lives, strengthen communities, and build long-term resilience. Chicago is advancing several climate initiatives that will have greater impact on the residents of Chicago beyond emissions reduction. In July 2025, the city hosted Aspen Ideas: Climate conference, which brought together global and regional policymakers, scientist and energy experts, innovators, artists and community leaders to share ideas, develop collaborative actions and share climate mitigating solutions. Clean energy investments are expected to stimulate local economies, especially through solar, wind, and energy efficiency projects. \nIn early 2025, Chicago City Council approved the Green Social Housing (GSH) Ordinance, which establishes an independent nonprofit developer under the Department of Housing. GSH will create mixed-income housing using green building standards, ensures permanent affordability without relying on federal subsidies like Low-Income Housing Tax Credits. The program will also reduce tenants' utility bills by an average of $572/year, as well as improves indoor air quality and supports climate goals by cutting building emissions. Green job creation is a major focus, with workforce development programs targeting underserved communities. Through the City's Greencorps Chicago is a 9-month paid training program targeting residents with limited access to traditional employment opportunities. The program promotes environmental stewardship while preparing participants for careers in industries such as horticulture and landscaping, tree care and urban forestry, and ecological restoration and invasive species management. Lowering utilities bills through energy efficiency upgrades and renewable energy adoption can help residents save money. In 2024, the city launched the Green Homes Chicago program, which is a city-led initiative that provides free energy efficiency upgrades to income-eligible homeowners, helping reduce utility costs and improve indoor comfort while advancing climate goals. The City of Chicago also plays a strategic and supportive role in advancing community solar programs through partnerships, policy, and outreach. By collaborating with local nonprofits on solar energy, the city is helping to empower its residents with the knowledge about the benefits and opportunities of renewable energy sources. The expansion of green spaces an opportunity to improve quality of life for residents and reduce urban heat islands through tree planting and nature-based solutions. In 2022 on Arbor Day, the city launched its Our Roots Chicago Programs, which set to plant 75,000 trees over five years. As of April 2025, over 60,000 new parkway trees have been planted throughout the city. The City of Chicago is taking an approach is holistic—climate action is not just about carbon, but about creating a healthier, more equitable, and economically vibrant city.

column19:
The City of Chicago has taken several concrete steps to ensure that the identified climate actions are equitable and inclusive, with compelling evidence across planning, budgeting, and implementation. In January 2024, Mayor Johnson and the Chicago City Council reinstated the Department of Environment to tackle the city's legacy of environmental racism, and to advocate for communities of color facing disproportionate climate risks. During the fall of 2023, the city conducted a Cumulative Impact Assessment (CIA). This assessment pinpointed communities that are most burdened by pollution—particularly on the South and West Sides—and to inform where equitable zoning changes needed to be made. As a result, the Hazel Johnson Cumulative Impacts Ordinance was introduced in April 2025. This landmark environmental justice policy will protect historically disadvantaged communities in Chicago by requiring cumulative impact assessments for new or expanding industrial developments within city limits. 

Along with the CIA, Chicago created the city's first Environmental Action Plan, which sets a clear goal that all Chicago departments will work together to improve environment, health, and quality of life in EJ neighborhoods by changing internal decision-making, policies, engagement practices, and resource allocation. Key strategies include improving data collection and transparency (like expanding air monitoring and creating real-time modelling tools), strengthening regulatory enforcement, changing zoning and development practices, increasing community involvement in decision making, and ensuring accountability through measurable metrics and regular reporting.

 Lead-Safe Chicago is the City of Chicago's comprehensive initiative to eliminate lead exposure from homes, water, and the environment—especially in communities most at risk. Chicago has among the oldest and most extensive lead service lines in the United States. Chicago's South and West Sides—home to many Black and Latino residents—have some of the highest concentrations of lead service lines. These communities already face compounded environmental risk; therefore, the city has made lead remediation a critical priority towards addressing health equity and climate justice. The Equity Lead Service Line Replacement Program covers 100% of replacement costs for households earning less than 80% of the area median income, or with children under six or elevated blood lead levels. Children under age 6 are most vulnerable because their bodies absorb lead more easily, and it can severely affect brain development, behavior, and growth The city implemented the Daycare Lead Service Line Replacement program to offer free replacement to licensed daycare facilities The Chicago Department of Public Health (CDPH) operate several lead-based paint mitigation programs as part of its broader effort to eliminate childhood lead poisoning. The Childhood Lead Poisoning Prevention program provides blood lead testing, case management services for children with elevated blood level and development assessment and referrals for additional services. The Lead Safe Housing Registry in Chicago is a public resource managed by the Chicago Department of Public Health (CDPH) to help families—especially those with young children—identify housing that has been inspected and deemed “lead safe.” 

The City of Chicago's Department of Environment released a Request for Proposals (RFP) to develop an updated Green Stormwater Infrastructure Strategy—the first since 2014. This updated strategy, mandated by the new NPDES permit effective April 2024, explicitly centers equity, targeting Environmental Justice (EJ) communities facing the worst flooding and pollution impacts. It emphasizes natural systems like permeable pavement, bioswales, and green roofs, aiming to provide both climate resilience and enhanced public access to green spaces.

column18: NYC's environmental justice law includes ten requirements for the city to consider when making the EJNYC Report, which was released in 2024. These requirements ensure that major climate, environmental, and health concerns are identified and measured, and that existing City programs to address those issues are also examined. The EJNYC Report includes: The locations and boundaries of the city's Environmental Justice Areas, A description of environmental justice issues that may be affecting Environmental Justice Areas, including: Locations within the city that are experiencing each issue, where possible, Recommendations for further data collection, research, or analysis that may be done to better understand which locations within the city are experiencing each issue, An estimate of current federal, state, and local investment per capita in renewable energy in Environmental Justice Areas as compared to non-Environmental Justice Areas in the city, A description of barriers to meaningful participation in environmental decision-making affecting residents of Environmental Justice Areas, Existing City programs and activities that advance environmental justice and allow the public to participate in City agency decision-making, Existing City programs and activities that allow for public engagement and participation in decision-making regarding the siting of facilities and infrastructure, Existing City programs, policies, processes, and activities that may cause environmental justice concerns. Changes that could be made to existing City programs and policies to increase participation by people in Environmental Justice Areas in decision-making that implicates environmental justice concerns, Latest environmental data, including (but not limited) to air and water quality, the location and characteristics of infrastructure owned and operated by the City, and violations of city environmental regulations, that may reflect environmental problems in Environmental Justice Areas, Environmental Justice programs proposed or in effect in other cities or states in the United States. https://www.nyc.gov/content/climate/pages/reports-and-publications/ejnyc-report
column19: New York City launched the first municipal environmental justice program in the nation to develop the forthcoming Environmental Justice for All Study and Plan. In 2017, New York City passed Local Laws 60 and 64 to assess environmental equity issues and develop a plan to incorporate environmental justice into the fabric of City decision-making. This legislation centers on three main products: a report, a mapping tool, and a plan. To carry out this work, the local law mandated that the Mayor and City Council appoint an independent Environmental Justice Advisory Board (EJAB) composed of environmental justice advocates, academics, and public health experts to work with the City on developing the comprehensive citywide Environmental Justice Study and Plan. The Study launched in 2023 informs the development of an Environmental Justice Plan incorporating environmental justice into the City's decision-making. The plan will identify potential citywide and local initiatives for promoting environmental justice and outline a set of discrete recommendations for better embedding equity and environmental justice into the City's decision-making processes. In addition, City agencies must work with the Advisory Board to develop plans to address environmental injustices in communities of color and low-income communities in consultation with the impacted communities. In early 2021, the City released an interactive map of the City's Environmental Justice Areas (https://experience.arcgis.com/experience/6a3da7b920f248af961554bdf01d668b/page/Data-Explorer/?org=nyc) and launched a citywide public engagement process to bring frontline communities to the table in developing Environmental Justice for All Study and Plan. The EJNYC Web-Portal) will be a public web-based portal and mapping tool based on the data and analysis from the EJNYC Report (https://www.nyc.gov/content/climate/pages/reports-and-publications/ejnyc-report). This portal will host interactive maps, a data repository, and information on relevant City programs relating to environmental justice. It will be used by City agencies to inform their environmental decision-making and will empower residents and organizers with the tools to continue advocating for the best outcomes for their communities. More information: https://www.nyc.gov/content/climate/pages/environmental-justice

column18: When planning for, investing in and delivering climate action, the GLA uses several tools to help quantify equitable and inclusive distribution: - Climate Risk Mapping - we are aware that high climate risk coincides with areas of income and health inequalities. This city-wide map overlays key metrics to identify areas within London that are most exposed to climate impacts with high concentrations of vulnerable populations. This map helps serve as a guide to prioritise and equally distribute investments, including through our grant funding programmes. - 10 Minute Walk Map - To help target action to areas where people currently live more than a 10-minute walk from a green space, we have created this 10-Minute Walk Map (with the help of Greenspace Information for Greater London CIC). It shows priority areas where Londoners may live more than an 800 metre walk (i.e. about 10 minutes) from an accessible green space of at least 0.02 hectares (a common size of pocket park).- Emerging work on identification of vulnerable properties for climate preparedness and prioritisation - We are in the process of establishing a database showing (i.) which of London's homes, buildings, workplaces, and critical infrastructure - such as care homes, GP practices, schools, early-years settings and hospitals - are vulnerable to heat risk due to climate change; (ii.) where they are located, (iii.) where data for the above two items sits, relative to the indices of deprivation for each of the 32 London boroughs, to support targeted interventions in: areas of high deprivation and inequality; and properties to which climate change poses the greatest heat risk. column19: The City of Los Angeles is actively working to ensure that climate action is equitable and inclusive by embedding environmental justice and community-led priorities across its planning and implementation processes. One of the city's landmark efforts was establishing the Climate Emergency Mobilization Office (CEMO) in 2021, which was the first of its kind in the United States. CEMO was created to ensure that frontline communities most impacted by climate change were centered in the city's climate policy development. This office has collaborated closely with grassroots and community-based organizations to co-design programs and initiatives that reflect community needs and lived experience. Los Angeles also utilizes the L.A. Equity Index to prioritize neighborhoods for climate mitigation and adaptation investments. The Equity Index assesses social, economic, and environmental indicators across the city to identify communities facing the greatest cumulative burdens and systemic inequities. This tool helps departments direct resources toward areas with the greatest need. In June 2024, the Department of City Planning completed the City's first Climate Vulnerability Assessment (CVA), which was developed in close partnership with community-based organizations in highly vulnerable neighborhoods. Through workshops, interviews, and participatory research, community partners shaped how the City understands vulnerability to key hazards such as extreme heat, wildfire smoke, drought, and flooding. The CVA will guide future climate adaptation efforts by identifying targeted, place-based investments to protect health, enhance resilience, and build adaptive capacity in the most at-risk communities. These initiatives reflect Los Angeles's commitment to an inclusive climate agenda that advances equity, strengthens local leadership, and ensures that those most affected by climate change are empowered to shape solutions.\n

Manchester recognises that climate action delivers wide-ranging social, economic, and environmental benefits. These opportunities will be outlined in the forthcoming Climate Change Plan https://democracy.manchester.gov.uk/documents/s56554/Manchester%20Climate%20Change%20Framework%20and%20Adaptation%20Plan.pdf for Manchester and have been documented in the Manchester Climate Change Framework 2020-25 (2022 update) and the GMCA Five-Year Environment Plan, and will be further developed in Manchester's forthcoming 2025-30 Climate Change Strategy.
Buildings and retrofit
Retrofitting homes improves comfort, reduces fuel poverty, and enhances resilience to extreme weather. Upgrading homes to EPC C could save residents £223 per year. Retrofit investment across Greater Manchester is estimated at £7 billion, supporting around 9,800 jobs in the Northwest.
Transport and mobility
Decarbonising transport improves air quality and health outcomes. Active travel could save the NHS £17 billion nationally over 20 years. Expanding public transport and EV infrastructure supports local businesses and jobs, while innovations in last-mile delivery could cut emissions by up to 26% by 2025.
Health and wellbeing
Energy-efficient homes reduce cold-related illnesses, while green urban spaces and active travel improve mental health and lower long-term healthcare costs. Every £1 invested in warm homes is estimated to reduce health costs by £0.42.
Adaptation and resilience
Investments in sustainable drainage, tree planting, and green corridors reduce flood risk, protect critical infrastructure, and enhance biodiversity, while improving neighbourhood quality.
Just transition and economy
Climate action underpins inclusive economic growth, creating new opportunities in construction, energy, and transport. A just transition ensures vulnerable groups benefit from lower bills, cleaner air, and access to green jobs.
Financing the transition
Achieving Manchester's 2038 net zero target is estimated to cost £10 billion. Alongside government support, Manchester and GMCA are working with DESNZ to develop blended finance models that leverage ESG-aligned private capital to accelerate delivery.

We're taking a holistic view of our climate adaptation and mitigation strategies. In particular, we're using various approaches to water and land management that have been successfully piloted throughout New Orleans and, when implemented together, are intended to create even greater neighborhood benefits—such as improved health, economic opportunity, environmental education, and recreation. We want to make sure everybody, including our disadvantaged and small businesses, have the opportunity to participate in this new “blue and green” economy. In order to make sure we're making these new opportunities available for our small local firms, the City 'dubundled' several of our green infrastructure construction and maintenance contracts, meaning they are broken down by project intervention type instead of by full project footprint. For example, rather than issuing a maintenance contract to a single, large contractor for all green infrastructure maintenance, the contracts for maintenance will be for specific interventions such as just the rain gardens, the bioswales, or the permeable pavement. This will allow smaller firms, especially DBE firms, to receive contracts for maintenance that they are qualified to execute on a smaller scale. This provides opportunities for growth of our local firms and contractors, allowing them to become experts in this new field. The debundling work is ongoing, there is also now a set aside program, although it is not specific to climate projects and those projects often are exempted because so much of the work is currently federally funded: https://nola.gov/set-aside/#:~:text=The%20Set%2DAside%20Program%20in,Disadvantaged%20Business%20Enterprises%20(DBEs).

We are currently developing the various requirements of expertise and licensure that will be needed to procure these contracts. Having smaller contractors that are specific to an intervention type will open the door for various contractors to work with the city. This is a cross departmental initiative for the City. Our Offices of Economic Development, Supplier Diversity, Public Works and the New Orleans Redevelopment Authority are working together to ensure that these contracts are available, and that local contractors are made aware of these opportunities. 

Within the Gentilly Resilience District, in the Community Adaptation Program, or CAP, is a $5 million investment from a 2014 HUD grant in residential stormwater management improvements to owner-occupied single-family homes with household incomes at or below 80% of Area Median Income located within the Gentilly Resilience District. The program is diverting and detaining stormwater runoff on over 200 properties with an average grant award between $10,000 and $25,000, and single contractors working on each of these small projects. The improvements are designed and installed at no cost to the homeowner. The first $5 million spent in this program was successful, got out the door and into projects quickly.

At the same time, the City is implementing the EPA's Climate Pollution Reduction Grant (CPRG), a $50 million federal award that provides resources to launch a suite of climate programs, including municipal building decarbonization, energy benchmarking, Solar for All subsidies, bike and e-bike expansion, and workforce development partnerships. CPRG ensures that federal climate investments translate into direct local benefits, creating new green jobs, improving health outcomes, and advancing equity in disadvantaged communities.

Likewise, Finance New Orleans (formerly the Finance Authority of New Orleans) has established a 'Green Bank' to make low interest financing available for homeowners and businesses for energy efficiency upgrades and drainage improvements. These include installation of permeable pavement, green infrastructure like rain gardens, and solar upgrades. Projects like this can lower insurance premiums and monthly energy costs. The upcoming Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund opportunity from the EPA could help significantly expand the green bank. New Orleans was recently selected to continue into Phase 2 of the Coalition for Green Capital's Municipal Investment Fund (MIF) alongside Finance New Orleans. This work is currently underway and focused on developing a roadmap and project pipeline for clean energy, solar, and resilience hubs that can attract large-scale investment. By building this pipeline, the City and Finance New Orleans are creating opportunities for accessible, low-interest financing that reduces household costs, builds community resilience, and strengthens local capacity for climate-resilient construction and clean energy deployment.

As noted above, adapting our infrastructure to our changing climate not only offers greater resilience to storms and flooding, but also is a key opportunity to expand our local economy. By promoting the engagement of local businesses in our blue and green economy, our city becomes more sustainable — environmentally and economically. 

In 2015, the City launched BuildNOLA to help train and build capacity for small and disadvantaged businesses and ensure that our local blue and green economy is equitable and accessible to all our local businesses. In its review of the City's 2017 Climate Action Plan, the Climate Action Equity Working Group (CAEWG) recommended that the City pay additional attention to encouraging more DBE participation in climate action work and to attracting more Black residents to jobs and businesses in the climate action economy. The City included many of the recommendations from the CAEWG in its updated Climate Action Plan, which was released in December 2022. Building on this foundation, the City has partnered with the Greater New Orleans Foundation on reports such as Economic Opportunity through Green Infrastructure: Equitable Access to Jobs and Contracts in Greater New Orleans, which explored opportunities and barriers for more equitable access to jobs created by resilience projects.

Additionally in November 2020, the City along with NOLABA and YouthForce NOLA was selected to participate in JP Morgan Chase's AdvancingCities Challenge. This three-year, $5 million grant supported the development of a robust blue/green infrastructure workforce pipeline that prepared high school youth, opportunity youth, people of color, and residents with low incomes for high-wage jobs in the growing water management sector. It also provided technical assistance, incubation, acceleration, capital access, and talent development programs for small and disadvantaged businesses, particularly firms led by people of color, to better compete for procurement opportunities.
 
Building on this momentum, the City is now implementing the EPA's Climate Pollution Reduction Grant (CPRG). Equity is a central requirement of CPRG, and New Orleans is ensuring that its $50 million award expands opportunities and benefits across historically disadvantaged communities. Programs under CPRG will include workforce development partnerships, energy efficiency and solar programs targeted at low-income households, a municipal building decarbonization program, and safe, accessible mobility investments such as bike lanes and e-bike rebates. With support from CPRG, the City is expanding its tree planting grant program, aiming to accelerate progress toward planting 40,000 trees by 2030, with an emphasis on stormwater management, neighborhood beautification, and heat reduction in underserved communities.

Equity is also guiding new climate resilience strategies. The City is developing its first Heat Mitigation Plan, which will prioritize neighborhoods most vulnerable to extreme heat, layering solutions such as reflective pavement, shade structures, cooling centers, and tree canopy expansion. The City is also developing a community engagement framework to ensure transparency, accountability, and community leadership in resilience and sustainability projects.

The City continues to advance access to renewable energy through its community solar program, designed to make solar accessible to renters and homeowners without suitable rooftops. By lowering energy costs and reducing exposure to energy insecurity, the program extends the benefits of clean energy to populations historically excluded from traditional solar markets.

Finally, the City is working within the transportation framework to provide safer and more equitable access to walkers, bikers, and public transit users. Expanded mobility options increase access to jobs, services, and recreation without requiring reliance on private cars, lowering transportation costs and emissions while enhancing equity and opportunity.

-	Improved health: The promotion of active travel, public transport, electric vehicles and green spaces all improve air quality which in turn has positive health benefits (for example: Reduced cardio-vascular conditions, reduced number of cancer cases). Active travel results in reduced obesity rates
-	Improved wellbeing (including mental health): More green spaces and cleaner streets combined with more active travel improves mental health and wellbeing
-	Safer communities: Streets that a cleaner and where residents recycle (as a result of climate action to reduce waste going to landfill) often are accompanied with greater community safety
-	Civic pride: Cleaner streets and greater green spaces promote civic pride
-	The circular economy: Actions taken by communities to reduce waste (including re-purposing food waste) and reuse items support the circular economy which directly contributes to resource efficiency by communities and residents consuming less.
-	Better and higher paid jobs: Green growth is shown to result in better and higher paid jobs. This is of critical importance in Newcastle, a city with a rich industrial heritage but one where de-industrialisation over the past 50 years has resulted in many low paid, low skilled jobs. Green growth can address this by providing new opportunities to communities.
-	Greater variety of jobs: The breadth and range of green growth jobs is a major opportunity for city residents, enabling them to pursue opportunities similar to their skillsets and of interest to them.
-	More money in residents pockets: Decarbonisation measures in residential homes result in lower energy bills, especially when combined with solar, resulting in those residents being better off.

Quantifying the equitable and inclusive distribution of climate action is achieved through three key tools:
-	Data driven analysis via the sustainability needs assessment: The sustainability needs assessment collects, analyses and present data on the Newcastle population profile, including its size, age distribution, socioeconomic status, gender and ethnicity. It collects and interprets a health profile of the city. This particularly focuses on respiratory, physical, mental and cardiovascular illnesses. It assesses and interprets carbon reduction efforts and their impact on health, especially respiratory outcomes in children and other population groups (taking a life course approach). It provides evidence on how Net Zero Policies and the 2030 Action plan supports Marmot City goals by addressing wider social determinants of health and reducing health inequalities.
-	Completion of an Equality Impact Assessment (EIA) as part of any climate action: The delegated decision process requires that an EIA is completed which considers the impact a project, policy or programme has on equality characteristics (sex, age, race, religion or belief, sexual orientation, gender reassignment, disability, pregnancy/maternity, parents and carers, socio-economic status). This is a data driven approach which evidences the impact. All climate change projects must follow this process.
-	Geospatial analysis of climate impacts: When analysing the impact of climate change we use geospatial tools to understand how these spread geographically - a key data set we use is the indices of deprivation (IND). This is a UK government measure of relative deprivation at the small area level in England. It combines information from seven different domains to produce an overall ranking of deprivation for each area. These domains include income, employment, education, health, crime, barriers to housing and services, and living environment. When considering the impact of climate change (flooding for example) we can clearly see which communities this impacts and then quantify this so as to see how to mitigate the impact to the most vulnerable.

column18:
Community engagement is a core part of the climate change teams activities, this includes engaging with schools, business and local communities. 
Since 2022, NCC has offered a funding scheme to support community climate action across Northumberland. This is now named the Environment and Climate fund and provides £50,000 funding per year in small grants to community groups - applicants can apply for funding between £250 - 5000 for their projects. The scheme is available for voluntary and community groups, registered charities, constituted groups or clubs, community interest companies, social enterprises, town and parish councils and faith groups provided the project will be inclusive and benefit the whole community. 
Through retrofit and home energy improvements, NCC's warmer homes scheme targets residents with the greatest need to reduce energy and heating costs. Installed improvements help to save money on energy bills, improve home comfort and reduce carbon emissions. Means testing applications and use of IMD data to identify eligible areas allows residents with the most need to be prioritised for national programmes such as the Home Upgrade Grant (HUG), Social Housing Decarbonisation Fund (SHDF) and the Energy Company Obligation (ECO) schemes. Progress is measured through tracking the average Energy Performance Certificate (EPC) ratings for domestic properties, the number of home upgrades and retrofits completed, and number of homes using low carbon heat sources. 
NCC are involved in building community partnerships to enable development of community owned district heating solutions. This action is specifically targeting off-gas grid rural communities. Progress is measured through tracking the number of off gas grid communities engaged in district heating schemes and the number of households/businesses in scope for district heating solutions when rolled out. 
Working alongside an Off-Grid Taskforce led by Community Action Northumberland, NCC have identified a number of properties that are off electricity grid. Many of these properties are reliant on expensive and high emissions fuels such as diesel. The analysis highlights multiple groups of off electricity grid properties and allows specific areas to be targeted. The aim of the taskforce is to improve the electricity supplies to these properties, assisting in reducing energy cost and decarbonisation of their electricity supply.

The jurisdiction has identified a wide range of opportunities and benefits arising from its ambitious climate action initiatives, which extend far beyond environmental improvements. These opportunities are embedded across key themes in the carbon neutral action plan, generating economic, social, and health advantages that contribute to the overall well-being of the city and its residents.

Transport:

Climate action in transport creates significant benefits, such as improving air quality and reducing pollution, leading to healthier communities.
Expanding vehicle-free public spaces enhances urban living by making streets more accessible and enjoyable for people.
Investments in safer cycling infrastructure promote active, healthier lifestyles, while also making it cheaper and more efficient for residents to move around the city.

Built Environment:

Climate-focused upgrades to housing and commercial premises lead to substantial reductions in energy bills for residents and businesses, improving affordability.
These upgrades also enhance living conditions, creating healthier homes and more productive workplaces.
The emphasis on sustainable construction fosters new skilled employment opportunities and stimulates growth in green industries, bolstering the local economy.
Reducing emissions from traditional gas boilers improves air quality and further supports public health goals.

Energy Generation:

Localised low-carbon energy generation strengthens energy security and reduces dependency on external sources.
By positioning the jurisdiction as a leader in low-carbon energy research and development, it attracts investment into sustainable infrastructure, bolstering the city's economic growth.
Businesses and communities benefit from lower energy costs, creating savings that can be reinvested into other areas of the economy.

Waste & Water:

Climate action helps maintain cleanliness and reduces waste, while creating job opportunities in the circular economy.
More sustainable waste disposal solutions lower costs for businesses and taxpayers.
These efforts also provide household savings, particularly in food bills, and ensure long-term security of water supply for the city.

Consumption:

Developing a sustainable food economy not only boosts local agriculture but also promotes healthier eating and tackles food poverty.
Community knowledge-sharing initiatives support the local food economy while enhancing food security and improving public health.
Climate-conscious consumption practices reduce the financial strain on individuals and foster a more resilient economy.

Carbon Removal:

The jurisdiction is focused on offsetting emissions from hard-to-reduce sectors by promoting carbon capture technologies.
Investments in land management practices help retain carbon, improve the environment, and contribute to long-term emission reduction goals.

Resilience & Adaptation:

Ensuring that climate adaptation is incorporated into future policies enhances the city's resilience to extreme weather and other climate-related risks.
Protecting properties and infrastructure from flooding and other climate impacts is a key benefit, reducing economic losses and enhancing public safety.
By preparing core services for a changing climate, the jurisdiction builds a foundation for long-term sustainability.

Ecology & Biodiversity:

Enhancing biodiversity not only protects local ecosystems but also contributes to urban cooling through increased green spaces and tree cover.
Carbon storage is enhanced through habitat creation, further supporting the city's carbon neutrality goals.
The preservation and expansion of green spaces create natural flood defences and strengthen ecological resilience, ensuring that both people and wildlife benefit from a healthier, more sustainable environment.

In summary, the jurisdiction's climate action plan drives a wide range of positive outcomes, from economic growth and job creation to improved public health and environmental resilience. These efforts are essential to building a sustainable, prosperous future for the city and its inhabitants.

column19:
The Council prioritises deep engagement with local communities, recognising that sustainable solutions can only be achieved when citizens are actively involved and empowered. By integrating community voices into the design and implementation of climate initiatives, we aim to create lasting benefits that are widely shared across all neighbourhoods.

Key actions taken to foster this inclusive approach include:

Community Engagement in Project Design and Implementation: We actively involve local communities in shaping climate initiatives from the outset. By inviting citizens to contribute to the planning and decision-making processes, we ensure that solutions are tailored to meet the specific needs and challenges of different neighbourhoods. For example, improving green spaces in communities is more effective when residents feel a sense of ownership and can see tangible benefits, such as enhanced recreation areas, better air quality, and increased resilience to climate impacts.

'Have Your Say' Forums: In partnership with Nottingham Trent University, we have established a series of 'Have Your Say' discussion forums, providing a platform for residents to voice their opinions, share concerns, and suggest ideas for climate action. These forums foster open dialogue, ensuring that all community members, including marginalised groups, have a say in shaping the city's climate strategy.

Digital Tools for Citizen Participation: We leverage technology to enhance engagement and make climate action accessible to all. The 'Green Rewards' App enables residents to log their own eco-friendly actions, from recycling to reducing energy consumption, and rewards them for their efforts. This app not only incentivises green behaviour but also allows citizens to track their personal contributions to the city's overall carbon reduction goals, creating a sense of collective achievement.

These efforts ensure that climate action benefits are distributed equitably across the city. By creating channels for ongoing engagement, we are working to ensure that all residents, regardless of their background or socioeconomic status, have the opportunity to participate in and benefit from the city's transition to a low-carbon future. This approach helps to build community resilience, foster inclusivity, and promote a shared responsibility for the success of our climate initiatives.

column18: The Portland Clean Energy Fund's (PCEF) Climate Investment Plan is intended to guide Portland's innovative investment in equitable climate action, and PCEF has detailed an extensive range of metrics to measure equitable outcomes. These metrics include workforce metrics on the utilization of diverse, minority- and women-owned businesses, contractor diversification, and numerous equity-focused targets for supporting low-income people of color, reducing energy burden in low-income households, retrofitting homes occupied by low-income families, increasing access to climate resilience assets to low-income communities and communities of color, and more. Additionally, city bureaus have increasingly integrated social and racial equity metrics into their asset management practices to ensure more and better investment in community assets that are accessible to communities that have historically been marginalized and underinvested.
column19:
A few examples of equitable climate action include: 
1) PCEF - Portland Clean Energy Community Benefits Fund. This investment fund was developed by and for frontline communities to directly benefit from climate action and investment. The Portland Clean Energy Community Benefits initiative was passed by 65% of Portland voters in November 2018. It provides a consistent, long-term funding source and oversight structure to ensure that our community's climate action efforts are implemented to support social, economic and environmental benefits for all Portlanders, particularly communities of color and people with low incomes. The initiative was supported by a broad coalition of groups and individuals and represents the first environmental initiative in Oregon led by communities of color. Since 2018, the program has issued a grant rounds for community investment. In the next few years, PCEF will invest over $700 million in community-led clean energy projects and climate solutions like energy-efficient upgrades to make apartment buildings safer and more comfortable during extreme heat and tree planting to increase shade in East Portland neighborhoods. https://www.portland.gov/bps/cleanenergy)

2) The City increased tree planting, especially in priority neighborhoods that are lower income and have greater urban heat island effect, such as East Portland. Approximately 3,500 trees will be planted each year through the PCEF Equitable Tree Canopy strategic program, which allocated $40 million over a five-year period to plant and establish trees in low-canopy areas of Portland, with attention given to the needs of East Portland. A community workgroup will help shape the scale of plantings and exact placement of the trees. 

3) Based on feedback from low income, communities of color, and tenant advocates, BPS is developing an annual energy reporting and disclosure of climate and health information in multifamily residential housing. BPS conducted a public comment period with the proposal in Spring/Summer 2024 and expects to bring an ordinance to City Council that will expand the Commercial Building Energy Performance Reporting requirement (Portland City Code 17.104) to include multifamily residential buildings. In addition, temperature standard for rental housing is also being developed by Portland Bureau of Planning and Development. As part of an update to the City's Housing Maintenance Requirements (Portland City Code Title 29, Chapter 30), BDS has been developing maximum temperature limits for at least one room per rental unit. This will reduce heat related illnesses and impacts on vulnerable populations during extreme outside temperature events. 

4) PCEF -funded climate resilience program Cooling Portland. Portland Clean Energy Community Benefits Fund (PCEF) staff gathered input from community partners and worked with the PCEF Grant Committee to develop and design a five-year program to connect vulnerable low-income Portlanders with efficient portable heat pump/cooling devices, in alignment with Portland City Code Chapter 7.07 (i.e., PCEF Code). Reduce heat related risk to vulnerable populations by distributing and installing portable heat pump/cooling units in households, prioritizing those with seniors among PCEF priority populations (low-income people and people of color). PCEF began distribution in 2022 with implementation taking place over a period of up to 5 years to distribute up to 15,000 portable heat pump/cooling units.

In 2016, OPCD created the Equitable Development Initiative (EDI), a set of strategies that emerged from our Growth and Equity Report, part of the Seattle 2035 Comprehensive Plan update. The EDI involves many different City departments coordinating to address equity in our underserved communities and displacement as Seattle grows. https://www.seattle.gov/opcd/ongoing-initiatives/equitable-development-initiativeIn May 2023 Mayor Bruce Harrell announced $13,550,000 in awards through the EDI, part of the City's effort to support property ownership among Seattle's diverse cultural communities in high displacement risk neighborhoods. The City awarded funds to community organizations for site acquisition and major capital projects, as well as capacity-building support to organizations that are still developing their plans for permanent spaces in Seattle.The Duwamish River Opportunity Fund (DROF) is a grant program that funds new and existing efforts focused on advancing priorities outlined in the Duwamish Valley Action Plan to address challenges faced by Duwamish River communities. The Duwamish Valley Action Plan is a City-community shared vision to promote collaboration and guide the City's work and investments in the Duwamish Valley. https://www.seattle.gov/environment/equity-and-environment/equity-and-environment-initiative/duwamish-river-opportunity-fundAcross the United States, race is the most significant predictor of a person living near contaminated air, water, or soil. column19: Race and social justice has been at the center of all climate action that the City of Seattle has pursued. Launched in 2015, Seattle's Equity & Environment Initiative (EEI) is partnership of the City and the community to deepen Seattle's commitment to race and social justice in environmental work. While Seattle has long been recognized as an environmental leader, we face many of the same challenges as the broader U.S. environmental movement: those who shape and benefit from environmental policies and outcomes are primarily white, upper-income communities. Those who do not benefit from progressive policies are overburdened with health, social, and economic impacts and the EEI seeks to flip those outcomes. The Equity & Environment Agenda guides our work in advancing racial equity in Seattle's environmental programs and policies. The Agenda lays out four key goal areas and recommended strategies in each area. https://www.seattle.gov/documents/Departments/OSE/Equity/SeattleEEAgenda.pdfSeattle expanded on its history of progressive climate action by enacting the Green New Deal Resolution (Res 31895), and Mayor Jenny Durkan introduced the Green New Deal Executive Order (EO-2020-01) directing all City departments to work together with the Green New Deal Oversight Board, the Environmental Justice Committee, and other key stakeholders to advance our shared goals.GND resolution: http://seattle.legistar.com/ViewReport.ashx?M=R&N=Text&GID=393&ID=3611579&GUID=ADF51F71-1823-4D7B-B599-9ED04DFD8860&Title=Legislation+TextGND EO: https://wayback.archive-it.org/3241/20211218155953/https://durkan.seattle.gov/wp-content/uploads/sites/9/2020/01/Final-Executive-Order-2020-01-Advancing-a-Green-New-Deal-for-Seattle_.pdf

column19: A key part of moving to a zero emissions world is to ensure it is a “just transition”. The principle of just transition is that a healthy economy and a clean environment can and should co-exist. The process for achieving that objective in the Climate Emergency Action Plan should seek to ensure that the substantial benefits of a green economy are shared widely, while also supporting those who stand to lose economically. We have committed to centering equity in the Climate Emergency Action Plan. For the actions in the CEAP, staff have initially focused on designing them to consider socio-economic inequities. That said, staff are committed to expanding beyond socioeconomic considerations as we move forward with implementation, particularly to better understand and centre systemic racial inequity, to understand impacts and barriers for people with disabilities, and to use an intersectional approach. One of the cross-cutting actions within CEAP to ensure that equity is integrated is the development of equity indicators, for which we hope to begin gathering disaggregated or spatial data on the impact of climate actions. Meanwhile, another action is the formation of a Climate and Equity Working Group, whose mandate included the development of a Climate Justice Charter. Staff are determining how to incorporate this Charter, developed with disproportionately impacted communities, into climate policy and programs to better address and integrate equity and racial justice. This, along with the City's Equity Framework, will guide staff work in this regard. (1) Climate Justice Charter for Vancouver, which was completed in 2022 and received for information in 2023. See: https://vancouver.ca/files/cov/climate-justice-charter-vancouver.PDF Description: The work to develop this Climate Justice Charter began on the traditional, ancestral, and unseeded homelands of the xʷməθkʷəy əm̓ (Musqueam), Skwxwú7mesh (Squamish), and səlilwətaɬ (Tsleil-Waututh) Nations by the Climate and Equity Working Group (CEWG). The CEWG recognizes the contributions of past and current generations towards surfacing the needs and hopes of those often denied a voice in climate discussions, including specifically citing how different marginalized groups are not included in decision making. Members of the 2021-2022 CEWG hope to have carried their work forward with this Charter. In regards to C40 staff requests for how specific climate actions were designed or developed based on the findings of the CJC and/or the goals outlined in the charter, see the work regarding City staff efforts to support the City's most heat-vulnerable residents: https://www.c40.org/case-studies/ica-cities-fund-vancouver/Specific metrics to measure how we are supporting the City's most heat-vulnerable residents are still TBD, but these actions began immediately in response to the values of the CJC and to prevent further death and destruction as a result of the June 2021 Heat Dome, which led to the death of 117 people. These actions include things like providing air conditioning to low income, disproportionately indigenous, residents in areas like the downtown east-side, most of whom are materially deprived and live in areas with higher temperature urban heat islands. The City is also investing in improved tree canopy in these areas. The CJC also inspired staff to insist upon disaggregated data collection during the 2022 CEAP model update refresh. (2) ZEETAP (Zero Emissions Economic Transition Action Plan), which was adopted in 2022. https://vancouver.ca/files/cov/2022-05-12-zero-emissions-economic-transition-action-plan-zeetap.pdf Goal: To accompany the City's Climate Action Plan by laying out the strategy to equitably facilitate the decarbonization of the economy that is in the implementation stage now. This plan has several directions with corresponding actions, but the first one is the most relevant to equity assessment as it looks to develop specific justice-oriented activities at three scales: activities for individuals, businesses, and the whole of the economy. Direction 1 - Action 4: Translate relevant climate information materials for diverse business owners. Potentially positive benefits for communities that primarily speak other languages to participate in policy making. Potentially negative impacts for smaller non-English speaking communities, if they are not included in these initiatives. Potentially negative impact for those working on initiatives if they do not have additional resources to support translation. Mitigation strategies: provide more support to planning work to include translation services, including the City of Vancouver's clear guidelines through its 'Language Access Policy' which has localized and jurisdiction-wide guidelines that include metrics on when and how to provide translation services: https://policy.vancouver.ca/ADMIN073.pdf

A short life cross-party Just Transition Working Group (JTWG) was convened by GCC following a commitment in GCCs Climate Plan. The JTWG created a Just Transition Implementation Plan that builds on the JTWG's initial 18 recommendations and explains how these will be delivered. It outlines how existing mechanisms for monitoring the progress of Glasgow's net zero work will be used to support a Just Transition element as well as aiming to develop new ways of doing so (https://www.glasgow.gov.uk/media/10564/Just-Transition-Implementation-Plan/pdf/Just_Transition_Implementation_Plan_Update_-_November_2024_1d81rg430fpbi.pdf?m=1751628792590). Glasgow assesses and monitors levels of fuel poverty in the city, including targets for its reduction, through the city's Housing Strategy. 

Glasgow also has a commitment towards increasing green jobs and skills supporting our young people in achieving positive destinations after secondary school. This is monitored and the city continues to invest in a just transition to net zero and climate resilient futures through the development of a Green Jobs and Green Skills plan supporting the upskilling and re-skilling of local communities, particularly young people those in areas of high SIMD, those with protected characteristics, those currently unemployed, or employed in high polluting sectors. 

Climate Ready Clyde generated a Climate Vulnerability Map (https://climatereadyclyde.org.uk/climate-vulnerability-map/) using data sources including deprivation, the 20 most deprived from Scottish Index of Multiple Deprivation (SIMD), flood risk postcode (areas subject to 1 in 200 year flood risk from SEPA Flood Risk Maps), and heat risk postcode (areas within the top two heat risk bands 4 and 5 from the 4EI Heat Hazard Index). Glasgow City Council's Centre for Civic Innovation (CCI) then used this map and overlaid their data on child poverty in Glasgow. Using these results, CCI identified three communities who were most at risk to climate impacts. This has been used to target funding. The City Change Makers project will guide participants from the identified communities through the steps required to turn their ideas for local climate action into reality.
column19:
Our regional partnership, Climate Ready Clyde, has developed a Climate Change Risk and Opportunity Assessment sets out the risks and opportunities posed by climate change to the end of this century, and highlights areas where more action is needed in the next five years. In response to this, Glasgow City Council developed its own Adaptation Plan to support the delivery of the above at jurisdiction.

Glasgow City Council has also developed a Climate Change Impact Assessment that proposed policies and projects must complete before passing through our Committees, similar to the EQIA process. Equalities Impact Assessments must also be completed for any policies or projects relating to climate change. 

In response to the impacts of climate change and its disproportionate impact upon lower income and under-represented communities, the Council committed to ensuring a just transition to a net zero society and set up a Just Transition Commission. This commission has prepared a report and set out actions that, if achieved will support and equitable and just transition for all citizens of Glasgow. 

The Council works across a number of local, national and international partnerships. These partnerships bring funding and research opportunities. Two such projects related to this are the Thriving Cities Initiative with the C40, which aims to support the development of more equitable and circular lifestyles and systems in the city, the other is a project with the Carbon Neutral Cities Alliance (CNCA) on developing strategies to increase inclusion and equity in climate policy making. Being part of organisations like the C40, the CNCA, as well as the Scottish Cities Alliance, 3Ci, and more allow us to benefit greatly from the experience of other cities across the world. 

Furthermore, the city are consulting with local communities on what a just transition should look like for Glasgow and Glaswegians; this has included a public consultation (June 2023) which sought the views of Glaswegians on their understanding of what a Just Transition means and how the Council can support action to bring about a Just Transition to a net zero city. In addition, as part of seeking to ensure our policies provide an inclusive transport system for all, GCC are involved in developing the national Inclusive Design guidance with the Scottish Government and Transport Scotland.

column16: The District has been working to assess the benefits of climate action on health and economic opportunity and inclusion in particular, firstly in the transportation and renewable energy sectors. In continuing to draw connections between climate and health, the District partnered with the WHO in 2022 to develop a local profile outlining the impacts of climate change on health, and opportunities to advance climate action and health equity together (see: https://www.who.int/publications/m/item/health-and-climate-change-urban-profiles--washington-dc). A few examples of assessing and pursuing these benefits are below. With resources provided by the EPA's Climate Pollution Reduction Grants, the District will expand and deepen the analysis of these benefits, particularly to low-income and disadvantaged communities. Health - Air Quality: Building on the District's Health Equity Report (https://dchealth.dc.gov/publication/health-equity-report-district-columbia-2018) the District has assessed local air quality impacts on public health and used those findings to determine where to prioritize investments in zero emission transportation solutions as replacements for diesel vehicles. One example is in prioritizing investments stemming from the Volkswagen Settlement to support conversion of diesel buses to zero emission electric buses on routes that travel through and serve neighborhoods with the poorest air quality (see: https://doee.dc.gov/page/volkswagen-settlement). The District's Air Quality Division is continuing to build on this framework by providing data and monitoring to continue to guide low-emission transportation investments citywide. Economic Opportunity and Inclusion: Renewable Energy & Energy Efficiency: Advancing economic opportunity and inclusion as the District advances energy efficiency, renewable energy, and materials recovery is also a key goal for the District. The city's DC Build Back Better Infrastructure Taskforce identified areas for economic growth and inclusion, and the Solar Works DC program - part of the District's Infrastructure Academy - is one example of a program already launched in the renewable energy space. Recognizing the growing solar industry in the District, spurred by the city's commitment to 15% of electricity coming from local solar by 2041 under the current Renewable Portfolio Standard, the Solar Works DC program recruits and trains District residents to become solar installers with a goal of helping unemployed and underemployed residents secure high-paying, long-term employment. Additionally, the Clean Energy DC Omnibus Amendment Act proposed new programs to support local businesses and residents through the Sustainable Energy Infrastructure Capacity Building and Pipeline Program. With a goal to increase the participation and capacity of certified business enterprises in the energy efficiency and renewable energy industries, the DC Sustainable Energy Utility established the Train Green program with offerings around energy efficiency, sustainability & healthy, building operations, renewable energy and solar, and heating, ventilation, and air conditioning. Finally, as the District implements a suite of policies and programs to reduce building energy demand and shift away from on-site fossil fuel combustion through implementing our Building Energy Performance Standards, Affordable Housing Retrofit Accelerator, and other rebate and incentive programs, the District is working to advance associated benefits of reduced utility burden for residents and improved indoor air quality.

column18: As the District implements the REACH Act, agencies are working to identify and quantify impacts and benefits to target communities. DOEE has conducted a first round of Racial Equity Impact Analyses (REIAs) to guide new program development and evaluate existing ones. With resources provided by the EPA's Climate Pollution Reduction Grants, the District will expand and deepen the analysis of these benefits, particularly to low-income and disadvantaged communities. Examples of initial efforts include the following: District's deployment of VW Settlement funds: DOEE's Air Quality Division conducted an analysis of local air quality and health data to identify communities overburdened by air pollution. Using that analysis, DOEE prioritized funding for projects to reduce emissions from diesel vehicles in these target communities. As the District continues to plan for mitigation actions and monitor air quality, including piloting more local air monitoring capability, we will work to quantify the impact of climate actions on local residents. Heat Sensitivity-Exposure Index: DOEE developed a new index as part of Keep Cool DC, our strategy to combat extreme heat, which combines air temperature data, with demographic factors about residents' age, income, race, disability, language, and health conditions like asthma and heart disease, which affect a resident's ability to cope with or recover from heat exposure. This allows the District to identify high risk neighborhoods for interventions and track action in these most vulnerable neighborhoods. In 2025, DOEE gathered updated data on temperature variations throughout the city which will be combined with updated demographic data to update the Index, allowing the District to track the impact of recent development, expanded tree canopy and new tree plantings, to see the impact of heat reduction projects in the areas of highest heat risk. Affordable Housing Retrofit Accelerator / Building Energy Performance Standards: The District has identified the 140 affordable housing buildings whose energy performance requires making improvements in order to comply with the Building Energy Performance Standards. DOEE launched the Affordable Housing Retrofit Accelerator in December 2021 to provide technical and direct assistance to support compliance. As upgrades are performed, DOEE is working to estimate benefits to residents, as well as overall community and energy-savings benefits, of these improvements. Additionally, the District worked with the Emerald Cities Collaborative (ECC) to estimate the job creation potential stemming from BEPS implementation (https://doee.dc.gov/sites/default/files/dc/sites/ddoe/service_content/attachments/BEPS_TaskForceMeeting_6-22-2021_slides.pdf). With the goal of supporting minority, women, and disadvantaged business enterprises breaking into or expanding skills in this sector, ECC launched its DC Contractor Incubator Cohort for 25 participants in 2023 and will launch its second cohort in Fall 2024 and track impact over the 2-year cohort cycles.
column19: The District's sustainability and climate plans have worked to identify, engage with and center vulnerable communities in their development and implementation, and following adoption of the REACH Act, District agencies and the DC Council are evaluating new and proposed policies and programs for impact on racial equity, including climate (see: https://www.dcracialequity.org/reia-database). One example of how the District is ensuring equitable climate action is in implementing its Climate Ready DC plan. The plan identified neighborhoods and communities most impacted by climate change and has been working with residents living in one of the most climate-vulnerable parts of the District since 2017 to determine how best to implement the climate adaptation plan in their community. As part of the project, DOEE launched the Equity Advisory Group (EAG), a community body made up of 13 residents chosen to be demographically representative of this Ward 7 community, to lead this effort. One of the EAG's key recommendations was to develop a community resilience hub to support residents, coordinate communication, distribute resources, and reduce carbon pollution. In 2020, the EAG produced a report on the components and services they felt most important in a resilience hub for their community and launched the Resilience Hub Community Committee to continue development of that concept. They have since selected the FH Faunteroy Community Enrichment Center as a pilot hub site, secured funding to provide solar and a battery system to provide resilient power in the event of an outage, and are pursuing funding to support key programming and ongoing community engagement. While work on this project continues, this group of residents has continued to guide engagement with their community on other resources, including recent work to identify flooding education and resources needed to help the disproportionate number of residents living in the floodplain in this community as compared with other District neighborhoods. See more: https://www.georgetownclimate.org/files/report/eag_recommendations_web_8.20.18.pdf; https://doee.dc.gov/node/1520366; https://faunteroycenter.org/resilience-hub-implementation/ A second example of equitable and inclusive climate action is the development and implementation of the District's Building Energy Performance Standards (BEPS), which is the first program in the country to require a broad swath of existing buildings to improve their whole-building energy performance. Recognizing the importance of ensuring that the benefits of living in modernized, healthy, efficient buildings should be available to all residents, regardless of income, the District's BEPS applies to affordable housing properties but has worked closely with the community to understand their specific challenges to implementation. Through an inclusive process -- recognized with the 2020 Community Leader Award for \'Excellence in Government, Advocacy, or Policy (Local Government)\' by the US Green Building Council National Capital Region -- affordable housing leaders provided recommendations on how to work with their properties under this new program (https://www.handhousing.org/wp-content/uploads/BEPS-Recommendations-FINAL2.pdf). That partnership positioned the District to attract federal stimulus funding to support compliance for affordable housing properties, and launched the Affordable Housing Retrofit Accelerator in December 2021 to provide direct technical and financial assistance to the 140 affordable housing buildings that must make efficiency improvements to comply with BEPS. The DOEE team has undertaken a racial equity impact analysis as they implement and monitor the program's first compliance cycle, to assess both the benefits and potential new challenges as the program gets underway. The District's Climate Commitment Act of 2022 also requires that District Government operations plan for carbon neutrality in a manner that advances racial equity and redresses past environmental and public health inequities, The District will deliver the plan this year in November (2025).
