column16: Our Climate Change Mitigation Strategy to 2050 included the results of comprehensive social and economic analysis of the costs and benefits of priority climate actions. This included social inclusion analysis conducted as part of stakeholder consultation, a survey of health impacts and benefits, a social impacts study and a comprehensive macroeconomic study of costs and benefits of priority actions for energy, buildings, transport and waste. Key benefits identified include (among others) increased energy security, local employment and productivity, and asset value; improved amenity, social cohesion, inclusion and health outcomes; and decreases in air and noise pollution, urban congestion and urban heat. The City is focused on leveraging the significant employment opportunities available in transitioning to a zero carbon economy. We intend to create an enabling environment for Melbourne businesses and universities to become the employment centre of a resilient zero-carbon economy. In 2023 Council established the Melbourne Climate Network to lead the transformation of the global economy towards net-zero, enabling job creation and economic opportunity for Melbourne through leading sustainable development of innovative technology for global impact. The Melbourne Climate Network an active network of over 750 climate businesses and start-ups has been financially supported by City of Melbourne. This group has in turn influenced the direction of the Economic Development Strategy (2025-2030) and influenced a pillar: a global powerhouse of innovation to include a priority to establish 'Melbourne as a leader in climate mitigation and adaptation technologies by harnessing the economic opportunities from the zero-carbon transition and the circular economy while preparing Melbourne to face the challenges associated with a changing climate.

City of Melbourne's Local Voluntary Review of progress against the Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) sets a baseline of the city's current performance, compiles exemplary practices, and assesses its performance in light of the SDGs to ask: “Are we pursuing a better future for all Melburnians?” The VLR report monitors all 17 SDGs, providing important insights into our progress in achieving equitable and inclusive climate action. For each SDG, the VLR sets up municipal targets, provides the general context with relevant data, including quantitative metrics, and exemplifies the city's action with implemented strategies. The VLR report concludes with an assessment of the localised targets based on data from 2015 until the most recent available value. Within each Goal, and the associated targets and indicators, the Review reveals both progress and room for improvement. This process will be completed every four years to track and report progress, and to inform the prioritsation of SDG-related actions under the Four-year Council Plan and Annual Plan and Budget process. Our ongoing commitment to the SDGs includes the UN principles 'leave no one behind'. 
The Climate Change and City Resilience branch are trialling a shared benefits assessment framework to encourage all project owners to think about broadening their project/program impact to include other environmental, climate, social, or economic outcomes. This is consistent with the SDGs and the interrelationship between all the goals. Project teams can self-assess their projects based on SDGs and identify areas to improve and outcomes to strive for.

The proposed Council Plan 2025-2029 strategic priorities and outcomes link to all United Nations Sustainable Development Goals and over 30 targets. The outcomes demonstrate a commitment to equitable and inclusive distribution of climate action.

•	Communities across the municipality have local access to clean, high-quality parks, waterways and open space 
•	Our residents and businesses are supported to transition to a resilient, net zero city and circular economy

column19:
City of Melbourne is ensuring that equity and inclusion is at the centre of our climate mitigation, adaption and resilience actions. For example:

The Fair Energy Futures Project was delivered by CoM in 2025 and funded by a Climate Neutral Cities Alliances Gamechanger grant. The project combined desktop analysis of energy hardship statistics and a comprehensive literature review to identify the root causes of energy hardship and the most vulnerable populations within the municipality. 17 local residents experiencing energy hardship took part in a comprehensive engagement process to identify the lived experiences of energy hardship and co-design effective solutions. This included the trial and evaluation of several interventions that could be delivered by Council. Insights from this project are informing the development of a support program for apartment residents, which Council has committed to in its Annual Plan and Budget 2025-26. 

An Inclusive Communications Toolkit for Extreme Weather has been developed to equip staff with the tools and knowledge to communicate extreme weather in ways that are inclusive, culturally safe, and resonate with our diverse communities. The toolkit was developed through community and stakeholder engagement and aims to improve the way we educate our diverse community about extreme weather, highlight Council's pivotal role in managing climate change impacts, and showcase ongoing initiatives for preparing our community. 

Community Cool Places Grants - Over summer 2024-25, the City of Melbourne funded seven community organisations across the city to operate as Cool Places during severe or extreme heatwaves in Melbourne. The Cool Places were free and open to all community members and residents, offering air-conditioned spaces, access to toilets, snacks, drinks and activities. Grants of up to $7,000 are again being offered for the 2025/25 summer period. During the period of 1 December through to 31 March, Cool Places are operational during a severe or extreme heat health warnings.

We partnered with Sweltering Cities to deliver a project titled 'Renters in apartments and the cost of keeping cool'. The research project identified the challenges apartment renters in the City of Melbourne face in keeping cool during extreme heat, with the goal to help increase awareness of the challenges faced by renters in apartments during extreme heat and enable advocacy efforts for affordable, sustainable cooling solutions for renters and communities. The research will enable CoM and relevant stakeholders to strategically advocate for solutions that reduce heat risk for private renters living in apartments.

CoM's heat health response summer delivery program included 11 Heat Smart Sessions (in various languages), distribution of over 1000 Cool Kits, provision of 7/11 drinks vouchers and cooling items for those sleeping rough and experiencing chronic homelessness, and activation of partner agencies who provide support services to those sleeping rough and experiencing chronic homelessness.

The Prepared Communities webpage was launched in August 2024 and provides information and resources to our community on how to prepare for emergencies. Collateral has been disseminated through libraries and community centres and promoted at workshops and community engagement events. An Easy Read version of the webpage is being created to make the information more accessible. 

Our Youth Climate Action Grants program provides funding to young people aged 15-25 to design and deliver climate-focused projects in their communities. TMG has formulated the Tokyo 2050 Strategy to make Tokyo one of the world's best cities that continues to grow and mature, allowing everyone to thrive and experience happiness. The strategy is a new guiding principle for TMG, which sets out the policies to be advanced through 2035 as milestones toward realizing this vision for the 2050s.
Strategy 20 of the Tokyo 2050 Strategy presents clear targets for achieving a Zero Emission Tokyo by mid-century. TMG has committed to reducing greenhouse gas emissions by at least 60% from 2000 levels by 2035, and is strengthening its actions to achieve this goal. As part of its mitigation measures, TMG will accelerate the introduction of renewable energy sources—including next-generation solar cells (Air Solar), floating offshore wind turbines, and geothermal heat—reflecting the unique characteristics of Tokyo's dense urban areas and islands. At the same time, we will maximize energy efficiency through enhanced thermal insulation and energy conservation in both residential and non-residential buildings, and expand renewable energy initiatives. Together, these efforts will secure a stable supply of clean energy for Tokyo residents.
As part of its adaptation measures, TMG will strengthen, in both structural and non-structural aspects, preparations for increasingly intense and frequent storms and floods caused by climate change as well as heat countermeasures, including efforts to mitigate the heat island effect and prevent heat stroke. In addition, TMG will promote agriculture, forestry, and fisheries industries that conserve the natural environment and are resilient to climate impacts. Through these forward-looking adaptation measures, Tokyo will evolve into a sustainable, adaptable city that minimizes climate risks and enables residents to live with peace of mind.
Please note that the above efforts to achieve a decarbonized society are consistent with the SDGs. For details, see page 456 of the Tokyo 2050 Strategy.
Reference: Tokyo 2050 Strategy Main Text https://www.spt.metro.tokyo.lg.jp/seisakukikaku/2050tokyo/#page=1 pp. 314-336

column19: The Tokyo Metropolitan Government (TMG) is committed to combating food waste in collaboration with consumers, food-related businesses, and municipalities.\nIn response to recommendations from the Tokyo Food Waste Reduction Partnership Council, which is comprised of food distributors, consumers, and experts, TMG formulated the Tokyo Food Loss and Waste Reduction Plan in March 2021. To promote the effective use of unused food, we are actively working to make use of emergency food supplies stockpiled at public authorities as well as aggressively leveraging food banks that support needy people and children's cafeterias in need of food. Specific initiatives include the provision of support tailored to the characteristics of municipalities, such as subsidizing part of the costs of their food waste reduction activities. In April 2021, we launched the full-scale operation of a matching system for unused food to link municipal and TMG's emergency food supplies with food banks. (https://www.kankyo.metro.tokyo.lg.jp/documents/d/kankyo/tokyo_torikumi-keikaku-files-030330_plan p.27） \nTMG is also actively working on the development of a comprehensive support system aimed at assisting vulnerable individuals in need of support during disasters. This initiative aligns with the Zero Emission Tokyo Strategy, the Tokyo Climate Change Adaptation Plan, and the Tokyo Regional Disaster Management Plan.Because of climate change, increased natural disasters such as floods, inland floods, storm surges, and landslides due to intensified heavy rains and typhoons are expected. In recent large-scale earthquakes, windstorms, and floods, the majority of the casualties have been the elderly, people with disabilities, and others who require special aid during disasters, and therefore, support is needed for those vulnerable people. Such individuals encompass a diverse range of demographics, including the elderly, persons with disabilities, infants, pregnant people as well as patients with serious illnesses.To ensure the safety of those individuals, TMG has formulated detailed guidelines for municipal governments in Tokyo. It is considered that vulnerable people are at high risk of being affected by disasters because there may be issues with such things as understanding information, evacuating, and securing the necessities of life. For this reason, the specific challenges faced by them are identified for each attribute. The guidelines also serve as a framework to support local municipalities in reaching out to people in need of support, establishing a roster of such individuals, formulating individual evacuation plans, and developing tailored measures to address their specific needs throughout the evacuation process. Under the Basic Act on Disaster Countermeasures, municipalities are mandated to compile a comprehensive list of individuals requiring support during evacuation, and TMG collaborates closely with them to help develop a robust evacuation system utilizing this database.TMG recently revised both the Tokyo Regional Disaster Management Plan for Wind and Flood Damage in 2021 and the guideline for local municipal governments in 2022. In response to the revision of the Basic Act on Disaster Countermeasures in May 2021, which made it an obligation for municipalities to make efforts to create individual evacuation plans for persons requiring assistance, TMG is strengthening support for efforts by local municipalities to address vulnerable people based on this guideline.

Kaohsiung City has formulated mitigation actions targeting nine major aspects. In the energy sector, it is promoting the phasing out of coal in cogeneration plants within its jurisdiction by 2025 and the establishment of renewable energy sources. In the industrial sector, to build a low-carbon industrial chain, the city has formed the Net-Zero Industrial Alliance. Through recommendations provided by experts from the Greenhouse Gas Inventory Consulting Group and the Energy Saving and Carbon Reduction Technology Service Group, emission reduction measures are implemented by identifying emission hotspots, thereby reducing climate-related costs arising from CBAM or domestic carbon fees. 
In the residential and commercial sectors, the city promotes the disclosure and improvement of energy efficiency in public and private buildings. The government provides subsidies for energy-saving appliances to support disadvantaged groups in participating in energy-saving and carbon reduction efforts. 
In terms of transport, due to the city's unique geographical features, Kaohsiung City has an uneven population distribution, with 95% of the population living in metropolitan areas that occupy 25% of the city's total area. Therefore, it relies on an integrated public transport network, including the MRT, light rail, buses, shared electric motorcycles and bicycles, Taxi+Bus, and YouBike 2.0, to provide convenient and safe transport for residents. Regarding equity, the city government is committed to reducing the gap between urban and rural public transport. 
In the environmental sector, the city is integrating energy resources, promoting the reuse of incineration bottom ash, updating incinerating plant equipment, and converting livestock manure into resources. In the agricultural sector, it promotes smart and eco-friendly farming and low-carbon fisheries. In terms of net-zero green lifestyle, it promotes eco-friendly restaurants/hotels, and plastic reduction alliances. In the carbon sink sector, it promotes afforestation and reforestation. In terms of just transition, it has established the 'Net-Zero Institute' to cultivate net-zero talents, formulated a just transition manual, promoted green finance, and issued green bonds, among other initiatives.

column16: In 2022 the City engaged the Institute of Public Policy and Governance at the University of Technology Sydney to assess the inclusiveness of the City's current environmental action areas and to recommend ways in which the City can deliver more equitable climate action for residents in its Local Government Area (LGA). The research identified that climate change affects everyone, but there are some groups of people who are more affected by its impacts than the broader resident population. They include: People living in social housing, People on low incomes, People experiencing homelessness, People living with disability, \tPeople experiencing mental health or chronic health issues, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, People >65 years old, Babies and young children <5 years old, People renting an apartment, New immigrants, non-citizens or people with refugee status, CALD speakers with limited or no English.\nMany of the people disproportionately affected by climate change impacts are already facing other barriers in their lives - and many belong to more than one group that already experiences disadvantage (intersectionality). Climate change compounds this disadvantage.\nBased on this research, it is clear that some types of climate action can help address other social issues. In particular, actions that support energy efficiency will help save money; and actions that help keep people safe during heat waves will address people with health or mobility issues.

column18: To enable climate equity decision making, the City developed visual mapping of climate-vulnerable communities within our boundary. A methodology was developed using census data and aligned to identified climate equity demographics. Each demographic group was normalised against other local government areas and the whole state. This information can be displayed as a collective or for each individual risk group. Using existing spatial data for surface temperatures (LANDSAT), canopy cover and building information, we are able to calculate vulnerability indices to understand where the most climate-vulnerable communities live, optimal areas to trial climate adaptation initiatives and support community groups with their initiatives. New spatial layers are being adding including flooding and ambient air temperature and they maps are being used across the City. The data is to SA Level 1. SA1s generally have a population of 200 to 800 persons, and an average population of about 400 persons. The City is also making the methodology available to other Greater Sydney councils and assisting them with the technical details of creating the maps.

Example 1 - Microclimate heat sensors - Over summer 2023/4 the City installed 200 bespoke temperature gauges across our local area to measure heat and humidity to help prepare us for hotter summers. This important study identified microclimates and will help us understand where we can concentrate the most appropriate heat adaptation actions. It'll also help us understand what is working already and inform the development of more cooling strategies to help our communities mitigate the worst impacts of rising temperatures. The locations for the sensors were chosen based on the spatial mapping of climate-vulnerable communities within our area (see question 1.4.5).
The results of the study were published in April 2025. For further information and to view the report, please refer to the following link: https://www.cityofsydney.nsw.gov.au/research-reports/mapping-summer-microclimates

Example 2 - Resilience Strategy 2023 - 2028 engagement
In 2023 the City developed its first Resilience Strategy. During the development of the strategy, the City undertook community engagement that focusses specifically on the priority communities identified by our climate equity research (see q1.4.3). Our objective was to understand the concerns, interests, and diverse perspectives on resilience challenges and inequities, especially those exacerbated by climate change, of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, people with disability, vulnerable community groups and social housing residents. We asked the community to share their experiences with emergency situations, their ideas on how our communities can be more prepared for emergencies and their thoughts on what will help our communities cope with the impact of shocks and stresses. The consultation focused on understanding community concerns, interests, and diverse perspectives on resilience challenges and inequities. We asked about four key topic areas: safe places in our community, the impacts of climate change, food security, and communication. Outcomes from the engagement shaped the Strategy and ensured we are addressing the needs of the most impacted communities.

This assessment is embedded in the City's Climate Action Plan (CAP) implementation and guided by an integrated approach that considers co-benefits such as:
•	Environmental benefits: improved air quality, biodiversity conservation, and enhanced urban resilience. The City's Air Quality Management Plan plays a pivotal role by identifying pollution hotspots and coordinating targeted interventions that reduce emissions from transport, industry, and informal settlements, complementing climate mitigation efforts.
•	Social benefits: job creation in green industries, improved public health outcomes, social equity, inclusion of vulnerable communities, and strengthened resilience through the City's Food Security Programme. This programme promotes urban agriculture, community gardens, and local food systems to improve nutrition, reduce food transport emissions, and enhance adaptive capacity in vulnerable areas.
•	Economic benefits: cost savings through energy efficiency, growth in the green economy, increased investment attraction via sustainable infrastructure projects, and enhanced local economic development through food security initiatives.
To ensure rigorous assessment and management of these opportunities and benefits, the City employs an Environmental and Social Management System (ESMS) which:
•	Provides a framework to systematically identify, evaluate, and manage environmental and social risks and opportunities associated with climate-related projects and programmes.
•	Ensures compliance with national legislation and international best practices, promoting transparency and stakeholder engagement throughout project life cycles.
•	Supports the City's commitment to a Just Transition by embedding social safeguards and equitable benefit sharing in climate action initiatives.
The City utilizes tools such as multi-criteria analysis, cost-benefit evaluations, and environmental and social impact assessments integrated into project design and decision-making processes. Stakeholder consultations—including communities and private sector partners—inform and validate the identification of benefits.
These assessments are mainstreamed into strategic planning frameworks such as the Integrated Development Plan (IDP) and sector-specific strategies, ensuring climate actions contribute positively to Johannesburg's broader socio-economic development objectives.

The City of Johannesburg employs a data-driven approach to quantify the equitable and inclusive distribution of climate action, ensuring that vulnerable and marginalized groups benefit from the transition to a low-carbon economy.
Data Sources and Quantitative Measures:
•	The City utilizes detailed socio-economic datasets from the National Statistics Institution and the Gauteng City Region Observatory (GCRO) at Wits University, which provide disaggregated data by income, gender, age, and geography. These data support the identification and targeting of groups disproportionately affected by climate-related transitions.
•	Studies on green jobs and the potential impact of electric vehicle adoption have highlighted demographic disparities, particularly the disproportionate effects on women. The City uses these findings to inform quantitative targets and equitable program design.
Community Engagement and Inclusive Planning:
•	The City conducts annual Community Based Planning (CBP) processes, which serve as grassroots platforms for residents to voice concerns related to equity and inclusion. Inputs from CBPs directly inform the design and implementation of climate and sustainability initiatives, ensuring they address localized needs and priorities.
Policies and Implementation:
•	In response to identified disparities, the City is implementing targeted regulations and incentives to promote green job creation for youth and women, aligning with the principles of a Just Transition.

The City of Johannesburg has implemented targeted actions to ensure equitable and inclusive distribution of climate benefits, focusing on vulnerable populations affected by urban heat stress, food insecurity, environmental degradation, and air pollution.
A recent study assessed urban heat impacts in informal settlements, revealing that low-income communities face disproportionately high heat stress. Real-time temperature measurements were piloted in three strategic informal settlement areas, with community volunteers actively involved in data collection—enhancing both accuracy and community empowerment.
These findings inform the City's broader climate adaptation and equity strategies. The ongoing Suncasa Nature-Based Solutions initiative uses this data to prioritize tree planting and urban greening in extreme heat hotspots, reducing heat exposure, improving air quality, and enhancing local well-being.
Complementing these efforts, the City's Food Security Programme promotes urban agriculture and community gardens in vulnerable areas to improve nutrition, reduce food-related emissions, and build local resilience. These initiatives create livelihood opportunities and foster social cohesion.
The City also integrates the Expanded Public Works Programme (EPWP) to provide temporary employment and skills development for marginalized groups. EPWP projects include urban greening, food security efforts, and critical environmental restoration activities such as alien vegetation eradication along river courses, which helps restore biodiversity, improves water quality, and mitigates flood risks.
Further supporting inclusive climate action, waste pickers and recyclers—a vital informal sector—are engaged through dedicated programs that enhance their livelihoods while improving waste management and reducing greenhouse gas emissions.
The City's commitment to addressing air quality concerns is strengthened by insights from the recent Air Quality Polling Report by Seriti Institute, which gathered community perceptions and priorities related to air pollution. The report highlighted disproportionate exposure to poor air quality in informal settlements and underscored the need for targeted interventions. This evidence supports the City's focused efforts on pollution reduction through integrated approaches like the Air Quality Management Plan and nature-based solutions.

The City of Toronto's TransformTO Net Zero Strategy (NZS) is grounded in the idea that reducing GHG emissions is not only necessary to avoid the worst effects of climate change, but that climate actions can also achieve multiple community-wide objectives. Equity: For cost of living, the Net Zero technical modelling indicates that average household energy costs decrease in the NZ pathway. In 2050 in the NZ pathways, households will be more efficient and, on average, energy costs will be 70 per cent less per month (energy and transportation combined), compared to the Do Nothing Scenario. These savings can be used to finance the building retrofits & electric vehicles. Lower household energy expenditures are particularly meaningful for lower-income households where energy & transportation costs make up a larger proportion of expenses. The Net Zero technical modelling determined that the cumulative social cost of carbon (SCC) of the Do Nothing Scenario between 2020 and 2050 is $94 billion. Implementing the NZS to reach net zero by 2040 will reduce the SCC to $35 billion, significantly reducing the burden of climate change on future generations. Toronto is actively working to ensure our programs & policies address the disproportionate impacts of our changing climate on equity-deserving groups and future generations. Using the TransformTO guiding principles and following a framework for equitable design & implementation of climate actions and programs will help to ensure that the transition to a net-zero Toronto occurs in a way that enhances equity, maximizes public benefit, and minimizes harms. Health: The NZS elucidates many health benefits of reducing GHG emissions and addressing the climate emergency, including less air pollution achieved through fuel switching, resulting in a 99 per cent reduction in local fossil fuel combustion for building energy and vehicle power compared to the status quo. Toronto Public Health has estimated that air pollution in Toronto from all sources gives rise to 1,300 premature deaths and 3,550 hospitalizations annually. The Net Zero pathway will dramatically reduce local sources of the GHGs that cause climate change and air pollutants that harm our health. Moreover, improved air quality as a result of electrifying transportation could deliver health benefits valued at nearly $750 million per year. Improved indoor air quality in dwellings and office space as a result of building retrofits will reduce health care costs and absenteeism at work. Reduced air pollution from the combustion of fossil fuels (on roads, in houses, and in electricity generation) will reduce asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Increased walking and cycling will reduce heart disease. The NZS also explores the benefits of managing extreme heat, a significant climate risk in Toronto. Building practices that reduce the heat absorption of roofs and hardscape materials and enhance greenspace, can help to reduce urban heat. These strategies together with building retrofits that improve the building envelope, insulation and ventilation; and community resilience supports for vulnerable people; can reduce the risk of heat-related illness & death. Greenspace maintenance and development (performed equitably citywide) to enhance climate change resilience will improve residents' cardiovascular & mental health and reduce obesity and cancer, and contribute to a sense of community & social cohesion. 

Climate resilience: Implementing the NZS will realize numerous improvements for Toronto, such as:
● Safer buildings during extreme weather (flooding, extreme heat/cold) as older buildings are retrofitted
● Homes that can keep the lights on during power outages, once outfitted with renewable energy & storage or connected to district energy systems
● Decreased stress on water & wastewater systems through retrofits and more stringent efficiency standards for new buildings
● Less urban heat island effect & flood stress through enhanced greenspace and tree canopy
● More back-up power from electric vehicles

Economic benefits: Climate change, climate resilience, & the economy are deeply connected. The Canadian Institute for Climate Choices recently examined >60 pathways for Canada to reach NZ by 2050 and found substantial GDP growth in all pathways, and on average, Canadians' incomes will rise. Benefits include: 
● Generating direct, indirect & induced jobs
● Lowering household & business energy demand, thereby saving costs, freeing disposable income for re-investment in the economy and improving business competitiveness
● Protecting households & businesses against energy price volatility
● Generating overall economic output (GDP) & associated tax revenue
● Mitigating future climate impacts that will be costly to society, & reducing the cost of adaptation by acting early
● Improving public health, and thus productivity, through improved indoor and outdoor air quality, reduced noise & improved building comfort

Based on the Accountability and Management Framework for the TransformTO NZS, Toronto established the Climate Advisory Group (CAG) with 26 members by 2022 who have been meeting quarterly since. The CAG comprises of community members who will act as advisors to the City on effective implementation of the TransformTO NZS and the Short-term Implementation Plan 2022-2025, with a focus on community-wide GHG emission reductions, climate resilience and equity. The goals of the CAG are to:
• Enable advice and peer review from Toronto's diverse community to inform community-wide implementation of the TransformTO Net Zero Strategy and the Short-term Implementation Plans;
• Ensure ongoing two-way information sharing and collaboration between the City and external parties; and
• Help mobilize all sectors and communities to move toward our shared goal of a zero-carbon, healthy, equitable, prosperous and resilient Toronto.

The Executive Director of the Environment and Energy Division will be responsible for reporting on the work of the CAG. The CAG will report out annually, at a minimum. The CAG will include Members representing the sectors with the greatest emission-reduction in the coming years in order to meet Toronto's 2030 community-wide interim targets. Sectors can include buildings, energy, transportation, finance, and waste. The City will include representation from Indigenous communities, youth and equity-deserving groups such as the Black community. Members should collectively bring the following skills and experience to the CAG:

• Understanding, skills, expert knowledge or experience with a sector that emits GHGs in Toronto;
• Lived experience and an understanding of diverse neighbourhoods and communities;• Knowledge in one or more areas of GHG emission reduction, climate resilience or climate planning;
• Reflect the cultural and social diversity of Toronto's community;
• A climate champion mindset and a desire to inform and mobilize sectors and communities to collectively achieve a future Toronto that is zero-carbon, equitable, healthy, prosperous and resilient.

More information on the Accountability and Management Framework is here: http://app.toronto.ca/tmmis/viewAgendaItemHistory.do?item=2022.IE29.10 https://www.toronto.ca/legdocs/mmis/2022/ie/bgrd/backgroundfile-224383.pdf https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/water-environment/environmentally-friendly-city-initiatives/transformto/

Equity Assessment 2 - Neighbourhood Climate Action Champions Program

Toronto launched the Neighbourhood Climate Action Champions program in 2020 to broaden public engagement and support for local community climate action. It is one of the first municipal programs in Canada to recruit and train residents to engage with their community on environmental issues and inspire climate action. Since 2020, the program has recruited and trained 75 individuals across the city. The role of Neighbourhood Climate Action Champions are to: communicate and educate residents about environmental and climate related topics and issues; and collaborate with residents to develop small-scale climate action projects that account for the diverse values and needs of their community. City staff provide capacity building training on climate change science, communications, climate action in Toronto, and project management to support community engagement. Climate Action Champions are required to commit at least 50 hours per year (4-5 hours per month) toward community outreach and each receives a one-time $500 honorarium.

Applications open annually and residents from equity-deserving groups are given priority. Applications are evaluated based on their demonstrable strength in:
●Understanding importance of neighbourhood / social cohesion, and local neighbourhood priorities
●Experience in working with equity-deserving groups, volunteering, and leadership
●Environmental / climate knowledge, understanding of the importance of climate action
●Understanding of engagement tactics and innovative ideas
●Demographic criteria

Meeting the net zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2040 target will require big changes and all Toronto residents and communities can do their part. Upon completion of training, a micro-grant of $2000 is provided to each Climate Action Champion to engage and work with residents to create a climate action project that address a need in their community. It is important that projects address the co-benefits of climate action as they will likely better resonate with the community and inspire action. The Environment & Climate, Outreach & Engagement team developed an equity lens tool to help programs and initiatives identify and address barriers that may be experienced by equity-seeking communities. The tool was used to evaluate the Neighbourhood Climate Action Champions program and the results can be found here: https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/water-environment/live-green-toronto/neighbourhood-climate-action-champions/

column18: Connecting climate action with social justice and social impact, social and green innovation, and inclusiveness remain a priority for the Municipality of Athens. To assess of the impacts of climate change in the city, and to address equity and inclusivity, it is necessary for the Municipality of Athens to regularly collect and enrich data on health, economy, environment and society, thus creating an up-to-date database. To this end, the Climate Action Plan and the recently adopted Climate City Contract include relevant indicators for each proposed action in order to create a transparent and accountable monitoring system. Each action is accompanied by a set of indicators that will correspond to and assess the wider benefits of its actions for the city. The Municipality of Athens has applied to access not-yet-published ELSTAT data from the most recent 2021 census in order to create detailed maps of vulnerable populations, green spaces, and socio-economic indicators across the city, including the number of people who benefit from specific climate actions across all 129 neighborhoods. For example, data will be used to analyze the access to new and existing green spaces, for all residents and for vulnerable groups. Through the REACHOUT program, the municipality is evaluating data to map walking distances to green spaces and through our target for at least 70% of residents to have access to a green space within a 15-minute walk from their home by 2030, we will consider the parts of the city that need it the most. This will allow the Municipality to assess how climate actions effect specific communities and quantify their equitable and inclusive distribution.

The Municipality of Athens continues to ensure that climate-related actions and public health services are equitably distributed across the city, making them accessible to all residents, particularly those in vulnerable communities. Key services such as municipal clinics in each district so that Primary Health Care is provided to all citizens, green roofs on school buildings (two per municipal district), and the digitization of city services for open access continue to be focal points of the city's efforts.
In addition to these ongoing initiatives, the Municipality of Athens is actively involved in European projects such as ARSINOE and FUSILLI, which enhance its focus on equity in climate action. Through the ARSINOE project, Athens participates in developing innovative climate-resilience solutions that consider social inclusion and the needs of vulnerable groups, ensuring that climate adaptation and mitigation measures reach all corners of the city. The aim of the ARSINOE project is to harness innovation to adapt to climate change in a range of key systems - from biodiversity to floods and sea-level rise, and from drought and water scarcity to heat waves and deforestation. The project is fully aligned with the objectives of the Athens Resilience Strategy for 2030, and its results will be used to guide the development of nature-based solutions, by taking into account feedback by citizens and other stakeholders.
The FUSILLI project complements this by focusing on sustainable food systems, working with communities to transform food environments and ensure that access to healthy, sustainable food is inclusive, particularly for disadvantaged populations. As part of this initiative, Athens has introduced several innovative food-related projects, including the creation of 14 communal vegetable gardens, including the establishment of a communal vegetable garden at the Athens Home for the Elderly. This initiative specifically targets the elderly population, fostering social inclusion, intergenerational interaction, and active participation in sustainable food production. These efforts are integrated into the broader Athens Urban Food Action Plan, which places a strong emphasis on equity and justice in the city's food systems
Furthermore, since 2022 and continuing through 2024, the Athens Business Green Toolkit has been developed to support small and very small enterprises of the Historic Centre of Athens to upgrade their operation based on the principles of energy efficiency and bioclimatic design. The programme supports businesses by financing technical measures such as interventions in the building envelope, upgrades of cooling/heating systems and appliances but also by measures to optimise energy use such as energy management systems. Since 2022, over €2.6 million has been distributed to 125 businesses, with plans to expand this support in the future
In terms of addressing heat vulnerability, the city maintains its Help at Home+ program, a lifeline for vulnerable residents such as the elderly and those with underlying health conditions. The program has been expanded to include volunteers from the Hellenic Red Cross, who assist with providing care during extreme heat. Residents can call a city helpline for assistance, whether for transport to air-conditioned spaces or other necessary care. The city's 25 Friendship Clubs offer older residents a place for daily creative activities, with seven of these clubs functioning as climate shelters during extreme weather. These cooling centers have extended hours during heatwaves to provide greater protection. The Municipality also operates six outreach crews from the Center for Solidarity and Reception, providing essential services such as water and food to homeless individuals during heatwaves. A 24-hour helpline offers additional support for those facing health challenges related to extreme weather.
The Municipality of Athens is also planning to install public water fountains in various locations across the city, particularly in areas with heavy foot traffic, as part of its initiative to tackle heatwaves, reduce plastic waste and provide equitable access to clean drinking water for all residents and visitors. This initiative ensures that all citizens, regardless of income level, can access free, sustainable hydration, contributing to both environmental sustainability and social equity.
By participating in projects like ARSINOE and FUSILLI and maintaining these critical programs, Athens ensures that its climate actions are both equitable and inclusive, addressing the diverse needs of its residents and prioritizing vulnerable communities.

column16: By implementing potential mitigation measures of the Bangkok Master Plan on Climate Change 2021-2030, not only the BMA can achieve GHG reduction targets to further support the national targets under NDC, but also employ co-benefits in terms of social, environmental, and economic aspects which can be described under the example of sectoral measures as follows:1) Reducing fossil fuels consumption in transportation systems helps to improve air quality leading to increased well-being of people, such as increasing the average life expectancy of the population, reducing the number of patients with respiratory disease and reducing employee absence rate, etc.2) Using renewable energy such as solar power generation systems help to improve the quality of life of the people in rural or remote areas where power grids are not yet accessible, reducing energy costs as well as reducing air pollution such as particulates and carbon dioxide from electricity generation from fossil fuels, etc.3) Promoting the use of energy conservation, for example, using LED bulbs, which use up to 90% less energy than incandescent bulbs, leads to energy saving. In addition, with the long service life of LED, maintenance and replacement costs are saved. Similar to the high-efficiency boiler improvement measure, it reduces fossil fuel consumption (diesel, natural gas, coal), fuel costs, and promotes technology transfer.4) Promoting waste management by raising community participation/awareness directly helps to reduce pollution that affects the surrounding environment, such as odor, soil, and water contamination. Additionally, it generates income from waste sorting and recycling.5) Increasing green spaces for recreation and sport helps restore urban ecosystems and create an environment that promotes well-being, makes people more healthy, and reduces health care costs. It also promotes the development of abandoned and unused urban areas for public benefit.In addition to the co-benefits outlined above, job creation is one of the most important co-benefits that mitigation measures can bring to the economy. In accordance with Bangkok's policy priorities, 3 mitigation measures including: 1) Rooftop solar PV deployment, 2) Construction and operation of a new Light Rail Transit (LRT) system, and 3) Improvement in recycling and compostingThese measures were assessed for their potential of job creation. The economic model used for rooftop solar PV measures in the energy sector is the EIM-ES (Economic Impact Model for Electricity Supply). For LRT measures in the transport sector and improvement in waste management a model developed by the C40 is used. In summary, the measures described above are likely to create tens of thousands of jobs. A majority of jobs would not be directly created from the measures but rather indirectly from relevant activities due to the multiplier effect. Specifically, 39,825 job-years could be created in 10 years' time from rooftop solar PV deployment. This is comprised of 20,108 job-years from direct employment in the power sector and 19,717 job-years from indirect and induced employment in relevant sectors. A new LRT system is likely to create around 148,000 jobs in total, of which most would emerge from construction, including 19,553 direct jobs in the construction sector and 128,109 indirect and induced jobs in relevant sectors. Operations and maintenance of the system would create only a few hundred jobs. Finally, increasing recycling and composting rates would create around 54,000-113,000 jobs, with 50,000-109,000 jobs from recycling and 3,733 jobs from composting. However, around 1,400 existing jobs at landfills could disappear in the meantime.

Adicionalmente, se conformó y acompañó la red de cuidadoras y cuidadores, en el marco del programa “Manzanas del cuidado” los cuales son espacios de la ciudad en los que las entidades distritales brindan tiempo y servicios a las mujeres cuidadoras y a sus familias para que ellas puedan estudiar emprender, emplearse o desarrollar otra actividades mientras las personas a quienes cuidan son atendidas. Conjuntamente se realizan actividades en pro de fortalecer capacidades comunitarias, donde se han desarrollado foros Inter locales, en donde se resalta la importancia de la prevención de Incendios forestales y el correcto manejo de los residuos (disposición final).\nFinalmente, se han establecido mesas de comunicación con la ciudadanía a través de la conformación y atención de veedurías climáticas, que condensan las principales preocupaciones e intereses de la comunidad y la academia, y con quienes se celebran reuniones periódicas para la resolución de inquietudes e inconformidades.

column16: Durante la elaboración del Plan de Acción Climática 2050 de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires, y en colaboración con C40, se realizó un proceso de identificación y priorización de acciones climáticas que tuvo como objetivo identificar las acciones necesarias para aumentar la ambición de los objetivos y metas de dicho plan, a partir de un análisis multicriterio, de manera participativa y transparente, que involucró un amplio espectro de actores para cada una de las etapas del proceso.La evaluación de las acciones tuvo lugar a partir de criterios de co-beneficios, que fueron seleccionados en línea con los ejes del Gobierno de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires. Estos co-beneficios fueron: calidad de aire y salud; espacios verdes; ingreso, pobreza y empleo; movilidad y nueva espacialidad; energía; gestión de residuos; y stakeholder engagement. A esta evaluación, se sumaron dos criterios de factibilidad: financiamiento, y autoridad local y aceptación política. Para realizar la priorización de acciones se utilizó la herramienta ASAP (“Action Selection and Prioritisation”), brindada por C40. De las 113 acciones climáticas consideradas para la evaluación de priorización, Buenos Aires seleccionó 19 principales según los criterios detallados anteriormente. Dado el contexto de pandemia iniciado en 2020, durante este proceso se incluyó la participación de una gran cantidad de áreas del Gobierno de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires de manera remota. Además, hubo participación de actores de la sociedad civil en la articulación a través de talleres y espacios de carácter virtual. A partir de este proceso de participación, se sumaron algunas acciones climáticas a las 19 priorizadas, las cuales se refieren a temas transversales como educación ambiental, calidad de aire, etc. Por otra parte, en colaboración con C40 se realizaron análisis específicos para algunas de las acciones climáticas del PAC 2050. Así, se realizó la valoración de los co-beneficios y equidad asociados a la implementación de dos acciones climáticas priorizadas por la ciudad: el plan integral de impulso al uso de la bicicleta y la generación de energía fotovoltaica. Se trata de dos medidas estratégicas, cuya implementación pretende constituir una experiencia piloto a través de la que se evidencie la capacidad que tiene la acción climática de generar beneficios que van más allá de la mera reducción de emisiones GEI o la resiliencia climática. El objetivo de este análisis fue poner en destaque y dimensionar los co-beneficios de estas acciones y, a su vez, actuar como desencadenante ante las autoridades municipales y suponer un punto de inflexión que fomente el compromiso e inversión en acción climática urbana, pasando de la implementación de los proyectos piloto a proyectos más ambiciosos de los que se esperen co-beneficios sociales, ambientales y económicos más amplios y equitativamente distribuidos. Se adjunta el informe final obtenido de dicho análisis (archivo “0.3 Co-beneficios de la Acción Climática Buenos Aires”) en el apartado 11- \'Información adicional\'.

column18: La elaboración del Plan de Acción Climática 2050 de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires contempló, en colaboración con C40, la incorporación del lente de inclusión, considerando tres aspectos claves para planificar y diseñar acciones climáticas con resultados justos y equitativos en la Ciudad. Estos fueron: la accesibilidad, la prosperidad y la ubicación geográfica. Al aplicar este abordaje, la Ciudad de Buenos Aires se propuso generar beneficios proporcionados respecto al acceso, costo e inclusión espacial de las acciones. Se realizó el análisis ICA (\'Análisis de Inclusión y Equidad\') con el objetivo de comprender quién puede acceder y beneficiarse de una acción climática y quién no, dadas las inequidades y necesidades existentes en la Ciudad. Se evaluaron las acciones en función de los grupos prioritarios -previamente identificados- alcanzados, los impactos positivos y negativos, la accesibilidad, la prosperidad, y el lugar, así como también, se elaboraron recomendaciones de políticas para que la Ciudad implemente acciones climáticas de manera inclusiva. Del análisis ICA realizado sobre las acciones priorizadas, se obtuvo como característica general un alto nivel de inclusividad. Se destacó el contemplar instancias de participación activa ya sea en sus etapas de diseño y planificación, como en aquellas de implementación y desarrollo. De igual modo, en términos generales, se consideró que las acciones impactan positivamente en la mayoría de los grupos prioritarios identificados y logran buenos resultados al ser analizadas a la luz de los tres principales criterios de inclusión: accesibilidad, prosperidad y ubicación geográfica.
column19: El Plan de Acción Climática 2050 de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires contempla el eje de acción \'Ciudad Inclusiva\'. El eje incorpora la inclusión de los grupos más vulnerables y actuar sin dejar a nadie atrás, a través de la implementación de seis acciones: (1) Integrando los barrios; (2) Vecinos más preparados; (3) Red de salud pública; (4) Buenos Aires limpios; (5) Alimentación sostenible y (6) Escuelas verdes. En el marco de la acción \'Integrando los barrios\', se destaca el caso de Barrio 20. Barrio 20 se encuentra en proceso de reurbanización desde 2016, año en el que se promulgó la Ley de reurbanización, zonificación e integración socio-urbana de la Villa 20 (N5705). En el marco de la Ley, se creó la “Mesa de Gestión Participativa para la Reurbanización del Barrio Villa 20” con el objeto de garantizar e instrumentar la participación activa de los vecinos del barrio en todas las etapas del proceso de reurbanización. La Gerencia Operativa de Cambio Climático de la Subsecretaría de Ambiente de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires asistió a Mesas Ambientales de Barrio 20 debido a su participación en el proyecto Coaliciones Urbanas Transformadoras (Transformative Urban Coalitions - TUC), de la Iniciativa Internacional del Clima (IKI). El proyecto IKI-TUC, desarrollado en articulación con el Instituto de la Vivienda de la Ciudad, es una iniciativa piloto de implementación de soluciones basadas en la naturaleza complementarias al proceso de reurbanización del Barrio 20. En 2023, y en conjunto con la Gerencia Operativa de Generación de Datos Territoriales, se instalaron 10 termómetros distribuidos heterogéneamente en el barrio para analizar la variabilidad de la temperatura y humedad ambiental en función de la configuración espacial de la trama urbana y monitorear el impacto de la incorporación de infraestructura verde urbana del proyecto IKI-TUC. También se realizó un proceso de ciencia ciudadana con vecinos del Barrio 20, con el objetivo de capacitar a los jóvenes “promotores ambientales” en el uso de tecnologías para el análisis de datos, difundir los resultados del monitoreo y sensibilizar a la comunidad con la problemática. Cabe destacar que el instrumental toma mediciones de temperatura ambiental y humedad desde su instalación en 2023 hasta la actualidad, que la información se encuentra disponible para la comunidad barrial y que la descarga de datos en Barrio 20 la realiza una vecina del barrio.

A jurisdição quantifica a distribuição igualitária e inclusiva da ação climática a partir de instrumentos legais e técnicos previstos na Política Municipal de Mitigação e Adaptação às Mudanças Climáticas de Curitiba, em tramitação na Câmara Municipal. O projeto de lei estabelece como princípio central a justiça climática (art. 3º, I), garantindo que as ações beneficiem de forma equitativa toda a população, com foco especial nas comunidades mais vulneráveis.

 

Entre os mecanismos já definidos em lei destacam-se:
- Instrumentos de informação e gestão (art. 31 e seguintes): Inventários de emissões e remoções de GEE, Avaliação de Riscos Climáticos e Inventário de estoques de carbono, que permitem identificar vulnerabilidades socioambientais e mapear os impactos climáticos com recorte territorial e social.
- Ação climática inclusiva (art. 5º, II): conceito normatizado que obriga a incorporação da equidade de gênero, do enfrentamento das desigualdades sociais e da participação de grupos historicamente marginalizados nos processos decisórios e de implementação.
- Sistema de Monitoramento e Avaliação de Impacto das Políticas Climáticas (art. 40): prevê coleta contínua de dados sobre emissões, adaptação e, de forma inédita, sobre a distribuição equitativa dos impactos e benefícios da política climática, garantindo que as métricas de justiça climática sejam institucionalizadas.
- Governança ampliada (arts. 36-39): o Comitê PlanClima, o Fórum Curitiba sobre Mudanças Climáticas e os Conselhos setoriais asseguram instâncias permanentes de participação social e de monitoramento inclusivo.
- Educação e comunicação (art. 52): programas de educação ambiental formal e não formal com linguagem acessível, abordando vulnerabilidades do município e responsabilidade compartilhada, para ampliar a participação cidadã.
Complementarmente, o município adota metodologias participativas como o Programa Fala Curitiba, que associa consultas populares ao processo orçamentário (LDO e LOA), permitindo que prioridades das comunidades sejam transformadas em investimentos, inclusive os relacionados ao clima.
Assim, a quantificação da distribuição igualitária e inclusiva da ação climática resulta de uma combinação entre dados técnicos (IBGE, Inventários, Avaliação de Riscos), instrumentos normativos (Lei do Clima) e processos participativos institucionalizados, que permitem monitorar de forma mensurável e transparente se os benefícios e custos da ação climática estão sendo distribuídos de maneira justa.
column19: O Projeto Bairro Novo do Caximba Gestão de Riscos Climáticos, que proporcionou intervenções em comunidades com vulnerabilidade socioambiental, envolvendo reassentamento de famílias, melhoria da infraestrutura, aumento da resiliência comunitária, valorização da economia local, promoção da economia circular e redução das emissões de GEE. Proporcionou engajamento e apropriação, além dos espaços projetados considerando a promoção intergeracional e a coexistência de gênero, acessibilidade universal e melhoria da educação e orientação profissional. O processo de engajamento com a comunidade da Caximba incluiu as seguintes atividades: Reuniões semanais com lideranças e moradores sobre o projeto envolvendo 850 famílias; Empoderamento dos jovens; Dever social da Companhia de Habitação para o serviço comunitário; Primeiro encontro LGBTQI+ na comunidade; Consulta pública promovida pela prefeitura e AFD; Rodas de conversa com mulheres, as únicas provedoras; visitas domiciliares; Oficina do Projeto, com o objetivo de trabalhar, compartilhar e alinhar o tema da resiliência ao aquecimento global com o projeto e construir uma resposta coletiva às ambições do Município e da comunidade em relação ao projeto. Curitiba está investindo em um amplo Programa de Agricultura Urbana para incentivar a produção e o consumo de alimentos saudáveis e garantir a segurança alimentar e nutricional de sua população. A ideia também busca otimizar o uso de recursos públicos e envolve diferentes partes interessadas - incluindo o setor privado, cidadãos e instituições - que trabalham juntas para melhorar o engajamento da comunidade, apoiar a implementação de hortas urbanas e programas sociais e fomentar o desenvolvimento de tecnologias inovadoras.\nDe 2017 a 2022, a cidade aumentou suas hortas urbanas de 60 para a marca de 1450 Hortas Urbanas - ocupando uma área de 176.589 m² em todo o território, sendo que 26 praticam a compostagem - que cultivam 126 toneladas de produtos por mês e beneficiam ~20 mil pessoas em comunidades da linha de frente, direta e indiretamente. As Hortas Urbanas são divididas em três categorias: Hortas Comunitárias, implantadas em vazios urbanos, onde os moradores são responsáveis pelo espaço; Hortas Escolares, criadas para engajar professores e alunos; e Hortas Institucionais, instaladas em unidades de saúde, ONGs e centros de assistência social para promover atividades de cultivo, terapêuticas e sociais. A Prefeitura oferece apoio técnico para avaliar a viabilidade de implantação, ministra treinamentos teóricos e práticos sobre cultivo e manutenção, além de oferecer insumos para o solo e plantio. Outro projeto é o \'Programa Reserva Hídrica do Futuro\', que consiste em fornecer água de qualidade e em quantidade para as necessidades básicas da população mais vulnerável durante o período de escassez hídrica, por meio da entrega de reservatórios e perfuração de poços.

Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality carries out the Participatory Budget project. The project in question is a platform that allows citizens to express their project ideas on environmental, disaster and social issues in public spaces.Thanks to the Participatory Budget project, an event was held on environmental pollution and climate change with the participation of the public in 2022 and year. 

Between December 2023 - March 2024, a training program on climate change awareness is planned for the young population. The training program aimed to raise awareness about sustainability and climate change among young people aged 17-29, encouraging them to act with common sense on the path to becoming a resilient city. The online training sessions, delivered by expert academics, covered a wide range of topics, including climate change, social and ecological sustainability, urban innovation, and green entrepreneurship. Cities have a critical opportunity to make the transformations needed to create more socially equitable, ecological, safe societies and economies as they work to manage and recover from these interconnected crises.With the perspective of getting rid of the devastating effects of COVID-19 among the C40 Cities of Istanbul, the Action Plan has been created with the goal of Green and Equitable Development.The Climate Change Action Plan focuses on green and equitable development through the action prioritization process. Employment and social justice criteria shape the prioritization process towards actions that will contribute to a green and equitable recovery. Prioritized mitigation and adaption actions shaped by green and equitable vision dimension are listed below:

MITIGATION ACTIONS

1) Encouragement of measures to increase energy efficiency in all buildings. 2) District-scale new clean energy development (heating, cooling, power) - microgrid (PV, hydrogen fuel cell, other). 3) Taking additional measures towards renewable energy generation, energy and water saving in the projects planned by KIPTAS and BIMTAS. 4) Purchase of new electric buses so that all buses can be electrified. 5) Making existing roads suitable for cyclists, and creating new separated bicycle paths. 6) Pricing for specific areas with high traffic. 7) Park and Ride expansion. 8) Develop programs to reduce or completely avoid any discarded food substance during the processing, using , storage, sale, preparation, cooking and serving of foods. 9) To prevent direct methane release to the atmosphere by capturing landfill gas from solid waste landfill and using it as electricity, heating or transportation fuel. 10) Optimize waste collection operations (routes, pickup schedules) to reduce environmental impacts and total GHG emissions. 11) Divert discarded materials from landfills by recovering and repurposing them into new products. 12) Supporting wastewater recovery and reuse. 13) Managing the supply lines and drinking water network with smart systems.14) Revise building and municipal code to encourage water use reduction, on-site water reuse, and recycling. 15) Application of sustainable rainwater solutions (rain gardens, use of permeable materials, storage, etc.). 

ADAPTATION ACTIONS

1) Increasing urban water storage capacity and preventing loss of function through leakage. 2) Tree planting in public spaces. 3) Cooling systems for critical infrastructure. 4) Rehabilitation of streams, green river banks. 5) Improve road drainage and keep drains clear. 6) Backyard and community gardening in vacant lots and parks, and roadside urban urban design agriculture.

While preparing the Istanbul Climate Action Plan, opinions and suggestions were received from all Istanbul stakeholders. This is important for the inclusiveness and transparency of the climate action plan. At the same time, meetings with the officials of 39 district municipalities within the borders of Istanbul are actively carried out in the preparation of the action plan and in the current projects.In addition, 'Participatory Budget' project has been provided to Istanbul citizens. Through Participatory Budget, our citizens have been asked about their opinions and suggests regarding climate change related issues. On the other hand, 'Climate Platform' has been found consisting of academicians, Non-Governmental organizations, climate activists and Istanbul citizens. Routine meetings were held on the Climate Platform by providing a discussion environment on the existing barriers, solution suggestions and good practice examples regarding greenhouse gas emission reduction and climate change adaptation actions such as water stress, drought, green space management, biodiversity, integrated transportation systems and renewable energy technologies.As Istanbul, we have ambitious goals to become a carbon neutral and resilient city. 

In order to achieve these goals, we carry out the following activities:

100 Carbon Neutral and Smart Cities MissionThe mission's purpose is to support 100 (100+12) European cities to achieve the goal of climate neutrality by 2030. All cities participating in this project are intended to become centres for innovation and experimentation and to serve as examples for all other cities. 

Call for Pilot Cities: NetZeroCities has published a call for pilot cities. Under this initiative, which is part of the Climate Neutral and Smart Cities Mission, pilot cities have been selected among European cities which submit innovative projects on how to achieve carbon neutrality until the year 2030. According to Istanbul's greenhouse gas emission inventory, stationary energy contributes the highest percentage (63-64%). Green and Carbon Neutral Transition Guide - Istanbul Model (Build4GreenIST) Project therefore supports action on energy used in buildings in the city. For this purpose, a guide has been established for green and carbon neutral buildings which are to be renovated in the context of urban regeneration. The guide can be reached by this link: https://build4greenist.ibb.istanbul/guide/ 

Within the context of the project, it is used sensors to monitor energy consumption in residential buildings in selected pilot region (Bayrampaşa KIPTAŞ Houses). Methodologies have been developed for data collection. Based on the data, a change in behaviour towards more efficient energy use promotes.

Adaptation Mission: Istanbul has entitled to become one of 215 signators of the EU Adaptation Mission which was initiated to support cities in their efforts to become resilient to climate change by 2030. The purpose of the Adaptation Mission is to prepare cities/regions for the current as well as future effects of climate change and to mobilise them to ensure adaptation. By this mission it will be possible to generate common benefits for municipalities working for the same goal, to test innovative solutions and to offer financial resources for future joint activities. 

Istanbul CCC: During the preparation of the Istanbul Climate City Contract, participatory meetings and workshops were held with a wide range of stakeholders, including all units of the Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality (IMM), all district municipalities of Istanbul, NGOs, universities, and chambers of industry. The Commitments Plan of the Istanbul Climate City Contract aims to establish the Istanbul Climate Platform, which will ensure that all stakeholders are engaged in the fight against climate change.

Istanbul GCAP: IMM participated in the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) Green Cities Program in 2021, began preparations for the Istanbul Green City Action Plan in May 2023 with technical and financial support from the EBRD, aiming for an environmentally sensitive and sustainable Istanbul.

Throughout the preparation of the Istanbul Green City Action Plan, numerous meetings and workshops were held with both internal and external stakeholders. These workshops conducted detailed needs analyses across all sectoral areas within the scope of the GCAP, prioritized Istanbul's environmental challenges, and discussed potential solutions.

Istanbul GCAP includes 52 actions in total, 17 of which are policy actions and 35 are investment actions. A total of 52 Green City Actions were shortlisted from a long list of hundreds of actions to support and encourage efforts to address the city's environmental challenges.

Peluang/Manfaat yang lebih luas dari Aksi Iklim meliputi: 1) Pengembangan Transportasi Berkelanjutan yang memiliki manfaat mengurangi polusi udara, mengurangi kemacetan dan meningkatkan kualitas hidup. Pengembangan transportasi berkelanjutan ini dapat mengurangi ketergantungan pada kendaraan pribadi serta mengurangi emisi karbon. 2) Pengelolaan sampah yang lebih baik yang memiliki manfaat dalam mengurangi resiko banjir, memperbaiki sanitasi, menciptakan peluang ekonomi dan mengurangi emisi gas rumah kaca dari dekomposisi sampah organik. 3) Penghijauan Kota dan Ruang Publik memiliki manfaat dalam penyerapan karbon, mengurangi panas kota, memperbaiki kualitas udara dan menyediakan ruang rekreasi. 4) Peningkatan efisiensi energi di bangunan gedung, memiliki manfaat mengurangi konsumsi energi dan biaya listrik, meningkatkan kenyamanan penghuni dan mengurangi emisi karbon. 5) Energi terbarukan memiliki manfaat peralihan ke ekonomi yang lebih berkelanjutan dan mengurangi dampak lingkungan. 6) Edukasi dan keterlibatan komunitas, manfaatnya meningkatkan kesadaran dan partisipasi masyarakat dalam menjaga lingkungan, memperkuat ketahanan pangan, mengurangi jejak karbon, memberdayakan warga dan membangun komunitas yang lebih tangguh. 7) Aksi Kolaborasi berupa Kolaborasi Sosial Berskala Besar (KSBB) baik pemerintah, masyarakat, akademisi, dunia usaha dan stakeholder lainnya. 8) Penerapan NBS (Nature Based Solution), Penerapan Nature-Based Solutions (NBS) di Jakarta dilakukan untuk mengatasi masalah banjir dan meningkatkan ketahanan kota terhadap bencana. Berikut beberapa contoh penerapan NBS di Jakarta¹ ²:
- Pembangunan Rain Garden dan Bioswale: Pemerintah Jakarta telah membangun rain garden dan bioswale di beberapa lokasi, seperti di Jalan Penjompongan Raya dan Tamai Boi Trans Park. Proyek ini bertujuan untuk mengurangi genangan air hujan dan meningkatkan infiltrasi air ke dalam tanah.
- Penambahan Ruang Terbuka Hijau (RTH): Pemerintah Jakarta berencana untuk meningkatkan luas RTH di kota untuk mengurangi limpasan air hujan dan meningkatkan kualitas lingkungan.
- Pengembangan Infrastruktur Hijau: Jakarta juga mengembangkan infrastruktur hijau lainnya, Jakarta seperti taman atap dan dinding hijau, untuk meningkatkan efisiensi energi dan mengurangi efek panas perkotaan.

column18: Semenjak dikeluarkannya Peraturan Gubernur pada tahun 2021, yaitu Peraturan Gubernur Nomor 90 tahun 2021 tentang Rencana Pembangunan Rendah Karbon Daerah yang Berketahanan Iklim, Pemerintah Provinsi DKI Jakarta berupaya melakukan kegiatan yang dapat mengurangi Emisi Karbon dan upaya Pengurangan Gas Rumah Kaca yang dimana Pemerintah Provinsi DKI Jakarta mempunyai target ambisius 30% di tahun 2030 dan Zero Emition di tahun 2050. Adapun cara Pemerintah Provinsi DKI Jakarta mengukur distribusi tindakan iklim yang adil dan inklusif adalah dengan bekerja sama dengan semua Satuan Perangkat Daerah (dimana terdapat 5 kelompok kerja yang terkait dengan upaya aksi iklim), sebagai contoh selama lima tahun terakhir : 1) Pemprov DKI terus menggalakkan pembangunan Taman dan Hutan Kota sehingga Ruang Terbuka Hijau (RTH) di Jakarta pun semakin merata dan diminati oleh Publik. Berdasarkan Data dari Dinas Pertamanan dan Hutan Kota (Distamhut) DKI Jakarta dimana sudah dibangun lebih dari 1.527 taman dan direvitalisasi serta lebih dari 200.000 pohon tertanam, dan sebanyak 91% luas wilayah Jakarta berada dalam radius berjalan kaki (800m) dari taman dan hutan kota. 2) Terlihat juga dari Jakarta sudah berkembang menjadi Kota Transit (tidak lagi memprioritaskan kendaraan pribadi dalam pembangunannya tetapi lebih memperhatikan pejalan kaki di perkotaan). Telah dibangun trotoar sepanjang 427 km, 314 km jalur sepeda, dan 67 bike sharing spots. Beberapa ruang publik di Jakarta sudah dibangun dengan menerapkan konsep Low Emission Zone, seperti Kawasan Kota Tua (Jalan Pintu Besar Utara, Jalan Kali Besar Barat Sisi Selatan, Jalan Kunir Sisi Selatan, Jalan Kunir Sisi Selatan, Jalan Kemukus, Jalan Ketumbar dan Jalan Lada). 3) Selain pembangunan yang diperbaiki, Pemprov DKI juga memfasilitasi Transportasi Publik yang dapat dijangkau hanya dengan berjalan kaki dalam radius 700m dari tempat tinggal sehingga sebanyak 86,8% warga tinggal dengan transportasi publik, ini menjadi 2x lipat peningkatannya. Pemprov DKI juga membangun Integrasi Ruang yg terdiri dari 9 simpul integrasi antarmoda (Interkoneksi Bawah Tanah, Terowongan Kendal, Integrasi Stasiun Tanah Abang, JPO Phinisi Sudirman, Halte Integrasi CSW, Integrasi Stasiun Tebet), 14 jembatan penyebrangan orang (JPO) baru, revitalisasi dan interkoneksi bawah tanah pertama MRT. Sistem Pembayaran Moda Transportasi publik juga sudah terintegrasi dengan Aplikasi JakLingko. 4) Pemprov DKI juga terus berkomitmen untuk mendukung upaya yang menjadikan Kota Jakarta sebagai Kota Beremisi Rendah. Salah satu program yang diwujudkan yaitu melalui Pembangunan Sekolah Net Zero Carbon dengan Green Building, seperti SDN Duren Sawit 14 Jakarta Timur, SDN Grogol Selatan 09 Jakarta Selatan, SDN Ragunan 08 Pagi, 09 Pagi, 11 Petang Jakarta Selatan dan SMAN 96 Jakarta Barat. 5) Pengelolaan Sampah menjadi prioritas. Sebagai antisipasi penuhnya kapasitas TPST Bantargebang, Pemprov DKI terus mempromosikan program Jakarta Sadar Sampah. Sebanyak 50% RW di Jakarta sudah melakukan pengangkutan sampah terjadwal, 141.418 rumah tangga sudah melakukan Pemilahan Sampah dan ternyata hal ini meningkatkan antusiasme masyarakat untuk mengolah sampah. Selain itu ada juga budidaya maggot/larva yang terbukti efektif mengurangi sampah organik dan memiliki nilai ekonomis sebagai pakan ternak. Inovasi dan kolaborasi bersama warga ini mampu menurunkan volume sampah di kota sebesar 24,85% di tahun 2021 dan 26% di tahun 2022. TPST Bantargebang juga sudah melalui peremajaan dan pengembangan teknologi sehingga sampah terolah bisa mencapai 250 ton/hari dari landfill mining eksisting dan PTLSa. 6) Solusi permasalahan sanitasi dan air limbah juga turut dilakukan untuk mengurangi pencemaran air di Jakarta, salah satunya dengan memanfaatkan Sistem Pengelolaan Air Limbah Domestik Terpusat (SPALD-T) Skala Permukiman. Sistem tersebut mengalirkan air limbah domestik ke jaringan perpipaan agar tidak langsung meresap dan mencemari tanah serta diharapkan bisa mengurangi penyakit bawaan air (waterbone diseases) yg disebabkan oleh saluran drainase lingkungan yang kotor atau air tanah yg tercemar bakteri E.coli. Adapun total keseluruhan Zona Pembangunan SPALD-T skala perkotaan yang direncanakan melalui Program Pembangunan Jakarta Sewerage System yaitu 15 Zona dengan Zona 0 sebagai Zona Eksisting (Waduk Setiabudi) dan 5 Zona Prioritas (Zona 1,2,5, 6, dan 8). Kapasitas Pengolahan Air Limbah Domestik Terpusat Skala Permukiman semakin meluas.

column19: The Lagos State Government conducted a Climate Risk Assessment to provide robust evidence and projections of localized climate risks and hazards, and prioritize sectors and actions that will meet short, medium and long-term adaptation needs of the State. This assessment was done across all the Local Government Areas and divisions in the State with focus on informal settlements. The climate hazards was identified from a combination of sources which include workshop, stakeholder meeting and field survey. The hazards identified include heat waves, inland flooding, river flooding, erosion, coastal flooding, thunderstorms, coastal and lagoon flooding, tropical storms and urban heat island. The corresponding adaptation actions were developed through stakeholder's input and consensus. A multi- criteria analysis exercise for each of the identified climate hazard was carried out. The implementation considerations for each prioritized action were discussed and assessed, and a roadmap of implementation steps was established. This was followed by a plenary discussion where feedback and comments were shared. For informal settlements, a corresponding adaptaton action that benefits these communities is the development of Sustainable Urban Drainage System by the other arm of the Ministry, Office of Drainage Services, which will take care of drainage channels which adresses surface water networks to pipes to ensure discharge into nearby watercourses within these localities which are susceptibke to flash flooding. In the same vein the Ministry has embarked on improving the Earth channels through continuous maintenance, cleaning and channelization.The State Government having a total understanding of the issue of flooding at local government, the State Government collaborated with the Local Government administrators to form a Tertiary Drain Maintenance Squad. The function of this squad is to ensure, continuous cleaning and maintenance of tertiary drains within the local governments. However, there isn't enough funding from local governments as the project should be done collaboratively. In the waste sector, to improve waste recycling in the State, Pakam offers the opportunity to build a clean and sustainable Lagos through its earn as you waste platform. The lack of collectors has created few setback but the solution is taking it one community at a time hence, the PAKAM app is used by Lagos residents to schedule pickup of recyclables from households by the nearest recycler. From the lekki corridor down to VI and Ikoyi wouldn't be a huge problem as every household there can start to schedule for any of their recyclable waste pickup. The areas around Ikeja, Kosofe, Anthony Maryland, Mende, Gbagada, ilupeju can also start to enjoy same service. Hotels, restaurants, can start to aggregate their recyclables waste now. Pakam is set to purchase at least a 3 million naira worth of recyclable waste on a daily from these areas which will help divert recyclables from landfills. The recyclers are prominently domained in informal settings, hence this helps to increase the earnings of this group of people, provide jobs whilst contributing to the city meeting her goals of diversion of recyclables from landfill.
