Key Area 1: Equitable and inclusive distribution of climate action regarding electricity charges on households. 

Electricity Charges Subsidy Scheme: [Input by FSTB]
The Government announced in 2008, 2011, 2012, 2013, 2019, 2021, 2022 and 2023 the provision of a maximum total subsidy of $14,000 to each eligible residential electricity account (“the subsidy schemes”). The sum has been fully credited to each residential tariff electricity account registered with CLP Power Hong Kong Limited (“CLP”) and The Hongkong Electric Company, Limited (“HK Electric”) from September 2008 to August 2009, from July 2011 to June 2014, from January 2020 to December 2020 and from June 2021 to May 2024. The subsidy can only be used for paying electricity charges. Any unused subsidy can be carried forward to pay billed electricity charges under the same account until 31 December 2025 or the close of the account (whichever is earlier). https://www.fstb.gov.hk/en/treasury/fin_rel_shc/electricity-charges-subsidy-scheme.htm 

Apart from the existing subsidy schemes, to balance the impact on people's livelihood of the recent transition to cleaner electricity generating systems in Hong Kong, the bureau implemented the electricity charges relief scheme in January 2019. A monthly electricity charge relief of 50 has been granted to each eligible residential electricity account for 60 months. To alleviate the impact of tariff increase on households during this transitional period in moving to a low carbon future, the Government provides a new round of electricity charges relief to each eligible residential electricity account in Hong Kong a maximum electricity charges relief of 1,200 over 24 months (i.e. 50 per month) from January 2024 to December 2025. The relief can only be used for offsetting electricity charges. Any unused relief can be carried forward to offset electricity charges under the same account until 31 December 2025 or the close of the account (whichever is earlier). https://www.news.gov.hk/eng/2020/04/20200421/20200421_141104_732.html 
https://www.eeb.gov.hk/en/energy/ecrs.html 
https://www.info.gov.hk/gia/general/202309/29/P2023092900275.htm 

Special Tariff Relief Mechanism during Energy Crisis: this mechanism would be triggered if Fuel Clause Charges (FCCs) increased as a result of persistent surge in fuel prices amid an energy crisis, leading to an increase in Total Tariff (defined as Basic Tariff Rate plus FCC) of more than 20% for HKE or more than 10% for CLP
compared with January of that year. If the mechanism was triggered, the two power companies would make contribution from their non-Scheme of Control accounts to provide Special Tariff Relief to low-consumption residential households, subject to a cap.
 https://www.legco.gov.hk/yr2024/english/panels/ea/papers/ea20241119cb1-1493-4-e.pdf

Key Area 2: large-scale green and equitable advancement of public transport: 
On 10 December 2024, the Government promulgated the Green Transformation Roadmap of Public Buses and Taxis, outlining the future direction and policy objectives aiming for the green transformation of buses and taxis in an orderly manner. The Government has introduced various supporting measures, including earmarking $135 million (about US$17 million) and about $470 million (about US$60 million) respectively under the New Energy Transport Fund to subsidise the purchase of 3 000 electric taxis (e-taxis) by the taxi trade and about 600 electric buses (e-buses) by the franchised bus operators. Another $50 million (about US$6 million) has been earmarked under the Fund for subsidising wheel-chair accessible e-taxis. The Government is also adopting a multi-pronged approach to encourage the trade to expand the network of charging facilities. It is expected at least 500 fast chargers across Hong Kong will be installed by the end of 2027 to support the anticipated increase in electric vehicles (EVs). The Government has also launched the Dedicated 100% Loan Guarantee Scheme for Battery Electric Taxis, which enables taxi owners to take out loan with a better interest rate for purchasing e-taxis. column16: Climate neutrality is a challenge that Madrid has accepted with a social perspective that will allow the city to bring urgent transformations with people´s actions and decisions. Madrid wants to achieve climate neutrality but always by guaranteeing equity and inclusiveness in the climate actions that will take place. The Roadmap towards climate neutrality of the City of Madrid identifies co-benefits of mitigation policies associated with the climate action. It implies an evolution of many of the current urban models and a social and economic transformation. In this process, the importance of the co-benefits that will occur in association with decarbonisation actions should be highlighted. Energy efficiency actions on the building stock will have the associated effect of improving the quality of housing, especially in the most vulnerable buildings and areas of the city, and will also improve the conditions of access to energy, reducing situations of energy poverty. The evolution in mobility will have a direct effect on the city's air quality and noise impact, due to the reduction in demand and the penetration of new technologies. The incorporation of behaviours such as teleworking or the development of proximity urban planning will lead to a reduction in the demand for travel and will increase the presence of non-motorised transport such as pedestrians and cyclists. The development of offsetting mechanisms, such as the creation of carbon sink forests, will substantially increase the presence of nature and biodiversity in the city with all the associated benefits that this entails. In addition to the mitigation actions, there will also be Climate Change Adaptation actions in the city. To the reduction of climate impacts produced by these measures, we should add the multiple benefits they provide, from the improvement of citizens' health, the quality of public spaces, the stimulation of local economies, water management or the reduction of insurance costs, among a myriad of other effects. It is also important to integrate into the design phase of projects criteria that implement nature-based solutions (NBS) and increase vegetation in the city. Continue to disseminate among the different areas of the City Council to work and support the planning and design of streets using green and blue infrastructure. That way we will integrate climate change adaptation criteria into the specifications and drafting of projects. Also, the study 'Madrid economic case' performed by Material economics in 2021 identified and prioritized the climate actions not only from an economic investment perspective but also including co-benefits associated that would improve social cohesion, equity and citizens welfare.

column19: Madrid is making wide engagement with urban stakeholders a central dimension in its transition to net zero, learning how other cities face the same risks, through active participation in city networks such as C40, Covenant of Mayors or EuroCities.Madrid City Council is actively working with C40 network how to increase action on community-led development, inclusive climate action and infrastructure projects that achieve major environmental, health, social and economic benefits, especially in low-income and vulnerable communities and how to deliver bold climate action that benefits all residents equitably.Citizen engagement is also critical for the fulfilment of the 'Mission of smart and climate neutral cities' of EU, which Madrid is part of. Change is for the citizens and Madrid wants to promote their participations in the different processes, plans and actions. An example is the need to disseminate climate objectives to society in non-expert language, reviewing the strategic axes of the Roadmap with this social perspective. In order to reduce the barrier of participation of marginalized group a working group was launched with the participation of social organisations such as Oxfam, Save the Children, Porticus, EAPN, Fuhem, among others, to learn from their experience and working together on emission reduction policies to ensure that all segments of the population are taken into account (leaving no one behind). It Is a project finance by Porticus and in collaboration with itdUPM that is going to deliver an updated Roadmap towards Climate neutrality in the late months of 2024. The aim of this process is to study the positive or negative impacts on different groups of the actions and measures that de Roadmap stablishes. That's why the participation of social organisations is the key to make a successful review to learn from their experience but also to represent different population such as children, elderly people, poverty energy homes...etc for the redesign of the lines of action.Another important target of this review is to identify cobenefits associated to the lines of actions of the Roadmap to integrate a deep social strategy such as green jobs, circular economy or eco-system services for the different groups.In addition, during these years, a set of strategic areas of action have been selected to create a portfolio of pilot projects with the aim of connecting them and some other initiatives that, together, will multiply their individual potential and they will have greater impact than they would do on their own. heat wave study in the “San Cristóbal” neighbour hood in Madrid, City of Madrid conducted a study of social dimension of adaptation to climate change in \'San Cristobal de los Ángeles\' neighbourhood (LINK Dimensión social) in 2022 (may 2022 - October 2022). This study is to targeting a low-income neighbourhood of the city and focused on how public spaces can generate more resilience and contribute to the social cohesion of the community. To complete this study a series of indicators have been developed as well as temperature monitoring to detail the behaviour of low income neighbourhood residents during high temperatures. To this aim a set of different sensors were installed during this period but due to different issues heat temperatures and data are going to be monitored during 2023 summer time (may 2023 - October 2023).The study identified a series of environments or spaces where it is desirable to intervene to improve the climate well-being of the inhabitants. It is considered three dimensions of intervention as basic:- Open space and vegetation- Housing- Public, private (commerce), NGO and community facilitiesThrough the study findings, the City of Madrid plans to incorporate these insights from the study into the intervention plan in school environments with criteria for adaptation to climate change and improvement of air quality that is going to keep working during 2024. This project focuses on design public spaces near schools through nature based solutions and improving air quality balancing the space between pavement and road to give prominence to pedestrians by creating places in these areas where people could keep relationships after school hours.Another example, Madrid wants to develop a working network between different departments of Madrid City Council and private areas, that will improve the relations between workers and will promote a feeling of teamwork in future projects. This municipal training initiative is already taking place by celebrating monthly meetings, that will last one year, and where workers from different departments can create connections in workshops where they can also learn about climate change basics and principles. This is the perfect way, not only to improve communication in future projects, but also to design them with different perspectives and opinions, so climate adaptation is more inclusive.

column16: De manera general, la Estrategia Local de Acción Climática (ELAC) 2021-2050 y el Programa de Acción Climática de la Ciudad de México (PACCM) 2021-2030 se alinean a los compromisos del Plan General de Desarrollo de la Ciudad de México, el cual consiste en transitar hacia una ciudad sustentable, sana y resiliente; que concilie los límites que impone el ambiente natural de la cuenca, la reducción de las desigualdades sociales y la aspiración de mejorar la calidad de vida de las actuales y futuras generaciones. Por lo que, en cada una de las acciones de los 8 ejes estratégicos el PACCM describen los beneficios y cobeneficios específicos por la implementación de las mismas. \nEl diseño, ejecución y seguimiento de las medidas implementadas en el PACCM, identifica los beneficios de la acción climática en la garantía de múltiples derechos humanos y la reducción de brechas de desigualdad en la ciudad, así como los aportes al alcance de compromisos internacionales y nacionales para el desarrollo sustentable. \nEl desarrollo y actualización del Programa incluyen etapas de análisis costo-beneficio social y priorización de medidas, para seleccionar y financiar las medidas con mayor potencial en materia ambiental, económica y social en la reducción de las desigualdades urbanas.

column18: En la Ciudad de México, los efectos negativos del cambio climático afectan a todas las personas, pero impactan de manera diferenciada por las dinámicas de género, por edad y condiciones socioeconómicas. Estas condiciones también generan percepciones diferentes entre mujeres y hombres sobre las causas y responsabilidades para la acción climática. \nA partir de los resultados del “Diagnóstico para conocer los impactos del cambio climático en mujeres y hombres de la Ciudad de México”, se detectó que existen diferencias significativas en cuanto a las percepciones del tiempo, patrones de movilidad, sensación de vulnerabilidad, roles y tareas, frente a los impactos del cambio climático entre hombres y mujeres. La política climática de la Ciudad de México parte de los avances en los diálogos e intercambios para la formación de una agenda ambiental con perspectiva de género. A pesar de que los impactos climáticos afectan a todas las personas y todos los sectores de la sociedad, existe un consenso sobre la mayor vulnerabilidad de determinados grupos de personas ante el cambio climático, especialmente quienes se encuentran en situación de pobreza. Las personas en situación de pobreza cuentan con menor acceso a servicios básicos, sufren una mayor incidencia de enfermedades y perciben ingresos bajos e inestables. Además, se encuentran más expuestas a eventos como sequías, inundaciones y tormentas, que afectan los recursos de los que dependen; cuentan con una limitada capacidad de adaptación a los impactos actuales o futuros causados por el cambio climático. Los impactos diferenciados también se reflejan en la percepción del fenómeno y la forma en la que las personas lo viven día con día. Las personas en hogares de clase económica media y baja han expresado haber padecido más los efectos del cambio climático al tener menos recursos para enfrentarlos. Sin embargo, las personas en hogares de clase media-alta y alta han percibido algunas implicaciones del cambio climático en su vida diaria, pero reconocen que otras regiones del mundo padecen aún más sus efectos. En ambos sectores económicos, se reconoce que las niñas y los niños, además de las personas adultas mayores y las personas con alguna discapacidad son los grupos con mayor vulnerabilidad climática, debido a los padecimientos en su salud a consecuencia de los cambios del clima, situación que se intensifica si viven en situación de pobreza o sin acceso a servicios de salud.Por ello, es tarea irrenunciable de la política climática desarrollar medidas cuyo objetivo prioritario sea reducir las desigualdades ambientales, socioeconómicas, territoriales y de género. La vulnerabilidad climática, expresada como una de las múltiples formas de rezago y desigualdad en la ciudad, orientará las estrategias de acción climática hacia la búsqueda del bienestar y la dignidad humana. \nA partir de análisis costo-beneficio social, del análisis territorial de la marginación y la vulnerabilidad social y climática y de otros indicadores socioambientales (i.e. desigualdad de género, acceso a servicios básicos, acceso a áreas verdes) se priorizan las intervenciones territoriales de los proyectos establecidos en el PACCM.
column19: En el marco de los derechos humanos establecidos en la Constitución Política de la Ciudad de México, las acciones climáticas dispuestas en la Estrategia de Acción Climática (ELAC) 2021-2050 y el Programa de Acción Climática de la Ciudad de México (PACCM) 2021-2030, garantizan el derecho a una vida digna, a la igualdad, a la ciudad, al desarrollo sustentable y a un medio ambiente sano como los derechos llave para la justicia climática. La transición hacia una ciudad incluyente y justa, promueve a su vez, la defensa de múltiples derechos interrelacionados, como la salud, el agua y saneamiento, la alimentación, la vivienda digna, la educación, la ciencia, la movilidad, el espacio público, la información y la participación pública. Desde esta perspectiva, la ELAC y el PACCM, buscan en su planteamiento y puesta en marcha, apoyar los esfuerzos para que las personas gocen de un libre ejercicio de sus derechos y construyan, de manera solidaria y compartida, un futuro sustentable y resiliente. Con ese fin, la política climática identifica la siguiente medida estratégica y transversal de inclusión y derechos humanos: “Generar y actualizar información que permita conocer las causas y los impactos diferenciados del cambio climático y su relación con las brechas de desigualdad por grupos sociales y económicos, así como identificar las áreas de oportunidad de la acción climática para reducirlas y garantizar así los derechos humanos” Para leer más al respecto, consultar el capítulo \'POLÍTICA CLIMÁTICA INCLUYENTE Y TRANSFORMADORA\' de la ELAC y el PACCM.\nLo anterior, se alinea al capitulo \'Ciudad sustentable, preparada frente al cambio climático\' del Programa provisional de Gobierno 2024-2029, el cual tiene como objetivo, consolidar a la Ciudad de México como un modelo de sostenibilidad y resiliencia ambiental mediante la reducción de emisiones contaminantes, la restauración y conservación de ecosistemas estratégicos, la promoción de una economía circular y el desarrollo urbano sustentable. A través de la gestión integral de residuos, la protección del suelo de conservación, la expansión de áreas verdes, el fomento de energías limpias y la movilidad sustentable, se garantizará la calidad del aire, y la adaptación al cambio climático, asegurando un entorno habitable, equilibrado y próspero para todas y todo. De igual manera, se velará por el bienestar animal con una visión de derechos.

The City of Milan views climate action as a catalyst for social equity, improved health, economic development, and enhanced quality of life, hence seeking to promote an integrated climate-neutral urban development. Among the different opportunities and benefits of climate action, the most relevant for the Milanese context concern:
- social inclusion: all climate actions of the Municipality are guided by the principle of equity and aim to mitigate the impacts of climate change that disproportionately affect the most vulnerable as well as to avoid that the costs of the transition to a low carbon economy take a toll on the population groups in weaker economic conditions. Hence, projects focused on creating a 15-minute city, increasing urban green areas, reducing heat islands, making public space more livable and accessible also offer the opportunity to reduce inequalities and reinforce social cohesion.
- the improvement of air quality and public health brought by investments in sustainable mobility, energy efficiency, waste management, and urban green spaces, which constitutes the main rationale behind the development of an Air and Climate Plan (and not simply a Climate Action Plan).
An analysis of the wider benefits of climate action was carried out in 2023/2024, when, in the framework of the EU Cities Mission, the City of Milan developed its Climate City Contract, aiming to anticipate and enhance local climate mitigation and adaptation actions as outlined in the Air and Climate Plan (ACP). This acceleration is expected to generate numerous inter-connected co-benefits for the city and its community:
- Social co-benefits: improved health (physical and mental); improved housing quality and accessibility/affordability; reduced energy poverty and vulnerability; improved equity, social inclusion and cohesion; improved urban liveability, with positive impacts on economic dynamism. 
- Economic co-benefits: higher and better employment, helping enhance overall economic development and social cohesion; augmented prosperity, through new investments and industries; fostered innovation;increased energy independence.
- Environmental co-benefits: improved air quality; a greater biodiversity, strengthening city's resilience as well as social and cultural services; reduced noise pollution.

The assessment of the co-benefits of the Climate City Contract builds on previous analysis, carried out during the development of the Air and Climate Plan to estimate the direct and indirect impacts of its climate actions. For instance, an impact assessment was developed to evaluate the benefits of implementing different sets of measures to reduce air pollution as well as their impacts on externalities (e.g. the costs incurred by society for increases in illness and mortality rates, work days lost, etc.), comparing a reference situation with different scenarios where the EU Limit Values or the WHO Guidelines are respected. Another example is the pilot cost-benefit analysis of a set of decarbonisation actions, conducted in the framework of the European project 'Healthy, Clean Cities - Deep Demonstration: Milan 2019' to assess the overall economic sustainability of the ACP and support the definition of individual actions. For more info on these, please see previous CDP Reports. 

Also, In 2021, with the support of C40, a Workforce Equity Assessment was carried out, outlining the employment potential and equity implications of climate interventions aligned with Milan's climate plans. The study showed that each climate intervention cluster analysed has the potential to deliver between 7.5 and 10.6 total job years per EUR 1 million invested at the city level, with the buildings cluster estimated to generate the highest number of supported jobs years, followed by urban cooling and flood resilience interventions. Also, climate interventions provide the potential to upskill Milan's existing workforce.

The Monitoring programme of Milan's Air and Climate Plan (ACP) is divided into six levels, including: 
- “Level 5 - INCLUSIVITY”, which refers to the actions of Area 5 of the Plan (citizens and stakeholders engagement) and evaluates whether the implemented actions are truly inclusive, able to involve the entire population and city users, as well as all areas of the city. The rationale behind this Monitoring Level is that effective social inclusion can be ensured through equity of access and use of services and urban areas, and in parallel, by targeting the most vulnerable citizens. Four dimensions of equity are prioritized: 
1. Population, i.e. the capacity of the action to fill asymmetries and discrepancies in relation to various variables related to SDG10 and the possible causes of discrimination cited in the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, namely: age, ethnic background, income and social background, disability, gender, sexual orientation, belief and religious faith; 
2. Urban geography, i.e. the capacity of the action to adapt to and address specific urban geographical and social characteristics, as well as its ability to act on the entire city area and on all Municipalities and not just on some portions of it; 
3. Participation, i.e. the ability of the action to involve large parts of the population in its planning, execution and evaluation, through participatory processes, local co-design of spaces and services and civic activism, with the aim of increasing the empowerment of all citizens and social cohesion. 
4. Territorial development, or the ability of the action to promote local socio-economic development with particular attention to the enhancement of employment and the creation of new businesses and jobs. This equity dimension is assessed in the sixth level of monitoring. 
- “Level 6 - SOCIO-ECONOMIC IMPACTS”, which measures the social progress and economic development produced through the implementation of the ACP, in particular in terms of creation of new professional skills, new jobs and new businesses. As socio-economic impacts can be positive or negative, expected or unexpected, to make these characteristics explicit, the indicators have been divided into: a. benefits, where the effect is positive and prodiced in a direct and voluntary manner (expected) on the specified subjects involved (beneficiaries and stakeholders); b. negative externalities, when it is a negative effect caused collaterally by an intervention aimed at achieving benefits for others on the identified subjects; c. co-benefits, if the positive effect is generated by an intervention in an indirect manner (not expected) on the indicated subjects.

To ensure equitable and inclusive climate action, the City of Milan designs and implements measures targeting specific areas of the city (e.g. low-income peripheral neighborhoods), vulnerable population groups (e.g. children, the elderly) and certain social issues caused or exacerbated by climate change. Two main examples:
GREEN AND THRIVING NEIGHBORHOODS FOR RESILIENT COMMUNITIES (GTNRC): Supported by C40 and Z-Zurich Foundation, the GTNRC programme aims to improve quality of life and strengthen resilience to extreme heat at neighbourhood scale. By prioritising people and their interaction with the place they live in, it promotes a holistic approach to public space transformation, integrating 15-Minute City principles with community-based climate adaptation solutions in the design and implementation of spatial and social interventions. 
In 2024, the City selected the district of Crescenzago as first pilot area, due to lack of quality public spaces, increasingly high temperatures and elevated concentration of people particularly vulnerable to heat waves. 
The first phase of GTNRC consisted in the assessment of the community needs of the neighbourhood of Crescenzago through the Climate Resilience Measurement for Communities (CRMC) tool, developed by Z Zurich and adapted to Milan's context. This instrument is based on the 5C-4R framework, combining a series of indicators of sources of resilience (five complementary 'capitals': human, social, physical, financial and natural - 5C) with four properties derived from resilient system-thinking (4R), that can help people withstand and respond to shocks. These baseline assessments served to identify key vulnerabilities and opportunities to improve well-being through tactical and longer term interventions developed in subsequent phases of the programme, such as “Camp Turroni” summer pilot, which launched Milan's first School Oasis connected to a tactical urbanism intervention, transforming the Perasso primary school's courtyard into an attractive and cool public space for the summer. 
Following this, a local action plan was developed identifying three priority actions to strengthen community resilience: School Oasis, Tactical Shade, and Cooler Home projects. 
In 2025 two pilot shading structures have been set up to enhance the thermal comfort of public spaces. During summer, different parameters are monitored, like temperature and humidity levels, with a view to implement additional structures throughout the city. This is complemented by a pilot information campaign to help residents keep their homes cooler and safer during heat waves, reducing energy costs. 
https://www.comune.milano.it/web/milano-cambia-aria/progetti/quartieri-resilienti
ACTION PLAN AGAINST ENERGY POVERTY: Based on the guidelines endorsed by the City Council in December 2023, the first draft of the plan to tackle energy poverty and vulnerability titled 'Towards a Common Energy Wellbeing' was approved in December 2024. The plan aims to provide relief to situations of energy poverty as well as to mitigate the risk factors aggravating energy insecurity. In 2025, the Plan has been subjected to a public consultation process, where citizens can make comments to improve the contents and support the Administration in finalizing the strategy. 
The plan has been developed by a working group composed of officers from the Environment, Welfare & Health, Housing, and Technological and Digital Innovation departments of the Municipality, leveraging on existing efforts, coordinating different initiatives and creating the basis for a new stream of work, multi-departmental and across services to citizens. The composition of the group reflects the double objective of the plan: on the one hand, it aims to identify and support families experiencing severe economic difficulties in adequately addressing extreme hot or cold temperatures, with serious impacts on health. On the other hand, it intends to continue to pursue decarbonization and the improvement of air quality, promoting a fair and inclusive energy transition for all.
In the meanwhile, ongoing activities to tackle energy poverty include: Energy Poverty Helpdesk, within the Energy One Stop Shop; “EnerPov - Energy Poverty Zero” project; Progetto Arredi (Furnishing project). Additionally, in 2024 energy poverty trainings for social workers and other front-line workers, mostly from the Welfare & Health and the Housing Departments, were organized. The objective was to up-skill them to function as a referral system for the existing Energy Support Desk by helping identify situations of hidden energy poverty and inadequate thermal comfort in the homes of at-risk citizens and address them to appropriate services and resources.

Prior to the adoption of the 2018 Climate Action Plan, the city of Paris has conducted a study to assess the socio-economic impacts of the energy and climate transition. Focusing on individual, economic, social, and political impacts as well as effects on employment, well-being, equity, and overall balance across the city, the study revealed that many measures implemented under the Paris Climate Plan will contribute to enhancing the well-being of citizens by improving the quality of their immediate environment.
(https://cdn.paris.fr/paris/2025/07/17/ey_c40_paris_social-impact-study_final-report-twjJ.pdf) 

These results were later confirmed and quantified more precisely with the study conducted by the Office Français des Conjonctures Economiques (OFCE) on the costs and benefits of the Parisian net zero transition. Focusing on local emissions, the study assessed energy savings reaching 2 billion € by 2050, meaning that the annual estimated costs of transition would be compensated by 2042 by the annual savings. Social co-benefits, mainly in health through air quality and building improvements, were estimated to reach up to 1,8 billion € 2035 and plateau around 1,3 billion € until 2050. Job wise, the study estimated a creation of 13 000 to 16 000 jobs for the region, representing an added value of activity in between 1 and and 1,7 billion €, and 3 billion € France wide. 
(https://www.ofce.sciences-po.fr/pdf/pbrief/2025/OFCEpbrief145.pdf)

Additionally, the City of Paris conducted in 2021 a resilience and vulnerability diagnosis in the context of climate disruption, using the latest scientific climate change models. Lastly, the City of Paris is working to Identify areas of environmental health fragility. The findings of this assessment provide support for the policies outlined in the Paris Climate Plan, particularly in terms of adaptation measures. These include greening the city, strengthening water management strategies, promoting solidarity towards vulnerable populations, and controlling water consumption. 
(https://cdn.paris.fr/paris/2021/11/16/088fcde428650ff1e3d9680f155a54a7.pdf)

The city regularly conducts city-wide studies on various equity-related topics such as: Update demographic, economic and social data for Paris, to understand gender gaps and trends. In 2022, an analysis was carried out and confirmed the narrowing of certain social gaps between the population of those neighbourhoods and that of Paris over the recent period (social indicators, educational success, economic dynamism, living environment), while at the same time indicators of precariousness remain high and gaps in employment and professional integration persist. The workshops also highlighted a number of issues that are becoming increasingly important in working-class neighbourhoods, including environmental health. 
(https://www.apur.org/sites/default/files/synthese_referentiel_evaluation_contrat_ville_paris.pdf?token=dWE_XFh9)

Circular economy helps combat climate change by reducing CO2 emissions from economic activities. It goes hand in hand with the development of new modes of production and consumption, generating new activities and creating sustainable jobs that cannot be relocated. That's why the job creation made possible by the development of the circular economy in Paris, and the resulting creation of value, have been defined as monitoring indicators for the Paris Circular Economy Plan. The quantification of jobs linked to the circular economy in Paris (document to be consulted as an attachment to the response) makes it possible to estimate the number of jobs in Paris at 66,500 FTE (full-time equivalent) in 2016. They represent 2.9% of Parisian jobs and generate an annual added value of 7 billion euros. (https://cdn.paris.fr/paris/2025/07/17/circularjobsquantifying-tLrg.pdf)

Since the adoption in 2016 of the Paris Environmental Health Plan, Health Impact Assessments (HIA) have been made. HIA is a science-based decision-making process that incorporates participatory approaches whenever possible. It helps contextualize research data and facilitates the implementation of projects by enhancing their legitimacy and social acceptability. HIA allows all stakeholders involved in a policy or project to address the social, economic, and environmental issues that may impact health and well-being. The main objective is to take into account health issues in the new urban planning projects, directly from the inhabitants, theirs needs and habits. 9 studies have been released since 2017, and most of the outcomes have been integrated to the new urban projects. Overall, these studies and assessments highlight the wider opportunities and benefits associated with climate action in Paris, such as improved well-being, enhanced public health, increased social cohesion, and greater resilience in the face of climate challenges. The Plan was actualized in 2024.
(https://cdn.paris.fr/paris/2024/12/09/ppse-2-ekaF.pdf)

The City of Paris is dedicated to creating an inclusive and sustainable future, guided by the fourth Paris Climate Action Plan. Through collaborative efforts and extensive stakeholder engagement, Paris aims to reduce social disparities, bridge gender gaps, embrace a more circular economy, and address areas of fragility in environmental health.

Regarding equity, two major challenges lie in the fight against energy poverty and adapting to heatwaves. The City of Paris already works effectively to help disadvantaged households, notably through the numerous aids that exist to support households in fuel poverty (the Fonds de Solidarité Logement (FSL), “Paris Énergie Familles” (PEF) - Paris Famille assistance scheme (10 million euros a year for 43,000 families)). Renovation remains crucial in combating both fuel poverty and climate change. The City of Paris has supported the energy renovation of over more than 50,000 social housing units and 30,000 private homes. These programs are maintained and strengthened and the City is stepping up its actions to combat fuel poverty by adopting a dedicated plan in November 2021. This program is based on three objectives: 
- Improve knowledge of the territory and the players involved, so as to better act on the diverse realities of fuel poverty in Paris; - - Facilitate the legibility and accessibility of aids, to better reach those eligible for assistance from the City; 
- Set up a 'Local Intervention Service for Energy Management' - “Service Local d'Intervention pour la Maîtrise de l'Energie” (SLIME 2022-2025) - with a priority focus on residents of working-class neighbourhoods, and designed to create an individualized service for people and households identified.
(https://www.paris.fr/pages/le-slime-une-nouvelle-facon-d-alleger-la-facture-energetique-23035)

Heatwaves are recognized as a pressing social issue in Paris, particularly affecting vulnerable groups. The city has implemented support measures like the 'REFLEX' program and the 'Fabrique de la Solidarité' initiatives, along with a comprehensive Heatwave Plan. Cool islands, mapped across Paris, provide refreshing spaces for the public, while initiatives such as vegetation planting and building adaptations contribute to heatwave resilience. The brochure 'Adapting to heat waves in Paris' details these refreshing measures and their importance.
(https://www.paris.fr/pages/fortes-chaleurs-crise-sanitaire-evenements-climatiques-prenez-les-devants-avec-reflex-23373)

Comprehensive studies and evaluations have highlighted existing disparities and challenges in Paris. Report on the implementation of actions in working-class neighbourhoods has identified progress in reducing social disparities but also highlighted challenges like poverty, employment disparities, digital inclusion, and access to healthcare. Gender inequalities have been examined, revealing gaps in various aspects of city life. The study on circular economy jobs showcases the potential for economic growth and sustainability, with circular economy practices generating sustainable jobs. A mapping exercise has identified the Parisian territories most impacted by unfavourable environmental and social conditions, and where sensitive populations are particularly present, in order to develop a prioritized and adapted response to reduce social and territorial health inequalities. 

As part of an agreement between the City of Paris and the French Economic Observatory (OFCE), the OFCE is conducting a study on the 'Energy and Environmental Transition of the City of Paris: Economic and Financial Impacts,' with results expected by the end of 2024. This study will include a modeling of the employment impacts of the actions outlined in the climate plan. Given the strong interconnection between Paris and the Île-de-France region in terms of urban planning, employment, and economic activity, the appropriate scope for conducting an impact assessment of the economic policies implemented by the City of Paris is the Île-de-France region. The analysis will therefore be conducted at this regional level, with localized imputations to the strictly Parisian level when possible. The modeling will assess:
• The number of jobs created and lost by sector at the local level. A breakdown by type of employment impacts may be considered.
• The impact on the regional GDP level and the GDP level of the different represented sectors.
• The impact on the purchasing power of households in the Île-de-France region.

By addressing these multifaceted challenges, Paris aims to create a more inclusive and equitable city. Through partnerships, policy implementation, and engagement with diverse communities, the city seeks to build a future where everyone can thrive. Together, let us work towards a Paris that is both sustainable and fair, leaving no one behind.
column19:
Social housing : The City invests heavily annually in the creation and renovation of social housing. With the double target of reaching 40% public housing and renovating 5000 units per year, these investments reached 384 M€ in 2024, representing 20% of its investment budget. These investments, representing more than 1,5 billion euros since 2020 are crucial to meet the climate action plan targets, by increasing the performance of residential building, all the while ensuring a better supply of a better quality of affordable housing. From 2001 to 2024, the rate of social and public housing went from 13,4% and 17,1% to 23,1% and 33.8% respectively, while the rhythm of renovation is on a steady 5000 unit per year annual pace since 2023. 
(https://indicateurs-transition-parisdata.opendatasoft.com/pages/indicateur/?id=climat-renovation-energetique-des-logements)

Energy precariousness : In 2023, a Local Intervention Service for Energy Management and a €400,000 fund to help with minor repairs is now offered. The SLIME program aims to scale up the identification, guidance, and support for households facing energy precariousness. Within this framework, 1,200 home visits are scheduled by 2025 to carry out energy diagnostics and provide long-term support, as well as distributing emergency kits. Since September 2022, more than 400 reports have been recorded: 30% are eligible for SLIME, 32% concern social housing provided by the City, 33% involve other landlords. The most prevalent City districts are the 18th, the 11th, the 19th and the 20th.

Reinforcing actions for people in precarious situations: The Paris Solidarity Guide Summer 2023 caters to the needs of vulnerable and homeless individuals during the summer. It provides a comprehensive list of available assistance. Street outreach activities are intensified, including the distribution of water bottles from Eau de Paris, refillable at any of the 1,200 drinking fountains in the city. Additionally, the inaugural summer edition of the Night of Solidarity took place on june 27. A total of 817 individuals were identified as homeless, compared to 707 in the same three districts in January, representing a 15.5% increase. However, this significant rise should be approached with caution due to the absence of comparative data from previous summers. Additionally, the results obtained in the 8th, 12th, and 20th districts cannot be extrapolated to the entire territory of Paris. After analyzing all questionnaires in September, a more precise overview of the current situation and encountered profiles will be provided. Among the initial findings, a decrease in the number of homeless families and couples is notable. Only 5.5% of the counted individuals were in such situations within the three tested districts, compared to 19% in January.
(https://www.paris.fr/pages/le-guide-solidarite-a-paris-ete-2023-est-disponible-23880https://www.paris.fr/pages/nuit-de-la-solidarite-ete-2023-23860)

Oasis schoolyards, creating inclusive and refreshing spaces for all: Parisian school playgrounds are being transformed into 'oases' to enhance daily livability and inclusivity. Recognizing their significance, school courtyards, spanning over 70 hectares and evenly distributed across the city, are targeted as crucial leverage points. These areas, currently predominantly asphalted and impermeable, contribute to the urban heat island effect and are inaccessible to the public on weekends when the need for refreshing spaces is high. The renovated courtyards provide a range of improvements, including more natural spaces, increased vegetation, better management of rainwater, water points, facilities for children, peaceful areas, and improved spatial distribution. The main goal is to enhance the well-being of children. These transformed courtyards, serving as refreshing oases within neighborhoods, are accessible to the public after school hours and serve as safe spaces for vulnerable individuals during heatwaves. From the beginning, the Oasis approach engages the stakeholders most affected by the courtyards' transformation, including students and adults. The goal is to gather input and reach a consensus on the new layout. Co-design tools involving children and adults from participating schools have been developed. As of 2023, around 130 courtyards have already been transformed into Oasis spaces in Paris.
(https://www.paris.fr/pages/paris-s-adapte-au-changement-climatique-18541#plus-de-1-300-lieux-frais)

Beyond those two major challenges, the city of Paris also strongly acts on : 
- Participatory engagement with frontline communities to deliver just transition: concertation actions in schools and working-class neighbourhoods 
- Supporting solidarity-based et sustainable food outlets 
- Being watchful to gender equality in development operations 
- Assessing the impact of Paris Climate Action Plan on air quality 
- Climate migrations (Research agreement)

column16: Salt Lake City is at the center of the Wasatch Front, a metropolitan area holds the vast majority of Utah's population. This means that climate-related issues that impact Salt Lake City nearly equally impact our surrounding communities, including drought, wildfire, and emissions into our shared regional airshed. For this reason, Salt Lake City regularly works closely with surrounding communities on shared air quality, climate, and water conservation efforts. One such example is the Community Renewable Energy Program. For several years leading up to 2019, Salt Lake City worked with its electric utility provider Rocky Mountain Power to achieve a net-100% renewable electricity supply for the jurisdiction's entire community. Recognizing that several nearby communities, as well as some rural, were working toward targets, legislation was ultimately proposed and adopted during the 2019 Utah legislative session, called the Community Renewable Energy Act (H.B. 411). The legislation enabled Rocky Mountain Power and communities that made a formal commitment to net-100% renewable electricity supply to participate in the Community Renewable Energy Program. As of 2022, 18 Utah communities are participating in the program and are on track to be supplied with net-100% renewable grid-supplied electricity by 2030.

Launched in 2016 and expanding through 2024, Suvidha Centres are public-private partnership facilities providing sanitation and hygiene services to low-income communities. These centres, located in 14 areas across Mumbai, offer clean toilets, purified drinking water, laundry services, and showers, impacting over 350,000 people annually. The initiative emphasised the inclusion of women and children, ensuring their safety with features like security cameras and panic buttons. Additionally, the centres incorporate water-saving technologies that have collectively saved over 100 million litres of water. By employing local community members to manage these centres, the initiative promotes social inclusion, improves health outcomes, and generates green jobs in the sanitation and water management sectors.

As a step to provide equity in budget allocations, BMC introduced the Gender Budget in 2009-10 and has been releasing it every year to address the specific needs of women and marginalised groups. Since more than half of Mumbai's population resides in densely populated slums, where inadequate infrastructure increases the challenges of daily life, particularly for women and children. Due to the largely unauthorised nature of these settlements, individual toilets are scarce, water supply is intermittent, and drainage systems are preliminary. Given the economic vulnerabilities of slum households, life in these areas is especially difficult for women, who face risks to their safety, hygiene, and dignity. The Gender Budget for 2024-25 allocates resources to implement gender-sensitive policies across multiple sectors, including the construction of community toilets designed for women.

Our Climate Action Playbook, which defines several actions Philadelphia can take to advance towards our climate goals, assesses each action along 4 impact pillars: Equity, Health, Environment, and Economy. In each of these 4 pillars actions are further assessed for impact along subcategories: Equity, Mobility, Community Capacity, Poverty Reduction, Health, Wellbeing, Public Safety, Heat Preparedness, Flood Preparedness, Environment Green Space, Waste Reduction, Carbon Pollution Reduction, Economy Jobs, and Cost Savings Competitiveness.
	
-	Lower Municipal energy costs - Between 2017 and 2022, the city's Municipal Energy Office has saved $9.4 million in municipal energy costs (paid for by the City's general fund) through improved operational practices and capital and rebuild upgrades. The City will continue to reduce these costs through actions outlined in the Municipal Energy Master Plan. 
-	Improved quality of life - since most of Philadelphia's emissions come from our buildings, decarbonizing these buildings (improving energy efficiency, scaling adoption of energy efficient, clean energy technologies for heating and cooling) is key to reducing our carbon footprint. Building decarbonization actions improve air quality, lower energy costs, and improve indoor comfort for occupants. For the city's energy burdened residents, these actions are especially impactful as they reduce energy burden (which has downstream impacts on financial and housing security) and increase energy security.
-	Economic opportunity - To achieve the city's clean energy transition, a significant number of jobs, especially in the building decarbonization sector will be needed. This has the potential not only to create significant economic opportunities for all Philadelphians, especially the city's historically marginalized communities by creating pathways for good quality, family-sustaining jobs in the clean energy economy. 
- Nature-based approaches - to build resilience to climate change, several departments are prioritizing nature-based solutions to address extreme heat and flooding. This approach has wider benefits to the community as increasing vegetation and green space has been proven to help sequester CO2, improve air quality, increase biodiversity and reduce crime.

column18: The Office of Sustainability uses equity metrics across a broad range of socio-demographic indicators to ensure that climate action is equitable and inclusive. These metrics include social indicators (including race), economic indicators, public health indicators and energy security / access / burden indicators to direct climate planning and climate action. OOS uses these indicators at the neighborhood and census tract level to identify communities disproportionately vulnerable to climate impacts including heat, flooding and energy access, and develop solutions and plans that specifically focus on these communities. OOS also uses these indicators to direct clean energy workforce opportunities to underserved communities to ensure that the benefits of climate action are equitably accessible to all Philadelphians. Other City Departments also include equity metrics in planning and implementation (specific examples include the Philly Tree Plan for urban greening and the Urban Agriculture Plan). \n\nThe Office of Sustainability is developing a publicly accessible mapping tool that will identify Philadelphia neighborhoods disproportionately impacted by environmental hazards and lacking equitable access to key services and environmental amenities that would strengthen their resilience - Philadelphia's environmental justice (EJ) communities. The EJ tool will include environmental, health and socio-demographic indicators. OOS is developing this tool to guide decision-making and policy. It may inform decisions around program development/evaluation and the allocation of resources. This tool will also serve educational and advocacy purposes and increase data accessibility for residents and community-based organizations.
column19:
In 2024, the Office of Sustainability (OOS) recently released the Energy Poverty Alleviation Strategy (EPAS), a multi-stakeholder informed actionable roadmap to ensue equitable energy access, affordability, and security. The report includes 25 suggested projects under three umbrella strategies: Support and strengthen Philadelphia's energy programs and services to address challenges in access, delivery, programmatic gaps, and scaling; Implement and advocate for enabling legislation and incentives at the local and state level; and strengthen and support the city's community and partner network.
With the help of various federal grants and NGO/CBO partnerships, three of these projects are currently underway. 

OOS also recently launched a citywide, inclusive public engagement process to support the update to the City's Resilience Plan. This two-year engagement process will include outreach and input from multiple stakeholders, including communities, youth, sector leaders, advocacy organizations and the private sector. Specific focus and resources have been dedicated to reach frontline communities—those that are impacted first and worst by climate change. This engagement will ensure that Philadelphia's most vulnerable communities have a role in identifying and prioritizing climate action. The updated Resilience Plan will be released in 2027, and will be heavily based on the feedback provided by frontline communities on the environmental disparities they are facing. OOS is also resourcing and working with community-based organizations across the city to better reach underserved populations and to support community-level resilience planning. 

OOS manages the Community Resilience and Environmental Justice (CREJ) Fund that distributes grants to frontline and fenceline community-serving organizations, provides technical assistance and educational programming for grantees, and builds organizational networks through an annual convening. The CREJ Fund has a primary goal of materially and sustainably changing conditions and increasing community resilience to climate change. $470,000 has been granted to 37 organizations over two grant rounds since 2023. 
OOS also manages an interdepartmental Environmental Justice & Climate Resilience Committee. The Committee brings together City departments to share information and work collaboratively to address the cross-cutting issues of environmental justice and climate change. It serves as a forum for dialogue, learning, idea-sharing and collective decision-making and creates a space to collaboratively develop policy, plans and programs that advance environmental justice and climate resilience.

column16: The 2021 Climate Action Plan (CAP) outlined strategies and actions to achieve net-zero emissions by 2040, while creating solutions that serve intersectional challenges of racial and social equity, public health, economic recovery/just transition, and resilient communities. The CAP is now being updated; both the last plan and the current draft plan contain goals across seven sectors (Responsible Production & Consumption, Transportation & Land Use, Energy Supply, Building Operations, Healthy Ecosystems, Housing, and Water Supply), with a broad range of strategies addressing both climate and equity. During the preparation of the last CAP in 2021, a study assessed the socioeconomic impact of implementing climate mitigation strategies in San Francisco. The study found that fully implementing the CAP would result in savings for the City of over $2.7 billion. This is the total of savings realized from reduced resident morbidity and mortality, reduced utility costs, and other reduced social costs. In addition, San Francisco recognizes the opportunity to address historical inequities through the implementation of climate actions. For example, the city uses an Environmental Justice Communities Map (developed in 2023 to identify the city's most vulnerable and environmentally burdened communities) to inform the performance of city projects and programs. In particular, the Environmental Justice Communities Map is a cornerstone for climate mitigation programs, such as the Climate Equity Hub, which provides free home electrification to low-income residents. This approach ensures that climate action brings opportunities and benefits to the wider community, and particularly to communities that are historically underserved.

column18: Every strategy and action in the CAP undergoes a Racial and Social Equity Assessment, a process developed by the San Francisco Environment department. The assessment analyzes each strategy and action in the plan, considering impact areas that address the fair the distribution of potential benefits and potential negative impacts of climate action, and the root causes of racial disparities in San Francisco. As San Francisco updates the plan for 2025, the City is in the midst of reviewing and incorporating the recommendations of this equity review in the plan's final strategies and actions to ensure support for disadvantaged communities and advance environmental justice.

O município de São Paulo conta com diversas ferramentas para monitorar espacialmente e temporalmente indicadores sociais e ambientais. Uma delas é a plataforma Geosampa (https://geosampa.prefeitura.sp.gov.br/PaginasPublicas/_SBC.aspx), que conta com uma série de camadas (temas) que apresentam indicadores geolocalizados sobre assuntos como transporte, cobertura verde, rede de drenagem, equipamentos culturais, entre outros.

Em formato semelhante, o ObservaSampa apresenta indicadores que cobrem outras temáticas, como assistência social, direitos humanos e cidadania, atingimento dos Objetivos do Desenvolvimento Sustentável (ODS), entre outros. Os indicadores podem ser desagregados em vários níveis, como região, subprefeitura e distrito, permitindo o acompanhamento do desenvolvimento de ações de forma comparativa em âmbito local.

Além disso, os diversos planos, como o Plano Diretor Estratégico (PDE) e os planos setoriais, como o Plano de Ação Climática (PlanClima), preveem ações distribuídas espacialmente de forma a atender as distintas demandas da cidade. O PDE, por exemplo, divide o município em macrozonas e macroáreas que devem receber intervenções urbanísticas distintas, visando a atender necessidades sociais, ambientais e econômicas particulares.
column19: Com a finalidade de assegurar a distribuição igualitária e inclusiva da ação climática, são estabelecidos indicadores para o Município de São Paulo, utilizados como base para o planejamento, implementação e monitoramento das ações. As ações são realizadas levando em conta as necessidades de toda a população, com enfoque nas parcelas de maior vulnerabilidade social, ambiental e econômica. Alguns indicadores que podem ser citados como exemplo são a cobertura vegetal por habitante; emissão de dióxido de carbono (CO2) pela frota de ônibus municipais; resíduos coletados no Ecoponto (ton); número de árvores plantadas no município; dentre outros indicadores. Cada um dos indicadores pode ser usado como base para o cumprimento de metas e objetivos de ações/planos/programas e de comitês municipais que visam distribuição igualitária e inclusiva da temática climática. Os indicadores e seus dados podem ser encontrados em plataformas de gerenciamento de dados, como ObservaSampa, Infocidade e GeoSampa. Entre os documentos /ações produzidos pelo município, a partir da coleta e análise de dados nesse contexto estão: Inventário de Emissões de GEE: para quantificar e comparar as emissões de Gases do Efeito Estufa (GEE) no Município de São Paulo, é criado um inventário que analisa as fontes de emissão e o total de gases gerado. O inventário leva em conta fontes como os diferentes meios de transporte, resíduos, energia estacionária, processos industriais, agricultura, silvicultura e demais usos de produtos e da terra. Dessa forma, torna-se possível comparar os dados quantitativos relacionados às emissões e, com isso, determinar o possível aumento ou redução desses poluentes na atmosfera e suas causas. Além disso, a \'emissão de dióxido de carbono (CO2) pela frota de ônibus municipais\' pode ser encontrada na plataforma Monitor de Ônibus SP. ....Ações de arborização/ expansão da cobertura vegetal: A cobertura vegetal do município, bem como o número de árvores plantadas, são dados que podem ser encontrados no Plano Municipal de Áreas Protegidas, Áreas Verdes e Espaços Livres (PLANPAVEL). Ainda, a quantidade de árvores plantadas no município é um dado disponibilizado pela Divisão de Arborização Urbana da Secretaria do Verde e Meio Ambiente do Município de São Paulo. Pode-se observar que entre os anos de 2016 e 2023, os anos de 2019 e 2020 foram aqueles que obtiveram maior sucesso, com 38.741 e 36.624 árvores plantadas, respectivamente. O a quantidade de árvores plantadas em 2019 e 2020 a quantidade de árvores plantadas. Em 2023, até o mês de junho, foram plantadas 19.412 árvores nas ruas. Gestão de Resíduos: Já os dados relacionados à resíduos gerados e coletados no município, como a coleta domiciliar, coleta seletiva e resíduos coletados em ecopontos, são disponibilizados pelo SPRegula e, ainda geridos pelo Plano Municipal de Gestão Integrada de Resíduos Sólidos (PMGIRS), que estabelece estratégias para o manejo de resíduos, visando a redução, reutilização, reciclagem e o aproveitamento energético de resíduos sólidos, além da disposição adequada dos rejeitos no meio ambiente. O plano conta com uma série programas relacionados ao gerenciamento de resíduos, incluindo também a educação ambiental. Plano de Ação Climática: dados do Plano de Ação Climática de São Paulo (PlanClimaSP) indicam melhorias na distribuição igualitária e inclusiva da ação climática. column18: In the main city document describing the plan to achieve climate neutrality: Warsaw Green City and Climate Action Plan, there are actions dedicated to inclusive distribution of climate action: Tackling energy poverty. Warsaw is in the process of planning a support system for residents who may be affected by climate action. column19:
In August 2022, Warsaw signed an agreement with the National Fund for Environmental Protection and Water Management on the implementation of the STOP SMOG programme within the city. As part of the agreement, the city has pledged to retrofit 200 single-family buildings in the city by the end of 2024. As part of the programme's implementation to date, the city is carrying out an inventory of single-family buildings of potential programme beneficiaries among Warsaw residents. This mainly concerns people who are poor and have coal-fired heating sources, who have been identified by Social Welfare Centers, and people who have applied for a city grant for replacing heat sources but have given up due to a lack of funds for their own contribution (despite a high % subsidy from the city). Regulations have been adopted to define the rules for implementing the program and carrying out the first retrofits. Warsaw is one of the few cities in the world to receive financial support from a new Inclusive Climate Action Cities Fund. The ICA is managed by C40 Cities, a global network of cities working together to tackle the climate crisis. Warsaw (as a member of C40) was selected to participate in the project through a rigorous process and will benefit from the first round of disbursements from the ICA fund. Each city received a grant (of up to USD 60 000) to implement projects that remove specific socio-economic barriers to accelerate climate action that is equitable, inclusive and benefits all residents, especially communities vulnerable to global warming. Warsaw addressed the issue of energy poverty among low-income groups through the project 'Carbon-neutral and affordable renovations for all in need' (CARE). The aim of the project was to provide special care for residents affected by energy poverty and to increase the energy efficiency of municipal housing. The CARE project ran from July 2023 to June 2024. As part of the project, a database of municipal buildings in the city was developed using data from various public sector sources. It will collect data in three thematic groups: - energy classes of buildings; - heat sources; - social criteria relevant to exposure to energy poverty. The data from the database was used to develop an algorithm that identifies buildings whose residents are particularly vulnerable to the negative effects of energy poverty. This tool supports the process of thermal modernization in Warsaw and the fight against energy poverty by objectively identifying municipal buildings that should be thermally modernized and renovated as a matter of priority. In addition, the data indicates the locations where the effects of the measures will bring the greatest benefits to both the city and its residents. The tool was used, among other things, to select buildings for the ELENA programme, which involves the preparation of design and technical documentation for the thermal modernization of 50 municipal buildings in Warsaw.
The City of Warsaw organizes and offers residents who do not have air-conditioned accommodation so-called cooling areas during heat waves. These are places in municipal buildings or those belonging to external partners where people can take a break from the high temperatures during heat waves and cool down, drink water, sit down, and rest. These places have been organized to protect vulnerable groups (the elderly, children with their guardians, people with cardiovascular diseases) from the effects of heat.
The City of Warsaw is a partner in the innovative science project NEEST 2023-2025 which outcomes were models for just transition on technical, environmental, social and financial issues. The project focuses on city quarters and presents comprehensive solutions that support just transition in urban areas with a high degree of challenges.

창원시는 산업도시이자 기후위기에 취약한 도시로서, 기후변화 대응을 단순한 온실가스 감축 차원을 넘어 경제·사회·환경적 기회 창출의 전략적 계기로 인식하고 있다.

1. 경제적 기회
1) 녹색산업 전환: 기계·조선·자동차 부품 등 주력 제조업을 저탄소·에너지효율형 산업으로 재편하면서, 새로운 녹색 일자리 창출이 기대된다. 특히 수소·연료전지·전기차 부품 산업은 창원시의 미래 성장동력으로 자리잡고 있다.
2) 지역경제 활성화: 재생에너지 보급과 그린 인프라 구축 사업은 지역 내 중소기업의 참여를 확대하여 내수 기반을 강화하고, 중앙정부·국제기구 공모사업을 통한 외부재원 유치도 가능하다.

2. 사회적 기회
1) 시민 건강 증진: 도시숲·바람길숲 조성, 쿨루프·쿨페이브먼트 도입, 대기오염 저감은 폭염·미세먼지로부터 시민 건강을 보호한다.
2) 사회적 형평성 강화: 취약계층을 대상으로 한 에너지 효율 개선 지원, 냉·난방비 지원, 무더위 쉼터 운영은 에너지빈곤 해소와 사회적 형평성을 강화한다.
3) 참여·인식 제고: 기후행동 캠페인, 시민·기업 공동 실천 프로그램을 통해 사회적 연대와 참여가 확대된다.

3. 환경적 기회
1) 생태계 보전: 수변·녹지축 확충은 생태계 회복력을 높이고, 도시 내 탄소흡수원을 강화한다.
2) 재난 회복력 향상: 침수 취약지 개선, 방재 인프라 보강, 스마트 재난대응체계 구축은 폭우·태풍 등 기후재난 피해를 최소화한다.
3) 도시환경 개선: 저탄소 교통체계 전환(전기·수소버스, 자전거·보행 인프라)은 교통혼잡과 소음을 줄이고, 도시의 지속가능성을 높인다.

결론적으로, 창원시의 기후행동은 ▲산업구조 전환과 녹색 일자리 창출, ▲시민 건강과 사회적 형평성 강화, ▲재난 회복력 및 생태계 보전이라는 광범위한 경제·사회·환경적 혜택을 창출하는 핵심 전략으로 작용한다. 이는 단순한 온실가스 감축 목표 달성을 넘어, 도시의 지속가능성과 경쟁력을 강화하는 전환점이 되고 있다.

column18:
창원시는 기후행동의 효과가 지역사회 전반에 균등하게 돌아가도록 다양한 정량적 지표 체계를 활용하여 평가하고 있다. 이는 정책 설계, 실행, 모니터링 전 과정에서 반영되어 공평성과 포용성을 보장한다.

창원시는 이행평가·센터 운영·인프라 조성·시민참여 확대를 통해 기후행동의 공평성과 포용성을 확보하고 있으며, 여기에 에너지 복지·건강안전·사회참여·지역균형 지표를 통합적으로 관리하여 정책의 형평성과 효과성을 강화하고 있다. 이를 통해 모든 시민이 균등하게 기후행동의 혜택을 누리는 지속가능도시 창원을 실현하고 있다.

1) 이행평가
창원시는 「제2차 기후변화 적응대책 세부시행계획」을 수립하고, 향후 5년간 7개 부문 39개 사업을 대상으로 매년 이행평가를 실시한다. 각 사업의 진행 상황, 성과, 미흡 분야를 정량적으로 분석하여 정책의 실효성과 형평성을 강화한다.

2) 탄소중립지원센터 운영
창원시는 탄소중립지원센터를 통해 시민 교육·체험 프로그램을 운영하며, 참여율·만족도·실천율을 정량화한다. 이를 통해 기후행동의 교육·참여 기회가 특정 계층에 집중되지 않고 전 시민에게 균등하게 분배되도록 하고 있다.

3) 기후적응 인프라
폭염 물길쉼터, 그늘숲길, 쿨링포그 등 기후적응형 인프라를 조성하고 있으며, 이용률·접근성·효과성을 정량적으로 측정한다. 이로써 기후적응 인프라가 소외 지역이나 취약계층에 편중되지 않고, 전 시민이 안전하게 혜택을 누리도록 한다.

4) 시민 참여 프로그램
'우리에게 남은 탄소시간' 캠페인, 자전거 출퇴근 챌린지, 공유텀블러 프로그램 등 다양한 시민 참여형 프로그램을 운영한다. 각 프로그램의 참여율, 온실가스 감축 성과, 생활습관 변화 등을 수치로 관리하여 사회 전반에 균형 있는 효과를 확산시킨다.

창원시는 기후행동의 효과가 지역사회 전반에 균등하게 돌아가도록 정량적 지표를 활용해 평가하고 있다.

1) 에너지 복지 지표
- 취약계층 대상 에너지 효율개선 사업(고효율 조명·단열재·냉난방기 지원)으로 절감된 에너지 비용과 참여 가구 수를 산출.
- 에너지빈곤 가구 비율 개선 정도를 연차별로 추적.

2) 건강·안전 지표
- 무더위 쉼터 이용자 수, 폭염·한파 응급환자 발생 건수, 홍수 방재시설 설치 전후 침수 피해 저감률 등으로 시민 건강·안전 개선 효과를 측정.

3) 사회적 참여 지표
- 탄소중립 캠페인 참여 인원, 시민·기업의 실천율(예: 온실가스 감축 활동 등록 건수)을 정량화.
- 교육·워크숍 참가자 수와 만족도 조사 결과를 반영.

4) 지역균형 지표
- 침수·폭염 취약지역을 중심으로 한 인프라 투자액과 설치 건수를 데이터베이스화해, 공간적 형평성을 확보.

창원시는 에너지 비용 절감, 건강·안전 효과, 시민 참여율, 지역별 인프라 분배와 같은 다차원 지표를 통해 기후행동의 공평·포괄적 분배를 정량적으로 평가하고 있으며, 이를 향후 정책 우선순위와 예산 배분에 반영하고 있다.
column19:
창원시는 기후변화 대응의 효과가 특정 계층이나 지역에 편중되지 않고 시민 모두에게 균등하게 분배될 수 있도록 다양한 정책과 사업을 추진하고 있으며, 이를 정량적 지표로 관리하고 있다.

1) 이행평가(Annual Implementation Review)
- 주체: 창원시(총괄), 부문 소관부서, 탄소중립지원센터
- 조치:「제2차 기후변화 적응대책 세부시행계획」의 7개 부문·39개 사업에 대해 연 1회 이행평가 실시(진도율·성과·형평성 점검).
- 절차/기준: 사업별 KPI(취약계층 수혜율, 공간적 분포, 안전·건강 개선지표 등)로 성과-형평 동시 평가 → 미흡 과제는 다음연도 예산·사업계획에 개선조치 반영(피드백 루프).
- 증빙: 연차별 이행평가 보고서(부문별 실적표/지도), 개선계획서, 예산 조정 내역.

2) 탄소중립지원센터 운영(교육·참여의 포용성)
- 주체: 창원산업진흥원(창원시탄소중립지원센터)
- 조치: 기후교육·체험프로그램(시민·학생·기업·취약계층 맞춤형) 연중 운영.
- 절차/기준: 프로그램 참여율-만족도-후속실천율을 표준 양식으로 계량화, 저소득·고령·장애 등 접근성 배려(시간·장소·이동지원) 의무화.
- 증빙: 분기별 참여대상 분포(연령·지역·소득층) 통계, 만족도 설문, 후속 실천 등록 건수(예: 절전·재활용 실천 인증).

3) 기후적응 인프라의 형평 배치(Spatial Targeting)
- 주체: 기후적응·안전총괄, 도시·녹지·하천·도로 부문
- 조치: 폭염 물길쉼터, 그늘숲길, 쿨링포그, 그늘막, 쿨루프 등 인프라를 취약지역 우선 배치.
- 절차/기준: GIS 기반 취약성 지도(고령인구·저지대·내습 이력·열섬지표)를 활용해 동(洞) 단위 우선순위 산정 → 설치 후 이용률·접근시간·피해저감률 계량화.
- 증빙: 공간배치 도면, 설치대수/투자액 동별 분포표, 설치 전후 온열·침수 피해 지표 비교.

4) 에너지 복지의 보편·선별 결합(Universal + Targeted)
- 주체: 에너지·복지 부문
- 조치: 고효율 조명/단열/냉난방기 지원, 냉·난방비 지원, 노후주택 효율개선.
- 절차/기준: 에너지빈곤 지수(소득·주거형태·에너지비 지출비중)로 대상 선정의 투명성 확보, 동별 수혜 편차 20% 이내 목표.
- 증빙: 수혜자 수·절감 에너지비(KWh/원), 에너지빈곤 가구율 연차 추이, 동별 수혜 격차 지표.

5) 시민 참여형 감축·순환 프로그램(Behavioral & Community)
- 주체: 시·센터·시민/기업/NGO
- 조치: '우리에게 남은 탄소시간' 캠페인, 자전거 출퇴근 챌린지, 공유텀블러 등 참여 인센티브형 프로그램.
- 절차/기준: **참여자 수-지속참여율-감축성과(kgCO₂eq)**를 디지털로 집계, 소득·연령·지역별 참여편차 모니터링 및 취약계층 참여 장려 인센티브 운영.
- 증빙: 프로그램별 등록·완료·재참여율, 감축량 총계, 사회집단별 참여분포.

6) 교통·안전의 공평 접근(Transport & Safety Equity)
- 주체: 교통·안전 부문
- 조치: 대중교통 편의·안전 시설(그늘막, 정류장 쿨링, 환승보행 개선), 자전거·보행 인프라 취약권역 우선 확충.
- 절차/기준: 정류장까지 도보 접근시간 10분 이내 커버리지, 보행약자 동선 개선, 야간안전 조도 기준 충족.
- 증빙: 대중교통 접근성 커버리지 지도, 보행약자 경로 개선 실적, 안전지표(사고·조도) 개선.

7) 지역균형 투자·지출 투명화(Fiscal Equity)
- 주체: 기획·재정
- 조치: 기후대응 관련 투자액·수혜량의 동별(행정동) 공개로 공간적 형평성 확보.
- 절차/기준: 예산 편성 시 '형평성 체크리스트'(취약지역 우선/동별 편차/1인당 수혜액) 의무 적용.
- 증빙: 동별 1인당 투자/수혜액 표, 연차별 편차 축소 추세.

8) 공감·접근성 제고(Accessibility & Inclusion)
- 주체: 전 부문
- 조치: 다국어·쉬운문장 안내, 수어·점자·모바일 접근성, 야간·주말 교육 등 보편 설계(Universal Design).
- 절차/기준: 프로그램·인프라에 접근성 인증 체크리스트 적용, 장애·고령·이동제약 대상의 실접근성 점검(현장점검 포함).
- 증빙: 접근성 자체점검표, 보완조치 이행률, 이용자 불만·개선 처리 기록.

9) 데이터 공개와 외부 검증(Transparency & Assurance)
- 주체: 시·센터
- 조치: 연차 성과·공간분포·수혜지표를 시민 포털/보고서로 공개, 외부전문가 자문 및 시민위원회 점검.
- 절차/기준: 핵심지표(KPI) 메타데이터 표준화, 동일 지표의 연차 비교로 신뢰성 확보.
- 증빙: 공개대시보드(또는 연차보고서), 외부 자문회의록, 시민위원회 권고안·이행현황.

창원시는 연차 이행평가-공간기반 취약성 분석-보편·선별 복지-참여·교육의 정량관리-형평 예산으로 이어지는 통합체계를 통해 기후대응 혜택의 공평·포괄적 분배를 보장한다. 

모든 사업은 KPI(수혜율·접근성·건강·안전·감축량)로 평가되며, 결과는 공개·검증을 통해 다음연도 계획과 예산에 반영된다. 특히 취약지역·계층 우선 원칙과 접근성·포용 설계를 의무화하여, 기후행동의 효과가 전 시민에게 균등하게 확산되도록 관리하고 있다.

column15: Wider opportunities/benefits are considered at the action planning stage
column16:
Seoul measured environmental benefits (i.e. air pollutants reductions) and economic benefits (i.e. industrial and economic impacts) when establishing the 2050 Seoul Climate Action Plan. 

- Air pollutant reduction: Air pollutant emissions are expected to be lowered by 50~60% in 2050 compared to 2016 levels when the climate action plan is implemented. 

- Industrial and Economic impacts: Carbon neutral projects in the energy sector are expected to lead to production inducement impacts worth 17.9 trillion KRW and create 120,000 jobs annually
column17: Yes, the jurisdiction is designing or implementing climate actions that address the needs of frontline communities most impacted by climate change
column18: When developing the climate action plan and the Seoul Carbon Neutrality and Green Growth Plan, Seoul sets specific targets for each project to achieve its GHG reduction goals. These targets are established through research conducted by research institutions and in coordination with relevant departments. Seoul is focused on reducing emissions from buildings and transport, which are the largest contributors to the city-wide greenhouse gas emissions. To ensure the successful implementation of these climate action projects, it is essential to fairly distribute greenhouse gas reduction targets among different projects based on their priorities. Additionally, it is crucial to scientifically calculate the greenhouse gas reduction effects of each project by applying greenhouse gas emission factors provided by the government or developed by Seoul.
column19: Seoul included measures to enhance equity in its 2050 Seoul Climate Action Plan. Seoul is taking various actions to support the vulnerable populations. For example, to minimize flood damage caused by heavy rainfall, we have provided flood barriers to residents living in semi-basements. To support vulnerable groups during heatwaves and cold spells, we provide energy vouchers.

column11: Report how your jurisdiction assesses the wider environmental, social, and economic opportunities and benefits of climate action.
column14: Yes, wider opportunities/benefits are assessed for all climate actions
column15: Wider opportunities/benefits are considered at the post-implementation monitoring and evaluation stage
column16:
Taipei City has identified a wide range of opportunities and benefits from its climate actions, aligned with the goals of reducing carbon emissions by 40% by 2030 and achieving net-zero by 2050. These opportunities extend beyond carbon reduction to drive economic growth, resilience, and social well-being:

Clean Technology and Green Industry Development - Promote energy-saving improvements across public and private sectors, provide subsidies and incentives for efficient equipment replacement, and foster the ESCO model to expand the green economy.

Water Security and Sponge City Initiatives - Strengthen flood prevention, river restoration, and green infrastructure. By 2030, 80% of urban areas will adopt green infrastructure, rainfall tolerance will reach 88.8mm/hr, and 16% of water will be recycled.

Low-Carbon and Sustainable Transport - Expand the MRT and bus networks, promote electrification of buses and scooters, and target full electrification of urban buses by 2030, with 35% of new scooters sold being electric.

Energy Efficiency and Smart Infrastructure - Implement the Residential and Commercial Electricity Saving 2.0 Plan, expand smart grids, and modernize incineration plants and power facilities to improve energy efficiency and reduce emissions.

Circular Economy Development - Implement the “Circular Taipei Strategy Roadmap 2.0,” advancing at least 60 measures across 22 strategic aspects, building an innovative ecosystem that creates circular value and reduces resource waste.

Advanced Waste Management - Enforce plastic restrictions, furniture repair, and kitchen waste reuse. Promote the recycling of bottom ash, fly ash, and other construction materials, ensuring their reuse in public projects.

Sustainable Food and Urban Agriculture - Promote urban agriculture for recreation, therapy, and resilience, supporting biodiversity, climate regulation, flood mitigation, and food education, while preserving farmland such as the Guandu Plain for future generations.

Overall, Taipei's climate actions not only reduce emissions but also create green jobs, strengthen urban resilience, promote resource efficiency, and improve citizens' quality of life, making the transition to net-zero an opportunity for sustainable urban transformation.
column17: Yes, the jurisdiction is designing or implementing climate actions that address the needs of frontline communities most impacted by climate change
column18:
Taipei City ensures equitable and inclusive distribution of climate actions through a well-established civic participation framework. In 2015, the City established the Citizen Participation Committee and launched the Citizen Participation Website to institutionalize participatory mechanisms. These mechanisms include:
1.Institutional design: Citizens outside the government are selected through open recruitment to join regular meetings, which are live-streamed and recorded for transparency.
2.Digital participation tools: The City developed i-Voting procedures and uses the official LINE account to deliver timely information and collect feedback.
3.Integration into policy processes: Operational procedures for public works and urban planning projects require citizen participation, ensuring opinions are incorporated into administrative decisions.
4.Information disclosure: The Open Data Platform provides wide access to datasets across sectors, promoting transparency and accountability.
5.Participatory budgeting: The City organizes proposal workshops, community meetings, and voting processes across districts, supported by academic partners to strengthen inclusivity and fairness.
Through this framework, Taipei City embeds civic participation into decision-making, ensuring that climate policies and actions are inclusive, transparent, and equitable.

Through the Sustainability Incentives Scheme the City of Adelaide supports residents and businesses to implement technologies and practices to reduce their impact on climate change. These incentives are reviewed regularly and redirected where appropriate to ensure the most equitable use of resources and to support residents and businesses to overcome the financial barriers to implementing these actions. Through our review process we analyse disaggregated and spatial data such as type of incentives applicant type e.g. homeowner, tenant, concession card holder, small business, not for profits, multi-story commercial, and location of project. 

The community consultation that informed the Climate Action Plan 2022-2025 and subsequent Integrated Climate Strategy 2030 sought to engage with sectors of the community that will be most impacted by climate change but do not always have input into climate action. This included engagements with the City of Adelaide's Access and Inclusion Advisory Panel, Reconciliation Committee, and the City's youth. The City of Adelaide recognises the disproportionate impact of climate change on the city's homeless population in its Homeless Strategy - Everyone's Business, released February 2024. The Homeless Strategy recognised that climate change is worsening homelessness both in terms of being a driver and how homelessness is experienced by individuals through health and wellbeing effects, and the ability to access support. Extreme weather events have real impacts, and the response must be broader than existing code red and blue procedures to ensure the burden and impact of climate change are not disproportionately experienced by marginalised people. Among other actions, the Homeless Strategy commits to investigating whether community infrastructure is made available in response to extreme heat and cold weather. 

The City of Adelaide also released a Housing Strategy in February 2024 which includes a goal of “Innovation and sustainability in housing”, focusing on adaptive reuse, electrification and housing diversity. Improving the quality of homes so that they use less energy, have lower bills and are more comfortable to live in is a key focus, to support the community with affordability while also addressing the climate crisis. The Housing Strategy calls for that State Government to amend its Planning and Design Code to ensure all new homes are all-electric from 2025. This will support our rental community in particular, which makes up half of all City homes and who are unable to initiate such changes, while taking climate action.
