column16: City departments use the Phoenix 2021 Climate Action Plan funding justifications for many projects. GHG emissions in Phoenix are being reduced through investments in clean energy by both the city, through solar projects on city properties and transitioning to LED streetlighting, and our local utilities' efforts to green the electricity grid. Phoenix has a weatherization assistance program that budgets roughly $1.3 million per year through local utilities, focusing on low- and middle-income households to reduce energy expenses. In January 2025, the Phoenix City Council adopted a target for the Energy Access Plan to increase household participation in low-income energy assistance programs by 25% by 2030. City libraries served as cooling centers with extended evening hours in 2024 and 2025 to provide heat relief. Water resilience is central at the city with the Mayor's Save Water Pledge being made permanent in May 2025. Phoenix also piloted the Chilled Drinking Water Initiative that is an initiative to keep Phoenix residents and visitors hydrated and healthy while on the way to work, school, appointments, and play. Phoenix's growing network of chilled water stations supports people who walk, bike or use scooters, while reducing single-use plastic waste. The City published a Green Stormwater Infrastructure (GSI) Handbook for Residents in November 2024 to help educate the public about how to capture and use stormwater for water conservation and ecosystem support (https://www.phoenix.gov/newsroom/environmental-programs-news/3333.html). The city is continually investing in public transit through the Transportation 2050 program with planned investments to increase bus service miles, 75 miles of bus rapid transit, 21 additional miles of light rail, improved accessibility for pedestrians, and other active transportation modes. The Phoenix City Council has approved a zero-emission bus plan to transition the city's 500-bus fleet to battery electric and fuel cell electric by 2040. In addition, the city's Transportation Electrification Action Plan provides a pathway to support 280,000 electric vehicles in the city by 2030, along with improving accessibility to micromobility options. As of 2025, 16 Phoenix libraries had EV charging stations installed. Since July 2024, the Shared Micromobility Program has enabled users to complete over 505,000 miles using shared scooters in the City of Phoenix. The Phoenix Local Food Systems Program achieved over 90% of its goals from the 2025 Food Action Plan. The City of Phoenix Local Food Systems Program created the Cultivating Food Resilience Documentary highlighting major achievements (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=b0k18Ey20yk ). Phoenix is developing the 2030 Food Action Plan with extensive community engagement, including visioning workshops with residents, food system businesses, and nonprofits. The final plan is expected to be completed by December 2025. The city encourages a culture of water conservation, with a goal to reduce water consumption to 155 gallons per capita per day by 2030. The city has also invested in water infrastructure and is planning to build a direct potable water reuse plant by 2030. Advanced water purification technology is being implemented at the rehabilitation of the Cave Creek Water Reclamation Plant (CCWRP) (https://www.phoenix.gov/administration/departments/waterservices/development-infrastructure/cave-creek-plant.html). Phoenix is also making investments in renewable energy that will use biomass from forest restoration efforts in Northern Arizona, reducing the risk and spread of wildfires that will protect the watershed that Phoenix relies upon. The Phoenix area experiences extreme heat. The Phoenix City Council adopted the Shade Phoenix Plan in 2024, focusing on trees and engineered shade to support a cooler city. Phoenix's ¡Sombra! The Celebration of Shade project commissioned artists to create nine shading and cooling installations in response to extreme urban heat (https://sombraphx.org/ ). The Parks and Recreation Department planted 1,500 trees in 2024. The city has approved a housing plan that establishes a goal of creating or preserving 50,000 homes by 2030 to address the housing shortage in Phoenix; achieved 5 years ahead of schedule with over 53,000 units as of December 2024 (https://www.phoenix.gov/newsroom/housing-news/3341.html ). The city is creating financial tools related to climate action, such as the 'Blue Bank' that provides loans to incorporate cooling tower projects that reduce electricity consumption. Phoenix is working with C40 Cities to estimate the number of good, green jobs resulting from climate action. The city is also participating in C40 Cities Reinventing Cities to transform the city's Resource Innovation Center into a hub for the circular economy, reducing waste while promoting economic growth (https://www.c40reinventingcities.org/en/professionals/winning-projects/resource-innovation-campus-1613.html ).

column18: The City of Phoenix quantifies the equitable and inclusive distribution throughout the planning and implementation of climate action with resident and business stakeholder engagement, through public workshops and surveys as examples. The city's Climate Action Plan (CAP) was approved by the Phoenix City Council in 2021. The CAP was developed, in part, using a climate hazard assessment developed with RTI International, the Maricopa County Multijurisdiction Hazard Mitigation plan and a report the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency in 2020 called “Indicators of Community Vulnerability to Extreme Events: Considering Sites and Waste Management Facilities” (https://www.phoenix.gov/content/dam/phoenix/oepsite/documents/climate/cdp/UrbanVulnerability_R9_July2020_Clean_v2.pdf ). The focus of the hazardous assessment was the exposure of vulnerable communities during extreme events. Extreme events considered included droughts, flooding events, and extreme heat events and how these events would be exacerbated by climate change. Census-block level data was presented throughout the community engagement process for the climate action plan in 2021. The 2021 CAP process included the development of a climate action plan framework, in collaboration with 29 city departments, and included a round of stakeholder engagement with input received from the local community guiding the development of the draft climate action plan (https://www.phoenix.gov/content/dam/phoenix/oepsite/documents/climate/cop039%20climate%20action%20plan_fin_hr.pdf ). The draft, presented in English and Spanish, had its own round of community engagement shaping the final climate action plan that was presented to City Council. For more details on the extent of community engagement, please see the Equity and Environmental Justice Chapter within the City of Phoenix Climate Action Plan 2021 Edition (https://www.phoenix.gov/content/dam/phoenix/oepsite/documents/climate/2021climateactionplanenglish.pdf). The City of Phoenix collaborated with C40 Cities in the development of a quantitative economic and market assessment published in 2023 related to the creation of good, green jobs by 2030 as a result of the mitigation and adaptation actions within the City of Phoenix Climate Action Plan 2021 (https://www.c40.org/case-studies/creating-local-good-green-jobs-in-phoenix/). The results of this work show that climate action could generate and support over 100,000 jobs in Phoenix and its supply chains by 2030. The report also provides key recommendations that will aid councilmembers and policymakers in creating and implementing climate action programs that ensure equitable outcomes for all residents within Phoenix.
column19: There are several aspects to equity at the city, some of which are included in the Phoenix 2021 Climate Action Plan (CAP) (https://www.phoenix.gov/content/dam/phoenix/oepsite/documents/climate/2021climateactionplanenglish.pdf ). The creation of the CAP included widespread community engagement. A draft CAP was provided to the public in both English and Spanish for feedback on improvement and to learn what City residents wanted in their CAP. The City is developing an updated 2025 Climate Action Plan that will employ similar strategies for equity and inclusion as the 2021 CAP. Creating a more inclusive and equitable city is central to all Phoenix actions and activities, prioritizing investments in previously underserved communities, proactively seeking community input on all major climate policy and related budget decisions, and embedding equity in all climate actions. Actions such as installing solar energy generation systems on City housing neighborhoods and promoting equity in the distribution of resources to overburdened communities demonstrate commitment to sustainability investments in all of our communities. Phoenicians are already experiencing impacts from climate change, from hotter, drier summers to record-breaking fire seasons and worsening air quality. We are all impacted by climate change, but some experience these impacts much more acutely than others. Black, Indigenous, and People of Color, lower-income individuals, historically underrepresented groups, children, older adults, and those experiencing multiple environmental burdens are disproportionately impacted by climate change. Phoenix pledged in the 2021 CAP to provide social protection and affordable access to essential public services, especially to the overburdened. The City's Transportation Electrification Action Plan for electric vehicles is equity-based. The transportation sector is Phoenix's largest source of greenhouse gas emissions. The Electrification Plan includes equity considerations when identifying locations for EV charging accessible by the public, fleet, and City employees. In the Food work the city is doing, the Funds to Feed Program provided funding for community and grassroots organizations, nonprofits, and health centers to recognize and enhance food delivery occurring in the community by the community. Using a hyperlocal approach, 10 organizations were able to continue and expand their work, create new partnerships, and obtain additional funding from other sources for their work. Equity was embedded in this program through the inclusion of residents impacted by food insecurity and by grassroots organization members to provide input and ideas on how to effectively promote the program and how to design the grant application and reporting requirements in a way that encouraged participation by Black, Indigenous, and People of Color. Phoenix continues to participate in C40 Cities projects such as 1) C40 Cities Green Jobs Analysis and Workforce Equity Assessment Report for the city of Phoenix's Climate Action Plan, and 2) the Reinventing cities (https://www.phoenix.gov/content/dam/phoenix/oepsite/documents/climate/cdp/City%20of%20Phoenixs%20C40%20Cities%20Leadership%20Standard%202b%20Two%20Examples.pdf?appId=aemshell). The City of Pittsburgh undertook the Pittsburgh Equity Indicators project in 2017 and a second report in 2019 to assess annual progress toward equitable opportunities and outcomes for Pittsburghers of all races, genders, and incomes, and to inform the City's investment decisions moving forward. The Equity Indicators project is a follow up of the city's OnePGH Resilience Strategy and covers 4 main topics: Housing, Transportation, Infrastructure, and Environment; Civic Engagement and Communications; Education, Workforce Development, and Entrepreneurship; and Health, Food, and Safety.
The City is using the Equity Indicators to begin to untangle the deep roots of inequality that exist in this city. By integrating the Equity Indicators into the work of City government, we are aligning budgets, assigning staff, and developing policies to increase staff effectiveness and efficiency, and provide a government that works for people.

In 2024, the City of Pittsburgh has kicked off work to develop Pittsburgh's first Citywide Comprehensive Plan, which will build off the Climate Action Plan 3.0 and incorporate climate justice and just transition principles. The City seeks to address the root causes of climate change, while simultaneously addressing a range of racial, social, and environmental injustices. These systemic injustices continue to exist in all many aspects of life for Black, Indigenous, and other non-White communities throughout the city. Racist land use policies and practices at the federal, state and municipal levels of government that targeted Black residents in many US cities, including Pittsburgh, have left a legacy of spatial and economic segregation that has been passed on from generation to generation. This is not the only story of Black life in Pittsburgh. Despite the struggles Black residents endured they persevered. Pittsburgh's Black residents inspired and influenced the city and the region through the creation of small businesses, cultural institutions and civic organizations. Black residents continue to reshape the city's social and political structures to advance equal rights, equal justice and equal access for all Pittsburghers.
As Pittsburgh continues to transition from an economy driven by extraction to one that is regenerative and multi-sectoral, we have an opportunity to center the health, safety and success of all city residents and communities. Envisioning a city where all residents have access to clean air and water systems, means that Pittsburgh must develop sustainable land use practices, emphasize the use of renewable energy, and provide economic opportunities in all clean economy sectors. The City wants to ensure all Pittsburghers have access to the economy of the future in a place that embraces its rich diversity of cultures, traditions and abilities welcomes immigrants and refugees, and unlocks innovation that is needed for the city to thrive.
This comprehensive planning process should not only strive to address past land use failures but ensure every resident in every neighborhood sees themselves as part of the future prosperity of the city. For this reason, the process must recognize and consider how the interrelated cultural, social, environmental and economic factors have on land use and related policies proposed in the Plan.
For more information and to sign-up for future community engagement related to Pittsburgh's Comprehensive Plan process, please visit our EngagePGH page here: Citywide Comprehensive Plan EngagePGH Webpage

column16: Climate and resilience planning efforts have economic benefits that extend beyond the more obvious infrastructure and community benefits. Many companies are looking to meet climate goals because of company policy, and in considering locations for development, factors such as transportation and access to clean and renewable energy are critical to hitting their targets. Amazon's recent search for new office headquarters, for example, brought tens of thousands of high-paying jobs and billions of dollars in investment to cities that were selected, in part due to their prioritization of climate action. Building community infrastructure and improving Tampa's carbon footprint will draw companies such as these to the region. The Tampa Bay Partnership has recently released a publication addressing the business case for addressing climate in the region. The Partnership's report suggests that building resilience into urban infrastructure could save communities more than two dollars for every dollar spent. One primary concern is sea level rise. The report suggests that in the six-county region of the Tampa Bay Regional Planning Council (TBRPC), daily tidal inundation may result in $2.9 billion in property value loss, with an associated $34 million in sales, tourism and property tax lost annually by 2045. By 2070, $238 million could be lost annually. The future, however, is not so certain. TBRPC has issued multiple possible scenarios for how much waters may rise, ranging from 2 to 8.5 feet above 2000 levels. These findings, supported by recent National Ocean and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) research, explain that future conditions are highly dependent on trajectories of increased heat, uncertainties of ice-mass loss, and change in ocean dynamics, which are all impacted by efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. In an indirect way, future flooding and the impacts within coastal communities are dependent on our actions today.

column18: Past plans and studies in Tampa included extensive outreach to Tampanians across the city, providing invaluable input and helping to define goals and priorities. For example, during the development of Resilient Tampa, more than 1,720 residents were reached through a Community Input Tool, and dozens of stakeholder and departmental meetings informed the report's 56 actions. The Regulatory Approach to Sea Level Rise project held multiple outreach seminars and a community symposium, with opportunities for feedback. Some of the climate adaptation programs have focused on historically underserved communities. For example, the Extreme Heat Playbook currently being worked on in partnership with the University of South Florida and Resilient Cities Catalyst has a project boundary defined by the East Tampa Community Redevelopment Area (CRA). This has included surveying at community events and workshops in partnership with the City of Tampa's Department of Partnerships and Community Engagement.
column19: To pinpoint concerns within communities that were underrepresented in previous planning processes, the Climate Action and Equity Plan took deliberate steps to engage these citizens. The City partnered with the CLEO Institute (CLEO), a non-profit, nonpartisan organization that has worked across the state to build climate literacy through advocacy and education, because of their expertise and successful record of accomplishing this task with other cities. CLEO developed an ambassador program that recruited leaders from specific neighborhoods, enlisting them as part of the outreach and education team. Their work was focused on establishing comfortable conversations guided by the topic of climate change. Ambassadors and CLEO staff fostered community connections within East Tampa, Sulphur Springs, North Tampa, West Tampa, and the southern end of South Tampa. This group was responsible for direct communication with the neighborhoods, and connected community members with outlets for civic engagement and media resources. With the help of CLEO, ambassadors participated in news interviews, and panel discussions and had their community leadership skills highlighted in community listening sessions. Efforts included community listening sessions to discuss areas of concern and educate citizens about the impacts of the climate crisis; door-to-door solicitations to distribute fliers and recruit for events; surveys to complement the listening sessions; and informal conversations within the neighborhoods. The surveys highlighted prioritized areas of concern for residents, gauged climate literacy, and helped those that couldn't attend listening sessions to have a voice. Residents expressed specific concerns about extreme weather events, flooding, and the lack of public transportation. The shared goal was to explain the Climate Action and Equity Plan program and above all, to listen to stories and convey that the City was interested in hearing their voice. When trust had been established, they exchanged surveys and other information. The listening sessions conducted by CLEO as part of their outreach strategy led to many conversations about the daily life of Tampa citizens. The ambassadors alongside CLEO were able to inform the city of difficulties surrounding bus routes being cut, high energy burdens, flood, and stormwater issues as well as the lack of connection between government initiatives and community benefit. Many of the community's difficulties have direct relationships to the climate crisis. Several of the concerns brought up during these workshops are addressed through initiatives in the Plan.

column16: To maximize the impacts of core benefits (the tangible benefits in addition to the reduction of GHGs) and achieve the goals of the City's Climate Action Plan, the City prioritizes the needs of residents in Communities of Concern. By empowering residents and including them in the decision-making process, the City believes it can be successful in mitigating the effects of climate change with substantial impact in our most vulnerable communities and improving quality of life for all. The CAP is one part of the City's comprehensive and coordinated approach to addressing climate change referred to as “Our Climate, Our Future.” Our Climate, Our Future currently also includes Climate Resilient SD, the Municipal Energy Strategy, Building Decarbonization efforts, Blueprint SD and climate equity initiatives. This comprehensive approach allows the City to align initiatives during the planning stage around the City's climate goals and leverage additional benefits, such as clean air, resilient communities and infrastructure, and increased access to green spaces. While reducing GHG emissions is the main objective of this Climate Action Plan, related challenges and benefits experienced by our residents each day were considered for planning and will inform implementation. Core benefits may not have a direct or indirect impact on reducing the effects of climate change, but they warrant consideration in the interest of public health and safety, economic resiliency and overall quality of life. The first step to empowering communities to achieve greater access to opportunity is to understand the core benefits most important to them and use this information to directly influence the development and implementation of the CAP. The following core benefits were identified from the extensive engagement process that took place during the development of the draft, utilizing online surveys, phone banking and community forums. Air Quality -Indoor air quality -Outdoor air quality Public Health -Reduce pollution and litter -Increase access to healthy and affordable food -Increase walkability -Increase access to parks, green space, and recreation -Increase safety (e.g., pedestrian, bike) Jobs & Economy -Local investment generated -Potential for local jobs -Increase affordability of transportation Resiliency -Reduce heat island effect -Increase natural habitat -Improve biological resources (i.e. trees, green spaces) -Improve water quality -Increased independence for local resources (i.e. energy, water). Core benefits were also assessed for each of the 89 strategies within Climate Resilient SD and closely correlate to the core benefits within the Climate Action Plan. Core benefits within Climate Resilient SD include City Services (maintaining critical city services), public health and safety (protection of public health), Historic and Tribal Cultural Resources (protection of resources), Greenhouse gas reductions, economic continuity, social equity, water quality, nature resource protection and air quality improvement, and recreation and green space access. Tel Aviv-Yafo has prioritized social justice and inclusiveness within its climate action initiatives by integrating climate policies with existing social programs. This approach ensures all residents, especially vulnerable populations, benefit from mitigation and adaptation efforts.
Key initiatives include:
•	Social Services Integration: The city's 'municipal climate preparedness mechanism' has embedded social services representatives into its steering and planning committees, guaranteeing that the needs of vulnerable populations are considered in all decision-making.
•	Improving Livability: The Social Services Department runs a comprehensive program to improve living conditions in at-risk neighborhoods. This includes direct interventions, such as providing ceiling fans and plants, offering training and consultation services, and making home improvements.
•	Apartment Climatization: The flagship Home Climate Adaptation Program provides tangible, physical upgrades to vulnerable residents' apartments. These upgrades, which include installing ceiling fans, sealing cracks, and replacing windows, directly improve indoor thermal comfort and energy efficiency.
•	Demonstration Centers: The city plans to establish at least three demonstration centers in public buildings. These centers will act as knowledge hubs, showcasing practical solutions for residential energy efficiency and climate adaptation.
•	Equal City Policy: The Municipal Resilience and Social Equality Authority developed a broad plan to address inequality in various areas, from personal safety and public spaces to economic opportunities and gender equality.
•	Affordable Housing: A new policy mandates that all new residential projects must include a certain percentage of affordable housing units built to green building standards. This policy, which includes an income test for eligibility, aims to create a more equitable and diverse housing market.
These initiatives are designed to promote social justice, build community resilience, and ensure a more equitable city by reducing the cost of living and improving living conditions for all residents.

column18: The policy decision-making process of climate action of the city of Turin is supported by scientific approaches, models and tools, analytically and quantitatively describing the various urban systems to evaluate the possible impacts of the strategic choices and decisions undertaken. The objective is to create skills and models to accompany the choices of the political decision-maker, developing knowledge of the possible scenarios and alternative strategic options and awareness of the consequent impacts on the different interacting domains without suggesting any scenario or option as preferential. Political choices are supported by a science-based approach. This approach has to make it possible to quantify the main relevant variables of the climate and sustainability-related actions, that are emissions and costs. Pertinent other aspects to quantify are the reference configuration of the system, the possible multi-dimensional impacts deriving from different future scenarios, and the evolution of the system itself over time, thus enabling the monitoring of the progress of the transition according to the implemented policies. This quantitative approach requires the availability and systematic management of the data to describe the urban systems (e.g., energy consumption and production, installed capacities, emissions, building stock and energy classes, mobility data, and macroeconomic data). In order to make the decision-making process effective and able to produce a positive impact, the city has carried out a constant interactions and a continuous dialogue with the social fabric of the city to make individual citizens, companies, and social entities aware of the cost/benefit ratio of the energy transition detailing the strategic choices according to the peculiarities of the different realities of the urban territory. Furthermore, the city has promoted an intense dialogue with the city's actors and stakeholders directly involved in the transition actions (multi-utility companies operating in the area, corporate, banking system, trade associations, investors, research institutions), thus fostering a coherent vision and shared sustainability goals, and consequently orienting, in a coordinated way, political and business decisions, investment plans and corporate strategic choices. Finally, given the complexity and multidimensionality of the transition process, having a systematic approach might open concrete opportunities for the growth and development of the whole city.

Singapore has integrated the concept of just transition in our national climate action plans by supporting affected groups and workers through skill development and new job opportunities in the green economy. 

Singapore's Green Plan 2030 outlines strategies for sustainability and climate action, including initiatives such as promoting green finance, increasing energy efficiency, and fostering innovation, which support a just transition by creating economic opportunities and enhancing worker skills in green sectors. One way the strategy is implemented is through Singapore's SkillsFuture initiative that supports lifelong learning and skills development where workers can access funding and resources to gain new skills needed for green jobs. 

Singapore introduced a carbon tax through the Carbon Pricing Act on 1 January 2019, which applies to all facilities with an annual direct emission of 25ktCO2e or more without exemptions. The revenue is used to support decarbonisation efforts, support businesses in improving energy and carbon efficiency and cushion the impact on households. Beyond legislative measures, Singapore has introduced the Climate Friendly Household Programme (CFHP) in two phases from November 2020 to Dec 2027. The CFHP lowers the barrier for households to purchase water-and energy-efficient appliances by lowering the upfront cost of such appliances, allowing households to enjoy energy and water savings.

Singapore has also invested heavily in our public transport system to ensure it is convenient, well-connected and fast, with inclusive infrastructure. This not only creates a more liveable environment through reducing emissions from the transport sector, but also ensures connectivity for all segments of society.

Santiago de Cali evalúa las oportunidades y beneficios de la acción climática de manera integral, considerando impactos ambientales, sociales y económicos en la planeación y ejecución de proyectos.

Ambientales. Cada acción se valora por su capacidad de reducir emisiones, restaurar ecosistemas y mejorar la resiliencia. El inventario de GEI (4,17 MtCO₂e en 2010) sirve como línea base para estimar reducciones: la electrificación de 60 buses del MIO en 2022 evita unas 4.000 tCO₂e/año, mientras que la restauración de más de 150 hectáreas urbanas y periurbanas entre 2019 y 2024 fortalece la captura de carbono y la biodiversidad. Proyectos como el Ecoparque Corazón de Pance mejoran la calidad hídrica y protegen nacimientos de agua que abastecen a más de 600.000 habitantes.

Sociales. Se prioriza la reducción de vulnerabilidades y la mejora de la calidad de vida. Las inversiones en drenaje urbano y protección de laderas disminuyen el riesgo para más de 250.000 personas que habitan en zonas de amenaza alta. La arborización y los corredores verdes en el oriente mitigan olas de calor que han aumentado 1,5 °C en las últimas tres décadas, aportando salud pública y bienestar. Los proyectos de cooperación internacional también generan inclusión social: programas recientes en 2023-2025 han vinculado población migrante y jóvenes a empleos verdes y procesos de educación ambiental.

Económicos. La acción climática se evalúa como motor de innovación y eficiencia. La transición energética abre acceso a financiamiento climático y cooperación internacional, mientras que la economía circular y el aprovechamiento de residuos generan nuevos mercados locales. La estimación de la inversión en electromovilidad (más de 1,2 billones COP en la próxima década) se compensa con ahorros en combustible, reducción de gastos en salud por contaminación y mayor competitividad urbana. Asimismo, la gestión climática atrae cooperación externa: en 2025 la ciudad anunció nuevos proyectos apoyados por GIZ y Swisscontact en economía circular y empleabilidad.

En síntesis, Cali mide las oportunidades climáticas desde una perspectiva de co-beneficios: reducción de emisiones, mejora de la salud y la seguridad de sus habitantes, creación de empleo verde y atracción de capital internacional. Esta visión integrada es la base para cumplir con los estándares de liderazgo de C40 y avanzar hacia una ciudad resiliente, inclusiva y baja en carbono.

La ciudad de Santiago de Cali cuantifica la distribución equitativa e inclusiva de los impactos de la acción climática mediante la integración de información socioeconómica, ambiental y territorial en sus sistemas de planificación y seguimiento. Estos datos provienen de fuentes oficiales como el Departamento Administrativo de Planeación Municipal (DAPM), el DAGMA, la Secretaría de Movilidad, el DANE, el SIAC y los reportes de rendición de cuentas que se publican de manera anual.

Periodicidad y mecanismos de cuantificación

El seguimiento se realiza de forma anual, articulando indicadores ambientales (calidad del aire, cobertura arbórea, espacio público efectivo) con indicadores sociales (índice de pobreza multidimensional, acceso a servicios básicos, densidad poblacional).

Se emplean herramientas de georreferenciación para relacionar la ubicación de proyectos climáticos (corredores verdes, humedales restaurados, sistemas de transporte limpio, programas de eficiencia energética) con la distribución de la población en comunas y corregimientos.

Dimensiones de equidad analizadas

Territorialidad: se evalúa la cobertura de infraestructura verde por comuna, priorizando zonas con menor espacio público verde por habitante (actualmente alrededor de 4,8 m²/hab, por debajo del estándar OMS).

Riesgo climático: se cuantifica la población expuesta a inundaciones y olas de calor según mapas de riesgo del DAGMA e IDEAM, cruzados con densidad poblacional y nivel socioeconómico.

Calidad ambiental: el Observatorio Ambiental de Cali reporta datos de calidad del aire (PM10, PM2.5) que se cruzan con localización de población vulnerable (niños, adultos mayores, comunidades en zonas de alta movilidad).

Movilidad sostenible: indicadores de viajes diarios en transporte público y modos activos (ciclovías, caminata), con énfasis en la cobertura en barrios de estratos bajos y periferia.

Participación social: número de mujeres, jóvenes y comunidades étnicas vinculados a procesos de restauración, educación ambiental y proyectos de eficiencia energética.

Herramientas utilizadas

Encuestas comunitarias y procesos de participación en los consejos de planeación y juntas de acción comunal, que permiten validar la percepción de equidad en la distribución de beneficios.

Mapas de calor socioambientales que integran calidad ambiental, déficit de espacio público y riesgos climáticos, para focalizar la inversión en zonas con mayor vulnerabilidad.

Indicadores del PAC Cali 2021-2030, como reducción de emisiones de GEI en sectores de transporte y energía, porcentaje de áreas verdes nuevas creadas, y porcentaje de viviendas beneficiadas con programas de eficiencia energética.

Uso de los datos

Los datos permiten priorizar las comunas con mayor déficit de espacio público verde, alta exposición a contaminación atmosférica y vulnerabilidad socioeconómica para recibir primero intervenciones como corredores verdes, arborización urbana y soluciones basadas en la naturaleza.

Se incluyen criterios de equidad territorial y justicia ambiental en la formulación del Plan de Desarrollo Municipal y en la implementación del PAC, garantizando que los beneficios ambientales no se concentren en áreas de alto ingreso.

Los resultados se incorporan en los informes anuales de rendición de cuentas, donde se presentan avances en indicadores de resiliencia urbana, movilidad limpia, acceso equitativo a servicios ecosistémicos y participación comunitaria.

Guayaquil ha identificado oportunidades y beneficios significativos derivados de la acción climática, los cuales se expresan en dimensiones ambientales, sociales y económicas, consolidando un modelo de desarrollo más resiliente y sostenible.
En la dimensión ambiental, la ciudad avanza en la recuperación y protección de ecosistemas urbanos y periurbanos —como manglares, esteros y áreas verdes— que cumplen un rol fundamental en la regulación climática y la conservación de la biodiversidad. La creación de corredores ecológicos y zonas de amortiguamiento hídrico contribuye no solo a la protección de especies, sino también a la reducción del riesgo de inundaciones. Asimismo, los programas de arborización y reforestación han comenzado a contrarrestar el efecto de islas de calor, mejorando la calidad del aire y aportando al bienestar ciudadano.
En la dimensión social, las acciones climáticas permiten disminuir la vulnerabilidad de la población en asentamientos informales a través de estrategias de reasentamiento y mejoramiento integral de barrios. Estas medidas aseguran un acceso más equitativo a vivienda segura, servicios básicos y equipamientos urbanos resilientes, fortaleciendo la justicia territorial. La educación ambiental también se ha convertido en una herramienta clave: a través de programas municipales se promueve la participación activa de mujeres, jóvenes y adultos mayores, fomentando una cultura de corresponsabilidad climática y un mayor sentido de pertenencia frente a los desafíos ambientales.
En la dimensión económica, la transición hacia un modelo de menor huella ambiental abre nuevas oportunidades de competitividad y empleo. El impulso a la economía circular y la gestión sostenible de residuos sólidos genera trabajo inclusivo y al mismo tiempo reduce la presión sobre los ecosistemas. De manera complementaria, los proyectos de movilidad sostenible y eficiencia energética mejoran la competitividad urbana al disminuir la dependencia de combustibles fósiles y reducir costos operativos. La infraestructura resiliente, por su parte, garantiza la continuidad de las actividades comerciales y de servicios en zonas estratégicas, protegiendo la economía local frente a eventos climáticos extremos.
Durante el año 2023, el Municipio de Guayaquil, en coordinación con URVASEO, desarrolló charlas comunitarias de capacitación orientadas a la correcta disposición de desechos sólidos en los hogares, fortaleciendo la conciencia ciudadana en la gestión responsable de residuos. De igual manera, junto con EMAPAG, se impulsaron procesos formativos en el marco del Mes Mundial del Agua, promoviendo el uso responsable y eficiente de este recurso vital. Estas iniciativas reflejan un esfuerzo constante por vincular la acción climática con la formación ciudadana y la corresponsabilidad social.
Finalmente, es importante destacar que las propias dependencias municipales cuentan con amplias áreas verdes, que constituyen un activo estratégico para la ciudad. Estos espacios generan un impacto positivo al aportar sombra, biodiversidad y regulación microclimática, reforzando el compromiso institucional con la sostenibilidad ambiental.
En síntesis, Guayaquil reconoce que las oportunidades derivadas de la acción climática no se limitan a la protección ambiental, sino que abarcan también beneficios sociales y económicos, consolidando un camino hacia un territorio más inclusivo, competitivo y resiliente.

column18:
La Municipalidad de Guayaquil incorpora criterios de equidad e inclusión en la planificación y ejecución de su acción climática, asegurando que los beneficios lleguen de manera prioritaria a los territorios y comunidades con mayor vulnerabilidad social y ambiental. Este enfoque está institucionalizado en los instrumentos de ordenamiento territorial, como el Plan de Desarrollo y Ordenamiento Territorial (PDOT) y el Plan de Uso y Gestión del Suelo (PUGS), que establecen lineamientos para orientar la inversión pública hacia las zonas críticas expuestas a riesgos climáticos.
La cuantificación de la distribución equitativa e inclusiva se realiza mediante un sistema de indicadores y diagnósticos que permiten evidenciar el alcance real de las políticas y programas ambientales. Entre estos mecanismos destacan: 1) Diagnósticos territoriales de vulnerabilidad, que identifican zonas críticas en función de riesgos climáticos, condiciones socioeconómicas precarias y déficit de servicios. 2) Indicadores de acceso a vivienda, servicios básicos y equipamientos resilientes, con el fin de monitorear la reducción de brechas en las áreas más expuestas. 3) Monitoreo de proyectos estratégicos como arborización, corredores verdes, drenajes pluviales sostenibles y procesos de reasentamiento de barrios informales ubicados en zonas de riesgo.
A estos instrumentos se suma un esquema de indicadores de cobertura territorial y poblacional, donde se cuantifica el número de beneficiarios de programas ambientales desagregados por edad, género y ubicación geográfica. Este enfoque asegura que los proyectos no solo reduzcan emisiones y fortalezcan la resiliencia urbana, sino que también promuevan la equidad social al priorizar a las comunidades más vulnerables.
Asimismo, la Municipalidad implementa capacitaciones y programas de educación ambiental en gestión de residuos, uso eficiente del agua y adaptación comunitaria al cambio climático. De este modo, se facilita un acceso equitativo a la información y a las oportunidades de participación.
En el diseño y ejecución de áreas verdes, actividades comunitarias y proyectos ambientales se incluyen mesas de participación ciudadana, donde intervienen mujeres, jóvenes, líderes barriales y representantes comunitarios. Esta práctica no solo fomenta la corresponsabilidad, sino que también asegura la inclusión de diferentes sectores sociales en la toma de decisiones sobre acción climática.
En síntesis, la Municipalidad cuantifica la distribución equitativa e inclusiva de la acción climática mediante un conjunto de herramientas técnicas (diagnósticos e indicadores) y sociales (participación y desagregación de beneficiarios), que permiten garantizar que las inversiones y programas ambientales respondan a criterios de justicia social, territorial y ambiental. Este enfoque asegura que los beneficios de la acción climática —como la reducción de riesgos, el acceso a espacios verdes, la mejora en la gestión del agua y la vivienda segura— se distribuyan de manera justa y prioritaria entre quienes más lo necesitan.
column19:
Entre las principales acciones destacan:
•	Reconversión de zonas no urbanizables en áreas verdes y de protección ambiental, integradas en el Plan de Desarrollo y Ordenamiento Territorial (PDOT) y el Plan de Uso y Gestión del Suelo (PUGS). Estos instrumentos delimitaron áreas no aptas para la expansión urbana, condicionan los usos de suelo en zonas de riesgo e incorporan parámetros urbanísticos orientados a la resiliencia y a la protección de ecosistemas estratégicos como manglares, esteros y corredores hídricos 
•	Programas de regeneración urbana resiliente, que incorporan drenajes pluviales sostenibles, parques inundables y corredores verdes, como parte de las soluciones basadas en la naturaleza priorizadas en sectores de alta vulnerabilidad, reduciendo riesgos de inundaciones urbanas y fluviales 
•	Movilidad sostenible y segura, con intervenciones como pasos peatonales verdes en la Vía a la Costa y ciclovías en áreas periféricas, que amplían el acceso a transporte limpio y no motorizado en sectores alejados del centro urbano
•	Educación ambiental y participación ciudadana, mediante talleres comunitarios y mesas de diálogo. En coordinación con URVASEO, se desarrollaron capacitaciones en barrios periféricos sobre la clasificación y correcta disposición de desechos sólidos, mientras que con EMAPAG, en el marco del Mes Mundial del Agua, se ejecutaron campañas educativas sobre el uso responsable del recurso hídrico dirigidas a familias, instituciones educativas y organizaciones barriales
•	Iniciativas de economía circular inclusiva, que fomentan la gestión sostenible de residuos y el reciclaje con participación de recicladores de base y comunidades locales, generando beneficios sociales y ambientales al mismo tiempo
•	Programas de reforestación con criterios de equidad territorial. El Plan de Reforestación 2022-2026 de Parques EP contempla la plantación de 15.000 árboles nativos en Áreas de Conservación Municipal, parques y avenidas, priorizando zonas urbanas expuestas a calor extremo, sequías e inundaciones. Este programa combina arborización, mantenimiento agronómico y sensibilización ciudadana, generando beneficios ambientales y sociales en sectores estratégicos de la ciudad
•	Cooperación internacional y multilateral, como el Proyecto Huella de Ciudades (CAF), que permitió calcular por primera vez la huella de carbono e hídrica de Guayaquil, establecer un portafolio de proyectos de mitigación y adaptación, y transferir metodologías para gestionar de manera autónoma los indicadores climáticos locales
•	Evidencia de inclusión social y territorial:
•	Se han desarrollado diagnósticos de vulnerabilidad parroquial, que consideran factores de pobreza, densidad poblacional, servicios básicos y exposición a amenazas climáticas (inundaciones, aumento del nivel del mar, olas de calor urbano). Estos diagnósticos han identificado “hot spots” en sectores como Tarqui, Pascuales, Letamendi y Monte Sinaí, donde se concentran las intervenciones municipales
•	La planificación y ejecución de proyectos se realizan con criterios de equidad territorial, asegurando que áreas verdes, drenajes sostenibles y espacios resilientes lleguen también a barrios periféricos y no se concentren únicamente en las zonas céntricas
•	La participación ciudadana es un eje transversal: mujeres, jóvenes, adultos mayores y líderes comunitarios participan activamente en talleres y mesas de diálogo, lo que garantiza inclusión social en la toma de decisiones y corresponsabilidad en la gestión climática
•	El impacto de las acciones se cuantifica mediante indicadores de cobertura territorial y registros de beneficiarios desagregados por edad, género y sector geográfico, lo que permite demostrar que los beneficios de la acción climática alcanzan a los grupos más expuestos y vulnerables
•	En conjunto, estas medidas no solo fortalecen la resiliencia climática y reducen riesgos ambientales, sino que también evidencian un enfoque de justicia ambiental, equidad territorial y participación ciudadana, garantizando que los beneficios de la acción climática se distribuyan de manera inclusiva en todo el territorio cantonal.

column16: Salvador avalia os impactos e benefícios mais amplos da ação climática por meio de uma abordagem transversal, integrada e orientada pela justiça climática, que considera os aspectos ambientais, sociais e econômicos em seu planejamento urbano e na formulação de políticas públicas. Essa avaliação se dá principalmente a partir de instrumentos como o Plano de Mitigação e Adaptação às Mudanças Climáticas (PMAMC), o Plano Estratégico de Salvador, o Plano Diretor de Desenvolvimento Urbano (PDDU) e os Inventários de Emissões de Gases de Efeito Estufa (IEGEE), que fornecem dados técnicos, diretrizes e metas para a ação climática na cidade.\nSalvador reconhece que os impactos das mudanças climáticas recaem com maior intensidade sobre as populações mais vulneráveis, justamente aquelas que menos contribuem para o agravamento do problema. Por isso, o PMAMC, especialmente por meio do eixo Salvador Inclusiva, incorpora a justiça climática como princípio orientador, buscando garantir que os custos e benefícios da ação climática sejam distribuídos de forma equitativa entre todos os cidadãos e ecossistemas da cidade. O plano promove o fortalecimento da participação popular, na formulação, implementação e monitoramento das propostas de adaptação e mitigação.\nA cidade entende que o acesso à informação, educação e capacitação é essencial para qualificar a participação social e fortalecer o engajamento da população. Assim, investir em ação climática significa também criar oportunidades para promover mais dignidade, igualdade e inclusão, ao ampliar o acesso a serviços essenciais como saúde, saneamento, energia limpa e trabalho digno, ajudando a reduzir desigualdades sociais históricas.

column18: A literatura evidencia que a crise climática afeta de forma desproporcional os países mais pobres, e dentro desses, incide de maneira ainda mais severa sobre os grupos mais vulneráveis. Esses grupos correspondem à parcela da população que apresenta maior exposição aos impactos climáticos e menor capacidade adaptativa, em razão de déficits históricos de infraestrutura (como habitação precária e ausência de saneamento básico), acesso limitado a serviços públicos e carência de recursos sociais e econômicos que permitam mitigar ou responder adequadamente aos efeitos do clima.\nNo Brasil, essa realidade é particularmente visível nos grandes centros urbanos, como Salvador. Na cidade, populações de baixa renda, idosos, mulheres e crianças tendem a estar mais suscetíveis aos efeitos adversos das mudanças do clima, sobretudo em áreas de risco ambiental ou socialmente vulneráveis. \nNesse contexto, a integração entre as agendas de inclusão social e de ação climática, que juntas compõem o conceito de justiça climática, torna-se fundamental para a promoção do bem-estar da população soteropolitana nas próximas décadas. Por isso, as políticas climáticas municipais devem ser deliberadamente inclusivas e igualitárias, de modo a não reproduzirem ou agravarem as desigualdades já existentes.
column19: A cidade do Salvador é entrecortada por uma falha geológica, tornando a cidade mais suscetível às consequências de riscos climáticos como deslizamentos, inundações e à elevação do nível do mar. De fato, mais de 45% da população vive atualmente em áreas de risco, considerando-se que a cidade conta com 160 áreas de risco mapeadas. Esse contexto geográfico, associado a um processo histórico de ocupação acelerada e desordenada de áreas irregulares, causa um aumento na ocorrência de desastres naturais e sociais no seio da população mais vulnerável. Diante deste cenário, a Defesa Civil de Salvador elaborou o NUPDEC e NUPDEC Mirim, projetos baseados em metodologias participativas, com o objetivo de mobilizar, sensibilizar e capacitar moradores de comunidades onde os riscos de deslizamentos e alagamentos são evidentes, assim os transformando em multiplicadores. Para disseminar conhecimento sobre tais adversidades, o projeto promove uma série de encontros, onde são compartilhadas experiências relacionadas à organização comunitária, voluntariado, análise de riscos e primeiros socorros. Além disso, são oferecidas informações detalhadas sobre a estrutura administrativa municipal e seus principais programas de apoio. Através dos NUPDECS, os moradores adquirem habilidades para lidar com situações de risco, assim capacitando a população vulnerável a reconhecer os sinais iniciais de incidentes, a identificar postos de vistoria e a agir de maneira adequada caso ocorram situações de emergência e de desastre climático. O projeto conta igualmente com NUPDECS Mirins, voltados para crianças e adolescentes, assim conscientizando e capacitando essa porção tão vulnerável da população que possui grande capacidade de multiplicação e viabilizar a continuidade geracional deste conhecimento. Os participantes dos NUPDECs são inseridos no Sistema Municipal de Proteção e Defesa Civil, se tornando agentes no desenvolvimento de ações de prevenção de desastres e de ações de resposta aos mesmos. Esta participação social se traduz em uma maior resiliência das comunidades frente às adversidades, promovendo uma melhor gestão de riscos, de maneira a incentivar comportamentos seguros, diminuir as vulnerabilidades locais e propiciar segurança e bem-estar para os cidadãos no curto e longo prazo.

column18: Si bien la ciudad hace los esfuerzos para priorizar la equidad e inclusión climática en el diseño, planificación e implementación de la acción climática, no se cuenta con los recursos para hacer una evaluación cuantitativa de la distribución. Quito realiza un análisis cualitativo en temas de equidad y mapeo de actores en territorio a nivel de todo el DMQ. Por ejemplo, en el Proyecto Solutions Plus, enmarcado en la Acción Área Cero Emisiones en el Centro Histórico tiene como objetivo permitir un cambio transformador hacia la movilidad urbana sostenible a través de soluciones de movilidad eléctrica innovadoras e integradas, que se implementan como pilotos en 10 ciudades a nivel global, entre las que consta Quito. Como parte de los resultados se efectuó una evaluación de impacto a los usuarios de los vehículos para evidenciar sus necesidades y requerimientos, para determinar si cumple con los objetivos planteados; así mismo, se realizó un análisis de cobeneficios para la acción más ampliada de área Cero Emisiones, donde se evaluó los cobeneficios de las acciones de aumento de peatonización en la salud, además, se efectuó una evaluación cualitativa como un primer análisis para asegurar que estos cobeneficios se distribuyan de la manera más equitativa posible.Para esta evaluación se priorizó un análisis sobre género, informalidad y condiciones laborales, discapacidad y edad. A partir de ello, se efectuaron sugerencias a ser tomadas en cuenta con el objetivo de dar un paso más allá en la construcción de un Centro Histórico de Quito sostenible y equitativo, la distribución justa entre los grupos vulnerables de estos cobeneficios puede garantizarse mediante la consideración de acciones que incentiven, por ejemplo, a las mujeres en la caminata, como la generación de estadísticas que mejoren el conocimiento del acoso en las calles, invertir en la seguridad, estudiar la viabilidad económica para que los espacios públicos tengan en cuenta las necesidades potencialmente diferentes de mujeres y hombres; y transformar las normas sociales. Los ancianos y las personas discapacitadas pueden verse beneficiados también si se garantizan los criterios de accesibilidad universal y seguridad necesarios. De esta forma, los avances en materia de reducción de emisiones en el Centro Histórico de Quito contribuirán a la integración de todos los grupos poblacionales contribuyendo a un centro sostenible e inclusivo.Otra acción que la ciudad implementa por más de 20 años, que tiene un fuerte enfoque de equidad e inclusión es el proyecto Agrupar, el cual ha trascendido a política pública con la Estrategia Agroalimentaria de Quito; AGRUPAR se enmarca dentro de la política de inclusión social y la macro-visión Quito Produce del Municipio del Distrito Metropolitano de Quito, no solo contribuye a la seguridad y soberanía alimentaria, sino que también tiene la capacidad de contribuir a mejorar los ingresos de sus participantes, así como generar ahorros a través del consumo de su propia producción.

column19: Making Climate Equity a Reality in San Antonio: Planning for Equitable Action Addressing major structural and institutional inequity, such as housing discrimination and neglected public infrastructure, will require the involvement of those affected by these issues in the policy planning process. - Climate action can be a catalyst for workforce development and job creation by moving laborers from legacy industries into fields and trades associated with mitigation, adaptation, and resilience that provide job stability, living wages, and safe and healthy working environments.
- Publicly communicating climate action efforts can help Indianapolis compete with other cities and regions for economic development and tourism opportunities by aligning with the sustainability priorities of organizations seeking a new headquarters location or a new convention host. 
- Deployment of climate action policies, like independent and community solar arrays or other renewable energy projects, have the potential for economic savings for the Indianapolis residential and business communities who could save money on their utility bills by being energy independent. Municipal investments in clean energy and the circular economy in particular offer responsible stewardship of taxpayer dollars as less budget needs to be allocated toward overhead and waste management.
- Climate action provides benefits to the local agricultural community and urban gardeners by helping to mitigate changing and unpredictable climate patterns that pose risks to crop yields and income potential.
- Policies that help to preserve vital ecosystems and species native to Indianapolis have unquantifiable cultural and environmental benefits for our shared local landscape.
- If climate action policy leads to more prepared neighbors and more resilience to extreme weather events, that would mean decreased costs for emergency response and decreased emotional/physical toll on emergency responders themselves due to flooding, heatwaves, tornadoes, or other disasters that threaten lives.

Indianapolis's sustainability and resilience plan has two overarching goals. One is to increase community resilience by prioritizing equity in policy, planning, and project implementation. Thus, equity is incorporated in every initiative that we do.

In 2020, the Indianapolis City-County Council implemented “Budgeting for Equity” which is a process through which racial equity is incorporated into budget planning for every city and county department. It is a tool that has created a formal and structural way of not only identifying how departments are integrating equity into their budgets and initiatives but also helping identify where the gaps are. Addressing these gaps and the historical inequities associated with them is key to the health and safety of our entire City, and we are proud to reintroduce Budgeting for Equity for its fourth consecutive year. The work continues, and we are committed to ensuring progress and accountability throughout the enterprise. The 2023 Budgeting for Equity Tool (BET) is designed to:   
• Identify whether budget requests advance equitable outcomes for residents.   
• Assess the equity impacts of budget decisions for potential burdens and benefits to communities of color, low-income communities, and historically marginalized communities. 
• Ensure that programs, projects, plans, and investments help reduce disparities, defined as significant, avoidable, and unjust differences in conditions or outcomes for one population vs. another.   
• Increase community engagement in program improvements, budget reductions, and overall budget development.   
• Allow city agencies/departments to create, promote, or foster policies, programs, and procedures that are equitable across race, income, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, ability or disability status, religion, citizenship, etc. 

In 2021, the City of Indianapolis released three overarching goals, outlining their racial equity and strategies: 
- The City of Indianapolis is committed to the diversity, inclusion, and racial equity of its employees. 
- The City of Indianapolis is committed to significantly increasing its communication, collaboration and feedback with the city's residents. 
- The City of Indianapolis is committed to racial equity in its delivery of programs and services, with each department and agency working to identify and prioritize programs and services that reverse systemic racism.

In 2024, the City of Indianapolis was awarded a $15 million Charging and Fueling Infrastructure grant from the U.S. Federal Highway Administration. The awarded proposal included plans to construct publicly available electric vehicle chargers at parks and libraries around Indianapolis - with at least 40% of the projects residing in neighborhoods most in need of cleaner air. The City has not received an update on the status of this funding since January of 2025.

The City of Indianapolis was also a member of two successful coalitions for Solar For All grant funding from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, awarded in 2024. One awarded proposal included plans to conduct a feasibility study of community solar on a closed city-owned landfill; a project known as 'brownfields to brightfields.' The other awarded proposal included plans to install rooftop or ground-mounted solar at roughly 1,200 low-income qualified, resident-occupied homes to decrease their energy burden and improve their resilience. The Future-Ready City Master Plan is aligned with and furthers the goals of Orlando's sustainability goals. The Plan will be mindful of our local ecology and provide a complementary set of strategies to improve city climate resilience while contributing to a sustainable and healthy economy for the City of Orlando. Orlando's sustainability goals and strategies are aligned with the United Nation's Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and aim to better incorporate strategies and initiatives that address social equity, climate resiliency, and smart technology and innovation across multiple focus areas:
1.	Clean Energy: Provide resilient, reliable, affordable, and sustainable energy service to all, by improving energy resilience during and after severe weather events, reducing utility consumption, and leveraging emergency tech to support clean energy goals. These will help the city rely more on renewable energy sources, make residents' power sources more reliable, and help them recover from climate hazards such as hurricanes. Doing so will also mitigate the spread of illness and injury during these events. Improving the city's emergency response and public health awareness will also increase the capacity to keep Orlando's population generally healthier. Heavier reliance on clean energy will enhance the quality of air.
2.	Green Buildings: Implement projects in neighborhoods that are particularly susceptible to poor water quality, poor air quality, and urban heat islands. By making our building infrastructure more environmentally friendly, we can also improve the quality of our residents' resources and quality of life.
3.	Local Food: By increasing green space in the city, residents will have more comfortable living conditions through increased tree canopy, shade, and lower urban heat island effects. Urban agriculture will also help engage the community and provide food to food-insecure neighborhoods. The additional green space can provide pollinator habitat, increased filtration of runoff water, and increase environmental resilience to extreme weather events.
4.	Transportation: This will improve transportation systems to provide safe, affordable, clean, and accessible multimodal options for all. This will help lower-income residents who may have less access to private transportation while ensuring cleaner air and less congestion.
5.	Water Conservation: This will improve water quality, reduce consumption, increase storage capacity and reclaimed water usage, and implement stormwater infrastructure to minimize extreme weather impacts.

column19: Following the death of George Floyd in 2020, the city increased its investments to address systemic racism in our community through economic development support for women and minority-owned businesses; job training programs; affordable housing; education and youth programs; and police policies and training, including banning all choke holds and no-knock warrants and updating their use of force policy. The Strategic Roadmap led by the Mayor's Office is bolstered by six priorities: housing, safety, mobility, prosperity, operations and culture. The opportunities we have identified are largely due to the large-scale transition to clean energy and clean transportation, reducing waste and increasing circularity, protecting natural resources such as water, greenspace, and tree canopy and resiliency work necessary to achieve carbon neutrality and prepare for potential impacts of climate change. The first wider opportunity this work brings is support for the prosperity priority of the Strategic Roadmap. Reducing emissions and pollution in our community can significantly improve the health and well-being of low-income residents and communities of color. Reaching our climate goals will require significant growth and change to industries and sectors within energy, transportation, waste, natural resource protection, and building construction and maintenance. Not only will businesses and jobs in these areas grow, but climate action will support growth in new and emerging technologies to reduce pollution. It supports the strategic goals the City is working toward of increasing physical health and economic health.
The second wider opportunity this work brings is supporting the Strategic Roadmap pillar of housing. Through support for clean energy and energy efficiency, which will help residents reduce energy costs climate action is specifically supporting the strategic goal of housing stability by keeping homes and home ownership or renting more affordable. 
The third wider opportunity this work brings is supporting the Strategic Roadmap priority of mobility. The Columbus Climate Action Plan supports increasing access to pollution-free transportation options like walking, biking and increasing availability of electrified public transportation and vehicle fleets. This supports the City's strategic goals of increasing transportation availability and increasing sidewalks, crosswalks and trailways.
and resilient communities.

This work supports the City's Strategic Roadmap priority of safety. column18: Climate change mitigation and adaptation actions contribute to a wide variety of benefits for the communities where they are implemented. These benefits typically span multiple sectors and include improvements to public health and air quality, social equity, environmental quality, economic prosperity, and local workforce opportunities. In order to assess the true value of the actions recommended in the Columbus Climate Action Plan, an analysis of expected benefits was conducted and used to inform the recommended strategies and actions as well as the prioritization of those strategies. A literature review of peer cities formed the foundation for the development of expected benefit categories that aligned with Columbus' climate action goals and community priorities. Four expected benefits were identified through this analysis: Climate justice, human health, environmental quality, and economic prosperity. The approach is intended to help the City balance the emissions reduction potential of each of the strategies with the priorities of the community as a whole to ensure the plan meets the City's wide-ranging expectations and desired outcomes. Each action of the plan were evaluated for contributions to each of the expected benefit categories. The scoring measures are outlined below for the positive, negative or neutral impacts, including where there are places to refine implementation plans for positive community outcomes. -1 : Strategy will have a negative impact on the expected benefit category-0.5 : Strategy is likely to have a negative impact on the expected benefit category, but the impact is dependent on how the measure is implemented0 : Strategy is unlikely to have an impact on the expected impact category, or has a neutral impact balance0.5 : Strategy is likely to have a positive impact on the expected benefit category, but the impact is depended on how the measure is implemented 1 : Strategy will have a positive impact on the expected benefit category. The City has also begun convening a Strategic Change Network comprised of staff from every to department to work on putting more metrics and quantifiable goals in place that support the Strategic Roadmap. The Sustainable Columbus office is participating in these meetings to ensure the goals and metrics within the Columbus Climate Action Plan are reflected and will lead to specific, quantifiable equity goals tied specifically to climate action.
column19: The 2021 US EPA report on climate change impacts within marginalized communities showed that people of color are most likely to live in areas that will be most-impacted by climate change, should global temperatures continue to rise. The 2020 US Census found that the population of the City of Columbus increased 15% over the previous ten years to over 900,000 residents. The Black, Asian, and Latino populations of Columbus are also growing significantly, which further underscores the urgency to center equity and environmental justice in all of our climate action work. Columbus' Climate Action Plan (CAP) recognizes that we must lead our sustainability efforts with equity at the forefront . We acknowledge that our climate work must co-create solutions with residents and community groups to deliver meaningful change. In 2021, the City worked with BIPOC and woman-owned businesses to hold focus groups and a survey to help deepen understanding of how sustainability is understood and viewed by communities of color. The results made it clear the City has room for improvement in how we communicate and engage with these communities around climate-related issues. This work led the City to have further emphasis on co-creation processes that involve residents from the very beginning of program and policy work. Turning lessons into action, the City invested in a local non-profit IMPACT Community Action to hire 3 neighborhood-based Community Advocates to help with engagement and outreach during the Equitable EV Readiness Ordinance process. The Community Advocates live in “Opportunity Neighborhoods” - priority neighborhoods for city services that underwent historic disinvestment -- and are compensated for their time, expertise and relationships to gain meaningful, honest feedback from residents. Their feedback was valuable throughout the Equitable EV Readiness Ordinance process, and remains valuable for all of our other outreach efforts on other climate related issues. Columbus has continued to invest nearly $3 million with IMPACT annually to create and support its Climate Justice Initiatives team. That includes funding for the EMPOWERED! program, a clean energy jobs training program with a focus on providing equitable access to good paying careers in the clean energy sector for people of color, women, and youth in Opportunity Neighborhoods. The program has had over 60 graduates who are primarily black or people of color, with many obtaining good paying jobs with employers such as Connect Housing, a sustainably minded housing manufacturer, AEP Ohio and Illuminate USA, a solar manufacturing facility. The funding also supports expansion of weatherization to residents up to 300% of the Federal Poverty Level and an energy efficient appliance replacement program. The energy efficient appliance program includes the Clean Clothes Initiative to provide new, energy efficient washers and dryers to income qualified residents. This was a top requested item from residents previously unfunded, and 98% of household recipients are black and 92% are female-headed households. The funding for IMPACT also supports a Climate Justice Director staff position. Columbus remains committed to equitable climate action, particularly in the American Addition neighborhood as we work with community to create a net-zero neighborhood. This historically Black neighborhood of 237 plats was first established in 1898 and was purposefully disinvested in by the City for decades, until around the late 2000s. To further the commitment, the City of Columbus applied and was selected to be one of 25 cities nationally participating in the Bloomberg Sustainable Cities initiative. This effort focuses specifically on the nexus of climate and building black wealth, and is a collaboration with the Mayor's Office and Office of Diversity and Inclusion. As part of the initiative, Columbus is receiving an Innovation Team of 3 Full Time staff that will be specifically focused on American Addition and creation of a net-zero neighborhood as well as technical supports and federal funding support. Another example is investing over $600,000 to do a pilot low-moderate income Solar Co-Op effort with national non-profit Solar United Neighbors. This will provide over 20 income qualified homes with free solar and battery backup. It was critically important to the City to include battery backup as part of this effort to increase the resiliency of our community, especially as in the summer of 2022 a week-long power outage during a prolonged heat wave had significant negative impacts on our low-income residents and communities of color. This pilot has already begun illuminating challenges and potential solutions to ensure better program design in the future, and how we can ensure disadvantaged communities are directly benefitting from the clean energy transition.

Edmonton and Alberta are home to the world's best energy innovators and we can use our strengths to lead this transition. We have competitive advantages, including the ability to produce near zero emission hydrogen at a lower cost than virtually any other jurisdiction in the world. Edmonton is home to significant expertise in sustainable building practices and green building technologies. It is home to the highest number of net-zero residential buildings in Canada. Construction and engineering is a key sector of Edmonton's economy. We have the expertise and innovative building technologies the world will need. The homes built in Edmonton today are more energy efficient than homes built a decade ago. 
The Community Energy Transition Strategy imagines a future where homes in the coming decade will be even more comfortable, energy efficient, and resilient as well as having lower energy costs than the homes we have today. This pathway also imagines an unprecedented energy efficiency retrofit effort (over 350,000 residential buildings) that could create a thriving retrofit industry and significant local job opportunities.
The way a city is designed and built has a direct impact on how people get around, connect and experience their city. Observations from 27 major urban centers across North America showed that cities with higher levels of energy efficiency, reduced GHG intensity, higher rates of “green” buildings, greater availability of sustainable transport options tend to have: higher rates of employment; higher GDP per capita; lower rates of violent crimes; higher levels of educational attainment; lower levels of perceived stress among residents (improved mental health); a greater sense of community; and higher levels of investment in new commercial and institutional buildings. 
Edmonton has potential to be designed and re-built to connect us to each other, to our communities and to our local businesses. We can have a city that helps each of us save money on the ways we move around, while also reducing the amount of time we spend driving, ultimately helping to create a healthier lifestyle. We can have a city that is attractive to top global employers by providing the lifestyle their employees are looking for. Urban planning practices are changing, and Edmonton has already shown bold transformative leadership in developments such as Blatchford. Continuing to catalyze those bold and transformative urban planning decisions across Edmonton and implementing the City Plan will help to create a vibrant and thriving low carbon city.
To limit global warming to 1.5°C, actions that actively remove carbon from the atmosphere are needed. These actions include nature based solutions (such as planting more trees and protecting existing carbon sinks) and technological options (such as using carbon capture equipment). Nature based solutions help support attractive, healthy urban places and carbon capture technology can grow prosperity in our region. The Edmonton Metro region is home to state of the art CO2 carbon capture and storage technology and infrastructure, such as the world's largest capacity CO2 pipeline and a significant carbon capture and storage facility. This is our competitive advantage and these strengths position the region to attract and grow carbon capture investment and jobs.

This is a methodology for measuring access, environmental justice and equity has been developed to help identify areas where residents and businesses may not have access to daily needs, choices for housing, a diversity of employment, or safe and healthy environments. The Equity Metrics described and mapped herein were used to 1) inform the development of Goals and supporting Policies, Projects and Programs in the Comprehensive Plan; 2) to identify priorities for Community Planning Areas for subsequent mapping and planning efforts within sub-geographies throughout the community; and 3) to assess and track progress towards becoming a more equitable, fair and just city over the next 20 years. As future initiatives are implemented, the data will be updated to be more accurate in relation to the efforts.
