column19: Ensuring inclusivity and equity in everything we do is a key priority at the City of Charlotte. The Office of Sustainability and Resilience works closely with the Office of Equity, Mobility, and Immigrant Integration: https://www.charlottenc.gov/City-Government/Initiatives-and-Involvement .\n as well as with the Corridors of Opportunity Team: https://www.charlottenc.gov/Growth-and-Development/Corridors-of-Opportunity .Please see the Comprehensive Plan for further details on how equity and community-engagement is integrated into city growth policy: https://cltfuture2040plan.com/wp-content/docs/01-CF2040_Policy-Plan.pdf . Charlotte works through an equity lens when implementing our Strategic Energy Action Plan. A lot of this work centers around the geographic location of pilot programs and reducing barriers to new technology and programs in historically red-lined and/or disadvantaged communities. Our SEAP document has an Action Area focused on Resilient Innovation Districts, however, implementation of that action item is focused not in separately designated districts, but within our Corridors of Opportunity. Since Summer 2020, Charlotte has embarked on transformational work in six historically under-invested corridors. The pivotal work includes collaboration among 8+ City departments, Mecklenburg County, non-profit organizations, and for-profit corporations working together to make systemic changes and build economic opportunity in each corridor. Strategic engagement resulting in playbooks and ongoing community engagement began along two more corridors. These partners represent a diverse group of fields including a financial center, medical centers, and various other organizations focused on helping Charlotte achieve sustainability goals. These strategies intersect to create a healthy, sustainable city. Advancing that work in 2023, the city has partnered with CleanAIRE NC and Sol Nation to initiate GreenPrints, a blueprint for environmental justice. The project aims to develop community-informed strategies to tackle environmental justice and climate inequities in six (6) of Charlotte's historically disadvantaged corridors. GreenPrints will be plans that include equitable climate action strategies for historically marginalized and underinvested communities by aligning with the City of Charlotte's Corridors of Opportunity program, mitigating injustice in the following focus areas: air quality, urban heat, energy burden, tree canopy, and legacy pollution. That project is ongoing with the goal of having a GreenPrint for each of the six (6) corridors and to secure seed money to start implementation. Other project implemented through a lens of equity include our PoleVolt program, wherein we installed pole-mounted EV chargers in Corridor, or Corridor adjacent, neighborhoods, while also placing EV Arcs in similar locations, improving access to EV charging. Additionally, we have been focused on a pilot for an Affordable Mobility Platform (AMP) reducing EV charging barriers at affordable housing sites in and adjacent to our corridors. The City of Charlotte recently created a partnership with Duke Energy to address energy burden. The program seeks to provide deep energy retrofit to high energy-use, low-income households. Duke Energy will be coordinating the program and providing the energy retrofits with the city funding home rehabilitation needed to enable the energy retrofits. Other projects include energy-efficient technology workforce training through our RENEW Program, and a CATS Electric Bus Pilot. More information on our SEAP and implementation can be found here: https://www.charlottenc.gov/City-Government/Initiatives-and-Involvement/Sustainability/SEAP . The implementation of the CATS eSERVE Academy: CATS eSERVE Academy - Charlotte Area Transit System trains individuals for high-demand technical roles and offers workforce development opportunities with the CATS. The GreenPrints program; GreenPrints: A Blueprint for a Greener, Healthier Charlotte - CleanAIRE NC aims to incorporate green infrastructure for neighborhoods that have been historically underinvested. The Comprehensive Area Plan: Welcome Letter - Charlotte Future 2040 has a focus on reaching policy goals of equitable growth by 2040. Charlotte is also one of 25 cities to join the Bloomberg American Sustainable Cities: Charlotte Selected as a Bloomberg American Sustainable City - City of Charlotte where it will receive historical levels of federal funding for implement transformative local solutions to build low-carbon, resilient, and economically thriving communities.

Sofia Municipality systematically assesses the wider opportunities and benefits of climate action through its SECAP 2021-2030, the Green City Plan, Vision Sofia 2050, and most recently the Climate City Contract (CCC) developed under the EU Mission for 100 Climate-Neutral Cities. These frameworks integrate sectoral risk and vulnerability analyses with planning tools such as spatial planning, resilience assessments, and digital modelling to capture both direct impacts and wider co-benefits of climate measures.

Environmental benefits: Significant reduction of greenhouse gas emissions, improved air quality, expansion of urban green and blue infrastructure, enhanced resilience to heatwaves and flooding, and preservation of biodiversity.

Social benefits: Improved public health outcomes through reduced exposure to air pollution and heat stress, creation of shaded and cooled public spaces, inclusive public engagement in climate initiatives, and greater access to affordable, sustainable energy.

Economic benefits: Job creation in the green and circular economy, attraction of EU and private investment, reduced household energy costs through efficiency programmes, and increased resilience of the local economy to climate and energy shocks.
Governance and innovation benefits: Strengthened interdepartmental coordination, enhanced capacity for data-driven decision-making (e.g. via digital twins and GIS-based adaptation planning), and closer collaboration with academia, civil society, and business.
Collectively, these benefits show that climate action in Sofia is not only about emission reductions—it delivers measurable improvements in social inclusion, economic competitiveness, innovation, and quality of life, while firmly aligning the city with EU climate neutrality goals for 2030.

Sofia Municipality quantifies the equitable and inclusive distribution of climate action using demographic and spatial data, programme participation indicators, and health metrics, as outlined in its Sustainable Energy and Climate Action Plan (SECAP 2021-2030 / ПДУЕК). The plan includes sectoral SWOT analyses that identify vulnerabilities by age, gender, socio-economic status, and health condition, ensuring that climate policies address the needs of those most at risk.

GIS-based mapping and disaggregated datasets are applied to monitor access to clean heating, green and cooled public spaces, and energy efficiency improvements across different districts. Programme indicators - such as the number of households supported through appliance replacement schemes, uptake of building retrofit measures, and observed improvements in local air quality - are systematically tracked.

This evidence-based framework, embedded in both the SECAP and the Climate City Contract (CCC), ensures that vulnerable groups - elderly residents, children, and low-income households - benefit proportionally from climate measures. By combining quantitative indicators with spatial equity assessments, Sofia guarantees that climate action contributes to reducing inequalities and supports a just and inclusive transition.
column19: Sofia Municipality embeds equity throughout the design and implementation of climate actions. Vulnerable households received free replacement of polluting heating appliances, combined with one-to-one support from municipal advisors and outreach teams to ensure accessibility and proper use. Over 8,300 households transitioned to cleaner systems, directly alleviating energy poverty and reducing exposure to harmful emissions.\nInclusive governance mechanisms were established: citizens, NGOs, academia, and businesses were engaged from the early design stage, ensuring that measures addressed local needs. Projects such as greening of dusty urban areas, creation of shaded “cool islands,” and walkable neighbourhoods were prioritised in districts with higher climate vulnerability. \nPublic consultations and local offices facilitated participation, while information campaigns reached over 400,000 citizens with tailored messages on air quality, health, and energy savings. This combination of targeted support, participatory design, and continuous outreach ensures that climate action in Sofia is both inclusive and equitable, with measurable social, health, and environmental benefits for frontline communities.

Short-term Opportunities
(1) Energy Systems: Investments in energy-efficient technologies such as smart grids and renewable energy sources (solar, biomass) aim to reduce emissions, improve air quality, and enhance energy independence. Spatial data helps identify priority areas, ensuring effective and equitable energy distribution.
(2) Green Infrastructure: Urban greening measures—including tree planting, green roofs, and urban agriculture—will mitigate heat island effects, enhance biodiversity, and provide carbon sinks. Densely populated areas are prioritized using spatial analysis.
(3) Capacity Building and Awareness: Frontline communities will be engaged through awareness campaigns and workforce training. Disaggregated data ensures targeted support for vulnerable groups, preparing them for participation in the green economy.

Medium-term Opportunities
(1) Sustainable Mobility: Investment in public transit, cycling infrastructure, and vehicle electrification will reduce congestion and emissions. Equitable access is ensured via spatial data, with initiatives like electric Kavalir vehicles improving mobility for elderly and disabled residents.
(2) Circular Economy: Improvements in recycling, reuse, and waste reduction will reduce landfill use, conserve resources, and generate economic opportunities. Waste data supports efficiency and promotes energy-from-waste systems.
(3) Retrofitting and Renewable Energy: Energy retrofits, solar installations, and district heating upgrades will reduce energy costs and improve living conditions, particularly in low-income areas. Initiatives like “Save the Homes” simplify access to these improvements.

Long-term Opportunities
(1) Climate Neutrality and Resilience: By 2030, Ljubljana aims to reach climate neutrality. This will reduce fossil fuel reliance and create green jobs in energy, construction, and infrastructure. Technologies such as carbon capture and green hydrogen are also being explored.
(2) Urban Regeneration and Sustainable Growth: Sustainable spatial development and investment in renewable energy will regenerate underserved areas and strengthen the city's status as a green leader. Nature-based solutions will enhance biodiversity and resilience.
(3) Health and Well-being: Improved air quality, reduced noise, expanded green spaces, and more non-motorized transport will yield significant public health benefits. Measures like electric boats will also improve quality of life and urban attractiveness.

(A) Environmental Context:
Ljubljana's actions reduce emissions and air pollution, support biodiversity, and improve resource efficiency through circularity. These impacts are monitored throughout implementation, particularly in energy and transport sectors.

Climate action is projected to generate significant economic activity and investment. Ljubljana anticipates ~€7.8 billion in climate-related investments by 2030, supporting green entrepreneurship and job creation in construction, energy, and mobility sectors.

Wider benefits are integrated across planning, implementation, and monitoring phases. Spatial and socio-economic data guide equitable targeting.

column18:
The City of Ljubljana quantifies equitable and inclusive climate action impacts through a data-driven approach based on the Energy Climate Atlas, an integrated analytical-reporting platform developed and operational since 2018. The platform consolidates diverse data sets across sectors such as energy, transport, buildings, spatial planning, green infrastructure, environmental quality, and climate risk exposure.

To identify and address inequalities, the city uses key indicators aligned with the Climate City Contract (CCC), including:

(i) Building energy performance and retrofitting potential

(ii) Use of different energy sources and energy poverty risks

(iii) Modal split, availability of sustainable mobility options, EV uptake

(iv) Urban tree cover, access to green areas, and cooling infrastructure

(v) Exposure to heat islands and other climate-related hazards

(vi) Rates of separate waste collection and local waste production

These indicators are used to establish baselines and assess distributional impacts of climate actions, particularly among vulnerable population groups. Although data are primarily collected and analysed at the city level, spatial mapping enables targeting of specific areas with low access to climate-related benefits or higher exposure to risks.

The CCC Action Plan (Section 3.2.2) explicitly states that these indicators are used to monitor implementation and outcomes of mitigation and adaptation measures. Progress is regularly reported through city and national mechanisms (e.g., LEK reporting, City Council).

The indicators inform:

(a) Ex-ante assessments of proposed measures to ensure equitable design;

(b) Ongoing monitoring of implementation and adjustments based on results;

(c) Post-implementation evaluation to track changes in access and benefit distribution.

The city also integrates qualitative inputs from 17 district communities and stakeholders through participatory meetings, co-creation processes (e.g., workshops, surveys), and pilot projects (e.g., targeting vulnerable urban areas).

This combined quantitative and participatory monitoring framework enables Ljubljana to ensure that climate action outcomes are equitably distributed and that no group is left behind in the city's transition toward climate neutrality and resilience.
column19:
The City of Ljubljana is implementing several targeted actions to ensure that climate action benefits are distributed equitably and inclusively across all segments of the population, particularly vulnerable and underserved communities.

1. “Save the Homes” - inclusive energy retrofits (2024-ongoing)

This program supports energy retrofitting of residential buildings. The goal is to reduce energy bills, improve thermal comfort, and lower emissions while enhancing equity in the built environment.

2. Sustainable city card and accessible E-mobility (2023-ongoing)

The Sustainable city card (Trajnostna mestna kartica) provides affordable or free access to sustainable mobility services, including public transport, bike-sharing, and the Kavalir electric vehicle system. Kavalir vehicles, operating in pedestrian zones, are free of charge and serve individuals with limited mobility. These initiatives aim to reduce transport poverty and ensure equitable access to low-emission transport options.

3. Participatory planning through district communities (2021-ongoing)

Ljubljana's participatory governance model involves all 17 district communities (četrtne skupnosti) in the co-creation of climate policies. Vulnerable groups, including the elderly, youth, people with disabilities, and migrants, are actively engaged through consultations, focus groups, and surveys. Their input shapes the design and location of interventions such as green infrastructure, mobility hubs, and cooling areas.

4. Data-driven equity mapping with the energy climate atlas (2018-ongoing)

Since 2018, Ljubljana has used the Energy Climate Atlas - a geospatial decision-support platform - to collect, analyze, and visualize data on energy use, transport, natural environment, and population vulnerabilities. The platform supports the equitable planning of climate actions by identifying hotspots of risk and opportunity, enabling more targeted and inclusive interventions.

5. Public drinking fountains

In Ljubljana, public drinking fountains (62) provide residents and visitors with free access to clean and safe tap water. They operate from spring to autumn and are regularly maintained by the city to ensure water quality and functionality. Their locations are also marked on city maps and apps, making it easy for people to find them and stay hydrated. The fountains were introduced as part of the city's sustainable measures to reduce plastic waste and to help people cope with heatwaves.

6. Community gardens

The City of Ljubljana supports urban gardening as a way to promote self-sufficiency, healthy food production, and social inclusion. It has established nine community gardening areas, equipped with infrastructure such as tool sheds, compost bins, rainwater collectors, parking spaces, bicycle racks and playgrounds. Vižmarje-Brod also provides accessible plots designed for people with mobility impairments. 

7. Identification of urban heat islands in Ljubljana

The Hotspots Ljubljana project, initiated by the cultural association Prostorož, aimed to identify urban areas in Ljubljana that become excessively hot during summer months. Residents were invited to use the interactive platform to mark locations they perceived as uncomfortably warm. This participatory mapping effort resulted in the identification of cca. 700 'hotspots' across the city. The findings were shared with the City Municipality of Ljubljana to inform urban planning and climate adaptation strategies. In addition, a network of 32 stationary sensors has been established to monitor temperature and humidity in real time. Data from these sensors will enable the development of a digital platform that will display temperature dynamics at various locations throughout the city.

These measures reflect Ljubljana's commitment to embedding climate justice and social equity into all stages of climate action. Actions are regularly monitored and refined through feedback loops and data-driven analysis, ensuring they continue to meet the needs of the most affected and underserved residents.

column18: Auckland Council commits to protecting our environment strengthening our economy and building a more equitable future by cutting emissions from the sectors most responsible for the climate crisis. This means putting inclusive climate action at the centre of all urban decision making. Auckland Council supports affordable fares and low cost transport options, such as, walking and cycling, enables equitable access for whānau and communities to jobs education and other opportunities leads to an enhanced quality of life for all. There are clear risks to equity that we need to address, and some actions may produce inequitable outcomes. Equity issues need to be clearly identified, assessed and made transparent as part of any decision-making process. We have applied an equity lens throughout the development and implementation of Te Tāruke-ā-Tāwhiri: Auckland's Climate Plan, considering the implications of our actions on all Aucklanders and making sure that we are not leaving anyone behind in our transition to a zero carbon and climate resilient region, However this plan also has the potential to create a much fairer and vibrant Auckland through well designed actions, as well as, Auckland Council, central government, business, Māori and communities all working together.
column19: Three climate actions are described as evidence. Actions #1 and #2 are part of the Shoreline adaptation programme (SAP). SAP is planning for the future of Auckland's 3200km of shorelines, beaches, cliffs, harbours and estuaries in response to the impacts of climate change erosion and flooding, as well as sea level rise. SAP utilises Dynamic Adaptative Pathway Planning (DAPP) to proactively address the long-term uncertainties posed by climate change. (#1). Whangaparaoa Shoreline Adaptation Plan. The plan, approved in 2022, has set the long-term strategic direction for management of the shoreline of the Whangaparaoa peninsula. It outlines decisions on how Auckland Council owned coastal land and assets will be sustainably managed against the impacts of coastal hazards and climate change across the short (20 years), medium (20-60 years) and long (60+ years) term. Community engagement and mapping assessment helped identify communities affected by coastal hazards and highlighted areas of interest (equity assessment evidence). Most of Whangaparaoa shoreline areas can be managed over the next 100 years with little to no active intervention. For some of the lowlying shoreline areas, the escalating risk of coastal inundation and rainfall flooding, as well as sea level rise will require managed realignment of assets in the medium or long term. The need to set back assets out of the areas susceptible to coastal erosion and instability where possible has also been signalled. To summarise, equity assessment evidence includes community engagement, mapping, assessment around coastal hazards and highlighted areas of interest. (#2). Manukau Harbour South Shoreline Adaptation Plan. The plan, approved in 2023, has set the long-term strategic direction for the management of shoreline of Manukau Harbour South. The adaptive strategies which guide how Council-owned coastal land and assets will be sustainably managed have been informed by: (1) Local iwi, acknowledging the cultural values and associations of iwi which centred on supporting local iwi objectives and aspirations. (2) The objectives of the local community, identified through community engagement. (3) Technical inputs including hazard risk, coastal hazard and climate change projections, ecological and policy framing. (4) Advice from infrastructure and assets owners/managers. Council-owned land and assets within the area can largely be managed in the short to medium term with 'no active intervention' to 'limited intervention'. The need to 'hold the line' in select locations responds to the presence of critical infrastructure and high social value. In the longer term, areas will require 'managed retreat' of assets and uses to manage risks from coastal hazards, rainfall flooding and the impacts of climate change. This provides the opportunity to support natural systems and maintain the highly valued natural character of the coastal environment. To summarise, equity assessment evidence includes community engagement, mapping, assessment around coastal hazards and highlighted areas of interest. (#3). Manurewa Urban Ngahere Action Plan 2022. This plan, approved in 2022, is intended to deliver on Auckland Council's Urban Ngahere (Forest) Strategy. The Strategy acknowledges the multifaceted benefits of Auckland's urban ngahere in social, environmental, economic, and cultural aspects. Communities will benefit from the strategy, including 181,194 Māori population (11.5% of the city total). According to the latest assessment in 2021, Auckland's average urban canopy cover stands at 18%, with five local boards falling below the 15% target, including Manurewa. To address these gaps, local boards have developed action plans aligned with the Strategy (e.g., Manurewa local board). The Auckland Council 2019 report on extreme heat effects highlights that the most vulnerable areas, including Manurewa local board. These regions face heightened risks due to heat exposure and possess limited green cover to mitigate extreme heat impacts. Manurewa Urban Ngahere Action Plan connects parks and open spaces, continues to explore planting opportunities to increase biodiversity and encourage important community initiatives. With the extent of the urban ngahere in the Manurewa area having now been assessed (mapping), there is a need for a large number of planting projects to be committed to in the short and medium term. This will ensure that a flourishing urban ngahere can continue to develop into the future to reduce the adverse effect of extreme heat and to gain the benefits that the “lungs of a city” can bring to its inhabitants. To summarise, equity assessment evidence includes community engagement, mapping, assessment around extreme heat hazards and highlighted areas of interest for future planting.

Council papers, project briefs, business cases, programme reports, and other key documents assess and highlight the wider opportunities and benefits of climate action. Some of the co-benefits identified for the city include:

•Better public health: Promoting active transport, such as walking and cycling, helps improve physical and mental health.
•Improved air quality: This is achieved through reducing emissions from vehicles as a result of improved active and public transport and a shift to e-mobility. This is supplemented by ongoing greening of the city landscape through tree planting and wetland restoration, which act as carbon sinks by sequestering GHGs and other air pollutants.
•Healthier homes and lower energy bills: Improving the insulation of Wellington's old, inefficient housing stock through initiatives like the Warmer Kiwi Homes scheme helps keep homes warm, dry, and affordable to heat. This reduces health issues such as respiratory illnesses linked to dampness, lowers energy bills, and ensures our most vulnerable populations live in healthier conditions.
•Improved access to green spaces: Expanding and protecting green spaces provides easy access to nature, supports thriving biodiversity, and delivers nature-based solutions in both urban and natural environments. Access to these spaces improves mental well-being, lowers stress, and strengthens community connection. 
•Reduced noise pollution and safer streets: Less car dependency and more walking, cycling, and public transport mean quieter, safer streets, reducing crash risks and creating more pleasant urban environments.
•Intergenerational fairness: Acting decisively on climate change today ensures that the costs of inaction are not passed to future generations of Wellingtonians.
•Reduced noise pollution and safer streets: Less car dependency and more walking, cycling, and public transport mean quieter, safer streets, reducing crash risks and creating more pleasant urban environments.
•Cultural connection and partnership with mana whenua: Embedding mātauranga Māori (Māori knowledge) in climate solutions strengthens cultural identity, supports kaitiakitanga (guardianship), and fosters a stronger sense of place.
•Improved disaster preparedness and community resilience: Through connecting climate adaptation planning and disaster management work, enabling communities to prepare for any unexpected events.

The WCC Climate and Sustainability Fund considers equity in the selection of projects to fund, with priority given to projects that demonstrate equity across communities in relation to access to climate action information and the ability to act. 

Our work on low-carbon and active transport considers accessibility of different modes for our communities and improving safety for all road users, including the most vulnerable.

Māori communities are likely to be disproportionately affected by climate change. Therefore, the Council has taken many initiatives targeting Māori communities to ensure equitable and inclusive distribution of climate action. The Council has been working with Ngāti Toa to trial a Māori Mara Kai project to improve nutrition, building capability to maintain healthy, productive soil through Earthworkers courses and composting. The council has also been setting up small funding pools that local kaupapa Māori organisations can draw on to strengthen and showcase Māori growing practices and teach sustainable food production and gathering.

The pilot area for our Local Community Adaptation Planning programme area was selected based on a range of criteria, including exposure to hazards and the social vulnerabilities of the community. The pilot is taking an equity principles-based approach and will be evaluated on the fairness of the process and consideration of intergenerational equity.
column19:
The Council is focusing on equity in its approach, seeking opportunities to work with communities that are traditionally less engaged with government programmes. The Council's goal is to provide them with developmental opportunities. Activities to support community climate action over the last year include:
• Face to face connection with 49 different community groups on community climate activities, and specific support provided to 22 groups.
• Development and delivery of a community climate leadership training course in partnership with Voice of Aroha.
• Delivery of a Wellington-specific community climate conversation webinar.
• Participation in and supporting community events.

An example of where we have considered equitable distribution of climate action is in our community adaptation planning. We used a multi-criteria analysis to prioritise areas for our community adaptation planning pilot. The spatial analysis considered the exposure to a range of climate hazards for public places & infrastructure, homes & communities, Māori taonga (sites of significance) and culture and non-Council-owned assets. This was then combined with consideration of populations, deprivation and qualitative assessment of adaptive capacity and readiness to engage. This analysis informed the selection of our pilot area, and a similar approach will be used to prioritise future areas for community adaptation planning.

Besides the community adaptation planning, there are a number of initiatives that the Council has taken to ensure equitable distribution of climate action:
• Supporting public share micro-mobility: The Council has allowed for public share micro-mobility to operate since 2018, increasing the cap on the number of e-scooters to 1000 in April 2024 to meet increase market demand and introducing e-bikes into the market in 2023. In the FY24 we saw 840,615 public share e-scooter trips maintaining a steady level of demand while there were 33,979 public share e-bike trips taken in Wellington. The Electric micro-mobility share scheme review 2024 showed that approximately one-fifth to one-quarter of trips reportedly reduced car ownership, as well as noting health and fitness, and equity and accessibility are the positive impacts 
of using shared micro-mobility.
• Kai and Climate Sustainability Fund: Co-funded between Council teams and Te Toi Mahana, the Kai and Climate Sustainability Fund is a twelve-month pilot supporting projects led by city housing tenants. Inspired by the Stone Soup fund for community gardens, a participatory decision-making model is being co-designed with tenants to allocate available funds.
• Māori Kai Sovereignty Network: The Council established a Māori Kai Sovereignty Network intended to disperse funding for mana whenua and Māori-led kai and soil sovereignty projects. The first network hui was held in July 2024.
Community gardening: Increased expressions of interest for new community gardens and orchards indicate growing community engagement with sustainable food practices. The Stone Soup fund is allocated by the network of established community gardens to assist with running costs. Funds have been budgeted to assist with set-up costs for new gardens, which pose a financial barrier for some groups. 
• Support for community-led programmes: The Seeds to Feeds Foundation has received funding to support communities to host and run a series of events encouraging locals to grow, forage, produce, cook, and share more food in their neighbourhoods. Garden to Table has been supported to continue their work with children in schools, developing skills and knowledge to grow and prepare nutritious kai in ways that uphold the mana of the natural world. GROW Pōneke was a three-month programme of community-led food initiatives and events encompassing Local Food Week, Neighbours Aotearoa and Community Gardens Open Sundays, brought together and promoted by the Council. Kai Kitchen continues as a strong community event in Linden with 80 to 90 people attending each time. Newlands and Tawa Community Centres now also offer a free soup lunch for their communities. The demand for food support has increased as unemployment rates rise across the city. We established a growing fund for Te Toi Mahana (previously City Housing) tenants to increase their access to affordable, healthy food and gardening knowledge. 

All the examples of climate action listed above are featured in the Council's latest Te Atakura - First to Zero update, which serves as Wellington City's blueprint for achieving net zero emissions by 2050. The full report can be accessed here: https://wellington.govt.nz/-/media/environment-and-sustainability/climate-change/files/te-atakura-first-to-zero-2024-update.pdf

<Long-term: Urban New Deal Project>
The Urban Regeneration New Deal project, which started in 2017, aims to improve the physical environment in response to urban decline, supplement deficiencies in existing urban regeneration efforts, and strengthen residents' capacity to realize residential welfare, restore urban competitiveness, and promote social integration. Until now, the maintenance of old houses has been carried out through urban renewal projects, primarily resulting in the construction of apartments. The need for urban regeneration arose due to issues such as insufficient public interest and inadequate consideration for the socially disadvantaged in existing maintenance projects.
Accordingly, the Special Act on Urban Regeneration Activation and Support was enacted in 2013, and the Urban Regeneration New Deal project is currently underway, starting with leading areas for urban regeneration in 2014. In 2017, the government selected it as a major national project, attracting significant attention, and proposed a target investment of 50 trillion KRW over five years. In response, Goyang City made urban regeneration an immediate priority, carrying out New Deal projects in Hwajeon and Wondang in 2017, Ilsan and Samsong in 2018, and Neunggok and Seongsa in 2019, becoming the self-governing body advancing the largest number of Urban Regeneration New Deal projects in the country.
Most of these projects are still in progress, making it difficult to measure performance as they require a long period and evolve alongside residents rather than being implemented unilaterally. Recognizing the importance of project management after completion, a village management cooperative was established in the Wondang area, where the project was completed in 2020. This cooperative aims to discover and promote initiatives for basic living infrastructure, facility maintenance and management, and revitalization of the local community and economy. Efforts are being made to secure the sustainability of village revitalization.

<Middle-term: Project to Utilize Idle Space in Villages to Create Green Space (2018-2022)>
This project has been continuously discussed, and through the gathering of citizens' opinions, packs such as Ssamzie Park, Garosup, and Urban Forest were created in idle village spaces with citizen participation. A total of 28 locations were designated as key promises of the 7th popular election. The resident participatory budget was actively utilized, and sites were determined by collecting local residents' opinions and conducting field surveys. 
By securing an auxiliary project cost of about 14 billion KRW, functional forests such as “fine dust reduction forests”, “urban heat island reduction spaces”, and “rainwater gardens” were created to expand green spaces and respond to climate change. Additionally, through the Goyang Hope Tree Planting Project, trees that were cut down or abandoned due to various developments were donated to create forests and green spaces in the city center. By the second half of 2020, 36 parks were created; although the pledged target amount was 3.12 billion KRW, 16.58 billion KRW was secured. Through this, the urban forest area per Goyang citizen increased from 8.4 m2 in 2018 to 9.6 m2 in 2020.
Green spaces around residential areas were expanded to respond to rapid climate change, providing greenery to citizens through planting projects and creating parks that serve as places for local residents to communicate. It is also meaningful in that it provided leisure spaces by promoting greening projects within living areas at a time when long-distance travel was difficult due to COVID-19 restrictions.

<Short-term: Goyang City River Green Forest Road Creation for Climate Change Response>
Goyang City has created a pleasant living environment and responded to climate change by establishing a wind corridor that ecologically connects surrounding forests and green areas through the creation of the Goyang River Green Forest Road. In 2019 and 2020, green forests were established along a 25 km selection encompassing Daejang Stream, Dochon-Gongneung Stream, Changneung Stream, and Hyangdong Stream. Ahmedabad's Climate Resilient City Action Plan (CRCAP) 2023, focuses on addressing the city's climate vulnerabilities while ensuring equitable socio-economic development. The CRCAP is designed with vulnerability/equity assessments, ensuring its benefits reach the city's most vulnerable populations, particularly those in informal settlements and low-income communities.

The Ahmedabad Heat Action Plan (HAP) 2019 is a significant transformative action, which targets high-risk groups such as outdoor workers, the elderly, and children. Through a vulnerability assessment, the plan prioritises those most susceptible to extreme heat and includes public health interventions, awareness campaigns, and infrastructure improvements such as cool roofs and shaded areas.

Similarly for the solid waste management sector, Ahmedabad has employed more than 13,000 sweepers as outlined in Chapter 3.4 of the CRCAP 2023. The city has employed more than 500 women rag pickers for segregating dry waste received at Refuse Transfer Stations (RTS). AMC has developed a 100 MT dry waste MRF, with automatic machinery, over 4,000 sq m land at Piplaj on PPP model, operated and maintained by NEPRA which has further employed and integrated rag pickers with mainstream. Additionally, the city has implemented 3 Material Recovery Facilities at Khadia, Sola and Vasna (100 TPD capacity each), which will generate further employment opportunities as mentioned in section 7.3.6 of the Ahmedabad CRCAP. These measures not only contribute to waste reduction but also drive social and economic benefits by empowering marginalised communities.

Climate Actions proposed under Climate Resilient City Action Plan include opportunities, social and environmental benefits. The proposed actions will create an estimated 480,000 green jobs from Implementation of renewable energy measures (solar and wind power) in buildings, municipal infrastructure, and electric buses. The proposed actions also quantified total vulnerable people (including elderly people, children, women, people with special needs, slums, vendors etc.) benefited due to proposed actions.

column18: El departamento municipal de Políticas Sociales trabaja de manera continua en la detección de situaciones genéricas de pobreza , siendo en ese ámbito una de las líneas de trabajo de los Servicios Sociales la información, el asesoramiento y el acompañamiento a las personas para reducir los gastos energéticos y evitar llegar a situaciones de pobreza energética. Una de las acciones llevadas a cabo es el asesoramiento para comprender las facturas de energía, tomar decisiones y reducir el gasto. Se trata de una atención personalizada y asesoramiento para comprender mejor las facturas de luz y gas, analizarlas y realizar una propuesta para reducir los costes. Por otro lado, el departamento de Territorio y Acción por el Clima ésta participando como colaborador en el proyecto europeo POWERPOOR cuyo objetivo es desarrollar programas de apoyo para la ciudadanía en situación de pobreza energética y fomentar el uso de esquemas alternativos de financiación (por ejemplo: comunidades energéticas y crowdfunding). Dentro de este proyecto se ha desarrollado un kit de herramientas dirigidas a reducir la pobreza energética, incluyendo tres herramientas on-line y una guía. Este kit de herramientas constituye la base para las formaciones y los programas de apoyo que se han utilizado durante el proyecto. Así mismo, el proyecto está formando a personas de perfiles diferentes que se certificarán como Asistentes de Pobreza Energética y Mentores de Comunidades Energéticas para poder ayudar a las familias vulnerables. Se ha puesto en marcha también una serie de jornadas de sensibilización para explicar a la ciudadanía, pymes, comercios, personas autónomas y demás entidades que colaboran en el desarrollo y bienestar de la ciudad en qué consisten las comunidades energéticas, razones por las que comenzar un proyecto de energía comunitaria, qué tipo de proyectos se pueden poner en marcha, cómo hacerlo realidad y qué beneficios económicos, medioambientales y sociales van a suponer para tu comunidad. En el enlace siguiente se puede obtener información sobre esta actuación: https://www.vitoria-gasteiz.org/wb021/was/contenidoAction.do?idioma=es&uid=u_5e206eba_17eb8dc7fb2__7f91.\nFinalmente, el AVG establece una líneas de concesión de ayudas económicas destinadas a financiar el gasto energético en la vivienda habitual de las personas con escasos recursos económicos, correspondiente al suministro de electricidad, gas, u otros combustibles. column19: El proyecto de rehabilitación energética de barrio de Coronación (Vitoria-Gasteiz) recibió la financiación de la Comisión Europea través del programa SmartEncity, y una financiación adicional del Gobierno vasco, a través del Departamento de Medio Ambiente, Planificación Territorial y Vivienda. Direct reduction of energy consumption and greenhouse gas emissions: either by transitioning to renewable or less polluting energy sources and by increasing the energy efficiency of consumption, such as the replacement of the municipal fleet by electric vehicles, of the greater supply of more accessible and zero emissions public transport, energy efficiency measures at the buildings level, among others. 

Increasing the energy autonomy of the city: With the use of renewable energy, namely with the production of solar energy within the city borders, the city's resilience and autonomy is expected to increase in face of energy needs, both from the point of view of cost and availability, a transition that is considered essential in the face of the uncertainty of energy costs, and which translate into clear economic benefits, as well as from the point of view of reducing consumption and production costs. This could lead to significant benefits in reducing energy poverty in the city. 

Improvement of air quality: through the reduction of GHG emissions and by the implementation of nature-based solutions (mainly trees and green cover, which contribute to air pollutants removal). 

Increasing landscape quality and promoting biodiversity: The focus on green and blue infrastructures and nature-based solutions, such as the requalification of streams and water lines, the expansion of green spaces of public access and other forms of green infrastructure increases the quality of the city landscape and, simultaneously, benefits biodiversity and boosts services provided by ecosystems. 

Increasing health and well-being: By reducing air pollutants (reducing emissions), increasing the availability of public space appropriate for the use of soft transportation modes, and expanding green and blue infrastructures, the health and well-being of the population can be incremented. Increasing the safety, pleasantness, functionality and availability of soft transportation modes, citizens will be more prone to use this option for (at least) short distance displacements, walking and biking more (daily physical activity).The availability of parks and water sheds significantly help fight the heat island effects during summer and heat waves (which will be more frequent), creating cooler buffers and, consequently, protecting the health of the population, particularly the most vulnerable. Simultaneously, parks appeal to physical activity and walking. 

Economic benefits: either by saving energy and/or by local decentralized production of renewable energy, the citizens and organisations will be able to significantly reduce energy costs in the medium and long term, either by saving energy and/or by local decentralized production of renewable energy, the citizens and organisations will be able to significantly reduce energy costs in the medium and long-terms. New green jobs related with, for instance, with renewable energies and energy technologies will increase. 

Social benefits: preparing the city for the impacts of climate change will reduce the number of people displaced or relocated from their housing/employment sites, allow for greater security/protection of vulnerable populations, and increase water and food security. 

Given the benefits listed, Porto believes that the transition presents a valuable opportunity to enhance the quality of life for its citizens, ultimately benefiting the entire city and region. The empowerment of the community, enabling individuals to make informed energy decisions, will play a crucial role in this process. This shift will also promote a change in societal norms, fostering a culture of sustainability and environmental responsibility. Furthermore, the region will become increasingly attractive for investment in innovative and sustainable projects, further driving economic growth and reinforcing these positive changes.

column18:
The Municipality of Porto has several monitoring tools that ensure climate actions are aligned with an integrated and strategic medium- and long-term vision, while promoting their equitable and inclusive distribution. These mechanisms also ensure a balanced coordination between social, economic and environmental dimensions, ensuring that municipal policies and interventions contribute coherently to truly sustainable development. 

Among the reference instruments, global reports such as the Sustainable Development Goals 2030 Voluntary Local Review (VLR) (conducted every 10 years) and the Sustainability Report (published annually) stand out, offering a comprehensive perspective on local progress in sustainability. The VLR, for instance, enables the alignment of climate action strategies with specific indicators and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), allowing for effective performance evaluation. For instance, under SDG 1 - No Poverty, the Municipality of Porto has focused on social housing, rental support, and housing requalification to improve comfort and reduce energy costs. A key initiative is the Porto Energy Elevator (PEER), funded by Horizon 2020 and developed with the Porto Energy Agency, aiming to combat energy poverty and promote clean energy, and so providing monitoring on this field. This project also led to the creation of the Porto Energy Hub, a one-stop shop supporting the community in adopting sustainable and efficient energy practices. 

These cross-cut reports are complemented by major municipal plans with indicators tailored to the reality of the territory, such as the Municipal Master Plan, the Municipal Climate Action Plan, the Municipal Housing Charter, the Municipal Health Plan, the Mapping of Porto's Food Environment, the Municipal Sustainable Urbanisation Plan and the Circular Economy Roadmap. For instance, the assessment made within the Municipal Housing Charter concluded that, in Porto, energy poverty is a reality in almost a third of the households and tend to be more significant in the parish of Campanhã. Indeed, Campanhã stands out not only for having the highest concentration of social housing but also as the most economically and socially disadvantaged population (30% lives in social housing). The integration of the data from the several plans resulted in the creation of an Urbanisation Plan for Campanhã, being drawn up with the aim of coordinating the necessary transformation of this area in a planned manner. 

The municipality of Porto assures that 13% of its residents live in social housing (the national average is 2%) and has been working to improve their living conditions. To reduce the energy bill for these tenants and offer them better bioclimatic conditions and comfort, the Municipality is promoting the rehabilitation of the buildings through the improvement of the insulation of the dwellings, refurbishment of glazed spans and the installation of solar thermal collectors, contributing to the reduction of heating and energy costs. The investment surpasses 50 M€ in 3 years. This constitutes a good example on how the social, environmental and economic dimensions are integrated to meet the needs of the city and its citizens. 

In addition, many of the actions are implemented through specific projects with their own monitoring systems, such as Asprela+Sustentável, URBiNAT, LIFE - My Building is Green, NBRACER - Quinta de Salgueiros, the Campanhã Intermodal Terminal and the Porto Energy Hub, among others, which allow, in greater detail, the identification of needs and the measurement of the efficiency of actions. For example, the Asprela + Sustentável project was promoted with the aim of acting as a driving force for energy transition and an effective reduction of the carbon footprint in Porto. This project - the Energetic Community of Bairro de Agra do Amial - is the first energy community in Portugal to be classified as a Pilot Project by the Energy Services Regulatory Authority (ERSE). This pilot also allowed testing the technical and economic viability of innovative energy solutions and measuring how to effectively implement actions that benefit population. So far, this energetic community allowed a reduction of about 40% in the monthly energy bill of the residents. 

Together, these tools ensure a structured, coherent approach that is tailored to local needs, reinforcing Porto's commitment to fairer, more resilient and integrated development.

Some examples are: 

Renovation of social housing buildings: Enhancing energy efficiency and thermal comfort across 50 neighbourhoods, resulting in increased comfort and reduced costs for 13000 dwellings 

Porto Amigo: rehabilitation of degraded buildings belonging to disadvantaged households and the creation of housing solutions for homeless people. 

Municipal Network of Solidarity Restaurants: three restaurants, operating since 2016, provide approximately 550 daily meals, 365 days a year—totalling 200000 full meals annually—while donations from food distribution chains help reduced food waste. 

Zero Waste project: is an ongoing initiative with the aim to reduce food waste by redistributing surpluses to the neediest, which provided 289304 equivalent meals between 2015 and 2021. 

Urban Gardens network: transformative initiative repurposes unused urban spaces into cultivable land, enabling citizens—especially low-income families—to grow their own organic food on 500 allocated plots across 13 city locations, returning 120 tonnes of organic matter to the soil each year. 

EcoPorto: promotes circular economy practices by repairing and reusing appliances, furniture, and computers, with the aim of redistributing them free of charge to social entities and interested citizens or businesses. 

Porto Energy Hub: this service centre promotes energy savings and improved thermal comfort by providing families and businesses with tailored information on energy efficiency, renewable energy solutions, and building improvements, while fostering energy literacy through legal, financial, and technical guidance. 

ASCEND project: aims to create a Positive Clean Energy District in the vulnerable neighborhood of Lordelo do Ouro by promoting renewable energy communities, improving energy literacy, and reducing energy poverty through self-consumption solutions and increased photovoltaic capacity in social housing and public schools. 

Improvement of school buildings: by installing photovoltaic panels in 29 schools and municipal buildings, this initiative boosts energy autonomy, improves comfort and learning conditions, and promotes energy literacy among students through a digital gamification tool. 

My Building is Green: this pilot project, implemented at EB1/JI do Falcão in Porto, explored improving thermal comfort in schools while reducing energy costs, also enabling rainwater harvesting for irrigating green and agricultural spaces. 

URBiNAT: Created a new 4-hectare interstitial green park with 1,5 km of pedestrian paths connecting three social housing neighborhoods, transforming underused urban space to enhance mobility, access, and quality of life for vulnerable residents. 

NBRACER: will create a connected public green space along the Eastern Park - Alameda de Cartes - Antas corridor, enhancing biophysical flows and linking diverse social areas through accessible walking paths that promote soft mobility, nature contact, and recreational activities, while serving as a living laboratory for research on nature-based solutions and urban ecology, fostering social cohesion and community well-being. 

Requalification and creation of public spaces: improving streets, squares, and green spaces—creating new parks and gardens that combine climate adaptation with social benefits, enhancing biodiversity, carbon sequestration, and public health through leisure and nature contact, exemplified by projects like Asprela Park, S. Roque Park expansion, and Dr. Mário Soares Park. 

Integrated Education-Action Plan for Sustainability: the Plan provides biodiversity and nature workshops for all education levels, accessible to students from all social backgrounds, notably through the 'Adapta-te' project, which engages students in creating sustainability strategies for their schools on energy, waste, and water. 

Improving public transport: through metro expansion, a new metrobus line, and affordable pricing—offering a 30€ monthly pass for unlimited travel, free transport for youth under 23, and benefits for Porto Card holders—enhancing connectivity, reducing emissions, and increasing access to the city's economic, cultural, and environmental opportunities.

Through Louisville's key sustainability plans, Plan 2040, Sustain Louisville, and Prepare Louisville, the interconnection between climate mitigations strategies, adaptation
strategies, and other core goals of Louisville Metro Government, such as equity and quality of life is evident. For example, parks and green spaces are planned to both
mitigate climate change through carbon sequestration and enhanced biodiversity, and also as an adaptation and equity strategy to provide equitable access to nature,
shade, and clean air across the community, particularly in neighborhoods with lower tree canopy and fewer parks. As MSD addresses sewer overflow issues due to climate
change, LMG is finding opportunities to restore stream/river habitat, remove concrete channelization in streams, and provide recreational opportunities such as multi-use
trails. Important functions that our natural systems provide include pollination of plants and crops, protection of streambanks and riparian areas from erosion, shade and
cool waterways, water storage in floodplains, wetlands, or meadows during large storms, and natural filtration of toxins and pollutants. Natural systems also provide
recreational activities and aesthetic benefits to residents and tourists.

Additionally, there are numerous benefits of the new clean energy economy. The burning of fossil fuels, especially approximately in Louisville not only contributes to climate change, but harms our air quality in Louisville. With the opportunity of investing in efficiency in Louisville's buildings, we are not only reducing our contribution to the global climate crisis, but we are reducing our residents' and businesses' energy bills and increasing their comfort.

activities for residents with lower access.

LMG's Cool Roof Incentive Program offers a $1/square foot incentive on Cool Roof Rating Council rated reflective roofing materials installed on residential and nonresidential properties. Over half of these funds are reserved for our targeted high heat districts identified in a city-wide urban heat study. Most of these districts fall in west
Louisville.

Another key climate action/emissions reduction measure was the launch of Solar Over Louisville, a solarize campaign, in early 2022. In combination with the bulk
purchasing discount on solar offered to all residents, Louisville Metro created a Solar Grant Program to cover the full cost of solar installation for a handful of low-income

The City continues to plant native trees in marginalized communities and aims to ensure that a park or green space is within a 10-minute walk of every community, a goal aligned with the US Conference of Mayors '10-Minute Walk' campaign.

Omaha's Climate Action Plan includes a recommendation for an Implementation Equity review as actions are implemented, focusing on policy and program design to improve the impact of actions and overall community resilience. 

Examples of equity actions in the plan include:
Increasing public transit commuter ridership from 1.3% to 5% by 2035. Efforts to improve efficiency, convenience, frequency, and reliability of bus service, particularly in areas less well served, can increase public transit ridership and reduce GHG emissions.

Reducing the share of the population living in high energy poverty from 40% to 20% by 2035. Energy efficiency upgrades and renewable energy can lower energy bills for low-income households while also improving health and climate adaptation outcomes by improving indoor air quality, safety, and resilience.

Increase tree cover in priority neighborhoods from 24.9% to 27.9% by 2040. The weighted prioritization for increasing tree canopy aims to balance the potential for canopy growth
with the opportunity to increase equity, positively impact the most households, and mitigate heat
island effects. These priorities are weighted as follows:
• Potential for New Trees: 15%
• Low Income Density (equity adjustment): 30%

column16: In our Climate Action Plan, we have identified six co-benefits which are as follows: (1) improve health and well-being: Extreme climate events (such as floods and wildfires) and human activity (such as energy production, poor air quality and pollution) can negatively affect people's health, safety and well-being. Climate action should aim to remedy these impacts and improve public health and well-being. Actions with long-term health benefits also reduce public healthcare costs. (2) provide environmental benefits: Effective long-term climate action requires resilient natural resources. Healthy and resilient ecosystems provide invaluable services, including by acting as a buffer against the effects of extreme climate events or providing socio-economic benefits such as food or medicines to climate impacts (such as floods or fires), and the creation of green jobs (3) promote economic growth, development and job creation: In cities with competing objectives and critical socioeconomic needs, the socio-economic co-benefits that climate action provides should be explored and maximised. These benefits can include the creation of new economic and entrepreneurial opportunities, cost savings by promoting efficiency, avoidance of repair and rebuilding costs due to greater resilience (4) promote public service delivery Climate actions have the potential to provide or aid the delivery of basic services (such as clean water, clean air or healthcare) to residents, either by facilitating the direct provision of these services or by creating a better environment for service delivery (5) Promote inclusivity and equity: Climate action should promote inclusivity and equity in Tshwane. This can be achieved by improving the resilience of vulnerable people, promoting environmental justice and improving livelihoods through green opportunities and climate-resilience approaches, and (6) Aid COVID-19 recovery or relief: COVID-19 has had a devastating impact on the economy of Tshwane and on the health and wellbeing of residents. The baseline assessment study for the Circular Turku Roadmap identified more than 700 circular economy stakeholders, 270 of which were businesses engaged in circular economy. Many significant regional solutions that follow circular economy principles have already been implemented in energy production, water systems, waste management and industry development.

Turku has been developing climate budgeting for preparation, steering and monitoring its investments. In climate budgeting, the EU taxonomy classification of sustainable funding has been used as the framework for assessing the climate impacts of investments, which enables a multidimensional examination of environmental objectives and, for example, the utilization of green funding. In addition to climate change mitigation and adaptation, the approach incorporates objectives for water and marine resources, circular economy, pollution prevention, and biodiversity. 

City of Turku is chairing the Turku Region Air Protection Co-operative Group. The group consists of the environmental authorities of the region, together with 11 industrial partners encompassing the energy industry, shipyards, harbors, the building materials industry and others. Turku is monitoring ambient air quality at seven monitoring stations in the region. The emissions of air pollutants have decreased substantially with the emissions of greenhouse gases. In 2024, ambient air quality, as determined by the national 24-hour air quality index, was most commonly classified as good or satisfactory. Limit values were not exceeded.

We collaborate closely with the scientific community in providing knowledge about climate related health risks and their linkage to nature-based solutions and social equity. For example, in the Hercules project environmental and socio-economic parameters have been analyzed together with cohort health data on several time-steps in the largest cities of Finland. In many studies higher greenness has been associated with higher levels of physical activity. Importantly, the association between higher greenness and higher level of physical activity is stronger in the more disadvantaged areas. The studies have also shown an inverse association between residential greenness and depression, implying lowered depression risk for individuals with higher residential greenness.

We have also studied the evolution of spatial temperature differences during a 17 year period in Turku. The Urban Heat Island intensity showed a slight intensifying trend. Relative cooling of daytime temperatures was also detected at some observation sites e.g. as a consequence of forest growth and related micro-climatological change. Thus vegetation is a valuable measure to mitigate the Urban Heat Island effect and to reduce heat related mortality also in higher latitudes.

Gaziantep's climate action plans for mitigation and adaptation to climate change go far beyond environmental goals. They also provide multi-dimensional benefits and strategic opportunities in the fields of economy, society, health, and urban development.
1. Environmental Benefits

Improved air quality: The transition from coal to natural gas, investments in public transport, and the expansion of green spaces help reduce air pollution, offering major environmental and health benefits.

Biodiversity protection: Urban green spaces and nature-based solutions reduce pressure on local flora and fauna.

Water resource conservation: Rainwater harvesting, greywater use, and efficiency in agricultural irrigation strengthen the city's resilience to water scarcity.

2. Economic Opportunities

New job creation: Green sectors such as renewable energy, energy efficiency, recycling, and sustainable agriculture will generate green employment opportunities.

Energy cost savings: Energy efficiency in buildings and industry leads to reduced operating costs and improved competitiveness.

Access to external funding: Easier access to international funds (EU, UNDP, World Bank, etc.) supports infrastructure and transformation projects in the city.

Low-carbon export advantage: By aligning with border carbon adjustment mechanisms (CBAM), companies gain a competitive edge in European markets.

3. Social and Community Benefits

Health improvements: Reduced air pollution and increased green areas contribute to lower rates of respiratory diseases, especially among children and the elderly.

Reduced inequalities: Investments in natural gas infrastructure in low-income neighborhoods promote energy access and justice.

Public awareness and participation: Climate education and outreach campaigns raise public consciousness and strengthen participatory governance.

 4. Urban Resilience and Quality of Life

Reduced disaster risks: Strengthening infrastructure (e.g., flood prevention systems, early warning mechanisms) increases safety and climate resilience.

Mitigation of urban heat island effect: Green roofs, parks, and shading systems help regulate extreme temperatures in city centers.

Sustainable mobility: Expanding public transport, bike lanes, and pedestrian areas lowers carbon emissions while enhancing quality of life.

 5. Governance and Innovation Opportunities

Data-driven decision making: Climate action encourages the use of sensor technologies, carbon inventory systems, and digital platforms, enhancing smart city infrastructure.

Institutional capacity building: Training of technical staff and improved coordination between departments increase local governance efficiency.

Climate diplomacy: Leading climate action on national and international platforms boosts Gaziantep's visibility and fosters new collaborations.

 General Assessment: A Strategic Opportunity for Gaziantep

Gaziantep's climate action plans are designed not only to address climate change but also to promote:

Sustainable development,

Social justice,

Economic resilience, and

Comprehensive improvement in urban living.

In this context, climate action is not viewed as a burden, but rather as a strategic opportunity for Gaziantep

Below are the key approaches used by Gaziantep to measure the fair and inclusive distribution of its climate actions:
1. Socio-Economic and Spatial Impact Analysis

The neighborhood-level impacts of climate actions are analyzed to monitor whether investments are reaching low-income, disadvantaged, or climate-risk-prone areas.

Distribution of services such as green infrastructure, transport investments, and energy transition projects is assessed based on the socio-economic profiles of neighborhoods.
2. Monitoring Indicators Focused on Vulnerable Groups

The municipality monitors how women, the elderly, children, persons with disabilities, and migrants are affected by or benefit from climate actions through specific social indicators.

For example:

Access rates to green areas designed to mitigate heatwaves,

Availability of age- and disability-friendly public transport options,

The distribution of energy efficiency support across different income groups.
3. Participation and Representation Metrics

Participation data from public meetings, workshops, and surveys conducted during planning processes is recorded.

The representation levels of women, youth, and rural residents are evaluated.

This helps identify underrepresented or excluded groups in decision-making processes.
4. Equity-Based Investment Distribution Analysis

The city's climate-related budget and investment plans are analyzed through an equity lens.

Key evaluation questions include:

Are renewable energy projects concentrated only in industrial zones?

Are energy subsidies equitably reaching all income groups?
Monitoring and Reporting Systems

The Sustainable Energy and Climate Action Plan (SECAP) provides a monitoring framework that tracks both environmental and social impacts of climate actions.

Regular impact assessment reports include indicators related to social equity and inclusiveness.
Civil Society and Stakeholder Feedback

Feedback from NGOs, academic institutions, and the local community is used to assess whether climate projects are implemented fairly and effectively.

This feedback informs adjustments and improvements in ongoing and future climate initiatives.

Evidence and Details of Actions Taken by Gaziantep to Ensure Fair and Inclusive Climate Action

Gaziantep Metropolitan Municipality has taken several concrete actions to ensure that its climate initiatives are implemented in a fair and inclusive manner. These actions aim to reduce inequalities, include vulnerable groups in the transition, and ensure that the benefits of climate action reach all segments of society.

Below are key examples and sources of evidence demonstrating Gaziantep's efforts:

1.Climate Awareness and Education Activities

As part of “Climate Action Week,” Gaziantep organized a large-scale educational event targeting 400 students. Children received education on climate change, nature, energy, and water efficiency. They also participated in upcycling workshops, promoting practical awareness of sustainability.

Impact: This initiative fosters long-term inclusion by raising climate awareness among younger generations.

2.🏢 Gender-Responsive Decarbonization Plan for the Building Sector

Gaziantep implemented a Building Sector Decarbonization Action Plan, which addresses transformative actions under four key pillars: policy, finance, technology, and technical capacity/awareness.

Importantly, the plan includes “gender equality” as a cross-cutting theme, aiming to integrate inclusive development and stakeholder coordination into technical planning.

Impact: Embeds social and gender equity considerations in climate-related infrastructure decisions.

3. Inclusive Stakeholder Engagement in Climate Planning

Through its Sustainable Energy and Climate Action Plan (SECAP), Gaziantep conducted:

Citywide emissions inventory assessments,

Risk and vulnerability analyses,

And held inclusive workshops focusing on the building sector and climate adaptation.

These processes aimed to include a wide range of stakeholders and strengthen inclusivity in decision-making.

Impact: Diverse groups contributed to the planning process, improving ownership and equity.

4. Civil Society & International Cooperation

Gaziantep has actively engaged in national and international partnerships to strengthen its climate governance. Examples include:

As early as 2011, climate action plan workshops were held with the French Development Agency (AFD), Gaziantep University, and other stakeholders.

Gaziantep also joined the EBRD Green Cities Program, where 31 priority green actions were defined, focusing on both carbon reduction and quality of life improvements.

Impact: Strengthens equity by integrating global best practices and inclusive urban planning.

Kraków implements its pro-climate activities, ensuring equitable and inclusive distribution of climate actions. This is achieved in several ways:
- Climate education is addressed to all groups of Krakow residents. Starting with educational materials for children, through meetings with primary and secondary school students, ending with dedicated activities (climatic walks and workshops) for seniors.
- RES support programs concern people who cannot afford to finance these energy sources on their own.
- We are increasingly ensuring the participation of all residents through consultations, cooperation, civic budget and citizen assemblies; participants of citizen assemblies were chosen randomly, in accordance with statistic data: proper percentage of women and men, of all age groups, education levels, etc.
- Climate projects and events are organized in different places in Krakow to ensure easy access for the residents. Area activities are addressed to districts that are used by wide representation of residents - the Climate Quarter project concerns a district attractive for citizens and tourists, where Cracovians from all districts spend their time.
column19: Krakow strongly engages citizens in actions aiming at reduction of climate change: organizes citizens' assemblies (the first city in Poland to organize two assemblies; first assembly in 2021 was about climate, the second in 2023 about city mobility), carries experiments, pilot projects, engages residents to submit projects in the citizen budget (in 2022: 8,3M EUR, 185 selected for realization; in 2023: 8,3M EUR, 144 projects; in 2024: 10,5M EUR, 163 projects).\nMunicipality currently implements three grant programs targeted at Krakow residents. - Program for the development of RES in the area of the Municipality of Krakow, under which residents can obtain subsidies for the installation of solar collectors, heat pumps, photovoltaic installations. The largest share of renewable energy installations carried out with funding from the City of Krakow by the end of 2022 is held by photovoltaic installations (45.54%, 1,542 units). Slightly smaller shares are held by air-source heat pumps (32.31%, 1,094 units) and solar collectors (21.74%, 736 units). Ground-source heat pumps are by far the least common in Krakow, with only 0.4% (14 units). According to available information, by the end of 2022, a total of 10,049 photovoltaic micro-installations had been installed within the Municipality of Krakow. In 2023, another edition of the Renewable Energy Development Program took place in the Municipality of Krakow. A total of 165 projects were completed, including 113 photovoltaic installations, 7 solar collector installations, and 38 heat pumps. Additionally, 9 energy storage systems, 5 energy management systems, and 8 electric vehicle charging stations were implemented. The total amount of subsidies granted amounted to 482.7 thousand EUR. - Thermo-modernization program for single-family buildings for the City of Krakow, under which residents can obtain a subsidy for carrying out thermo-modernization works that will improve the energy efficiency of buildings, and reduce the costs of energy. Since 2018, 450 single-family houses received thermal modernization. The total amount of support granted is almost EUR 3,8 million. In 2023, there was no call for applications for the Thermal Modernisation Programme for Single-Family Buildings for the City of Krakow, due to the lack of financial resources for this purpose (funding was paid for two subsidies from 2020 for a total amount of 15,714 EUR.- In 2023, as part of the Low-Emission Economy Plan, financial expenditures were made for the thermal modernization of educational buildings, amounting to 346,242 EUR. In 2021, a citizens' assembly was held on climate protection, energy efficiency and the use of renewable energy. It resulted with 32 binding recommendations. The most important one concerns the preparation of the Krakow Climate Strategy by the end of 2022, presenting a plan to achieve climate neutrality, assuming at least a 30% reduction in greenhouse gas emissions by 2030 compared to 2018, at least 80% emission reduction by 2040 and achieving climate neutrality no later than 2050.\n

Mejora de la eficiencia energética y reducción de costos operativos: La modernización del alumbrado público, la implementación de tecnologías eficientes y la promoción de edificaciones sostenibles generan ahorros significativos y reducen emisiones.
Fortalecimiento de la resiliencia hídrica: La optimización del riego, la incorporación de especies nativas o de bajo requerimiento hídrico a través de corredores biológicos e islas de biodiversidad.
Reducción de la isla de calor urbana: A través de la conservación del arbolado, la creación de corredores verdes y el diseño bioclimático.
Impulso a la movilidad sostenible: La ampliación de redes de ciclovías y la promoción del transporte limpio generan beneficios ambientales y reducen la congestión.
Atractivo turístico y urbano: Las mejoras en calidad ambiental, paisaje urbano y sostenibilidad fortalecen la competitividad de Mendoza como destino turístico y ciudad atractiva para inversiones.
Promoción del empleo verde: Proyectos de eficiencia energética, energías renovables, economía circular y gestión de residuos generan oportunidades laborales y fomentan nuevos sectores económicos.
Acceso a financiamiento climático: La adopción de políticas alineadas con estándares internacionales permite acceder a fondos, cooperación técnica y financiamiento externo para proyectos de alto impacto.
