We can share some examples:
1. The Municipality of Almada created a concept of Renewable Energy Centers in which municipal buildings are grouped together so that solar production is redistributed among them more effectively. Part of the surpluses produced are transferred to disadvantaged communities within the area of action. The transfer process to 124 families in NER3VALES is currently in the final phase. The creation of a new NER ALMADACENTRO is underway, which will cover around 100 more families living in social housing nearby.
2. We are developing an innovative concept in the area of circular economy in a part of the city, Bairro Circular. Bairro Circular is a locally based initiative, located in the city of Almada, focused on Mercado das Torcatas, which aims to transform the community into an example of good sustainability and circular economy practices. With its dynamic development, Bairro Circular will be a space demonstrating the concepts present in the municipal Roadmap for Circular Action 2030.
This area of the city shows signs of an aging population and some economic stagnation, factors that increase its sensitivity to climate change, and which we intend to alleviate.
The Torcatas Market will be used as a space demonstrating circularity (itself circular), where we will centralize regular circular activities, such as events, training, workshops and fairs.
The Circular Neighborhood is also a space for the entire community: families, businesses, associations, schools and other local organizations that want to contribute to a more circular, collaborative and environmentally conscious economy. The objective is to create a network that involves people of all ages, origins and contexts, promoting interaction between different generations and cultures.
Whether to learn, share ideas, transform practices, or simply be part of a more connected and sustainable community, Bairro Circular is open to everyone:
• Families who want to explore and implement more ecological lifestyle habits;
• Entrepreneurs and businesses interested in developing more sustainable and innovative solutions for their businesses;
• Schools and associations that wish to get involved in educational and community projects;
• Individual citizens, motivated to contribute to a more sustainable and active neighborhood;

To empower businesses with knowledge and tools associated with the concepts of circularity when applied to their own economic activities, and promote the adoption of sustainable practices, free and personalized training actions will be carried out with the support of a specialized company, where they will be passed on knowledge about circular economy concepts, resource management and waste reduction, energy efficiency, and sustainable marketing.
Almada Municipality will award a seal of recognition to participating traders, who will differentiate themselves, attracting more environmentally conscious customers.

In a central area of the city identified as especially vulnerable to the effect of the Urban Heat Island due to the accentuated aging of its population, a project co-financed by the European LIFE program is underway which aims to increase green areas and tree planting, unpave, create areas of shadow, etc.

O Município de Matosinhos tem vindo a identificar várias oportunidades e benefícios na ação climática, de que são exemplo:
. Oportunidades Económicas - (a) Crescimento de Novos Setores: A transição para uma economia de baixo carbono pode estimular o crescimento de setores emergentes, como energias renováveis, eficiência energética, mobilidade elétrica e tecnologias verdes. Isso pode gerar novos empregos e atrair novos investimentos para a região. 
(b) Inovação e Competitividade: A adoção de práticas e tecnologias sustentáveis pode posicionar Matosinhos como um líder em inovação verde, aumentando a competitividade das empresas locais tanto no mercado nacional quanto internacional. Matosinhos tem explorado esta oportunidade com programas de incubação de ideias como: 
O projeto BluAct é um projeto que teve a sua génese na rede URBACT (que é um programa europeu de aprendizagem e troca de experiências na promoção do desenvolvimento urbano sustentável) e seguiu o exemplo da cidade grega de Piraeus, que implementou, em 2018, um concurso para apoiar o empreendedorismo sustentável em investimentos relacionados com a economia azul.
Matosinhos avança para a 4.ª edição do projeto. Desde 2018 já passaram pelo programa 21 projetos e destes, 9 foram incubados nas instalações da UPTEC MAR em Leça da Palmeira. Estão estimados volumes de negócio que rondam os 2 milhões de euros anuais.
O Colmeia, programa de inovação colaborativa desenvolvido pela Galp e a Câmara Municipal de Matosinhos, foi lançado oficialmente no QSP SUMMIT. O Colmeia é um programa visa impulsionar o empreendedorismo e a transição energética em Matosinhos , reunindo talento, start-ups e toda a comunidade em torno de soluções sustentáveis.
Matosinhos é parceiro na edição nacional do Climate Launchpad, é a maior competição de ideias cleantech do mundo. Já concorreram 79 equipas com 153 ideias de negócio submetidas e 4 vencedores Europeus.
. Turismo Sustentável - A promoção de iniciativas de turismo sustentável pode atrair visitantes interessados em práticas ecológicas, contribuindo para a economia local de forma sustentável.
. Benefícios Ambientais - (a) Melhoria da Qualidade do Ar: A redução das emissões de gases poluentes pode levar a uma melhoria significativa na qualidade do ar, resultando em benefícios para a saúde pública e bem-estar dos residentes.
(b) Conservação dos Recursos Naturais: A adoção de práticas sustentáveis pode ajudar na conservação dos recursos naturais locais, preservando a biodiversidade e os ecossistemas da região.
(c) Redução da Pegada Ecológica: A implementação de políticas de redução de carbono pode ajudar Matosinhos a reduzir sua pegada ecológica, contribuindo para a mitigação das mudanças climáticas globais.
. Benefícios Sociais: (a) Melhoria da Saúde Pública: A diminuição da poluição do ar e a promoção de modos de vida mais sustentáveis podem resultar em melhorias significativas na saúde pública, reduzindo a incidência de doenças respiratórias e outras condições associadas com a poluição.
(b) Cidades Mais Vivas e Sustentáveis: Iniciativas como o aumento de espaços verdes urbanos, promoção de transportes públicos e mobilidade ativa (como ciclismo e caminhadas) podem tornar a cidade mais agradável e habitável.
(c) Inclusão e Justiça Social: As ações climáticas bem planeadas podem garantir que todos os segmentos da sociedade beneficiem das mudanças, promovendo a inclusão social e a justiça ambiental.
(d) Qualidade de Vida: As ações climáticas podem resultar numa melhoria geral da qualidade de vida, com cidades mais limpas, saudáveis e prósperas.

A quantificação da ação climática foi prevista aquando do planeamento estratégico do PAESC/SECAP “Sustainable Energy and Climate Action Plan”. Este plano inclui várias medidas de adaptação e mitigação às alterações climáticas sendo que cada uma delas tem prevista uma metodologia de implementação e uma metodologia de monitorização articulada com indicadores de realização. Cada medida está igualmente enquadrada em vários setores estratégicos nomeadamente: Ordenamento do território e cidades, Recursos Hídricos, Segurança de Pessoas e Bens, Saúde, Energia e Industria, Biodiversidade, Agricultura florestas e pescas, Turismo e, por fim, Zona Costeira; assegurando assim a equitabilidade e inclusão das mesmas. 
Esta metodologia faz também parte do Plano Municipal de Ação Climática de Matosinhos (PMAC), desenvolvido este ano, no qual se concentram as diferentes políticas locais em matéria de mitigação, adaptação, erradicação da pobreza energética e promoção da qualidade de vida e bem-estar do Município. 
O modelo de monitorização contempla a avaliação, revisão e eventual introdução de novas medidas que possam surgir como úteis, existindo um sistema de monitorização focado na vertente da Mitigação, por ser aquela que melhor acompanha a meta da descarbonização. Por sua vez, as medidas de adaptação continuarão a ser acompanhadas conforme o plano de monitorização correspondente, estabelecido no âmbito do PAESC Matosinhos 2030.
Na vertente de adaptação a avaliação de riscos focou-se nas vulnerabilidades do Município de Matosinhos, atendendo inclusive à sua dispersão e ou frequência geográfica. As principais alterações projetadas poderão agravar, minorar ou manter as atuais vulnerabilidades climáticas do território concelhio. Estas alterações poderão ainda potenciar o aparecimento e desenvolvimento de outras vulnerabilidades e riscos, nas áreas e setores já afetados atualmente ou em novos a identificar. 
As alterações climáticas têm o potencial de aumentar a desigualdade social, afetando de forma desproporcional as comunidades mais vulneráveis. Por este motivo, o Município considera fundamental atuar sobre as vulnerabilidades de maior risco, com uma atuação transversal a toda a população, mas que de forma indireta garante a proteção das populações mais vulneráveis sujeitas a maior risco. 
A monitorização da componente de Mitigação desenvolve-se maioritariamente com recurso a informação sobre a utilização de energia e emissões de GEE, bem como ao nível da implementação de ações e medidas. As bases de informação para a realização da sua monitorização são essencialmente de fontes estatísticas, disponibilizadas publicamente, complementadas com informação de base local, sempre que seja possível recolher essa informação junto de diferentes atores, tendo em atenção o respeito pela privacidade da sua informação.
Por sua vez, no domínio da energia, Matosinhos elaborou em 2024 o Plano Municipal de Ação para a Mitigação da Pobreza Energética. Este Plano surge como consequência das diretivas europeias e da Estratégia Nacional de Longo Prazo para o Combate à Pobreza Energética 2023-2050 (ELPPE) que tem como principal objetivo erradicar a pobreza energética em Portugal até 2050, protegendo os consumidores vulneráveis e integrando-os de forma ativa na transição energética e climática nacional.
Este plano pretendeu promover a articulação da temática da pobreza energética na ação climática do Município de Matosinhos, nomeadamente como complemento ao Roteiro para a Neutralidade Carbónica Matosinhos 2030, enquadrando os principais planos e estratégias europeus, nacionais e locais nesta matéria. O mesmo possui uma componente de diagnóstico importante à identificação da extensão desta problemática no Município, identificando a população em risco, a extensão da vulnerabilidade e o mapeamento de entidades de interesse. 
Este documento apresenta uma proposta de plano de ação a promover a curto prazo (até 2030) e objetivos estratégicos de erradicação a médio e longo prazo (2040 e 2050), com mapeamento de iniciativas em curso e proposta de indicadores de avaliação de impacto, cronograma de implementação e identificação de entidades responsáveis pela respetiva implementação.
A par das demais estratégias possui também uma metodologia para acompanhamento e gestão de atividades com vista a garantir o sucesso da sua implementação, assim como a coordenação das partes envolvidas e a avaliação do impacto das ações propostas. Esta monitorização depende de um conjunto de dados de base estatística, bem como de informação local sobre os níveis de conforto e/ou desconforto térmico ou capacidade financeira para manter as habitações adequadamente aquecidas ou frescas. 
Neste sentido, é reforçado o compromisso com o qual o Município de Matosinhos pactua: o compromisso de não deixar ninguém para trás no processo da transição energética e caminho para a Neutralidade Carbónica (The pledge to leave no one behind).
column19:
A garantia de uma distribuição equitativa e inclusiva na ação climática é um dos desafios da resposta às alterações climáticas, contudo, esta é uma importante preocupação para assegurar que todos tem acesso a medidas de mitigação e adaptação independentemente das respetivas condições socioeconómicas.
Esta é também uma das preocupações do Município de Matosinhos que, de forma a garantir uma atuação equitativa e inclusiva elaborou, este ano 2024, o Plano Municipal de Ação para a Mitigação da Pobreza Energética, o qual pretende integrar as populações mais vulneráveis de forma ativa na transição energética. Este Plano é composto por um conjunto de medidas de ação que pretendem proteger e salvaguardar estes consumidores do risco de pobreza energética. 
O instrumento debruça a sua ação sobre 4 eixos: habitação, acesso a serviços de energia, implementação de uma ação territorial integrada e a aposta no conhecimento como forma de informar para o processo de decisão. As várias medidas pretendem: (I) aumentar o conforto térmico das residências, diminuir consumos energéticos através da promoção da eficiência energética, promover a produção de energia renovável,(II) assegurar o acesso ininterrupto a serviços de energia, (III) reforçar a ação das estruturas locais no combate à pobreza energética e (IV) capacitar os atores locais, aumentar a literacia energética de diferentes públicos-alvo, estimular a investigação e robustecer a oferta formativa em domínios deste compto. 
Para apoiar diretamente os cidadãos a implementar medidas de eficiência energética nas suas habitações e melhorar as suas condições de habitabilidade, Matosinhos disponibiliza, desde novembro de 2022, um balcão único (one-stop-shop) digital e físico denominado Matosinhos Energy Hub. Este balcão, desenvolvido no âmbito do projeto Porto Energy ElevatoR (PEER), financiado pelo programa Horizonte 2020 e coordenado pela Agência de Energia do Porto, compreende o aconselhamento acerca de soluções de eficiência energética e de energias renováveis, legislação aplicável, identificação de oportunidades e apoio a candidaturas para financiamento. É um exemplo concreto da atuação do Município de Matosinhos em prol da garantia da equidade e inclusividade nas políticas em prol do clima. No ano de 2023, foram feitos 49 pedidos de avaliação de potencial (inquéritos respondidos) e 41 atendimentos técnicos.
Também o projeto ATELIER que tem como objetivo contribuir para o desenho de cidades inteligentes, energeticamente eficientes, com planos de mobilidade sustentável e com integração de soluções de produção de energia renovável é desenvolvido numa área de intervenção com populações mais vulneráveis. Este projeto atua sobre o Conjunto Habitacional de Custió (Bairro Social) e estende-se ao troço do Rio Leça entre a Ponte da Pedra e a Ponte do Carro. 
A participação no ATELIER complementa as ações iniciadas em 2018 no Living Lab de Matosinhos, um projeto financiado pelo Fundo Ambiental, no qual foram desenvolvidas um conjunto de iniciativas de cocriação e inovação aberta com o objetivo de desenvolvimento de um espaço de teste, experimentação, e demonstração, em contexto real, de soluções tecnológicas, organizacionais e sociais integradas na intersecção entre mobilidade, energia, ambiente, edifícios e conectividade orientadas para a descarbonização da cidade. 
Outro exemplo pode ser dado através do projeto PROLIGHT. Um dos objetivos deste projeto compreende a implementação de uma solução de produção de energia renovável, através da implementação de painéis fotovoltaicos no Bairro de Carcavelos, com o objetivo final de poder dar origem a uma comunidade de energia renovável. Pretende-se através do envolvimento da comunidade e do desenvolvimento dos investimentos necessários poder beneficiar a população vulnerável deste Bairro, disponibilizando energia renovável a custos mais acessíveis. É também uma maneira de combate à pobreza energética desta comunidade. 
O próprio Laboratório de Cidadania pela Transição Climática promovido aquando do desenvolvimento do Roteiro de Neutralidade Carbónica de Matosinhos 2030 é um relevante exemplo de envolvimento da comunidade e de oportunidade de participação ativa de todos os cidadãos. 
A Câmara Municipal de Matosinhos implementou também medidas de promoção do transporte público, através da gratuitidade e ou redução tarifária, complementares às já existentes para jovens estudantes entre os 4 e os 23 anos, nomeadamente para os jovens com idade igual ou superior a 13 anos a estudar no concelho, reforçando a aposta no fomento da utilização do transporte coletivo como peça fundamental para a descarbonização. 
Poderá ainda destacar-se a abrangência do Mecanismo para uma Transição Justa ao território de Matosinhos o qual beneficiará as populações e empresas mais afetadas pela transição para uma economia hipocarbónica.

Como cidade histórica, Évora deve assegurar que as iniciativas de eficiência energética e renovação não comprometam o seu património cultural. A implementação de tecnologias inovadoras que respeitem a integridade patrimonial é fundamental, mas frequentemente encontra limitações regulamentares.
No centro Histórico de Évora muitas famílias enfrentam grandes dificuldades para melhorar a eficiência energética das suas habitações, o que as torna vulneráveis à pobreza energética. A necessidade de intervenções em edifícios antigos, que devem respeitar o património, aumenta os custos das melhorias. Assim, é crucial disponibilizar apoios financeiros a nível europeu e nacional para garantir uma transição justa e acessível.
O município de Évora é parceiro do projeto POCITYF - A Positive Energy CITY Transformation Framework, cujo objetivo é auxiliar as cidades históricas a tornarem-se mais verdes e mais inteligentes, respeitando ao mesmo tempo o seu património cultural e social.
Este projeto promove a redução de emissões poluentes e de Gases com Efeito de Estufa, através de uma rede de soluções tecnológicas inovadoras, contribuindo para a produção de energia limpa e para a descarbonização das cidades históricas. A implementação dessas soluções está associada ao envolvimento ativo dos cidadãos e à sua participação direta na tomada de decisões e no desenvolvimento sustentável do território.

Climate action led by Cascais Municipality represents a strategic opportunity to advance sustainable development, improve quality of life, and enhance urban resilience. In addition to reducing greenhouse gas emissions, Cascais's climate policies deliver broader benefits across several areas:

Improved quality of life: Cascais is expanding urban green areas through initiatives like the “Corredores Verdes” (Green Corridors), increasing access to nature and promoting thermal comfort in urban areas. Energy efficiency upgrades in municipal buildings and social housing also improve indoor comfort and reduce energy poverty.

Urban resilience and risk reduction: Climate adaptation measures are integrated into land use and coastal planning. Projects such as the “Duna da Cresmina” ecosystem restoration a help buffer storm surges and rising sea levels, protecting infrastructure and public spaces.

Sustainable mobility: Cascais has implemented a free public transport network (“MobiCascais”) that encourages modal shift and reduces car dependency. It is complemented by an integrated bike-sharing system and investments in pedestrian-friendly infrastructure, improving air quality and reducing congestion.

Green economy and innovation: The transition to a low-carbon economy supports new job creation in energy, mobility, and circular economy sectors. Cascais has invested in renewable energy, including installing solar PV panels on public buildings, and promotes eco-innovation through hubs like DNA Cascais, supporting green startups.

Citizen engagement and social cohesion: Through tools like the “Orçamento Participativo Jovem” (Youth Participatory Budget) and “Academia Jovem” (Youth Academy), Cascais empowers residents to shape climate and sustainability projects. Educational programs in schools and community centers raise awareness and build climate literacy.

Resource efficiency and circular economy: The municipality is improving water and waste management through smart monitoring systems and promoting reuse. 

Biodiversity and ecosystem services: Nature-based solutions are central to Cascais's approach. The municipality promote initiatives to plant native trees and create biodiversity corridors. Green infrastructure improves water retention, reduces flood risk, and enhances air quality.

Institutional capacity and collaboration: Cascais applies data-driven decision-making using tools like the “City Dashboard” to monitor sustainability indicators. Climate governance is cross-sectoral and integrated with national and European strategies, ensuring policy alignment and leveraging external funding opportunities.

International cooperation and visibility: Cascais is an active member of networks such as the Covenant of Mayors and reports annually to CDP, reinforcing transparency and commitment. These platforms foster knowledge exchange and position the municipality as a climate leader at the national and international levels.

In summary, climate action in Cascais generates wide-reaching co-benefits—improved health and comfort, increased equity, new green jobs, safer public spaces, and restored ecosystems. These actions strengthen the municipality's capacity to face climate challenges while building a more just, inclusive, and sustainable future for all.

Cascais Council is committed to ensuring that climate action delivers fair and inclusive benefits across all communities. To quantify and monitor the equitable distribution of climate initiatives, the municipality integrates social indicators, spatial analysis, and participatory tools in its planning and implementation processes.

Inclusive access to public services: Climate-related programs are designed to reduce inequality. For example, the free public transport system (MobiCascais) guarantees equitable access to mobility regardless of income, while energy efficiency upgrades in social housing target households vulnerable to energy poverty, helping reduce both emissions and inequality.

Participatory budgeting and engagement: Cascais tracks inclusion through its Participatory Budget (including youth and senior editions), where residents propose and vote on local projects. Many winning proposals focus on sustainability and equity—such as tree planting in underserved areas or inclusive green spaces. Participation metrics are disaggregated to assess demographic reach.

Education and capacity building: The municipality implements climate education programs across age groups and communities, including schools, NGOs, and senior centers. Attendance and engagement are monitored to ensure broad inclusion, especially among youth and vulnerable populations.

Open data and indicators: Cascais maintains a public “City Dashboard” that provides access to key sustainability and social indicators, including mobility usage by parish, energy performance, and public space distribution. These metrics help evaluate the territorial and social reach of climate actions over time.

Engagement with vulnerable groups: The Council works with social services and local associations to involve marginalized groups—such as migrants, older adults, and people with disabilities—in climate planning. Co-designed workshops and consultations ensure that these groups' specific needs are reflected in adaptation and mitigation strategies.

Equity in funding allocation: The distribution of municipal climate investments is tracked to ensure a fair allocation across parishes and communities. Projects that combine environmental impact with social equity receive funding priority.

Resilient infrastructure planning: Coastal defense projects, flood mitigation systems, and public space improvements are implemented with a focus on equitable access and safety. Interventions in higher-risk or historically underserved areas are prioritized to prevent further disadvantage.

Measuring co-benefits: The municipality evaluates climate actions not only by emissions reductions but also by social outcomes—such as improved mobility access, reduced energy bills, increased green coverage, and participation rates. These co-benefits are key performance indicators in project evaluations.

By combining technical analysis with community engagement, Cascais Council ensures that climate action contributes to both environmental sustainability and social justice. Equity is not treated as a secondary benefit, but as a core outcome—measured, monitored, and integrated into decision-making at all levels.
column19:
Cascais Council integrates equity and inclusion as key principles in its climate strategy, ensuring that no group is left behind in the transition to a resilient, low-carbon future. Several actions and programs illustrate this commitment:

MobiCascais - Universal access to sustainable mobility:
Cascais offers a fully free public transport network for residents and students, removing financial barriers to low-carbon mobility. The system includes accessible buses, electric minibuses, and bike-sharing, improving mobility for low-income groups, youth, and elderly citizens. Usage data is disaggregated by parish to monitor access in all communities.

Energy efficiency for vulnerable households:
The Council conducts energy retrofitting of municipal and social housing, targeting residents in energy poverty. Interventions include insulation, efficient lighting, and solar thermal systems. Selection criteria prioritize households with low income, seniors, and large families. The program tracks energy bill reductions and comfort gains per household.

Participatory budgeting with equity lens:
Cascais has one of Portugal's most established Participatory Budget systems, including youth and senior editions. Proposals are accepted from all residents and are voted by the public. Many selected projects focus on improving green spaces, mobility, and infrastructure in underserved areas. The Council tracks geographic distribution of submitted and approved projects to ensure balance across the territory.

Inclusive green infrastructure planning:
Urban greening initiatives such as Corredores Verdes and Reflorestar Cascais are planned with socio-spatial equity in mind. Areas with low tree canopy, poor air quality, and social vulnerability are prioritized. Green corridors are designed for accessibility, with shade, seating, and paths adapted for people with reduced mobility.

Climate education and capacity building:
Programs like “Programa de Sensibilização e Educação Ambiental” engage students and young people in climate action, ensuring intergenerational inclusion. In parallel, workshops for senior citizens are held through local associations to raise awareness of climate risks and build adaptive capacity. The Council tracks participation rates to ensure broad demographic representation.

Co-creation with vulnerable communities:
Cascais works with local NGOs and social services to co-design climate actions with vulnerable groups. Examples include coastal adaptation workshops with residents in exposed areas, and focus groups with older adults to shape heatwave response plans. Feedback is integrated into municipal action plans.

Monitoring tools and transparency:
The City Dashboard (www.cascaisdata.pt) includes data on social vulnerability, energy use, transport, and green coverage. These indicators are used to evaluate the social distribution of climate benefits. The platform promotes transparency and allows the public to monitor progress and disparities.

Equitable funding and project prioritization:
The allocation of climate-related funding is assessed by project type, location, and expected social co-benefits. For example, investments in drainage and climate adaptation infrastructure are prioritized in flood-prone, socially vulnerable areas such as Bairro da Adroana or Alapraia. Equity is embedded in the scoring criteria for project selection.

Inclusive policy alignment:
Cascais's local climate planning is aligned with broader equity frameworks, including the Social Charter and the Local Housing Strategy. Climate policies are designed to contribute simultaneously to SDG 13 (climate action), SDG 10 (reduced inequalities), and SDG 11 (sustainable cities).

These actions show that Cascais does not view equity as a separate goal but as a guiding principle in climate action design, implementation, and monitoring. The Council ensures that vulnerable populations benefit from the transition, actively shaping a fair and inclusive response to climate change.

We also use GIS mapping to track and visualize where climate investments are being made, overlaying this with demographic data to assess whether resources are reaching communities that are historically underserved or most vulnerable to climate impacts.

As evidence of how we quantify and track the equitable and inclusive distribution of climate action, the City of Tempe is actively collecting and analyzing data across multiple programs and sectors. Below are several examples:

Mobile Home Retrofit Program:
We recently launched an energy efficiency retrofit program for mobile homes. As part of our evaluation, we are collecting energy usage and utility cost data for each household for one year before and one year after improvements. This will allow us to assess energy savings, cost reductions, and GHG emissions avoided. Once post-retrofit data is available, we will develop a comprehensive project report to include in future CDP disclosures.

Municipal Building Energy Tracking:
The City conducts annual energy assessments of municipal buildings to identify opportunities for retrocommissioning and energy efficiency upgrades. We are integrating data into EnergyCAP, a software platform that tracks energy consumption and demand response performance. This platform will allow us to publicly share energy usage trends over time and highlight buildings that have undergone improvements. The public-facing dashboard is expected to be live before our next CDP reporting cycle.

Tree Steward Program & Urban Forestry Goals:
Our Tree Steward Program supports the city's goal of achieving 25% tree and shade canopy coverage, with a focus on planting in heat-vulnerable neighborhoods. We are currently collecting data on tree planting locations and land surface temperatures to evaluate cooling impacts and progress toward canopy goals.

Heat Vulnerability and Climate Action Targeting:
We use Heat Priority Scores, which assess census tracts based on a combination of heat exposure, vulnerability, and adaptive capacity. These scores guide decisions on where to target climate resilience investments, such as tree planting, cooling infrastructure, or outreach. Fayetteville has identified multiple co-benefits of climate action that extend beyond emissions reduction, improving community well-being, economic resilience, and equity.

Public Health and Quality of Life

Expansion of active transportation infrastructure (bike lanes, trails, pedestrian networks) promotes physical activity, reducing chronic disease risk while lowering vehicle emissions and improving air quality.

Increased tree canopy and green space helps mitigate urban heat islands, provides shade, and improves mental health and community livability.

Cleaner air and water from reduced fossil fuel combustion and stronger stormwater management lower respiratory illnesses and enhance public health outcomes.

Economic Development and Jobs

Investment in renewable energy, building retrofits, and efficiency upgrades stimulates local job creation in construction, engineering, energy services, and clean technology.

Fayetteville's strong base of educational services and workforce development programs positions the community to retrain workers for emerging low-carbon industries, helping cushion the transition risks.

Energy performance contracting and utility savings reduce long-term operational costs, freeing resources for reinvestment in community services.

Social Equity and Community Resilience

Prioritizing climate equity ensures that low-income and vulnerable neighborhoods benefit first from energy efficiency programs, utility savings, improved mobility, and resilience investments.

The establishment of the Climate Refugee Resettlement Fund demonstrates Fayetteville's commitment to humanitarian leadership, preparing to provide support for displaced populations while reinforcing its designation as a Welcoming City.

Environmental Protection and Biodiversity

Land preservation, riparian restoration, and urban forestry expansion enhance biodiversity, protect natural habitats, and strengthen Fayetteville's ecosystem services (flood mitigation, carbon sequestration, soil stability).

Converting flood-prone lands into parks and conservation areas increases recreational opportunities while protecting property and infrastructure.

Civic Engagement and Reputation

Visible climate leadership builds community pride and trust, enhancing Fayetteville's reputation as a forward-looking, sustainable city within Arkansas and nationally.

Engaging boards, commissions, and community partners through regular oversight fosters collaboration and civic participation in shaping a resilient future.

Commitment to Equity
Fayetteville's Climate Action Plan embeds equity as a guiding principle, recognizing that climate risks and benefits are not evenly distributed. The City prioritizes low-income, historically underserved, and vulnerable populations when designing and implementing climate initiatives.

Measures in Place

Targeted Program Design: Energy efficiency programs, renewable energy incentives, and utility rebate opportunities are directed toward low-income households to reduce utility burden and improve housing comfort.

Transportation Equity: Investments in active transportation, transit, and safe pedestrian networks are concentrated in areas with higher mobility needs, improving access to jobs, schools, and healthcare while reducing reliance on single-occupancy vehicles.

Resilience and Public Health: Expansion of urban forestry and cooling infrastructure is targeted in neighborhoods most vulnerable to heat, helping address health disparities.

Waste and Recycling Access: Recycling and waste diversion programs are tailored to ensure equal access across neighborhoods, even amid community resistance to some system changes.

Climate Refugee Resettlement Fund (2021): Established through a resident donation, this trust fund channels resources to local organizations providing refugee resettlement services. It demonstrates Fayetteville's humanitarian leadership and ensures future displaced populations benefit equitably from community resources.

Annual Budget Allocation: The City allocates $100,000 annually for Climate Action Plan implementation, with equity outcomes explicitly considered when distributing funds across programs.

Governance and Oversight

Boards and Commissions (Environmental Action Committee, Active Transportation Committee, Urban Forestry Advisory Board, Parks & Recreation Advisory Board) meet monthly to ensure equity considerations are built into projects and planning.

Annual Sustainability Report and community GHG inventories provide transparency and allow the City Council and public to evaluate how climate benefits are reaching all parts of the community.
column19:
Fayetteville has developed processes to ensure that equity and inclusion are measured, tracked, and embedded in climate action planning and implementation. Data is collected, updated, and reviewed on an ongoing basis, with major integration points during annual reporting cycles, long-range planning reviews, and plan updates.

How Data is Quantified and Used

Annual Sustainability Reporting: Fayetteville produces an Annual Sustainability Report that compiles greenhouse gas inventories and highlights progress on equity-focused actions, including access to transit, energy burden reduction, and resilience measures.

GIS Mapping and Analysis: The City uses GIS tools to map low-income neighborhoods, flood-prone areas, and heat-vulnerable zones, allowing staff and decision-makers to identify where investments in climate resilience (e.g., stormwater infrastructure, nature-based solutions) will most directly benefit vulnerable populations. These maps are regularly updated and used when reviewing long-range plans, rezoning applications, or land acquisition for preservation and nature-based deployment.

Transit and Mobility Equity: The City measures transit ridership and accessibility, with fare-free public transit and expanded bus routes ensuring equal access across income levels. Data on ridership patterns and coverage informs future transportation and emissions reduction planning.

Inclusive Governance: Fayetteville collects and tracks participation data from boards and commissions, which are open to non-voting residents as a way to incorporate diverse voices, including immigrant and refugee populations, into climate decision-making.

Housing and Development Data: Developments like Willow Bend Housing are evaluated for their role in providing affordable housing in areas with access to green space and community services, ensuring climate and social co-benefits are equitably distributed.

CAP 2024 Equity Focus: The 2024 Climate Action Plan explicitly integrates nature-based solutions, green space access, and equity prioritization. Data from GIS and demographic analysis is used to guide where investments in parks, tree canopy, and flood mitigation should occur first, ensuring underserved areas receive benefits early.

When Data is Collected and Reviewed

Monthly: Boards and commissions meet monthly to evaluate ongoing projects and equity considerations.

Annually: Data is compiled into the Annual Sustainability Report and greenhouse gas inventories, reviewed by Council and the public.

Every 5 Years: The Climate Action Plan undergoes a full update with a comprehensive equity review, informed by community data, GIS analysis, and public engagement.

column19: Although we are all negatively impacted by climate change, Black, Indigenous, and People of Color (BIPOC) are disproportionately impacted and aren't genuinely represented in the current environmental and climate change movement. The C4 vision is that, BIPOC and historically white environmental organizations will dismantle extractive systems and build new systems to combat climate change - centered in human wellbeing, the interconnectedness of life, and access to shared leadership. With a leadership team of 23 and led by BIPOC co-chairs, the City of Grand Rapids is one collaborating partner with 2 leadership team members. E.H.Zero will co-create with community policies and programs to equitably decarbonize Grand Rapids residential and commercial buildings and present them to Commission for consideration and hopeful adoption. column16: The actions laid out in the Framework are aligned with a “low-carbon pathway” that creates the best possible economic and co-benefits for the community, while balancing the need to minimize the negative effects of climate change and optimizing Regina's competitive advantage amongst other Canadian cities. The “low carbon-pathway” consists of “Seven Big” moves and summary of these and associated environmental, social and economic opportunities is provided below: Big Move 1: Building Retrofits: Retrofitting buildings presents a significant opportunity to achieve reductions in both energy consumption and GHG emissions. Retrofitting buildings also creates local jobs and generates cost savings for households and businesses. This big move has the potential to generate 5-10 person years of employment per million invested and contribute to enhanced equity.Big Move 2: Clean Heating: Most of the emissions from buildings in Regina currently come from natural gas used for space and water heating. In the future, new and retrofitted buildings will need to use more efficient and cleaner space and water heating systems. This is realized by switching out fuel heating systems to electric systems. Switching to clean heating (i.e heat pumps) can reduce utility bills because these systems are more efficient than most other traditional systems. This means that less energy can be used for heating and cooling a space, which translates into utility savings.Big Move 3: Net-Zero New Construction: Buildings and the heating and cooling systems within them are long-lasting assets. Encouraging net-zero new construction now means that fewer new buildings will be contributing to GHG emissions in the community, and fewer buildings will need to be retrofitted in the future. This also allows building owners and/or tenants to begin generating operational savings from lower utility bills right away and maximizes other co-benefits such as indoor air quality. This big move has the potential to generate 5-10 person years of employment per million invested.Big Move 4: Renewable Energy Generation: One of the most significant low-carbon transition opportunities the community can pursue is to increase renewable energy generation. Moving to these sources will allow the community to decrease emissions from the electricity grid, which is directly related to emissions levels from electricity use in homes and businesses and in electric vehicles. It also maximizes the emissions reduction benefits of building retrofits and fuel-switching. Wind, solar and hydropower produce little or no air pollution, therefore renewable energy generation translates into important health co-benefits. Local solar PV generation has the potential to generate above 10 person years of employment per million invested.Big Move 5: Low-Emissions Vehicles: Regina's transportation sector makes up 23 per cent of community emissions on a yearly basis. While not all vehicle trips can be avoided, there are viable alternatives to gasoline-fueled vehicles, which contributes to reduced emissions. Other benefits of low-emissions vehicles are that they are more efficient than gasoline- and diesel-powered vehicles, so they use less energy overall, and the ongoing operation and maintenance costs tend to be lower. In addition, Big Move 6: Increase Active Transportation and Transit Use: Efforts to increase transit use, walking, and cycling will be critical to reducing emissions from transportation. Active transportation provides many co-benefits related to health and community well-being. Expanding transit enhances equity , as it becomes accessible for more people. Also, this action has the potential to generate more than 10 person years of employment per million invested. Other specific actions within this big move such as transportation demand management and increase active transportation have the potential to generate 5-10 person years of employment per million invested. Big Move 7: Cleaning and Re-energizing Industry: -Regina's industrial sector represents one- third of energy consumption and GHG emissions in the community. The City is committed to continue its positive dialogue with industry stakeholders to encourage industry to consider their energy transition and to work together on solutions to mitigate the economic risk associated with the transition to a low-carbon economy. This big move has the potential to generate 5-10 person years of employment per million investedOverall, implementation of the Framework is expected to generate over 120,000 person-years of employment between now and 2050. This is equivalent to over 4,000 full-time equivalent jobs per year existing in the community, beyond job projections in the business-as-planned scenario. Expanding transit will generate more sustained employment than any other action. Building retrofits and solar PV installations will create an employment boom over the next decade and a half.

Currently our Municipality is not quantifying equitable distribution of climate actions, however we are in the process to set up measures and indicators. 

It should be noted that while reducing GHG emissions is the core goal of the Energy & Sustainability Framework (ESF) and the primary performance indicator, the City also measures success through a broader set of co-benefits and qualitative indicators that reflect social, environmental, and economic outcomes.

These include:

-Equity and inclusion, which were considered extensively in the development of the ESF and continue to be a key parameter when designing and evaluating community-facing initiatives such as the Property Assessed Clean Energy Program (PACE).

-Consideration of how programs impact vulnerable populations, frontline staff, and residents who may be disproportionately affected by climate hazards.

-Alignment with the Corporate Climate Adaptation Strategy, which incorporates equity and Indigenous worldviews to ensure resilience-building actions do not leave behind those most at risk.

Through this approach, the City is advancing beyond emissions accounting to capture the broader social and equity outcomes of climate action, which will become more formalized as indicators and tracking systems are developed.
column19: Community and stakeholder engagement was a vital component of developing the Energy & Sustainability Framework. Extensive input from the community was sought to ensure the unique conditions, constraints and community voices in Regina were heard and understood. The plan was influenced by input from: •A Community Advisory Group made up of community members from different sectors. •An Internal Advisory Committee made up of cross-departmental staff from the City of Regina.•Discussions with Regina's residents using a variety of outreach techniques and formats. •Research on best practice. Sustainability Solutions Group expertise from working with other municipalities across Canada. Meeting recordings and working drafts were regularly published on the City's public engagement platform Be Heard Regina, for the public to review and stay informed. Further information on engagement can be found in The Community Lens section of the Framework. Equity was a specific focus of engagement. For example, efforts were made to reach groups particularly impacted, or who may be underrepresented, such as youth. This included a virtual student forum to understand the benefits and challenges of potential actions from the perspective of youth in our community. The series of focus groups and interviews facilitated by Sustainability Solutions Group (SSG) included discussion on how the potential actions could be accomplished in an equitable manner, and there were also specific focus group sessions with equity-seeking groups and labour groups. Another example of how the plan is addressing equity is through Big Move #6 - Increase Active Transportation and Transit Use. Equity in transit is related to the general accessibility of the service to all populations, and the right to feel safe while navigating Regina. Providing reliable transportation to residents who cannot afford or prefer not to have their own vehicle plays an important role in reducing GHG emissions by creating a path towards an inclusive and less car-reliant community. In addition, the Framework provides projected cost savings to all residents from reduced energy expenses. In 2020, household energy expenditures were $6,333 and are estimated at $4,06 in 2050 after full implementation of the “low carbon pathway”.The development of the Framework is just the start of community and stakeholder engagement. As this is a community plan, residents and all sectors in the community will want to further explore what does the plan mean to them, how are they impacted and how do they benefit from it. Administration is committed to work with residents and the community to collectively answer these questions throughout the implementation of the “low-carbon pathway” as laid out in framework. Ensuring that programs are accessible to all segments of the community will be a significant focus of the implementation phase.

In 2020, Mayor Kincannon convened the Mayor's Climate Council to identify and evaluate strategies to achieve the community-wide emission reduction goal established by City Council in 2019. The cross-sector group of over 65 members included clean energy experts, conservation activists, advocates for equity, neighborhood representatives,
developers, business leaders, utility representatives, and more.

Council members and working groups (transportation, buildings/energy, waste, and equity) evaluated dozens of proven high-impact strategies for their impact to climate, economy, and community. Specifically, strategies were ranked based not only on emission reduction but also impact on equity and other societal benefits (air quality, public health, mobility and access, housing affordability, human services, and civic engagement). The strategies ranked highest by the Council across transportation, buildings/energy, and waste formed the basis for the City's 2021 Energy & Sustainability Work Plan, which directs the Office of Sustainability's work and more. These strategies include:
- Expand and improve bicycle and pedestrian facilities, connectivity, convenience, and/or safety in a manner that significantly increases the number of trips taken by walking or biking
- Make public transit investments that significantly enhance coverage, service quality, frequency, and/or speed
- Significantly accelerate community adoption of electric vehicles
- Partner with major local commercial fleet operators to transition to electric vehicles
- Create voluntary large, commercial, and multi-family energy upgrade program(s) (eg. incentives, technical assistance) that achieve deep energy savings (~25%+) in ~20%+ of buildings
- Amplify and opportunistically expand voluntary home energy upgrade program(s) that will achieve deep energy savings (~25%+) in 20% of homes
- Develop or amplify opportunities to invest in renewables at scale, including community solar and in-valley investments
- Research and develop strategies to promote opportunistic electrification (eg. replacement of fossil fuel-fired furnaces with electric heat pump technologies) in existing buildings over time
- Pursue food waste reduction and collection programs that capture ~80%+ of organic waste from all high-volume locations (eg. restaurants)
- Increase residential recycling through community engagement and education strategies
- Promote consumption-reduction approaches such as sharing and re-use through education campaigns
- Research pathways to offer organics (food/yard waste) collection for single-family and multi-family residential properties

Beyond the work plan, the City's Office of Sustainability continuously seeks opportunities to educate and engage other departments on the climate impacts and wider benefits related to their work. For example, staff provided technical assistance to the regional transit agency by calculating air quality and public health impacts of bus electrification.

In 2023, the City was awarded a Climate Pollution Reduction Grant from the EPA to lead a regional climate planning process for the 9-county metro area. The City is currently convening technical working groups (including a dedicated Equity group) and evaluating all climate actions for social, economic, and other factors beyond emissions reductions.

column19: Sustainability and Climate Action, and Equity, are two of the five main guiding principles in Envision Lakewood 2040, which means that the city's short and long-term goals and strategies integrate these principles in all aspects of its projects, from planning through completion. In 2024 and 2025, the City collaborated with the Jefferson County Health Department to provide no-cost home weatherization improvements to several residents living in one of Lakewood's manufactured home communities. The Jefferson County Hazard Mitigation Plan includes a detailed analysis of socially vulnerable geographic areas and populations in the county, including Lakewood. This has led to a Lakewood-specific Climate Hazard & Social Vulnerability Study. The study began in 2024 and evaluates the potential impacts of climate change on natural hazards that post the greatest risks to the city's residents, infrastructure, and economy, with particular focus on socially vulnerable communities. An extensive Tree Canopy Assessment completed in 2022 identifies areas of the City that will be targets for tree preservation and planting programs to reduce air pollution and urban heat island effects. The Hazard Mitigation Plan, Climate Hazard & Social Vulnerability Study, and Tree Canopy Assessment provide the data necessary to inform decision makers on how to prioritize resources and strategies to ensure that underserved populations benefit from the City's climate action work. column19: The Ciy developed a diversity, equity, and inclusivity lens after hiring a permanent DEI Advisor. DEI considerations are on a project-by-project basis to reflect on improving the outcomes of a project to incorporate inclusiveness and equity. Examples of ad hoc DEI lens usage include the following: Better Homes Peterborough, which is striving to financially support participants to lower household energy usage and also seeking to support rental property owners to participate in the program as well. Including rental properties can help low-income renters lower their energy bills and increase comfort after a renovation. Without this consideration for renters, a large segment of the population would be left out which would not be equitable for a City-funded program. Another example is the solar photovoltaic (PV) map that was created to enable all property owners to assess how suitable their buildings are for solar PV, with an estimation of the electricity savings provided. This free map will help businesses, homeowners, and rental property owners decide if pursuing renewable energy makes the most financial sense without the cost of a solar inspection (https://www.peterborough.ca/en/city-hall/climate-action-in-peterborough.aspx#Solar-Energy-Potential-Map). In addition, an integrated flood model that reviews all the sub-watersheds in Peterborough along with sewers, retention ponds, and LIDs correlated to the projected impacts of climate change is underway by the City. Once the model is completed it will have assessed every neighbourhood for vulnerability to flooding, regardless of proximity to historic floodplains. The City also launched a public bus route connecting Lakefield, ON, and Curve Lake First Nation to the city of Peterborough in 2021. The LINK (https://www.selwyntownship.ca/en/resident-services/bus-service-the-link.aspx) provides rural residents outside the city limits with public transit and supports individuals who cannot drive, low-income, and marginalized to access city services like medical care, which previously required trips to be made via taxis, carpooling, and personal vehicles. The LINK is supported in part by the Province, Curve Lake First Nation, Selwyn Township, and the City and will operate until 2025 unless more funding is allocated to keep the route operational beyond that year. Lastly, the City completed its new community climate change action plan that now aligns mitigation measures with reaching net-zero emissions by 2050. The CCAP utilized a DEI lens during its development to ensure that vulnerable and marginalized populations were included in the planning process. As a result of the DEI lens, an Equity Focused Group was added as an extra engagement activity to complement the other planned engagement activities.

The city's climate action efforts are intersectional in nature and aim to mitigate emissions at the largest scale possible while also improving the well-being of the community and enhancing its resilience to the increasing frequency and intensity of climate change anticipated. Properly designed, intersectional climate actions can move us away from fossil fuels, foster enhanced natural climate solutions and reduce material consumption while also improving racial, gender, and economic equity and making Boulder more resilient against a changing climate. 

The city has identified several benefits/opportunities of climate action. 
•	Local Economic Development of clean technology businesses: Investment in energy efficiency and local renewable energy development creates jobs. A Boulder County economic analysis projected that for every dollar spent on local energy programs, almost half remained in Boulder County. Expansion of programs to install solar and improve building energy performance will generate hundreds of additional jobs in the Boulder area. 
•	Increased energy security: Local renewable energy investments and related system improvements such as undergrounding, microgrids, and equipment upgrades will not only help achieve energy system change and emission reduction goals but will also improve the system's reliability, resilience and safety. These actions are also essential steps in building a local energy system capable of ensuring energy services during disruptive events. 
•	Social equity and 'just transition': A significant theme in the extensive community engagement conducted on climate issues is the importance of ensuring that the costs and benefits of a transition to renewable energy and other climate-related actions are shared equitably. A set of three goals for a “just transition” were developed in collaboration with community groups. Inclusion of these social equity goals can substantially improve the well-being of the community, particularly those most affected by unpredictable and rising energy costs and climate change impacts. 
•	Energy expenditures: As a community, Boulder spends approximately $300 million annually on energy, with over $120 million spent on electricity. The transition to a renewable energy economy with a significant proportion coming from local sources has the potential to significantly increase the money staying in the community related to energy expenditures. Investing in building decarbonization and electrification can reduce total energy consumption and can shift use away from more volatile and less predictable energy sources (e.g., natural gas).
•	Health and environmental impacts: There are significant local air and water quality impacts associated with fossil fuel use. Substantially reducing and eventually eliminating this use will have multiple environmental benefits while also reducing indoor and outdoor air and water pollution and related health impacts. For example, energy efficiency assistance to low-income communities can improve health and tree planting programs have been proven to improve mental health. Electrification of buildings and transportation reduces the production of ozone forming and particulate pollutants leading to improved air quality.
•	Reducing climate vulnerabilities: Many selected actions are chosen for their ability, not just to mitigate emissions, but to increase our community's adaptive capacity to the impacts we are already experiencing. Increasing tree canopy and carbon sequestration can help reduce temperatures on days with extreme heat. Coupling electrification with renewable generation (and dispatchable storage) can reduce the likelihood of power loss on days with extreme temperatures. Heat pump adoption, which is a strategy to replace natural gas for space conditioning can bring centralized cooling solutions to buildings constructed without cooling.

Quantifying the equitable and inclusive distribution of climate action is challenging due to the complexity of defining, measuring, and addressing diverse social, economic, and environmental factors across dynamic and heterogeneous communities. More broadly, the city has committed to collecting and analyzing meaningful data to advance racial equity in our community as a part of the city's Racial Equity Plan. Under this commitment, the city has created a racial equity index mapping tool to assess equity across geographic regions of Boulder. This tool is used by staff when using the Racial Equity Instrument (previously referenced) to determine an area's equity priority. 

Equitable and affordable access to energy is a key priority of the city's climate work, with an intention to ensure all community members have unburdened access to meet heating, cooling, and energy needs. While there have historically been national tools available that estimate incomes and energy expenditures for households in the US at a census-tract scale, the city's Climate Initiatives team is aiming to identify a more locally specific approach to measuring energy burden. To date, the city has worked with state implementers of energy assistance, weatherization and other low-income programing to track participation rates in these programs at the census-tract scale on an annual basis. The city will also soon have access to census-tract scale data from our serving utility that provide enhanced energy cost burden analysis and utility disconnect information.

The city is also partnering with Boulder County on a just-launched Climate Equity Fund to support community- based organizations, neighborhood groups and individuals to access climate funds and track this support. 

The city is also taking a data-driven approach to reach an equitable distribution of trees and their many benefits among its underserved communities. A cross-departmental effort, in partnership with the neighboring communities and non-profit organizations, intends to address the impacts of a warming climate, set urban canopy goals by subcommunity, and identify potential planting areas. The city is prioritizing planting in areas based on heat vulnerability, increased storm water runoff, and equity factors. The city has undertaken a variety of analyses and development of planning tools to manage and monitor urban tree canopy city-wide, including heat mapping analysis and canopy planning tools that intersect with equity data.

Lastly, the city prioritizes equity in quantification of our investments through our budgeting process. The city has worked to implement an outcome-based budgeting approach called Budgeting for Resilience and Equity, which aims to incorporate performance metrics and identify outcomes, advance cross-department and -program collaboration, and increase the transparency of the development of the annual budget and our investments as they align with community goals.

Fully addressing climate change will require immediate, system-scale action to create an equitable future, rapidly reduce emissions and accelerate technological innovation. The city's climate work is centered around three main focus areas, with equity and resilience as core considerations embedded in all climate programs and policies. The Energy Systems focus area has targets covering energy burden, resilience and reliability, wellbeing of building occupants, and clean mobility options. The Circular Economy focus area has targets covering equitable access to goods and services and promoting repair and reuse options. The Nature-based Climate Solutions has targets covering urban tree and soil landscape restoration, increasing tree canopy cover in areas of greatest need, reducing urban heat island in energy burdened neighborhoods, and equity-based opportunities to participate in the “green” sector jobs. 

Additionally, Boulder has committed annual budget to resource equity-focused engagement organizations. Community engagement led by these organizations has directly led to the design of new programs and prioritization of tax-funded investments. 

Some recent highlights supporting the City's work in an equitable distribution of climate action: 
•	Healthy and Resilient Mobile Homes and Colorado Affordable Residential Energy (CARE) Programs: The city is committed to enhancing community resilience to climate change, while also preserving manufactured and mobile homes, and permanently affordable and naturally affordable housing for community members. The city has partnered with Boulder County to offer grants for repairs and upgrades to mobile and manufactured homes that need emergency repairs or that experienced wind damage. The city has partnered with Energy Outreach Colorado, the state implementer of the CARE program, to provide no-cost energy efficiency upgrades for income qualified households.
•	Climate Disaster Emergency Preparedness Training: The city funds a community-led training program to help manufactured/mobile home residents prepare for climate disruption. The program leverages the lived experiences of residents who are motivated to help their neighbors by sharing their learnings. 
•	SmartRegs: Since 2011, the city has required that all licensed rental housing in Boulder meet a basic energy efficiency standard called SmartRegs. By requiring a minimum level of energy performance, SmartRegs lowers tenant energy bills and helps ensure rental units are upgraded with energy efficient technology. 
•	Recycling for All Community Members: The city and its partners, Eco-Cycle, Boulder Housing Partners (BHP), and FLOWS, hosted community recycling pickup days for 14 different manufactured home and BHP communities throughout 2023. This ongoing effort brings recycling services and knowledge to historically underserved neighborhoods. 
•	Climate Justice Collaborative in Boulder County: The city, in partnership with Boulder County, the City of Longmont and Philanthropiece, formed a county-wide Climate Justice Collaborative. The CJC strengthens and supports existing movements and organizations active throughout Boulder County. 
•	FLOWS: A spinoff group from the CU Environmental Center that is now based within the city's housing authority, Boulder Housing Partners, that develops leadership in climate and sustainability within low-income, immigrant, and BIPOC communities, supported by the city for climate mobilization and racial equity advancement.
•	Reducing Energy Burden Through Solar Gardens: The city and local partners have invested in community solar gardens, large solar systems that allow income-qualified participants to access clean, low-cost solar energy, while also bringing down energy costs, without installing equipment at home.
• Boulder Racial Equity Plan: Adopted in 2021, the plan guides prioritization of programs and resources to achieve meaningful change. The city developed a Racial Equity Instrument and has internal Justice, Equity, Diversity, and Inclusion (JEDI) teams in each department, including Climate Initiatives, along with mandatory staff trainings.
• Climate Equity Fund: Boulder County has launched a $2.5 million Climate Equity Fund in 2025 to support community-led climate action in historically underserved neighborhoods. The Fund is administered by Boulder County and prioritizes projects like energy upgrades, climate education, and green workforce development, with funding decisions made through a community-led grantmaking process. The CEF uses a participatory grant-making approach where affected communities help determine how to distribute the resources. Community voices have been present in all aspects of the fund from fund design, grant review, and program evaluation.

column16: The City of Santa Monica continues to identify opportunities and benefits of climate action. The City is advancing climate policy to reduce carbon emissions further by adopting more aggressive new construction codes, electric vehicle charger reach codes and policies focusing on electrification in existing buildings. Wider opportunities and benefits of building and transportation electrification identified include, healthier, safer, and less expensive homes. These benefits may also be felt more broadly with better access to clean outdoor air, robust ecosystem services, efficient mobility, decreased costs of energy and increased resilience to effects of extreme heat and sea level rise. In addition to improved day-to-day living conditions, continued climate action in the City of Santa Monica points to a significant reduction in future economic and social costs associated with infrastructure and public health if no action were to be taken. Climate action also presents an opportunity to broaden the local job market. With building electrification becoming more common, the City will need skilled workers to install electric appliances in existing buildings.

column16: The City of Dubuque has identified many opportunities and benefits of climate action. If implemented successfully, the CAP will enhance Dubuque's economic vitality, resilience, and viability as a healthy, livable city. The following 9 sections of Dubuque's CAP explain the opportunities/benefits related to each area. Buildings and Energy: Electricity from renewable sources is typically less expensive than fossil fuels, so by implementing renewables, we will be greening the economy and making the economic activity in the city more environmentally sustainable. Clean energy jobs are growing and employing more people, so more jobs are being created. Climate actions will result in annual savings for Dubuque businesses and households, and better planned and low carbon cities will have increased production, both of which will create social community and labor improvements by creating a stronger sense of community while providing job security and benefits. City Council will create a policy for city buildings to reduce energy usage and implement energy benchmarking. Transportation and Land Use: Implementation of Complete Streets and a connected system of transit, bike, and pedestrian infrastructure along with consolidation of residential zoning categories and emphasis on neighborhood designs that supports density and walkability will improve access to and quality of mobility services and infrastructure will develop systems and networks that allow for greater choice in where residents live, work, and how they commute. City Council will update, adopt, and fund a more comprehensive complete streets policy. Solid Waste and Recycling: The City is working on diverting, reducing, and reusing waste which will create improved resource efficiency in terms of energy by meeting the needs of the city with a lower level of resource input and promote a circular economy by supporting greater reuse and recycling of resources. Through prevention and waste recovery methods, the solid waste sector has potential to be zero waste. The City of Dubuque is currently working on a project to divert captured landfill gas for renewable natural gas use. Water, Wastewater, and Flooding: Creating a storm water infiltration plan and increasing flood resilience of infrastructure will address disaster preparedness and risk reduction by increasing the City's ability to respond to hazards and reduce the risks of said hazards. These ideas will also enhance climate change adaptation and resilience by making the City more able to withstand changes in the climate and quickly recover from disasters. Resources will also be conserved such as water by promoting increased water conservation and updating plans and standards in support of water conservation goals. City Council will update infrastructure standards to meet climate change projections. Climate Health and Safety: The City of Dubuque will educate and engage the public on extreme weather risks, expand cooling and warming facilities, implement air quality monitoring, and explore and address ozone impacts on local agriculture. All of which will improve public health by reducing mental and physical health issues, improve resource quality such as air quality. City Council will develop a comprehensive heat response plan that incorporates climate impact projections. Food: Improving the healthy food system resilience and supply safety net and strengthening farm to institution procurement will shift to more sustainable behaviors by supporting a lifestyle change that reduces emissions and is more sustainable and improves resource security such as food. City Council will pass a policy to procure locally sourced foods for events and City-managed facilities. Greenspace and Tree Canopy: Reducing, repurposing, and reimagining lawn space and utilizing parks and marginal City property for greater community use will address ecosystem preservation and biodiversity improvement by increasing connectedness of green spaces. City Council will create a tree preservation and planting ordinance and establish a policy incentive for homeowners converting traditional lawns to sustainable areas. Climate Economy: Dubuque will create a climate action market that supports and advances climate action strategies and explore climate action economic development and financing which will create economic growth by increasing the value of goods and services in Dubuque. City Council will establish a policy for funding climate initiatives and tax increment financing. Climate Action Capacity: The City of Dubuque will improve access to data for informed decision-making by collecting and sharing data through maintaining and updating design standards and plans for climate actions.

column19: The City of Dubuque recognizes that certain populations such as lower income, people of color, the elderly, disabled, children, etc. are more at risk, so the City is taking steps to ensure an inclusive and equitable environment for climate action. Every section of the CAP has equity considerations listed and taken into account when creating and implementing the accomplishments of goals and taking action. Therefore, Dubuque will help reduce/eradicate poverty, help secure tenure, and promote social inclusion and justice while also combating climate-related issues. Building and Energy: Lower income families may not be able to afford energy costs, energy efficiency improvements, or access to renewable energy. Renters might not have the ability to implement energy efficiency measures to buildings. Air pollution disproportionally impacts low income and communities of color due to building locations and characteristics. So, Dubuque plans to encourage equity for renewable energy, provide energy efficiency rebates and financial incentives, and improve energy efficiency and equity in residential buildings. The City will create a rental housing energy efficiency policy to qualify for rental licensing and deploy an incentive program for electrification. Transportation and Land Use: At risk populations may not have transportation or close public transportation access. There may not be affordable or reliable options for those with special transportation needs. So, Dubuque plans to build complete streets, increase housing options and affordability, increase public transit ridership, and increase pedestrian access and safety. City council will invest in bike paths, pedestrian paths, public transit, and fund neighborhood development. Solid Waste and Recycling: Recycling and composting programs may not be equally or readily available to all, and there may be other barriers like a lack of awareness, fees, etc. Populations situated near the landfill or composting center may experience bad odors and potential health issues. So, Dubuque plans to expand recycling options for multi-family equity and provide education. City Council will expand commercial and residential composting. Water, Wastewater, and Flooding: Low-income neighborhoods suffer more damage from flooding. Certain areas are more prone to flooding and sewer overflows due to impervious surfaces and less open/green space. So, Dubuque will better manage stormwater by creating open green spaces and educate, engage, and empower the public for flood mitigation. City Council will implement pricing preference for households to install water efficient fixtures, establish incentives to prioritize the development of green infrastructure, and prepare a flash flood risk map to identify at risk areas. Climate Health and Safety: Vulnerable populations are disproportionately represented within vulnerable environments and frequently lack resources to improve the adaptive capacity of their surroundings. So, Dubuque will work to reduce risks of health and safety created by ongoing climate impacts. City Council will update the City's emergency response plan and ensure that preparation and updates recognize and address likely climate change impacts. Food: People in low income neighborhoods may live in a food/nutrition desert or experience food insecurity. So, Dubuque will improve healthy food system resilience. City Council will identify potential sites for community gardens with a focus on expanding community equity. Greenspace and Tree Canopy: Lower income/ people of color neighborhoods usually have lower tree canopy coverage, and neighborhoods with vulnerable populations have the highest heat island impacts. So, Dubuque will promote and implement heat island mitigation improvements. City Council will identify vulnerable tree canopy sections and develop policies to incentivize, encourage, or require strategic tree planting for heat island mitigation. Climate Economy: Low income individuals are especially prone to the impacts of climate change and bear a greatly disproportionate share of the costs. So, Dubuque will explore climate action economic development and financing, particularly within underserved populations. City Council will explore the community development finance program to provide credit and financial services to underserved markets and populations. Climate Action Capacity: Individuals, organizations, and communities with a lower degree of adaptive capacity will suffer more harm from exposure to climate impacts and will recover more slowly. So, Dubuque will support the development of social networks to build social resilience. City Council will encourage development of affordable intergenerational housing with a focus on improved social connectedness across demographic cohort.

column18: While it is difficult to quantify the equitable and inclusive distribution of all climate action taken by the City, participation data from City of Palo Alto Utilities (CPAU) assistance programs helps quantify the City's effort to provide clean, affordable energy to lower income community members. CPAU offers a number of programs that help income qualifying resident's afford utility bill costs. The Rate Assistance Program (RAP) offers up to a 25% discount on portions of resident's utility bill who are experiencing financial hardship or have a medical condition that requires higher than usual utility consumption. RAP customers are also eligible for the Residential Energy Assistance Program (REAP) which provides hands on support to help residents permanently reduce their utility bill through energy efficiency measures. CPAU also provides direct rate relief through ProjectPLEDGE, which uses donations from residential and commercial CPAU customers to provide relief for Palo Altans who can not afford their utility bill when unexpected hardship strikes. Because CPAU provides 100% carbon free electricity, these programs help ensure accessible and affordable access to clean energy for all Palo Alto residents.\n\nIn addition, the City offers rebates to incentivize and make affordable a variety of actions residents can take to reduce emissions, protect water quality, and otherwise mitigate and adapt to climate change.
