The City of Palo Alto considers equity issues for all aspects of climate action. For example, Palo Alto recently completed the Multifamily Gas Furnace to Heat Pump Retrofit Pilot funded by a Climate Protection Grant from the Bay Area Air Quality Management District with additional funds from the City of Palo Alto Utilities (CPAU). The pilot aimed to identify viable retrofit options and validate the cost and benefits of retrofitting existing gas furnace systems with energy efficient heat pump alternatives at an affordable 24-unit multifamily apartment complex. Except for a manager unit, all apartments are reserved for adults with developmental disabilities. At the project level, the pilot provided direct benefits to residents through improved indoor air quality, bill savings, as well as increased comfort and safety, as reported in the post-retrofit survey. At the community level, the pilot will reduce the City's greenhouse gas emissions and serves as a case study for future electrification projects in multifamily buildings. It's projected that the pilot will result in energy savings of 71,804 kBTU per year and a greenhouse gas emissions reductions of 11.1 metric tons per year. CPAU plans to monitor billing data at the pilot site for at least 12 months after the retrofit and will publish updated results.

CPAU also programs also include rebates for EV charger installations at multifamily residences and nonprofit organizations. In 2024, CPAU led the installation of six Level 2 chargers at a 65-unit affordable housing project. As of December 31, 2024, a total of 263 EV charging ports had been installed at multifamily properties through the CPAU program, serving 814 housing units.

In a recent example of considering equity in climate adaptation planning, the City collaborated with Stanford University students to study the potential impact of extreme heat across geographies and demographics within the Palo Alto. The study will inform recommended solutions such as establishing an additional cooling center in the southern portion of the City or implementing cooling roofs on schools and commercial buildings.

column16: Take action on the climate emergency can achieve multiple community benefits — such as to build more resilient communities and improve people's health, quality of life and economic prosperity. It's an opportunity for governments to deploy policy and economic measures that reduce inequality, ensure people and nature are climate save, drive emissions reductions (e.g. through stimulating the renewables industry, investing in sustainable transport and creating low carbon business opportunities). It's also an opportunity for relocalisation — to lead lives that are less energy and resource intensive and wasteful; to be more connected to one another and create healthy environments. Continued global heating means that the average number of days in Melbourne over 35°C will likely increase from around 8.3 days per year to between 13 and 21 days by the 2050's. The impact of continued global heating on water supply shows that by 2040 the Yarra catchment area will see rainfall reduce by 2.7% annually and an expected 11% reduction in water flowing to waterways. While these impacts pose significant challenges, they also present an opportunity to create a more climate resilient city that improves liveability. Our city's green spaces, parks and reserves provide considerable physical and mental health benefits that need to be preserved to help people cope with the impacts of a changing climate. To address these challenges, we need to adapt the way we design, build and manage our infrastructure and assets - our parks and reserves, buildings, roads, streetscapes and drainage network. We will implement a range of on-ground solutions and embed climate adaptation approaches across Council's works, strategies and policies. There is considerable opportunity to reduce transport emissions and realise a range of co-benefits including reduced congestion, improved air quality, health, amenity and overall liveability of the city.

column19:
一、充分认识气候可行性论证评估工作的重要性
气候可行性论证是指对与气候条件密切相关的规划和建设项目进行气候适宜性、风险性以及可能对局地气候产生影响的分析、评估活动。开展气候可行性论证工作对应对气候变化、开发利用气候资源、合理控制建设成本、避免和减轻气象灾害造成损失以及提供风险管理决策依据等具有重要意义，能够避免或者减轻规划和建设项目实施后可能受气象灾害、气候变化的影响或者可能对局地气候产生影响，是涉及安全的强制性评估事项。
二、进一步规范气候可行性论证评估工作
国家级、省级、市级开发区、产业园区、新区和“标准地”等特定区域实行区域气候可行性评估制度。在区域气候可行性论证报告有效期内，对落户在该区域的项目，除危化品类项目应进行单个项目气候可行性论证外，在《目录》范围内的重点建设工程项目无需重复开展区域气候可行性论证报告中已有内容的评估工作。如区域气候可行性论证报告不能完全替代，且属于开发区内重点建设工程项目的共性评估内容，可增加相应评估章节作为对原有报告的补充完善。重点建设工程项目如确需另行开展气候可行性论证，要重点开展区域气候可行性论证报告中尚未覆盖的特性部分论证工作。对于未开展区域气候可行性评估区域的建设项目，应当按照《目录》范围开展区域气候可行性评估或单个项目气候可行性论证。气候可行性论证报告必须通过市级以上气象主管机构组织的评审。
三、协同推进气候可行性论证评估工作
气象部门要加强气候可行性论证评估工作的监督管理，及时公开具备气候可行性论证能力的机构名录，组织做好气候可行性论证报告评审工作，开展气候可行性论证工作执法检查，查处违法违规行为。在编制市、县级国土空间总体规划时，应将气候可行性评估纳入规划内容。发展和改革、自然资源、生态环境、住房和城乡建设、水务、文化和旅游等部门配合做好协同监管工作。

Rajkot's Climate Resilient City Action Plan (CRCAP) 2024, focuses on addressing the city's climate vulnerabilities while ensuring equitable socio-economic development. The CRCAP is designed with vulnerability/equity assessments, ensuring its benefits reach the city's most vulnerable populations, particularly those in informal settlements and low-income communities. The city has identified vulnerable systems and the affected wards through vulnerability assessment. The quality of life for the residents of certain wards is directly improved by measures to reduce system fragility. The following are some of the actions the city has identified:1) The city is putting out an air quality improvement plan, and its execution will help to enhance the air quality in the city as a whole.2) The city processes all municipal garbage, and the entire value chain for waste management generates a number of green employment.3)The city is converting its entire fleet of public buses to completely air-conditioned e-buses, giving bus drivers a comfortable working environment.4) The city has public/primary health centers close to the slum regions, and it is building new health facilities to offer nearby residents access to affordable health care.5)The city has been establishing an urban forest and planting trees along road sides in an effort to create green space and boost biodiversity in general. Through a vulnerability assessment, the plan prioritises those most susceptible to extreme heat and includes public health interventions, awareness campaigns, and infrastructure improvements such as cool roofs and shaded areas. 22 strategies and 78 actions have been proposed across all priority sectors to address 
vulnerabilities to urban heat, urban flood, and air pollution in the urban systems and areas 
Cost estimation is limited to actions where it was possible to provide an estimate. Actual budget requirement will be higher than this 
estimation. The proposed actions will create an estimated 57,661 green jobs from RE implementation in Industries, buildings and municipal infrastructure for water supply, solid waste and wastewater services.

Pemerintah kota berusaha memastikan bahwa semua kelompok masyarakat - termasuk warga miskin, perempuan, lansia, dan penyandang disabilitas - ikut terlibat dalam program seperti Kampung Iklim, penghijauan lingkungan, pengelolaan sampah, dan edukasi lingkungan.\nKota Medan melihat apakah bantuan atau program adaptasi iklim, seperti pembuatan drainase atau penyedotan limbah tinja, sudah menjangkau wilayah yang paling rawan banjir atau padat penduduk. Selain itu, Kota Medan memantau apakah akses terhadap informasi dan layanan ramah lingkungan bisa diakses oleh semua warga, bukan hanya kalangan tertentu. Melalui laporan dan data dari kelurahan, kecamatan, serta masukan dari masyarakat dan lembaga lokal, pemerintah bisa menilai apakah program iklim yang dijalankan sudah merata dan berpihak kepada kelompok yang paling rentan terhadap dampak perubahan iklim.\n

Kota Medan telah melakukan upaya distribusi aksi iklim yang adil dan inklusif, terutama menjangkau semua lapisan masyarakat dan wilayah rentan:

1. Partisipasi Berbasis Kelurahan dalam Proklim
Dinas Lingkungan Hidup (DLH) Kota Medan secara aktif menyosialisasikan Program Kampung Iklim (Proklim) di berbagai kelurahan seperti PB Selayang I (Kec. Medan Selayang) dan Sidomulyo (Kec. Medan Tuntungan). Pelibatan masyarakat langsung bertujuan meningkatkan adaptasi iklim dan pengurangan emisi gas rumah kaca melalui aksi lokal, hingga ke level lingkungan. Ini menunjukkan upaya pelibatan warga termasuk kelompok rentan dan wilayah pinggiran kota.

2. Pendidikan dan Literasi Lingkungan di Sekolah
Melalui program Penghargaan Adiwiyata, DLH Kota Medan membina sekolah-sekolah agar menjadi pusat prakarsa lingkungan. Kegiatan ini mengikutsertakan siswa, guru, dan masyarakat sekitar dalam edukasi pengelolaan sampah dan tindakan iklim, menyediakan akses pengetahuan ramah lingkungan bagi semua golongan, termasuk anak-anak di komunitas kurang beruntung.

3. Dialog Multi-Stakeholder untuk Mobilitas Inklusif
ITDP Indonesia bekerja sama dengan Pemerintah Kota Medan menyelenggarakan survei dan dialog bersama warga rentan untuk menghasilkan rekomendasi mobilitas inklusif — seperti akses pejalan kaki dan transportasi umum — melalui dokumen “Mobilitas Inklusif Kota Medan” dan “Konsensus Medan, Kota untuk Semua.” Ini menjadi dasar kebijakan kota yang memperhatikan kelompok rentan dan inklusi sosial dalam perencanaan urban.

4. Kolaborasi dengan Komunitas Pembelajaran Iklim
Palang Merah Indonesia Kota Medan memfasilitasi Community Climate Learning Centre, melibatkan warga kelurahan, anak muda, remaja, PKK, Babinsa, hingga penyuluh agama. Program ini menyasar edukasi iklim, pengolahan sampah, eco-enzim, green rooftop, serta inovasi energi alternatif. Model gotong royong ini memastikan akses ide dan teknologi iklim ke berbagai lapisan masyarakat secara inklusif.

column18: All Greater Amman Municipality (GAM) services are directed to all people living in Amman regardless of their legal status, background, origin, gender and age. this is reflected within GAM strategic plans and the type of projects we are implementing. some examples on the strategic planning level are as follow:- Amman resilience strategy: The IRC, in partnership with 100RC, carried out in-depth research to understand the scale of the problem and make practical recommendations that would align with Amman's goals and actions in the resilience strategy. Interviews, site visits and workshops formed the basis of the process. Based on their findings the IRC made the following recommendations: (1) Promote an inclusive approach to resilience (2) Develop an Inclusive Resilience Plan (3) Work through public private partnerships (4) Play a leadership role in the refugee response within Amman (5) Identify financing opportunities through foreign investment funding streams (https://resilientcitiesnetwork.org/downloadable_resources/Network/Amman-Resilience-Strategy-English.pdf).- Amman Green City Action Plan preparation phases were aligned with a public engagement plan : (Amman GCAP \'https://www.amman.jo/site_doc/AmmanGreen2021.pdf\' - page 30).- An action plan for Gender for Equitable Mobility was published in collaboration with FES - Amman (https://library.fes.de/pdf-files/bueros/amman/19445.pdf); The main objective of this Action Plan is to help bridge the gap between all the existing strategies and action plans related to or intersected with mobility and gender. The City of Amman is implementing the Climate Action Plan through the GAM Strategy 2022 - 2026 that is updated on a regular basis. It is emphasized that the GAM Strategy is gender-responsive and it integrates the principle of equity, especially given that the impacts of decarbonisation and the impacts of climate change and climate variability have disproportionate impacts accruing to vulnerable communities. Both the CAP 2023 and the GAM Strategy are aligned with the CAP 2019 and the GCAP 2021. The GCAP sets Strategic Objectives supporting low-carbon and climate-resilient development up to 2040, and contains an implementation plan that is integrated in the GAM Strategy that is reviewed and updated every four years.\nOvercoming social and cultural barriers to mode shift in urban mobility and public resistance to building energy code enforcement also feature as critical challenges. Ensuring equity and justice in the application of building energy codes to prevent negative financial impacts on vulnerable communities is a social imperative.\nity will also explore possibilities to integrate an internal risk management system for climate actions, minimizing the negative impacts while progressing towards achieving goals of the climate action plan. As stated in the Amman Resilience Strategy, 2017, the city will ensure equity and inclusivity by involving civil society, vulnerable communities and youth groups in various climate actions.
column19: Amman is divided into 22 districts. The climate change plan and Amman green city action plan focus on issues and actions within the institutional mandate of GAM; however, some environmental issues extend beyond political boundaries and GAM's remit. As such, many of the climate actions also require the engagement of National Ministries, agencies and other stakeholders, such as civil society groups, not-for profit organizations and the private sector. in the planning process; GAM did a technical assessment of the environmental data to identify the Priority Environmental Challenges in the city and the context of the interdependencies within which they arise in all the spatial boundary of the city. in Amman resilience strategy which is considered the bigger of sustainability and resilience planning, all actions were directed to vulnerable communities according to a research into vulnerable people including people with disabilities and refugees were undertaken to ensure inclusive and equity (https://resilientcitiesnetwork.org/downloadable_resources/Network/Amman-Resilience-Strategy-English.pdf). There is a bidirectional flow of interactions between GAM and its stakeholders. One the one hand, stakeholders are beneficiaries of the services that are provided by the city administration. On the other hand, stakeholders support GAM to deliver these services. On account of this interdependent relationship, the expectations, needs and interests of these stakeholders need to be accounted for in all work that is carried out by GAM, including infrastructure development, strategies and plans. The level of community engagement is dependent on the nature of the project. - Amman Green City Action Plan preparation phases were aligned with a public engagement plan : (Amman GCAP \'https://www.amman.jo/site_doc/AmmanGreen2021.pdf\' - page 30)A highly participatory approach was used for developing the GCAP. A Stakeholder Engagement Plan was put in place. A Project Steering Committee (PSC) for providing political guidance and support was set up . A Technical Committee made up of GAM's departmental expert was established. A total of 275 stakeholders from municipal government agencies, research centres, academics, embassies, civil society groups, Jordan-based companies, national government agencies, international NGOs, donor agencies, and International Financial Institutes participated in the process of elaborating the GCAP. The GCAP also benefitted from city-wide communication and awareness campaigns using social media platforms (the Amman in Green Online Campaign that reached nearly 500,000 inhabitants), a campaign mural in Rainbow Street and the Green Amman Contest.- An example of a project with a strong community outreach is the GIZ-led and sponsored project “Improving Living Conditions in Disadvantaged Areas in Amman via the Implementation of green infrastructure” (ILCA), which was jointly carried out by GAM and GIZ in partnership with the Jordan Ministry of Environment. This project was carried out with strong involvement of community representatives and local residents (including women, children, elderly, and individuals with special needs). By integrating their valuable inputs throughout all stages of the project, such as design, planning, and management processes of the rehabilitated areas, the ILCA project aimed to foster a sense of ownership among the local residents. A primary objective of the project was to prioritize the specific requirements of women, girls, and children, ensuring their safety, security, and access to convenient facilities. By meticulously addressing these needs, the project aimed to create an environment that fosters cohesion and convenience for all community members. The overarching goal was to enhance the quality of life in disadvantaged areas of Amman and promote equitable opportunities for social development. Moreover, the ILCA project served as a vital platform to raise awareness about the immense potential of green infrastructure in mitigating and adapting to climate change. By successfully engaging the community, considering the unique requirements of diverse groups, and highlighting the significance of green infrastructure, the ILCA project effectively demonstrated how collaborative efforts can bring about positive change. It serves as a model for future projects seeking to improve living conditions, foster community ownership, and create sustainable environments in disadvantaged areas.https://www.giz.de/en/worldwide/83767.html- Another example of waste soring project funded by GIZ (https://www.giz.de/de/downloads/giz2021-en-sorting-analysis-jordan-short.pdf) directed to different districts around Amman (High, medium and low income districts and a commercial area).

Davao City recognizes that climate action delivers wide-ranging environmental, social, and economic benefits that extend beyond emissions reduction. The City's Local Climate Change Action Plan (LCCAP 2024-2026) identifies co-benefits such as improved air and water quality, enhanced public health, sustainable livelihoods, and greater resilience of vulnerable communities.

Environmentally, initiatives such as urban greening, solid waste management, renewable energy promotion, and watershed rehabilitation contribute to biodiversity protection, temperature regulation, and reduced pollution. Socially, community-based adaptation and participatory planning strengthen local capacity, promote gender inclusivity, and enhance disaster preparedness. Economically, investments in climate-smart agriculture, renewable energy, and sustainable transport create green jobs and stimulate innovation while reducing energy costs in the long term.

The City also benefits from climate resilience initiatives that minimize disaster recovery costs, prevent damage to infrastructure, and sustain productivity across key sectors such as agriculture, tourism, and services. These actions align with the city's vision of being a “globally livable city and a center of excellence in climate change adaptation, disaster resiliency, and sustainable growth.”

column18: Davao City quantifies equitable and inclusive climate action through the integration of disaggregated socioeconomic and spatial data in local planning and monitoring processes. Data from the Community-Based Monitoring System (CBMS), POPCEN-CBMS survey provide household-level insights on poverty, access to basic services, and exposure to hazards, enabling planners to identify vulnerable groups—such as low-income households, women, children, elderly, and Indigenous Peoples.\n\nThese data inform the prioritization of adaptation programs and infrastructure investments in high-risk barangays, particularly those vulnerable to flooding, drought, and extreme heat. Equity and inclusion are also measured through participatory consultations and feedback mechanisms in project implementation, ensuring that marginalized sectors are represented in decision-making and benefit equitably from climate initiatives.
column19:
Davao City ensures equitable and inclusive climate action through a people-centered and data-driven approach embedded in its governance frameworks. The City Environment and Natural Resources Office (CENRO) and the City Planning and Development Office (CPDO) collaborate with barangay councils and sectoral groups to integrate vulnerability assessments and community needs into project design.

Key examples include:
• The Community-Based Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Program, which strengthens adaptive capacity among vulnerable barangays through localized training and early warning systems.
• The Urban Greening and Reforestation Program, which prioritizes tree planting and livelihood opportunities in upland and coastal Indigenous and low-income communities.
• The Sustainable Transport and Solid Waste Management initiatives, which reduce emissions while improving accessibility and health outcomes for urban populations.
• Integration of Indigenous Peoples' ancestral domain management within the climate planning process, ensuring alignment with UNDRIP and national IPRA laws.

These actions collectively promote social inclusion, environmental justice, and long-term sustainability. Through ongoing monitoring and participatory governance, Davao City continues to ensure that the benefits of climate action are equitably distributed across all sectors of society.

The Enhanced LCCAP for 2021-2050, aligned with the Philippines' National Climate Change Action Plan (NCCAP), is anchored on the City's aspiration for carbon neutrality, climate resilience, and inclusivity. These benefits are articulated in the Enhanced LCCAP outcome statements and are already being advanced through flagship programs across key sectors.

In food, water, and waste management, the City is working to increase the availability and accessibility of safe and healthy food through food security initiatives and urban farming programs. For sustainable food systems, availability and accessibility of safe and healthy food is increased through food security initiatives and urban farming programs. Sustainable food policy through the Healthy Public Food Procurement ensures that no public funds go to the purchase of unhealthy food and the Calorie Labeling Ordinance builds an environment that empowers consumers to make an informed choice that supports their dietary needs. Access to water resources is being improved through more equitable distribution and optimized urban water systems, guided by the City's Drainage Master Plan, which also supports flood mitigation. 

Quezon City is reducing the pressure of waste on the environment and ecosystems by pursuing a 50% diversion rate by 2030, driven by circular economy programs for both organics and recyclables. The City's flagship circular economy initiative continues to expand in collecting recyclables across barangays incentivized by providing environmental points that can be used to buy groceries and pay utilities. To further reach communities, orientations and pop-up booths continue to operate, encouraging more QCitizens to participate in trading. Following the success of the Kuha Sa Tingi Program, the newly launched Fill-A-Bottle (FAB) store program led by the Small Business and Cooperatives Development and Promotions Office (SBCDPO) also aims to promote sachet avoidance and to empower sari-sari store by becoming refill hubs for affordable common household cleaners such as fabric conditioners and dishwashing liquids. This is furthered by now expanding to the upcycling of textiles and tarpaulins with the Kilo/s Kyusi program and clothes swapping events to address the growing issue of textile waste driven by fast fashion. The program promotes the donation and reuse of pre-loved clothing.

On the reduction of food waste, the City now operates 43 biodigesters across barangays and urban farms by converting input kitchen and leftover waste to biogas for cooking and liquid soil conditioners. In collaboration with Scholars of Sustenance Philippines (SOS PH), Quezon City also rescued 35,780 kilograms of surplus food in 2024. Through the SOS Rescue Kitchen, with support from volunteers and QC Hall employees, 150,276 meals were prepared and distributed to communities in need.

In the area of health, equity, and social resilience, the City is addressing the risks of urban heat and drought through greening programs and the ongoing development of a Heat Action Plan. This plan will establish early warning systems, response protocols, and community-level safeguards, and its implementation is supported by the designation of a Heat Action Officer to coordinate measures and integrate heat-risk management across departments. These actions complement broader adaptation measures aimed at reducing the vulnerability of children, the elderly, persons with disabilities, and other at-risk groups, while inclusive planning frameworks embedded in the Enhanced LCCAP are designed to improve access to essential public services.

In buildings and energy, the City is implementing the Green Building Code, which requires energy-efficient and climate-resilient building design, with a target that 80-100% of building permits comply with the updated Green Building Code by 2025. Meanwhile, the Solarization Program aims to achieve 100% solar coverage for all viable city-owned buildings and facilities by 2030, while climate-proofed and ecologically efficient technologies are being deployed in city infrastructure to further enhance resilience and efficiency.

For sustainable mobility and transport, Quezon City is promoting active mobility by tripling cycling's modal share from 2.2% in 2016 to 6.6% by 2030, supported by the expansion of bike lanes from 55 km to 350 km, in partnership with national government and the private sector. Public transport is also being prioritized, with bus share expected to grow from 6.6% to 8.5% and railway share from 4.2% to 6.0% by 2030, aligned with the City's integration into Metro Manila's bus rapid transit and railway expansion projects.

Finally, institutional strengthening underpins all these efforts. The City is building the technical capacities of departments, stakeholders, and communities to deliver and monitor climate actions, supported by training programs under the Enhanced LCCAP and partnerships with C40 Cities and other international organizations.

column19: In 2020, the City completed the Inclusive Climate Action Stakeholder and Policy Analysis, which assessed how equity is embedded across strategies, policies, institutional processes, and governance structures. This was reinforced by the creation of the Climate Change and Environmental Sustainability Department (CCESD), which houses a Climate Change and Environmental Education Division mandated to institutionalize stakeholder engagement and inclusive climate action. The City also ensures representation of marginalized groups through the People's Council, where sectors such as persons with disabilities, urban poor, women, workers, senior citizens, youth, and neighborhood associations participate directly in development planning and investment programming. To further operationalize inclusivity, in 2024 the City issued an Executive Order establishing the Good Green Jobs (GGJ) Development Program, positioning climate action and employment generation as mutually reinforcing priorities, and designated a dedicated team to oversee implementation. Also in the same year, the City joined the Open Government Partnership (OGP), and by 2025 began consulting stakeholders in the budgetary process allowing civil society and community representatives to provide direct input into climate- and sustainability-related allocations.\n\nQuezon City also maintains comprehensive databases on women, children, the elderly, and persons with disabilities to inform development planning and investment programming. Inclusivity and equity are integrated into these processes through several measures: promoting gender equality in job and career opportunities; providing capacity-building programs to equip vulnerable groups with skills for participation in projects; using validated city-specific data to reassess the scale of social, economic, and environmental equity benefits; and strengthening knowledge exchange with academic institutions, development partners, NGOs, and the private sector. The City is also enhancing its technical capacity to implement monitoring and evaluation systems, fostering research collaborations with local universities to drive innovation, and sustaining national-local dialogues with agencies such as DENR, CCC, DOE, and DOST-PAGASA.

column18: THE construction of two retention ponds in Taman Buana Perdana to address floods is on track for completion by end June.Petaling Jaya City Council (MBPJ) Engineering Department director Ismail Shafie said the high volume retention ponds with a monsoon drainage network would allow for better surface runoff.“The flood mitigation project estimated at RM4mil, which began in November 2022, should be completed by the end of June.“One retention pond, measuring 40m by 60m, across Jalan Medan 29 is 80% completed and able to hold 4,800 cubic metres of water.“The second retention pond has a capacity to hold 2,880 cubic metres,” he said.Taman Buana Perdana is sandwiched between Jalan Sri Manja, Jalan PJS 3/29 and bordered by PJS 3/25.Ismail said Taman Buana Perdana, which has about 250 houses, had experienced floods in the past during heavy rain. The Low Carbon Society Blueprint for Iskandar Malaysia 2025 (LCSBPIM 2025) is a comprehensive climate mitigation strategy that outlines policies, actions, and programs to guide Iskandar Malaysia in becoming a strong, sustainable metropolis of international standing by 2025. It was developed through the SATREPS-JICA international research project (2011-2015), in partnership with IRDA, Universiti Teknologi Malaysia, Kyoto University, Okayama University, and Japan's National Institute for Environmental Studies.

The success of LCSBPIM 2025 led to Iskandar Malaysia's inclusion in the Global Covenant of Mayors for Climate & Energy (GCOM) in 2017, enabling ongoing access to international guidance and peer collaboration. In 2022, the blueprint was revised into the LCSBPIM 2030 - Climate Action Plan, broadening its scope to include climate adaptation and reaffirming a target of 70% reduction in GHG emissions intensity by 2030 from the 2010 baseline. This was funded under the 12th Malaysia Plan (RMK12).

Iskandar Malaysia's LCS blueprint is now widely recognized as a national and regional model. It has been referenced in the preparation of similar blueprints in Kuala Lumpur, Muar, Pengerang, and even in Semarang, Indonesia, with further replication across ASEAN cities supported by Japan. This blueprint has also helped secure support from the World Bank's City Climate Finance Gap Fund, which provides technical assistance for evaluating mitigation investments and flood risk resilience under LCSBPIM 2030.

At the international level, IRDA and Iskandar Malaysia have consistently participated in the UNFCCC Conference of Parties (COP) since 2010, showcasing progress in climate action, green infrastructure, and multilevel governance.

Complementing the blueprint is Malaysia's Low Carbon Cities 2030 Challenge (LCC2030C), a national initiative to accelerate GHG reductions in designated zones through integrated solutions such as energy efficiency, sustainable mobility, water conservation, and green infrastructure. In 2024, Johor emerged as a national leader, with multiple local authorities and private stakeholders receiving recognition under the LCC2030C awards program. Provisional certifications were awarded to MP Kulai and MB Iskandar Puteri for their government buildings, while Tanjung Langsat Industrial Zone 2 was certified as a low carbon zone. Diamond-level recognitions were granted to partners such as Iskandar Investment Berhad and MP Kulai, along with several designated low carbon zones in Sunway Iskandar Puteri, Pasir Gudang, and Kulai. In addition, Diamond Design awards were presented to Sunway Iskandar, Medini Net Zero CBD, and Ibrahim Technopolis (IBTEC)—highlighting the growing public-private commitment to green urban transformation across Johor.

Further cementing its leadership, Iskandar Malaysia was also recognized as a national winner by WWF Malaysia under the One Planet City Challenge (OPCC), reflecting its strong climate ambition, local action, and alignment with the Paris Agreement. This prestigious recognition highlights the region's role in advancing integrated, science-based climate strategies at the city-regional scale.

These recognitions, replications, and partnerships reinforce Iskandar Malaysia's ability to mobilize local and international climate finance, align with national carbon market goals, and operationalize SDG-aligned urban development at scale.

column19: Inclusivity and equity are in the center of the City Strategy. In Tampere, we have understood that achieving climate neutrality by 2030, and ensuring a just and inclusive urban climate transition, requires new ways of engaging citizens and making their sustainable choices as easy as possible. The transition must be socially justifiable and meaningful to people. By 2030, everyone in Tampere has to be able to live a climate resilient lifestyle and make climate friendly choices best suited for oneself, regardless of one's socioeconomic situation, neighbourhood, age, gender or health. This requires strengthening of cultural sustainability of our climate action. It means keeping everyone on board and working seriously towards cohesive and sustainable communities and the social and ecological change. To ensure this a new 4-year development program Climate Neutral Actions was established in 2022. The program concentrates on enabling behavioural change of citizens, especially in terms of their mobility and consumption. In addition, the program focuses on enhancing circular economy especially with the private sector, and furthermore coordinates and monitors city's own climate and environmental work, including biodiversity. The methods of the program are heavily focused on co-creation and empowerment. As a result, we will have climate actions tailored for specific city areas and groups of people, actions that actually are feasible for them in terms of their life situation and living location. As examples of our past actions, we have organised climate hero campaigns where citizens could share their favourite climate actions and calculate their carbon footprint. The city has also hosted Eco Impact dialogues for people to chat, share ideas, and get inspired. In another campaign the carbon footprint of four households was calculated and actions by which the household would achieve a so-called 1.5-degree life by 2030, were planned. Additionally, Tampere empowers its citizen by participatory budgeting, My2050 climate mobile game, and mobility carbon footprint calculator. Tampere has a continuous tradition of sustainability and climate work since first citizen engagement actions in 1990s. The climate neutrality goal has been explicitly stated in the city strategies and mayoral programs since 2017. We have separate councils for example for youth, elderly and disabled citizens. Citizens are also involved to the city planning process. People-centred housing, sustainable mobility, smart energy systems, circular economy and green and blue infrastructure, as well as co-creation with citizens, are at the core of our flagship urban investments, such as the new Hiedanranta city district. We also use data- and AI-driven solutions to develop smarter and more sustainable urban infrastructure and public services. Our annual climate budget is an important climate governance and transparency tool, which as part of the official financial statements makes visible the progress towards climate neutrality and the financial resources allocated for the measures. Achieving the above climate vision requires a change in our ways of doing and thinking in all spheres of urban development and urban life, and determination for working together. Citizen empowerment, humancentered actions and co-creation are at the core of our climate policy and all related actions. We are cocreating a climate neutral city and a just and resilient urban future for Tampere together with our citizens, communities, universities and companies.

In the city of Helsingborg, the social dimension of sustainable social development is addressed in the Quality of Life Programme (2016-2024), which sets out an overarching strategy for implementing the 2030 Agenda and the global goals in Helsingborg. A guiding principle for the 2030 Agenda work is social inclusion and that 'no one should be left behind', an ambition that is also expressed in, for example, the EU's Green Deal. The Quality of Life Programme is based on four orientations of will, which relate to different concepts of justice. Long-term responsibility relates to issues of global justice and solidarity with future generations. Participation relates to issues of participation and procedural justice, of making different groups and interests visible and recognised, and of opportunities for citizens to be heard and have their say. Lifelong activity relates to issues of good health, improved living environments and good access to various experiences and community services. Equality relates to issues of distribution and social integration, gender equality and giving all citizens in Helsingborg equal opportunities to grow up.

The Quality of Life Programme also includes goals for minimising climate impact and resource use, an ambition that is specified in more detail in the Climate and Energy Plan. In the implementation of the Climate and Energy Plan, consideration needs to be given to how different measures and initiatives contribute to achieving a good quality of life for all citizens in Helsingborg in accordance with the Quality of Life Programme. Below we summarise our analysis of the current proposal for a new Climate and Energy Plan (KEP) in the following main comments, which should be taken into account in the implementation of the new Climate and Energy Plan.

Habiteum 
Habiteum is the City of Helsingborg's dedicated workshop and innovation space for sustainable living and quality of life. It provides premises, outdoor areas, and tools—primarily from recycled or repurposed sources—that support hands-on, collaborative workshops focused on themes such as food, recycling, and water. 
Reflecting the ethos of “learning by doing,” Habiteum facilitates creative co-creation: citizens, associations, municipal departments and businesses join together in an equal and experimental forum where nature and sensory experience ground the conversation, making sustainability accessible and inspirational. 
In essence, Habiteum acts as both a maker space and a meeting place. It invites citizens to become co-creators of sustainable practices, supporting those who seek help in advancing their sustainability initiatives or who wish to test ideas in a shared space. 
As part of the city's broader Quality of Life programme, Habiteum aligns well with Helsingborg's strategic ambition to integrate environmental stewardship with well-being. It fosters inclusive innovation by encouraging experimentation, learning through doing, and bridging the gap between community-driven ideas and municipal support. 
In summary, Habiteum is a dynamic, tangible expression of participatory sustainability in Helsingborg. By combining sensory, nature-based engagement with creative co-creation, it empowers local stakeholders to contribute directly to the city's quality of life and sustainable development ambitions.
column19:
Climate Dialogues (Klimatdialoger) 
The Climate Dialogues are a participatory process designed to involve citizens, organisations and local stakeholders in Helsingborg's climate and energy planning. As part of the preparation of the new Climate and Energy Plan for 2025-2030, the city has conducted more than 25 dialogues with residents. 
The dialogues are structured around open conversations, workshops and interactive methods that allow participants to share perspectives, express concerns and propose solutions. The process ensures that diverse voices are heard and that local climate policy reflects community priorities and everyday realities. 
By using Climate Dialogues, Helsingborg builds legitimacy, transparency and trust in its climate governance. The method fosters a sense of shared ownership and responsibility for the transition, while providing the municipality with valuable insights that guide decision-making and implementation. 

Helsingborg Research and Innovation Fund (Forsknings- och innovationsfond) 
Helsingborg operates a municipal Research and Innovation Fund through its R&D unit, FoU Helsingborg. The fund supports projects that address societal challenges, including climate change, and encourages collaboration between municipal departments, universities, businesses and civil society. 
One flagship initiative is The (Exploring) City (Den (ut)forskande staden), which introduces new methods for municipal learning such as “hypothesis labs” and experimentation in real urban environments. These projects bring together researchers, practitioners and citizens to test innovative solutions, evaluate results and disseminate lessons learned. 
The fund ensures that Helsingborg remains at the forefront of applied research and innovation for climate neutrality. It strengthens the city's ability to work across organisational boundaries and to integrate scientific knowledge into day-to-day governance and strategic planning. 

Climate Municipalities (Klimatkommunerna) 
Helsingborg is an active member of Klimatkommunerna, a Swedish network of municipalities and regions working towards ambitious climate goals. The network facilitates peer learning, policy advocacy and joint initiatives that support the transition to climate-neutral local societies. 
As a member, Helsingborg benefits from shared expertise, benchmarking opportunities and representation in national policy dialogues. The city's progress is significant: since 1990, Helsingborg has reduced its territorial greenhouse gas emissions (scope 1 and 2) by more than 60 per cent. The remaining emissions are addressed through nature-based carbon sinks and continued systemic transformation. 
Participation in Klimatkommunerna provides Helsingborg with both recognition and accountability, while reinforcing its role as a frontrunner in Sweden's collective efforts to achieve climate neutrality by 2030. 

Miljöverkstaden (Environmental Workshop) is a municipal initiative within Helsingborg's Environmental Education and Behaviour Change Unit. Operating since 1989, it supports schools by delivering environmental and climate education through experiential, outdoor pedagogy. 
We partner closely with schools—teachers and pupils—to offer structured programmes tailored to different grade levels. These range from lessons on water, energy, and waste, to active, engaging formats such as “child traffic school” at Fredriksdal for first graders, designed to promote cycling and sustainable mobility. 
Naturskolan (the Nature School) forms a key component. It offers immersive, sensory-based learning for students from preschool through grade 6, held in Helsingborg's green surroundings such as Jordbodalen. Students engage in hands-on activities—planting trees, water purification, nature-based crafts and reflection—to foster a personal connection to environmental issues. 
Miljöverkstaden's methods actively integrate head, heart and hands: pupils gain knowledge through doing, reflection and creative expression. Their work is aligned with updated curricula emphasising education for sustainable development and entrepreneurial learning. 
The operation encompasses several municipal departments and partners: we collaborate with urban municipal departments and municipal companies—including NSR (waste), Öresundskraft (energy), and NSVA (water and wastewater)—to deliver comprehensive and contextually grounded programmes. 
In summary, Miljöverkstaden strengthens the link between environmental education and municipal knowledge-building by engaging young residents through immersive and context-based learning. It fosters sustainable mindsets early on, builds partnerships across municipal actors, and anchors environmental stewardship in everyday education.

Each action in Sunderland City Council's Low Carbon Action Plan has a key performance indicator or milestone, some of which help to quantify equitable and inclusive climate action. Examples of this include the number of homes assisted through various fuel-poverty and low carbon focussed retrofit schemes, installation of solar PV on schools, total external funding secured for decarbonisation and the number of residents engaged across the city. 
Many of the current projects in Sunderland that support equitable and inclusive climate action have used disaggregated and spatial data to quantify eligibility within the city. 
For example, the delivery of the Warm Homes Local Grant(WHLG) programme which commenced in April 2025 and runs for three years, is targeting fuel poor properties with energy efficiency and fuel poverty measures. The WHLG funds installation of electric air source heat pumps in low efficiency / low-income properties that have old and inefficient electric storage heaters, and LEAD provides help and support to residents to be more energy efficient in their behaviour. 
The Council uses the national government's open-source Energy Performance Certificate (EPC) database, Lower Super Output Area (LSOA) fuel poverty data, as well as internal Unique Property Reference Number (UPRN) data to target the least efficient properties which are most likely to house families suffering from fuel poverty. Data is recorded by SCC partners, Citizen's Advice and Green Doctors to ensure the target audience is reached for WHLG, LEAD and REDRESS activity. A similar process is also undertaken for the ongoing ECO4 / Great British Insulation Scheme project.
column19: Sunderland aims to ensure inclusive climate action. This is considered for both climate mitigation and adaptation.SCC in 2025 has mapped the city reviewing locations of energy sources, ICT and wifi coverage, opportunities to enhance EV charging, tree planting and improving green spaces, decarbonising and retrofitting homes and businesses and reviewing where Sunderland's most vulnerable communities live, to inform delivery of interventions to ensure all residents benefit from investment which will support them to live in a changing climate. Energy Advice: SCC participates in the regional programme LEAD. Working with Energy Saving Trust and Groundworks 'Green Doctors' this project offers residents free advice about domestic retrofit and the delivery process. Objective to educate and raise awareness about the retrofit process and how it helps cut energy bills. The project uses a data-led and community engagement approach to identify, residents in priority groups categorised as Hard-to-Reach.SCC is working with Groundwork and Citizens Advice (CAS) to deliver the OFGEM REDRESS 'Energy Savvy' programme in Sunderland. The priority of REDRESS funding is to help people who are at risk from cold homes and high energy bills, offering energy efficiency advice and support. Energy Savvy targets residents living in damp and mouldy homes. SCC continues to support business and community organisations with UKSPF-funded BREEZ to March 2026. The objective of BREEZ is to support SMEs and community organisations to upgrade inefficient heating, lighting and insulation systems with new, efficient upgrades. BREEZ provides 50% grant funding towards microgeneration and upgrades for business process equipment. From Jan 2024 - March 2025 SCC BREEZ supported 84 businesses and 35 community organisations. From April 2025 - March 2026, SCC is delivering BREEZ3 (more info at 9.1)Engagement: Young people live with the most severe impacts of climate change in the future. Sunderland views it as important to engage young people in the climate conversation. Climate change was voted the most important issue by Sunderland's young people at the Young People's State of the City, in November 2019 which informed the city's Low Carbon Framework and approach, and it is vital that youth voice is planning sustainable futures in the city. The 2030 Shadow Board set up the EGS young people's group which first met in Oct 2021. EGS brings together young people from all schools and young groups alongside reps College, and University to provide a forum where young people's opinions can be heard. Connecting with Sunderland's Youth Consortium, SCC is engaging with communities to improve access to EGS and diversify reach. EGS members are supported to meet termly; participate in volunteering opportunities; and discuss the city's plans. Members send a rep to the city's 2030 Shadow Board and feed into the Board's discussions.   The young people have grown in confidence and increasingly shape their own agenda.  19 members have attended the group sessions since September 2024, across 4 meetings and 1 volunteer session, as well as attending 2 Shadow Board meetings.  This year (2024/25) the group informed designs for Sunderland's Low Carbon School Charter Mark, & Sunderland's new sustainable mascot, Sunny Bee. Adaptation. A Climate Change Risk Assessment for Sunderland has been developed, aligned with the UK Climate Risk Independent Assessment (CCRA3). It recognises climate change impacts certain groups in different ways and to varying degrees, with low-income households and vulnerable groups facing the largest impacts. The risk assessment highlights how these groups need to be considered under each risk, to ensure adaptation actions are addressing those most impacted. \nFlood Risk: one of the social strategic and specific objectives of Sunderland's Local Flood Risk Management Strategy (LFRMS) 2016 (link and explained in 7.1) is to protect the most vulnerable communities and increase resilience to current and future flood risk from climate change. Green infrastructure: As part of the SCC LCAP, SCC has mapped existing green spaces across and identified areas with less greenspace. Along with tree canopy cover and tree equity data, this has helped to ensure citywide equity and inclusivity when planning nature-based solutions for climate adaptation and has influenced planting sites during the 2024-25 planting season. In 24/25 trees were planted across 9 urban sites in the Millfield area of Sunderland, which has low access to quality greenspace and nature. SCC have been awarded £490,000 funding (July 25) through Lottery Fund's Nature, Towns and Cities initiative. The project, over the next 3 years will bring organisations together to connect residents with nature. Funding will help communities to improve their health and wellbeing making it easier to access nature.  www.sunderland.gov.uk/article/35494/City-scoops-490k-lottery-funding-to-improve-residents-access-to-nature

column19:
Más allá de las disposiciones legales, la administración municipal de Montería reconoce y promueve los diálogos con la comunidad como base para garantizar la distribución equitativa e inclusiva de la acción climática. Las voces ciudadanas en la co-construcción del Plan de Desarrollo son determinantes no solo para identificar problemáticas, perspectivas y aspiraciones, sino también para construir confianza y legitimidad en las decisiones públicas. No se trata únicamente de un diseño técnico y político, sino de un proceso de acuerdos colectivos que ponen a Montería primero.

En este sentido, desde la administración se implementa una estrategia de participación, aprobada por el Consejo de Gobierno el 1° de enero de 2024, que articula tres modalidades de interacción: i) Encuentros territoriales en comunas y corregimientos, ii) Encuentros temáticos relacionados con los cuatro circuitos del Plan de Desarrollo y el Plan Plurianual de Inversiones, y iii) Encuentros con actores estratégicos del municipio. En el marco de esta estrategia se realizaron 36 encuentros de los 38 previstos, de los cuales 23 se llevaron a cabo con enfoque territorial (12 en zonas rurales y 11 en comunas urbanas), 5 fueron temáticos y 8 con actores estratégicos, logrando la participación de 4.760 personas.

La evaluación del impacto de la acción climática en Pereira revela un enfoque multifacético y dinámico, aunque inherentemente fragmentado. No existe un marco de evaluación único y centralizado; en su lugar, se manifiesta a través de los criterios y métricas de diversos actores, incluyendo el gobierno nacional, las entidades locales, el sector privado y la academia. La capacidad de la ciudad para evaluar los beneficios de sus iniciativas climáticas está directamente vinculada a su alineación con los compromisos nacionales y su éxito en la movilización de capital, la mejora de la calidad de vida y la implementación de mecanismos de gobernanza proactivos.

El análisis de las fuentes documentales identifica que los beneficios de la acción climática se evalúan en tres dimensiones principales:

Dimensión Económica: Los beneficios se miden en términos de la movilización de capital para proyectos sostenibles, la creación de 'proyectos bancables' y la generación de un 'retorno sostenible' a largo plazo. Se observa una creciente integración de la sostenibilidad como un factor de valorización y rentabilidad para la inversión privada.

Dimensión Social y de Gobernanza: Los indicadores de impacto social se centran en la creación de 'empleo verde,' la capacitación del capital humano para una 'transición justa,' y la mejora de la calidad de vida a través de políticas de movilidad y gestión de residuos. Un elemento distintivo es la evaluación del rol de la ciudadanía en la gobernanza ambiental, a través de la participación y los mecanismos de control social.

Dimensión Ambiental Directa: La evaluación se basa en métricas de mitigación cuantitativas, como la reducción de emisiones de Gases de Efecto Invernadero (GEI) y la gestión de residuos sólidos. Además, los organismos de control utilizan criterios de eficiencia, eficacia y cumplimiento legal para fiscalizar la gestión ambiental de las entidades públicas.

A pesar de estos avances, se identifica una debilidad principal: la falta de métricas estandarizadas y la desconexión entre las evaluaciones de los distintos actores, lo que dificulta una medición holística y consolidada del 'triple impacto' (ambiental, social y económico) de los proyectos. La fortaleza reside en una clara alineación de los planes locales con las metas nacionales de reducción de emisiones y en el fomento de un ecosistema de corresponsabilidad que va más allá de la gestión gubernamental.

column19: La evaluación de las acciones climáticas en Pereira se enmarca en una estrategia de gobernanza que busca la coherencia entre las políticas locales y los compromisos internacionales de Colombia. Los planes de gestión y los informes de progreso de entidades como el Ministerio de Ambiente y Desarrollo Sostenible (Minambiente) demuestran una clara alineación con los objetivos de la Contribución Determinada a Nivel Nacional (NDC) y las metas del Plan Nacional de Desarrollo (PND). Por ejemplo, el PND 2022-2026 establece objetivos para avanzar hacia una economía sostenible, productiva, innovadora y competitiva, armonizando la producción con la conservación de recursos y la mitigación del cambio climático.   \n\nUn objetivo central de esta alineación es la reducción acumulada de las emisiones de Gases de Efecto Invernadero (GEI). Se ha establecido la meta de reducir 52,2 millones de tCO2eq con respecto al escenario de referencia nacional, con un porcentaje de avance del 65,17% al cierre de 2022. Esta medición se basa en la existencia de nuevos proyectos de mitigación que han sido verificados, validados y certificados en los años recientes. Adicionalmente, el país ha definido un objetivo más ambicioso de reducir el 51% de las emisiones de GEI para 2030 y alcanzar la carbono-neutralidad para 2050, compromisos que guían la Estrategia Colombiana de Desarrollo Baja en Carbono-Adaptada y Resiliente (ECDBCAR). Este enfoque de largo plazo subraya la importancia de la planificación de mediano y largo plazo como un criterio fundamental de la evaluación de la acción climática.

A jurisdição de Palmas avalia as oportunidades e os benefícios da ação climática de forma integrada ao seu processo de planejamento estratégico. O Plano Diretor serve como o principal instrumento para identificar sinergias. Ações que cumprem múltiplos objetivos, como proteger o meio ambiente, promover a justiça social e estimular a economia, são priorizadas. As oportunidades são avaliadas com base em sua contribuição para os Objetivos de Desenvolvimento Sustentável (ODS), garantindo que a ação climática impulsione uma agenda de desenvolvimento mais ampla. No planejamento financeiro, as oportunidades são avaliadas pelo seu retorno sobre o investimento, economia de longo prazo para os cofres públicos e potencial de geração de 'empregos verdes'. A interação com cooperativas, associações e a comunidade em geral é fundamental para identificar oportunidades com alto impacto social, como o fortalecimento da cadeia de reciclagem.

A partir dessa avaliação, Palmas identificou e está implementando as seguintes ações estratégicas: Fomento à Economia Circular e Inclusão Social: Programa de Resíduos Recicláveis. Esta ação é vista como uma das maiores oportunidades para integrar as agendas ambiental, social e econômica; Redução direta das emissões de GEE (metano) ao diminuir o volume de resíduos orgânicos e recicláveis enviados ao aterro; Ampliação da vida útil do Aterro Sanitário, otimizando o uso do solo; Redução do risco de contaminação do solo e de cursos d'água; Fortalecimento e formalização da atividade dos catadores de materiais recicláveis, com criação de novas associações e cooperativas; Inserção de grupos marginalizados em uma cadeia produtiva estruturada, promovendo justiça social; Incremento direto na renda de todos os envolvidos na cadeia da reciclagem (catadores, associações, empresas); Melhoria das condições de saúde dos trabalhadores da cadeia e da população em geral.
A cidade identificou a transição energética como uma oportunidade chave para a resiliência econômica e a liderança climática. O Programa Palmas Solar estimula através de incentivos fiscais (redução de IPTU, ITBI, etc.), promove a economia local, gera empregos na área de instalação e manutenção, atrai investimentos e reduz o custo da energia para cidadãos e empresas, fomenta a mudança para uma matriz energética limpa e descentralizada e reduz significativamente a emissão de GEE no município. A troca de lâmpadas por LED gera economia direta e substancial no orçamento municipal através da redução da conta de energia pública e reduz o consumo de energia e a geração de resíduos sólidos (lâmpadas mais duráveis) e elimina o uso de materiais poluentes como o mercúrio.

Investir em capital natural é visto como uma oportunidade para melhorar a qualidade de vida e adaptar a cidade aos impactos climáticos. O Plano de Arborização Urbana, que tem como meta o plantio 200 mil mudas em 4 anos, combate às ilhas de calor (adaptação), sequestro de carbono (mitigação), agrega melhoria da qualidade do ar e aumento da biodiversidade urbana, melhora a saúde física e mental da população, embeleza a cidade e cria espaços públicos mais agradáveis, valorização imobiliária das áreas arborizadas e criação de empregos em viveiros, plantio e manutenção.

A Implantação de Parques Lineares ao Longo de Cursos Hídricos garante a proteção de nascentes e matas ciliares, criação de corredores ecológicos para a fauna e melhoria da drenagem natural, o aumento da qualidade de vida com espaços para lazer, esporte, cultura e educação ambiental, além de intensificar o potencial de atração turística e fomento a atividades econômicas ligadas ao lazer e bem-estar.

A jurisdição de Palmas reconhece que uma transição climática eficaz deve ser, por princípio, justa e inclusiva. Para garantir que os benefícios da ação climática alcancem prioritariamente as populações mais vulneráveis, foi adotada uma metodologia de quantificação baseada na análise de dados socioeconômicos e espaciais.
Antes da implementação das ações, as vulnerabilidades são quantificadas e mapeadas para orientar a alocação de recursos de forma justa. Foi desenvolvido um Índice de Vulnerabilidade Climática (IVC) que cruza dados socioeconômicos (renda, escolaridade, condições de moradia) com a exposição a riscos climáticos (como ilhas de calor e áreas de alagamento).
A alocação de investimentos em adaptação (ex: projetos de drenagem, arborização) é priorizada para as regiões com o IVC mais elevado. Quantifica-se o percentual do orçamento de adaptação que é destinado a essas áreas críticas.
Assegura-se que os benefícios de parques e áreas verdes sejam distribuídos de forma equitativa por toda a cidade. Realiza-se uma análise de distribuição espacial que sobrepõe o mapa de infraestrutura verde (parques, praças) ao mapa de renda média por setor.
Mede-se a área verde por habitante em diferentes faixas de renda, estabelecendo metas para reduzir o déficit em regiões de baixa renda.
Quantifica-se a distância média que os moradores de bairros vulneráveis precisam percorrer para acessar um parque urbano qualificado, trabalhando para reduzir essa distância.
O programa de reciclagem é avaliado por sua capilaridade e impacto social, além do benefício ambiental. A infraestrutura de coleta seletiva é mapeada e comparada com a demografia e o perfil socioeconômico da cidade.
Analisa-se a localização dos PEVs (Pontos de Entrega Voluntária) em relação à densidade populacional e à renda, garantindo que não existam 'desertos de reciclagem' em áreas periféricas.
Correlacionam-se o volume de resíduos coletado por ponto com o perfil da população atendida para direcionar campanhas de educação ambiental de forma mais eficaz.
A adesão aos programas de energia limpa é ativamente monitorada para evitar que os benefícios se restrinjam às populações de maior renda. Os dados de adesão ao Programa Palmas Solar e outros incentivos de energia renovável são analisados.
É feita a correlação entre endereços que receberam incentivos fiscais (como descontos no IPTU) com a faixa de renda da região. Essa análise permite identificar barreiras financeiras e desenvolver programas específicos, como projetos de geração de energia comunitária ou linhas de microcrédito, para democratizar o acesso à energia solar.
column19:
A Prefeitura de Palmas vai além do planejamento, implementando ações concretas que materializam o compromisso com uma distribuição justa e inclusiva dos benefícios da ação climática. As evidências desse direcionamento podem ser observadas em diversas áreas.
A gestão reconhece que, historicamente, parte da infraestrutura verde se concentrou em áreas de maior renda. Para reverter essa tendência e promover a justiça espacial, a diretriz atual para novos projetos é a priorização de regiões periféricas e de menor renda.
Projetos de implantação e requalificação de parques e praças estão sendo direcionados para setores que carecem desses espaços, como o Jardim Taquari, o Bertaville e o setor Santo Amaro. Esses novos espaços são concebidos como pólos de cidadania, integrando a criação de áreas verdes com a implantação de infraestrutura essencial (drenagem, esgoto) e equipamentos de esporte e cultura.
Dentro do Programa Coleta Palmas, a prefeitura implementou um sistema de monitoramento contínuo e adaptativo para garantir o acesso equitativo à coleta seletiva.
Com uma frequência quinzenal, as equipes técnicas monitoram o volume de resíduos coletados por tipo de material nos Pontos de Entrega Voluntária (PEVs). Essa análise de dados permite uma gestão adaptativa: se um PEV em uma área de menor renda apresenta baixo volume, isso aciona a necessidade de campanhas de educação ambiental focadas naquela comunidade, garantindo que a falta de informação não seja uma barreira à participação.
A evidência mais direta do compromisso com uma transição energética inclusiva é a integração de energia solar em programas de habitação de interesse social.
Um exemplo concreto é o Residencial Recanto das Araras I e II, onde as 1.424 unidades habitacionais foram entregues à população de baixa renda já equipadas com painéis fotovoltaicos. Esta ação remove a principal barreira de acesso à tecnologia (o alto custo de investimento) e proporciona um benefício econômico direto, reduzindo a despesa mensal das famílias com energia elétrica e combatendo a pobreza energética.

column19: 飯田市環境基本条例（前文）私たちの郷土、飯田市は、南アルプスや中央アルプスをはじめとする山並みに囲まれ、天竜川沿いの河岸段丘に発達した、伝統文化の息づくまちである。美しく雄大な自然に抱かれ、その豊かな水や緑は、古来より、市民生活に潤いを与え地場産業の発展を促すなど、様々な恵みをもたらしてきた。しかしながら、近年は、過去のような産業公害が減少する一方において、大量消費、大量廃棄型の社会経済活動の定着や無秩序な都市化の進展により、廃棄物の増大、生活排水や自動車などによる都市・生活型公害、身近な自然の減少、良好な景観の破壊など新たな環境問題が顕在化してきている。私たちは、ともすれば、生産の向上と便利な生活を追求するあまり、人類も生態系の中の一員であり、自然や文化の深い恩恵にはぐくまれて生存できることを忘れがちとなり、日々の活動による環境への影響は、地球的規模にまで拡大した。人類共通の重要な課題となった地球環境問題は、その解決に向けてわが国の地方自治体にも、大きな役割が求められてきている。今こそ私たちは、広い視野に立って、すべての人々が健全で豊かな環境の恵沢を享受するとともに、将来の世代に良好な環境を引き継いでいく責務を有することを認識し、環境への負荷を低減するため、すべての者の公平な役割分担の下に社会経済システムや生活様式の変革を図っていかなければならない。このような認識の下、私たちは、市民の総意として、美しい環境と文化の香りに包まれた持続的に発展することができる都市を、強い意志と行動により築くことを決意し、この条例を制定する。

Ao longo dos anos, a LP criou um ambiente que estimula o verde empregos e crescimento verde (orçamento anual aumentado de 75 mil euros para 1 milhão de euros).Ações relacionadas com a redução de riscos naturais, traduz-se em benefícios para a saúde pública da população, nemeadamente por reduzir a contaminação da água:- Bacia de Retenção das Hortas (Zero inundações) e sistema de alerta em tempo real- Delimitação das novas zonas ameaçadas pelas cheias com base nas Orientações Estratégicas de Âmbito Nacional e Regional - instrumento de planeamento que permitirá antecipar as reações do território face a situação de cheia.Guimarães é também proativo no reaproveitamento da água e eficiência hídrica, reduzindo os custos e aumentandp a segurança da água:- Guimarães lidera uma rede nacional para a circularidade da água- Projeto piloto: São as águas sujas das piscinas municipais que lavam as ruas da cidade de Guimarães- Substituição de relvados por prados de sequeiro, onde inexiste a necessidade de rega- Guimarães promove campanha para uso sustentável da água- a antecipação da deteção de fugas e a redução significativa das perdas - o melhor planeamento das intervenções de reparação- a redução do consumo de energia, uso de reagentes e emissões de CO2 associadas, com a consequente diminuição da pegada ecológica.Estratégias para redução de resíduos, separação de resíduos, reciclagem e reutilização ou gestão de resíduos biológicos, são alternativas viáveis e de baixo custo para a incineração aberta de resíduos sólidos e permitem a valorização energética de resíduos:- Zero Waste municipality- PAYT system- RRRCICLO- Guimarães tem vindo a regenerar sítios contaminadosVárias são as iniciativas e ações que promovem a Neutralidade Climática, destacando-se:Uma transição verde bem sucedida, colocando os cidação no centro, trará benefícios económicos, sociais e ambientais significativos - redução das emissões de GEE, redução da poluição atmosférica e sonora e os seus impactes negativos na nossa saúde e promoção da inovação:- Net Zero Cities- Bairro C: Compromisso Carbono Zero- EU Mission - Climate Neutral and Smart Cities- Iluminação pública de LEDVárias ações promovem aumento do uso sustentável da terra e do conforto bioclimático:- PDM- Brigadas Verdes- Guimarães mais Floresta- Expansão de espaços verdes - Biodiversity Action PlanOutras medidas têm como consequencia benefícios económicos, como a redução do risco de inundação (aumento do valor das propriedades nos locais onde o risco é efetivamente diminuído) e a substituição da iluminação pública convencional por LED (aumenta a eficiência energética e reduzir a energia consumida - poupança de energia). Finalmente, contamos com ações que promovem dignidade, oportunidade e igualdade, como o acesso de comunidades mais vulneráveis a energia limpa mais barata e , em alguns casos, melhoram a segurança nas ruas para diferentes grupos populacionais. Ao avaliar as ações climáticas, o Município identificou várias oportunidades e benefícios que se desdobram em diferentes áreas, conforme descrito a seguir.
A ação climática em Braga oferece oportunidades significativas para o crescimento económico local. Investimentos em tecnologias limpas, como energias renováveis e eficiência energética, não apenas reduzem os custos operacionais para as empresas, mas também criam novos empregos e setores económicos. A promoção de indústrias verdes e a modernização de infraestruturas podem impulsionar a competitividade local, atraindo investidores e estimulando a inovação. Além disso, iniciativas que visam a transição para a mobilidade elétrica e a construção sustentável podem resultar em economias substanciais no consumo de energia e na dependência de combustíveis fósseis.
Uma das principais vantagens da ação climática é a melhoria da qualidade do ar. A redução das emissões de gases poluentes, através de políticas de mobilidade sustentável e da promoção de transportes públicos, tem um impacto direto na saúde pública. A diminuição da poluição do ar contribui para a redução de doenças respiratórias e cardiovasculares, resultando em menos custos para o sistema de saúde e um aumento da produtividade. Assim, as iniciativas climáticas não apenas promovem a saúde ambiental, mas também beneficiam o bem-estar geral da população.
As ações climáticas promovem a construção de comunidades mais resilientes. Ao implementar infraestruturas verdes, como parques, telhados verdes e sistemas de drenagem sustentável, Braga não só mitiga os efeitos das alterações climáticas, mas também melhora a sua capacidade de resposta a eventos climáticos extremos, como inundações e ondas de calor. Essa resiliência tem impactos positivos na segurança da comunidade, na proteção de bens e na minimização de perdas económicas durante crises climáticas.
A ação climática também promove a coesão social e a inclusão. Projetos que envolvem a participação da comunidade e a colaboração entre diferentes setores podem fortalecer os laços sociais e aumentar a conscientização sobre questões ambientais. A promoção de iniciativas de mobilidade sustentável e de eficiência energética, com enfoque em grupos vulneráveis, garante que todas as camadas da sociedade se beneficiem das ações climáticas. Este enfoque inclusivo é essencial para criar uma cidade equitativa, onde todos têm acesso às oportunidades de desenvolvimento sustentável.
Braga possui um rico património natural e cultural que pode ser valorizado através de ações climáticas. A proteção e a recuperação de ecossistemas locais, como zonas húmidas e áreas verdes, não só preservam a biodiversidade, mas também enriquecem o ambiente urbano, tornando a cidade mais atrativa para residentes e visitantes. Além disso, a promoção do turismo sustentável, centrado em experiências que valorizem o património natural e cultural, pode gerar receitas adicionais para a economia local.
As iniciativas climáticas oferecem uma oportunidade valiosa para a educação e a sensibilização ambiental. Programas de educação nas escolas e nas comunidades, focados em práticas sustentáveis e na importância da ação climática, ajudam a formar cidadãos mais conscientes e proativos. Ao promover uma cultura de sustentabilidade, o Município pode inspirar uma nova geração a tomar decisões informadas que beneficiem tanto o ambiente quanto a sociedade.
A ação climática também pode estimular a inovação e a pesquisa. Braga tem a oportunidade de se tornar um laboratório vivo para tecnologias sustentáveis e soluções inovadoras. A colaboração com universidades, centros de pesquisa e empresas pode resultar em desenvolvimentos tecnológicos que não apenas beneficiam a cidade, mas também contribuem para o conhecimento global sobre práticas climáticas eficazes. A promoção de parcerias entre academia e setor privado pode acelerar a adoção de tecnologias limpas e soluções criativas para desafios urbanos.

column19:
O Município de Braga tem implementado várias ações concretas para assegurar a distribuição igualitária e inclusiva dos benefícios da ação climática. Essas iniciativas são projetadas para atender às necessidades de todos os segmentos da população, especialmente os grupos mais vulneráveis. Abaixo estão algumas evidências e detalhes dessas ações:
1. Programas de Educação e Sensibilização Ambiental
Braga desenvolve programas de educação ambiental nas escolas, com o objetivo de sensibilizar os jovens sobre as questões climáticas e a importância da sustentabilidade. Esses programas incluem atividades práticas, como oficinas de jardinagem e reciclagem, permitindo que crianças e adolescentes se tornem agentes ativos na promoção de práticas sustentáveis em suas comunidades. Um exemplo disto são as atividades desenvolvidas na Quinta Pedagógica de Braga e no seu recente Centro de Educação Ambiental onde mais de 100 atividades de educação às alterações climáticas pelas escolas do concelho. 
2. Incentivos Financeiros para Eficiência Energética
O Município lançou iniciativas de apoio financeiro para a implementação de soluções de eficiência energética, como a instalação de painéis solares em habitações de baixo rendimento. Este programa oferece subsídios e condições favoráveis de financiamento, garantindo que famílias de todas as condições socioeconómicas possam beneficiar da transição para energias renováveis e reduzir seus custos energéticos. O Programa Municipal de Combate à Pobreza Energética de Braga que pretende oferecer obras de renovação de eficneica energética a famailais desfavorecidas é um exemplo disso. 
3. Acessibilidade à Mobilidade Sustentável
Braga está a investir na expansão da rede de transportes públicos acessíveis e na promoção de alternativas de mobilidade sustentável, como a implementação de ciclovias e sistemas de partilha de bicicletas. A cidade desenvolveu um programa de bilhetes sociais que oferece tarifas reduzidas para cidadãos de baixa renda, garantindo que a mobilidade sustentável seja uma opção viável para todos. 
4. Projetos de Inclusão Social em Ações Climáticas
O Município tem promovido projetos que combinam ação climática e inclusão social, como a criação de hortas comunitárias em áreas urbanas desfavorecidas. Esses espaços não apenas promovem a agricultura urbana e a biodiversidade, mas também criam oportunidades para a comunidade se envolver em práticas sustentáveis e fortalecer os laços sociais.
5. Consulta e Participação da Comunidade
O Município organiza consultas públicas e workshops para envolver os cidadãos na elaboração de políticas climáticas. Este processo garante que as preocupações e sugestões de todos os grupos, incluindo os mais vulneráveis, sejam consideradas nas decisões sobre investimentos em infraestrutura e projetos ambientais. O Pacto de Mobilidade Empresarial de Braga que estimula as empresas a contribuir para a mobilidade sustentável da cidade é um exemplo desta participação da comunidade por via do setor empresarial. 
7. Parcerias com Organizações Locais
Braga colabora com organizações não governamentais e grupos comunitários para implementar iniciativas de inclusão e garantir que as ações climáticas cheguem a todos. Estas parcerias ajudam a identificar as necessidades específicas de diferentes grupos da população e a desenvolver soluções adaptadas.

column16: There are many direct and in-direct benefits to climate action. The City recognizes that through our climate work we are helping to foster a community that is more resilient to extreme events, healthy through improved mobility, access, and through cleaner air, more open and accessible green-space, and indoor environmental quality for residents. Some of these wider benefits can be hard to measure and track, such as improved mental health of city residents in response to improved greenspace, energy efficiency homes, and reduced noise from vehicle traffic. For example, the City has an Urban Forestry Master Plan, which lays out the pathway for increased tree canopy coverage throughout our urban environment. Urban trees provide a number of intangible benefits from sequestering CO2, increased shade (which has a growing importance as extreme heat becomes a greater issue every year), and mental well-being. The City is organized into various departments, and departments divided further into divisions. The Community Development Department is the main driver of climate related work in the city, but often collaborates with other departments to further the reach and affect climate work. For example, CDD often works with the Department of Public Works and the School Department to collaborate on greenhouse gas emission inventories, electric school buses, EV-charging, and education and outreach campaigns for a variety of topics (recycling, bicycle safety, etc.).

The Office of Sustainability routinely assesses the wider opportunities and benefits for most of the climate actions they initiate. For example, the City's 10K Tree Program's goal to distribute 10,000 trees to residents and businesses in 10 years, not only connects the program to climate change and the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions over the years but also, brings attention to human health (heat reduction by providing shade), improving air quality (clean air), economic saving (shading house can reduce energy cost) and providing habitat. The Office makes the program accessible to the City's historically disadvantaged communities as these neighborhoods were identified with a lack of substantial tree canopy coverage. Also, quantifies the impact of the program to demonstrate to city departments and Administration the co-benefits provided by the program beyond the obvious benefit, if possible. An example of a tree's benefits are showcased in the Treeplotter Inventory- https://pg-cloud.com/WestPalmBeachFL/

As it relates to planning, the Climate Resilience Assessment and Plan includes an analysis of economic factors, as well as demographics of residents and sensitive populations, and for each climate threat identified for the City and how each threat will impact the local economy and people. For example, 43% of the city's annual sales and 36% of the city's jobs/ employees were found highly vulnerable to rainfall-induced flooding, with specific vulnerable populations identified by neighborhood. The Climate Resilience Assessment and Plan also included an analysis of assets and properties at risk in various climate scenarios, including sea level rise and coastal & urban flooding, strengthening the connection between climate mitigation and adaptation and benefits to local property owners.

 In 2021, the City received a grant to update its Vulnerability Assessment, as it relates to flooding. The result of this assessment will be integrated into city planning process and future projects throughout the City by identifying which communities, neighborhoods, and/or sectors are most in need and would benefit the most from the work.

column18: We have identified the areas of the city that are vulnerable to climate-related risks using the Climate Resiliency Assessment. Also, the Heat Study helped to identify areas with low canopy and areas that needed tree planting. Using census tracks we have identified our LMI communities, so we can target neighborhood groups and organizations with programming and education.
