column19: The Climate Resilience Assessment and Plan considered 11 climate threats that could impact the City, including storm surge, sea level rise, water pollution, and extreme heat, and measured the impact of those threats on various assets, including people and socioeconomics. Particular sensitive populations were identified, including families living below the poverty line and elderly households. For each threat, the assessment mapped the impacts of those threats as they related to each asset and identified specific regions and/or neighborhoods in the City that were most vulnerable to the threat. These maps allow the city departments to visualize where climate threats are located and which communities are impacted the most thus providing another tool for them to use when determining what actions need to take place that will be most beneficial to the most vulnerable community as well as the city as a whole.\n \nThe City conducted a tree canopy assessment of the entire City in 2018 and identified the Historic Northwest Neighborhood, a historically disadvantaged community, as lacking substantial tree coverage. A Million Dollar Tree Fund was established in 2018 to improve the tree canopy in two areas of the City (Downtown & Northwest). The project has moved from planning to the execution stage in 2023, with planting 62 trees in the Historic Northwest and 101 trees in the Northwood Hills communities. The trees will provide shade for the residents and properties, thus reducing the energy burden felt by residents to cool their homes. As of 2025, the City has completed an update to its Tree Canopy Assessment, which includes revised goals for tree canopy planting throughout the entire City.

1. Improve the quality of natural resources (e.g., air quality, water quality) and promote health benefits.
New Taipei City has completed three key policies, including the phasing out of coal-fired boilers and the replacement of asphalt industry fuel from oil to gas in 2019, and the phasing out of coal-fired steam electricity symbiotic units in 2022, which has resulted in New Taipei City becoming a coal-free city starting in 2023.In addition, the city government has been integrating various resources. Through cross-departmental cooperation, New Taipei City has succeeded in decreasing PM2.5 concentrations in the jurisdiction through policies such as building a comprehensive public transportation system, expanding public bicycle system, promoting cleaner vehicles, and promoting the installation of continuous automatic air pollution monitoring facilities in factory boilers. In the future, we will move towards more strict air quality goals (annual average PM2.5 concentration below 10µg/m3 by 2030). In addition, policies such as waste management and the promotion of circular economy can reduce waste, improve water quality of rivers and reduce marine pollution.

2. Green Economy and Sharing Economy to Promote Green Job Opportunities.
(1) Green Economy.
A.Since 2013, New Taipei City has undertaken the replacement of traditional streetlights with energy-efficient alternatives. All streetlights were upgraded to LED by 2015, and in 2020, the city began replacing them with smart LED lights. This initiative not only reduces greenhouse gas emissions but also promotes green employment and enhances the competitiveness of the green technology sector.
B. The city's “Food Waste Reducing Restaurant” initiative encourages restaurants to use imperfect (ugly) fruits and vegetables as ingredients to minimize food waste.
C. Through the “Green Store” project, the city evaluates four major sectors—fast food chains, retail and wholesale stores, supermarkets, and restaurants—based on criteria such as source reduction, food conservation, recycling, environmental cleanliness, environmental education, and energy conservation. The program guides these key industries toward more energy-efficient and waste-reducing operations.
(2) Sharing economy: New Taipei City has developed a public bicycle rental system and promotes shared scooter and car rental services. The city also encourages service providers to establish operations within communities to enhance local accessibility and reduce private vehicle dependency.

3. Enhancing Social Equity
Projects such as the Food Sharing Network, which donates surplus or imperfect (ugly) fruits and vegetables to disadvantaged groups, and the Happiness Station, which redistributes reusable furniture and household items to low-income households, aim to support those in need while promoting resource reuse. These initiatives not only reduce waste but also help care for vulnerable communities and strengthen social inclusion.

4. Promoting Livability and More Efficient Land Use Patterns
New Taipei City continuously expands its public transportation network, including MRT routes, transit buses, shared bikes, and pedestrian corridors. In addition, reducing greenhouse gas and air pollutant emissions, it can also reduce the number of transfers for passengers, save travel time, and enhance the convenience of citizens' life. With a dense, comprehensive, mass transportation infrastructure, most of the public activities gather around the public transport station and achieve a high-quality transportation system and sustainable and efficient land use structure.

column18: 1.The New Taipei City Government has established a dedicated Sustainable Development Portal to regularly monitor and publish the outcomes of sustainability-related policies. In addition, the city released the “New Taipei City Voluntary Local Review on SDGs” in both 2019 and 2021, and published the “2050 Net-Zero Pathway and Climate Action White Paper” in 2022 to evaluate the progress of its sustainable development and climate actions.\n\n2.The New Taipei City Government, through its dedicated agency—the Department of Social Affairs—has established a long-term monitoring and support system for vulnerable groups, ensuring that climate policies are aligned with social data and assistance mechanisms to prioritize the needs of the most at-risk populations. The department implements the \'Shelter and Assistance Measures for Homeless and Elderly Individuals\' program, which annually tracks outreach efforts during periods of extreme heat and cold, including the provision of cooling spaces and cold weather supplies. The \'Good Day Love Platform\' records annual public donations made to vulnerable groups such as homeless individuals, elderly people living alone, children, and persons with disabilities. In parallel, the \'Food Sharing Network\' monitors the volume of imperfect fruits and vegetables donated to disadvantaged individuals within the city. Additionally, other government departments also incorporate considerations for vulnerable populations into their climate-related initiatives, further reinforcing the city's inclusive and people-centered approach to climate resilience.
column19:
1.Inclusion of Citizens' Views in the Formulation of Climate Policy
The New Taipei City Climate Change Response Steering Groups are composed of representatives from civil society organizations, academic experts, industry representatives, and government agencies, all of whom provide advice on the city's climate change mitigation and adaptation actions. Civil society members are drawn from some of the most prominent advocacy groups in Taiwan, including the Green Citizen's Action Alliance, Greenpeace, and the Taiwan Youth Climate Coalition. Industry representatives include the Taiwan Green Technology Industry Alliance, as well as members from the ESCO sector, net-zero building, and air-conditioning industries. Academic experts contribute their knowledge in areas such as energy transition, circular economy, and climate resilience. During both the annual plenary meetings and the biannual subgroup meetings of the Steering Groups, at least one representative from civil society is invited to provide input from the public's perspective and to advocate on behalf of disadvantaged communities.

2. Upholding the Principle of 'Leaving No One Behind'
In 2021, New Taipei City published its second Voluntary Local Review (VLR) on the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), integrating local policies with global sustainability objectives.
Recognizing that vulnerable groups are often the first and most severely affected by climate change, the city ensures that climate action incorporates the rights and needs of all populations, particularly those who lack a strong voice in policymaking. The VLR outlines a range of inclusive measures, including: employment support for persons with disabilities; provision of adequate learning resources for students in rural and remote areas; encouragement for disadvantaged youth to enlist in the military; creation of gender-friendly environments; year-round domestic violence prevention services; promotion of Indigenous agricultural revitalization in urban areas; development of social housing; establishment of a workplace sustainability center for women and older adults; intensive employment counseling for youth; and implementation of multicultural policies to support new immigrant communities.
Through the development of a green and circular model of production and consumption, New Taipei City continues to promote local economic development and sustainable future.

3.Caring for Climate-Vulnerable Communities
In line with the Climate Change Response Act, New Taipei City conducts climate risk assessments to identify high-risk areas under 1.5°C and 2°C warming scenarios and develops adaptation strategies for vulnerable groups. The Department of Social Affairs implements a disaster response plan focused on mapping the distribution and evacuation needs of at-risk populations, aiming to strengthen preparedness and ensure adequate support during emergencies.
For extreme cold, the city activates the Cold Wave Preparedness Plan when temperatures fall to 12°C or below, and enhances outreach when temperatures drop to 10°C, providing warm clothing, hot meals, and temporary shelters for homeless individuals and elderly residents.
For extreme heat, the Heat Response Measures Plan is triggered when temperatures exceed 36°C for three days or reach 38°C in one day. The plan includes wellness checks for elderly residents, public heat alerts, the opening of cooling centers, and the distribution of water and supplies to those in need.

4. the “Good Day” platform
Established in 2019, the “Good Day” Platform integrates local resources to support vulnerable groups in New Taipei City, including homeless individuals, elderly people living alone, children, and people with physical or mental disabilities. The platform allows citizens to select specific charity projects and designate donations to their preferred beneficiaries. As of the end of July 2024, the platform had raised over NT$4.897 billion in combined cash and in-kind donations and had provided support more than 54.53 million times.

5.Food Sharing Network
Established in 2016, the Food Sharing Network is a cross-agency initiative by New Taipei City that redistributes surplus food—mainly from public markets—to vulnerable groups such as the elderly, low-income families, and homeless individuals. The program supports both food waste reduction and social welfare goals.
The city partners with food suppliers, markets, and NGOs to collect excess produce and deliver it to community kitchens. To ensure food safety and expand reach to rural areas, three refrigerated trucks were introduced through public-private collaboration, improving both transportation and donor confidence.
Since 2020, donated food has been processed into frozen meal packs and canned goods to improve shelf life and convenience. This allows the program to serve more communities efficiently while reinforcing the city's commitment to resource circularity and inclusive food access.

Due to the aging farmers and fishermen, Pingtung County hoped to transform the idle land into solar photovoltaic farm through this project. With 20-year guaranteed wholesale rate, Pingtung County provided reasonable land rents for farmers and fishermen as stable alternative incomes. 2009年的八八風災侵襲南台灣，使得屏東縣部分地區發生淹水及斷電情形，尤以林邊鄉、佳冬鄉等嚴重地層下陷區最為嚴重，使得當地土壤鹽化情況加重，重創農漁養殖業。為協助災民重建家園、解決困擾許久的地層下陷問題，本縣發起「養水種電」計畫，結合太陽光電設置於不再適合耕作的土地，在家園恢復的過渡時期，透過台電公司20年「躉購制度」保證收購綠電方式，協助居民能有穩定租金收入，不僅引導當地產業轉型與土地復育，更奠定屏東縣綠能發展基礎。
考量屏東為農業大縣，為避免太陽光電設施與農爭地，並克服饋線不足，2019年於嚴重地層下陷區(東港鎮、林邊鄉、佳冬鄉、枋寮鄉全行政區)推動專案計畫，將不利耕作的嚴重地層下陷範圍拓劃為光電優先發展區域，不僅成功複製養水種電模式，亦透過土地「種電」達到暫時休耕恢復地力與涵養地下水的功能。

Typhoon Morakot hit southern Taiwan in 2009, resulting in flooding and power outages in some areas of Pingtung County. Soil salinization become worse in severe subsidence areas, such as Linbian Township and Jiadong Township, which severely damaged agriculture, fishery and aquaculture industry. In order to assist citizens to rebuild their homes and solve the long-tern problem of land subsidence, Pingtung County Government launched a project named “Aqua Solar Farm,” which installed solar PV panels in nonarable lands. During the period of home restoration, Tai-power Company purchases green electricity with 20-year guaranteed wholesale rate. Pingtung County provided reasonable land rents for farmers and fishermen as stable alternative incomes. Developing solar energy not only promotes industrial transition and land restoration, but also becomes the basis for developing green energy in Pingtung County.

Pingtung is a major agricultural county. In order to avoid competing land with farmers and overcome the feeder shortage, Pingtung County Government promoted “Sever land subsidence areas” in 2019 to develop solar PV energy in severe land subsidence area (Donggang Township, Linbian Township, Jiadong Township, Fangliao Township). It not only successfully replicated the model of “Aqua Solar Farm,” but also restored soil fertility and groundwater.

Çanakkale Municipality has identified a range of broader environmental, social, and economic benefits associated with its climate action efforts. These benefits are considered in both planning and implementation phases of policies and projects.

Key opportunities and benefits include:

Environmental benefits: Improved air quality through promotion of active transportation (cycling and walking), reduction of vehicle emissions, and increased green spaces. Waste reduction and sustainable land use planning also contribute to ecosystem protection.

Social benefits: Enhanced public health from cleaner air and increased physical activity; stronger community engagement through participatory environmental programs; educational benefits via climate literacy initiatives in schools and youth groups.

Economic opportunities: Lower municipal energy costs due to efficiency projects and renewable energy use; development of green jobs in areas such as recycling, clean energy, and sustainable mobility; increased attractiveness of the city for sustainable tourism and eco-conscious investors.

Climate resilience: Investments in urban green infrastructure and sustainable stormwater management enhance the city's resilience to extreme weather events and reduce long-term climate-related risks.

These co-benefits are an integral part of the city's approach to creating a livable, inclusive, and climate-smart future.

Çanakkale Municipality employs several methods to quantify the equitable and inclusive distribution of climate action benefits:

Data collection and mapping: The municipality collects socio-economic and demographic data across neighborhoods to identify vulnerable and underserved communities, ensuring targeted climate action.

Performance indicators: Key indicators such as access to renewable energy, public green spaces, and sustainable transportation usage are tracked and disaggregated by geographic area and social groups.

Community surveys and feedback: Regular surveys and public consultations help assess whether climate initiatives reach diverse population groups and meet their needs.

Monitoring social impact: The municipality measures outcomes related to health improvements, job creation in green sectors, and participation rates among marginalized groups to evaluate inclusivity.


Through these approaches, Çanakkale ensures climate actions benefit all residents fairly and inclusively.
column19:
Çanakkale Municipality has adopted a multi-stakeholder and participatory approach to ensure that climate action is equitable and inclusive. During the development of the Local Climate Action Plan, representatives from public institutions, universities, NGOs, youth, women's groups, and community volunteers were actively engaged through stakeholder meetings, climate workshops, and awareness sessions designed to encourage inclusive participation.

The municipality also launched a Climate Ambassadors Project, involving local volunteers in the decision-making process and strengthening civic engagement in climate governance. Through educational programs in schools and community centers, awareness on climate change is being raised among children, youth, and elderly populations, ensuring that all social groups have access to knowledge and participation opportunities.

In terms of sustainable infrastructure, the municipality's Wastewater Treatment Plant Solar Energy Project (GES) provides clean energy while promoting environmental sustainability and social equity. The project delivers both economic and ecological benefits by reducing reliance on fossil fuels.

These initiatives reflect a climate action strategy that integrates environmental goals with social justice, ensuring that no group is left behind in the fight against climate change.

column16: Medford's Climate Action and Adaptation Plan lays out the action Medford will take over the next five years, and the trajectory we'll take in the following decades, to minimize our carbon footprint, strengthen our city's resilience, and build a healthy and inclusive city for residents today and future generations. Medford met its goal to reduce municipal emissions by 20% by 2010, and subsequently met two more municipal targets: a 20% reduction in total municipal energy use from 2009 levels by 2014 (to achieve Green Communities status), and a 20% reduction in building energy use per square foot from 2009 levels by 2020 (to accomplish the US Better Buildings Challenge).

column18: Medford has four guiding principles for climate equity (as listed in the Climate Action and Adaptation Plan):1) Cultivate belonging and diversity - City projects, programs, and policies should strive to ensure all residents - regardless of their identities - feel like they belong in the city. This requires tackling implicit biases and assumptions within city government and the community as a whole about who is considered a \'true\' Medford resident. The city aims for all residents to feel represented by public officials, feel respected and validated at public meetings, and feel that they have the resources and support to become the city's next leaders. 2) Create equitable access to resources and communication - All residents deserve to have access to the resources they need to achieve their potential and lead healthy and fulfilling lives. Resources include program, information, tools, and opportunities that range from sustainable transportation options, to quality healthcare, to ways to save money on utilities. Equitable communication can look like adapting Medford's resources to reflect the diverse languages of the city's many cultural and language communities and providing interpretation services so each person's voice can be heard. By acting on this principle, the city is committing to building its cultural competency and breaking down communication and information barriers so that all residents are able to benefit from climate investments.3) Facilitate inclusive decision-making - Medford organizations, residents, and the city work in partnership to address the climate crisis. Decisions should draw on community members' lived experiences, defer to those who have been historically underrepresented in planning processes, and involve communities that will be most impacted by climate change. By pursuing this principle, the city intends to shift the decision-making relationship from \'city as lead problem solver\' to \'city as collaborator.\' Acting on this principle to implement the goals set in the CAAP and Comprehensive Plan, the city will seek ongoing opportunities for democratic participation, community ownership of projects, and community partnerships.4) Design and implement anti-racist policies - Anti-racist climate policies aim to reduce the disproportionate burden created by climate change on Black, Indigenous, and people of color, and ensure that benefits from climate action are shared equitably regardless of race. Accountability mechanisms in anti-racist policies ensure that all policies are continuously improved to center equity and social justice.
column19: (1) Medford Connectors - In 2020, Medford was the first municipality in Massachusetts to hire community members from each of the City's main language/cultural groups (Brazilian-Portuguese, Arabic, Haitian-Creole, Spanish, and African American) to serve as liaisons between the City and their communities for climate-related issues. They are largely responsible for ensuring that their communities receive the necessary climate-resiliency resources provided by the City and have the opportunity to serve an active role in shaping the City's future projects and plans. (2) The Climate Equity Council is an Ad Hoc committee (currently composed of the Medford Connectors and City staff) that advises the city on implementation of the Climate Action Plan, with a focus on representing the interests of previously underrepresented groups. Based primarily on Members' lived experiences and perspectives they've gathered from their communities, the Council provides feedback on proposed City actions, including neighborhood-specific projects, buildings and energy projects, stormwater projects, public health projects, and transportation projects. (3) Electrify Medford Coaches - Starting in 2024, Medford residents interested in reducing their energy bills and their carbon footprint can sign up (at no cost) to meet with a resident volunteer or City staff member to talk through the options available to them. Volunteers are Medford residents with different language backgrounds and experiences with electrification who have been trained on the relevant technologies and programs. Although it is a citywide program, the City has a grant from the Massachusetts Clean Energy Center to focus outreach efforts on environmental justice groups. (4) The outcomes of the MVP planning process—and specifically the identified priority area that called for strengthening social resilience and communication with non-English speaking populations in Medford—helped to launch an initiative led by the Medford Health Department to assess potential neighborhoods, potential partners, and community needs for the development of Resilience Hubs in Medford. This process was supported by an MVP Action Grant, discussed in further detail in Question 4. (5) Finally, the MVP process outcomes and the Climate Change Vulnerability Assessment (2019) have directly informed the development of the City's Climate Action and Adaptation Plan. A workshop was held with City staff and key stakeholders to identify actions for the development of the Climate Action and Adaptation Plan. This workshop was followed by extensive interviews with City and State-level staff to identify resilience-related actions that are already underway and upcoming priorities; a public workshop to develop the vision for the plan; a public survey, shared online and by staff tabling at public events, which further engaged the public in developing the vision for the plan; the launch of four Working Groups made up of City staff and residents to further develop strategies within specific topic areas, and an Equity Workshop to look at the equity implications of the strategies and opportunities to advance equity through this plan. A Community Dinner to further engage residents, specifically Medford's Haitian community, was hosted. This extensive outreach responds to the MVP priority area related to building social resilience and communication with residents, specifically non-English speaking residents. The strategies developed as part of the plan further address other priority areas identified in the MVP planning process (e.g., stormwater management and green infrastructure, the health of wetlands and riparian corridors, and reducing vulnerability in Medford Square, among others.)

column18: Los planes que se elaboraron cuentan con todo un enfoque inclusivo, equitativo, con enfoque de género y diversidad. Se definieron las poblaciones vulnerables de nuestra ciudad y se incluyeron en la elaboración de los planes y su validación. El enfoque de género está ligado con las dinámicas locales de la ciudad en todos los niveles de la vida pública, en donde se entienda la complementariedad de las políticas y el rol de las mujeres dentro de los sectores priorizados. Así que para los diferentes estudios se comprende el desempeño de las mujeres en el mercado laboral, la composición de su ingreso, sus patrones de movilidad, la participación política, las tendencias migratorias y cualquier otra interacción entre los sectores de la ciudad y el género. Por otra parte, de alguna forma integrar a las mujeres y entender el impacto de sus acciones sobre las brechas existentes. Para todos los proyectos se trabaja en la creación y en la validación con diferentes grupos etarios, precisamente para impulsar las diferentes visiones y perspectivas. Se cuenta con procesos de co creación de proyectos, políticas y otros. Y en el caso de la planificación climática ha sido así.
column19: Se cuenta con una oficina de género en la Municipalidad, y una unidad de promoción social que nos apoyan para integrar y para incluir el tema en los diferentes proyectos. Para la elaboración de todos los proyectos se ha incluido este enfoque y se trabaja con todos sectores en procesos de co creación y participación ciudadana. También se trabaja en procesos de gobernanza climática como la Comisión Cantonal de Cambio Climático. Se tienen planes de acción y trabajo con la comunidad y diferentes sectores. Se trabaja con las comunidades que están en primera línea, las más afectadas por el cambio climático y que se encuentran en sitios con mayor exposición. column18: Much of the assessment of climate equity in York has been assessed qualitatively, through Our Big Conversation in York's Climate Change Strategy and through Equalities Impact Assessments completed for Climate-related decisions that will impact York's residents. However, projects that seek to help the most vulnerable populations in York do involve quantifiable evidence to enable to equitable and inclusive distribution of climate change action. For instance, the HUG2 programme seeks to help homes which have off-gas heating systems to become more energy efficient and save residents money. The scheme uses eligibility criteria to focus on households particularly vulnerable to high heating costs (households may have a total gross income of up to £36,000 unless you are already in a qualifying postcode area). Similarly, our partners York Energy Advice by York Community Energy offer free support on energy issues to anyone in York on a low income, or aged 65+, or experiencing a long term physical or mental health condition or disability offering an example of how climate action support may use quantifiable data to encourage inclusive climate action. In terns of quantifying the equitable and inclusive distribution of climate adaptation actions, the Council utilises tools such as the Tree Equity Score UK. Trees are essential to public health and wellbeing, yet not everyone has good access to trees and their benefits where they live. Tree Equity Score UK is a map-based application that was created to help address disparities in urban tree distribution by identifying the areas in greatest need of people-focused investment in trees. The Council has utilised the Tree Equity Score in its adaptation focused efforts to increase tree canopy cover in York through its Green Streets programme. https://uk.treeequityscore.org/
column19: We engage with communities impacted by climate change in relation to the implementation of projects, however we have also undertaken city-wide engagement to inform the our Climate Change Strategy. Almost 2,000 responses were received, with 80% of respondents agreeing with York's ambition to become a net zero carbon city by 2030. A further round of engagement included focus groups that targeted underrepresented voices from the first Our Big Conversation discussion. These structured discussions have contributed to our understanding and the content of this Strategy and aided in increasing the inclusivity of the Climate Change Strategy. Our Equalities Impact Assessment of both our Climate Change Strategy and Emissions Reporting also demonstrates our commitment to considering the equality of our climate action. This assessment details the key findings and impacts of the Climate Change Strategy in terms of equality groups and human rights as well as mechanisms to mitigate adverse impacts and maximise positive impacts across these key demographics. We are also currently implementing the Local Energy Advice Demonstrator (LEAD) programme, which is focussing on Hard-to-reach communities and Hard-to-treat homes recognising that some groups need more support than others. Beşiktaş Municipality recognizes that climate action creates not only environmental gains but also significant economic, social, and health-related opportunities. These co-benefits are systematically assessed through the Sustainable Energy and Climate Action Plan (SECAP), launched in 2023, and the district-wide greenhouse gas inventory completed in 2024. The wider benefits identified span multiple policy areas and guide the district's long-term development vision.

Energy efficiency in buildings

Cost savings: Reducing energy consumption through retrofits and improved building standards lowers utility bills for residents, businesses, and public facilities.

Lower emissions: Decreased energy demand directly contributes to the district's 41.6% emissions-reduction target by 2030.

Improved comfort: Better insulation and ventilation enhance indoor air quality and thermal comfort, supporting health and well-being.

Renewable energy integration

Sustainable supply: Solar panel installations on municipal and residential buildings reduce fossil fuel dependency.

Energy independence: Local renewable generation increases resilience against global energy market volatility.

Economic development: Renewable energy deployment stimulates local green jobs and attracts investment in innovative technologies.

Electric mobility and transport

Reduced emissions: Shifting to electric vehicles (EVs) and low-emission public transport lowers transport-related air pollution.

Public health benefits: Cleaner air reduces respiratory illnesses and improves overall health outcomes.

Technological innovation: EV charging infrastructure positions Beşiktaş as a leader in sustainable urban mobility.

Waste reduction and recycling

Resource conservation: Enhanced recycling and zero-waste practices reduce demand for raw materials and protect ecosystems.

Economic efficiency: Efficient waste management decreases landfill costs and generates savings for the municipality.

Environmental protection: Prevents pollution, improves local air quality, and safeguards public health.

Water management and drought resilience

Conservation: Rainwater harvesting, graywater recycling, and efficient irrigation reduce stress on municipal water systems.

Cost savings: Lower water consumption decreases utility bills.

Resilience: Improved practices strengthen the district's capacity to cope with droughts and water scarcity, which are increasingly frequent across Istanbul.

Infrastructure resilience

Reduced risk: Climate-resilient design minimizes damage from floods, storms, and heatwaves.

Long-term savings: Proactive adaptation investments prevent costly post-disaster recovery.

Improved safety: Resilient infrastructure supports safer living conditions for residents and visitors.

Environmental awareness and education

Informed decision-making: Public education campaigns encourage responsible consumption and climate-friendly practices.

Community engagement: Social responsibility projects, trainings, and events build stronger community bonds.

Behavioral change: Awareness programs instill long-term sustainable habits across generations.

Urban green spaces

Enhanced livability: Expanding parks and recreational areas improves quality of life, reduces urban heat, and enhances city aesthetics.

Biodiversity: Green areas provide habitats for species and strengthen ecological networks.

Climate mitigation: Urban greenery contributes to carbon absorption and improves local air quality.

Cross-cutting benefits
Climate action in Beşiktaş provides cumulative opportunities across multiple sectors. Energy efficiency reduces municipal operating costs; renewable integration increases security; sustainable transport enhances health; and resilient infrastructure safeguards future generations. These actions also strengthen the district's reputation as a cultural and innovation hub, attracting visitors and investment while ensuring that climate neutrality and social inclusivity remain central goals.

Beşiktaş Municipality monitors the equitable and inclusive distribution of climate actions primarily through its existing performance measurement and citizen engagement systems. Regular performance reports are published both by the Climate Change and Zero Waste Directorate and by the municipality as a whole. These reports include quantitative indicators such as the number of projects completed, waste collected, energy consumption trends in municipal facilities, and progress on environmental initiatives. While not designed solely for climate action, these indicators provide measurable insights into the effectiveness and inclusivity of ongoing activities.

Residents also have continuous opportunities to provide input through multiple communication channels. The municipality maintains a 24/7 call center, dedicated email addresses, an online municipal portal, and active social media platforms. Citizens regularly use these tools to raise concerns, share suggestions, and provide feedback on environmental and climate-related services. All communications are digitally recorded, creating a dataset that can be used to evaluate community priorities and identify areas for improvement.

The “Recycle & Win” mobile application further supports monitoring by allowing residents to deliver recyclable waste to the municipality in return for incentives. The application records detailed log data, including the type and amount of waste delivered, user participation levels, and the growing number of active users. These records make it possible to track how different community groups engage with waste reduction initiatives and to quantify the inclusivity and reach of climate-related actions.

The broad accessibility of these monitoring mechanisms ensures that vulnerable and frontline communities—such as elderly residents, students, and low-income households—can benefit from climate-related programs at no cost. The combination of traditional reporting, digital engagement, and open communication platforms provides a foundation for monitoring whether opportunities and benefits are fairly distributed, even in the absence of formal survey data.

Beşiktaş Municipality has not yet implemented large-scale climate projects beyond the Sustainable Energy and Climate Action Plan (SECAP, 2023). Since a follow-up SECAP monitoring report has not yet been prepared, comprehensive outcome-based evaluations are not available at this stage. Nevertheless, climate-related actions are continuously monitored and assessed through the municipality's existing performance reporting systems, which provide transparency and accountability to residents. These mechanisms, combined with digital records and citizen engagement platforms, enable the municipality to measure progress in an inclusive manner and to identify areas for further improvement. Looking ahead, future SECAP updates and expanded monitoring efforts will allow Beşiktaş to strengthen its quantitative and qualitative assessment capacity, ensuring that the equitable distribution of climate action opportunities and benefits is tracked more systematically over time.

Beşiktaş Municipality is committed to ensuring that climate action opportunities and benefits are distributed equitably and inclusively across all segments of society. A key milestone in this direction has been the preparation of the Sustainable Energy and Climate Action Plan (SECAP), adopted in 2023. Based on the greenhouse gas inventory finalized in June 2024, the SECAP not only sets ambitious emission reduction targets (41.6% by 2030) but also incorporates measures designed to address the needs of different social groups and neighborhoods.

Beyond the SECAP, the municipality recognizes that climate action must be supported by continuous participation and inclusive governance. To this end, Beşiktaş regularly organizes public participation processes, consultation meetings, and workshops with local stakeholders, including residents, NGOs, academic institutions, and businesses. These interactions provide valuable insights into the needs of diverse communities, and the feedback collected helps shape municipal climate strategies in a way that reflects local priorities.

The municipality also maintains open and accessible communication channels to ensure inclusivity. Residents can provide input through the 24/7 call center, dedicated email addresses, an online municipal portal, and active social media platforms. All communications are digitally recorded, creating a transparent dataset that informs improvements in service delivery and climate planning. This ensures that vulnerable groups—such as elderly residents, students, and low-income households—have equal opportunities to share their perspectives and influence decision-making.

Digital innovation further supports equitable participation. The “Recycle & Win” mobile application enables residents to deliver recyclable materials to the municipality and track their contributions. The system records data such as types and volumes of waste collected and the number of active users, offering an inclusive monitoring mechanism that quantifies community engagement across different social groups.

Regular performance reports issued by the Climate Change and Zero Waste Directorate, along with the municipality's broader annual reporting, also contribute to equity monitoring. These reports include key indicators on waste management, energy consumption, green space development, and other sustainability measures, which allow the municipality to evaluate whether climate action outcomes are being fairly distributed throughout the district.

Looking ahead, Beşiktaş Municipality intends to strengthen its approach by expanding structured equity assessments, developing additional participatory tools, and incorporating lessons learned into future SECAP updates. By combining formal planning instruments with ongoing citizen engagement, digital feedback mechanisms, and transparent reporting, Beşiktaş ensures that climate policies remain inclusive, participatory, and responsive to community needs. This approach reflects the municipality's commitment to delivering climate actions that benefit all residents equitably while building resilience for the district as a whole.

Este plan busca generar una ciudad más resiliente y sostenible mediante la implementación de medidas concretas que reduzcan las emisiones de gases de efecto invernadero, mejoren la gestión de riesgos climáticos y fortalezcan la calidad de vida de vecinas y vecinos. La actualización periódica del plan permite evaluar los avances de las medidas ejecutadas, identificar oportunidades de mejora y coordinar los esfuerzos interdepartamentales, asegurando que Independencia cumpla con los compromisos locales y nacionales en materia climática.

El Plan de Acción de Cambio Climático 2025-2030 contempla el desarrollo de un proceso participativo, en el cual se realizaron dos sesiones de participación ciudadana.

La primera sesión consistió en un diagnóstico de los riesgos y oportunidades relacionados con la acción climática, así como con la adaptación y mitigación. En esta instancia, los vecinos y vecinas de Independencia pudieron identificar de manera cuantitativa, cualitativa y espacial los desafíos y oportunidades climáticas presentes en la comuna.

En la segunda sesión, los participantes tuvieron la oportunidad de priorizar las medidas formuladas a partir de la etapa de diagnóstico, calificando cada medida según su importancia.

Este proceso permitió generar un instrumento que refleja las necesidades de los ciudadanos de la comuna, incluyendo mapas de riesgos que facilitan la distribución estratégica de las medidas propuestas.

1. Vulnerability and Risk Assessments
The city uses Climate and Disaster Risk Assessment to identify priority areas and population groups most at risk (e.g., coastal barangays, informal settlements, low-income households).

These assessments inform the targeting of programs—such as relocation support, livelihood assistance, or ecosystem-based adaptation—to ensure resources reach the most vulnerable.

2. Barangay-Level Disaggregation
Data on climate programs (e.g., tree planting, flood control, energy projects) are disaggregated by barangay, allowing the city to track which communities are benefiting.

This helps monitor whether low-income or high-risk areas are equitably receiving support and infrastructure investments.

3. Inclusive Planning and Participation
The city conducts public consultations, sectoral workshops, and school-based programs to involve diverse groups—youth, women, fisherfolk, and indigenous peoples—in climate decision-making.

Participation is tracked through attendance logs, representation records, and feedback forms.

4. Monitoring of Social Co-Benefits
Climate actions are evaluated not only for environmental outcomes but also for social benefits, such as:

Number of green jobs created in marginalized communities

Access to clean energy or water services in poor barangays

Education and awareness programs conducted in public schools

5. Gender and Development (GAD) Integration
Batangas City incorporates GAD indicators in climate-related projects to ensure that women and gender-diverse groups are actively included and benefit equitably from climate actions.

Through these systems, Batangas City ensures its climate initiatives are fairly distributed, responsive to community needs, and aligned with inclusive development goals.
column19:
1. Barangay-Based Risk Assessments and Targeting
As part of its Local Climate Change Action Plan (LCCAP) and Comprehensive Land Use Plan (CLUP) 2019-2028, Batangas City conducted vulnerability and risk assessments at the barangay level.

These assessments identified high-risk coastal and low-lying barangays for priority climate adaptation investments such as drainage improvements, slope protection, and mangrove reforestation.

Programs are designed to prioritize informal settler families, fisherfolk, and low-income residents in these areas.

2. EBD Ecopark and Wildlife Rescue Center and Community Engagement

EBD Ecopark and Wildlife Rescue Center transformed a former dumpsite in Brgy. Tinga Labac into a forested area.

This project included partnerships with community members and private groups for tree growing and monitoring, offering volunteering and livelihood opportunities.

The program's next phases—such as creating a, amphitheater, mini-park, nursery, and wildlife sanctuary—are intended to serve as inclusive public green spaces accessible to all, especially nearby low-income residents.

3. Education and Public Awareness for All Ages
The city operates the Bahay Kaalaman, an interactive Climate Change and Clean Energy Hub in partnership with DepEd.

It offers free educational tours and learning sessions for students from public schools, ensuring equal access to climate education regardless of economic status.

The facility includes accessible displays and accommodates school visits from both urban and rural barangays.

4. Green Building Incentive Program
Through the Environment Code (E-Code), Batangas City promotes green infrastructure compliance by providing financial incentives (e.g., 25% building permit discount) to developments that incorporate sustainable, health-safe designs.

This program includes prescribed standards for accessibility, energy efficiency, and environmental impact, indirectly benefiting workers and occupants from diverse economic backgrounds.

5. Gender and Sectoral Representation in Planning
Batangas City ensures representation of women, youth, senior citizens, and sectoral organizations in planning bodies such as the City Development Council, Climate Change Committee, and DRRM Council.

The OPCC confirms the city's commitment to inclusive planning, citing the involvement of various sectors in crafting the LCCAP and updating the CLUP.

6. Public Consultations and Participatory Budgeting
During the planning and updating of the CLUP, CDP, and LCCAP, the city conducted consultations with barangays, civil society organizations, and local stakeholders.

Feedback from these sessions helped shape the prioritization of projects and ensured that marginalized groups could influence decision-making.

In summary, Batangas City goes beyond planning by embedding equity and inclusion in program design, community participation, education, and access to green services. These actions ensure that the city's climate response reaches not just the environmentally vulnerable, but also the socially and economically disadvantaged, in a fair and deliberate manner.

The council also work directly with key partners including counsellors, charities, and residents to implement place-based action, and to identify and work with individual communities to distribute climate action which affect a community to ensure that any action is meaningful and required for a certain area. Through our Place-based Working Programme, we are changing our relationship with local people, so that we can enable more people to shape their communities as citizens and not just deliver services to customers. The Communities Partnership Board will oversee and monitor the impact of the Inclusive Communities Framework. Individual organisations and services will, through evaluating work undertaken with communities, determine personalised framework implementation and action plans to improve or enhance practice. The ICF can be scaled up or down and can be applied in a way that is proportionate to the task. System leadership will be key to the framework's success in enabling a positive and consistent approach to our work with communities. The Communities Partnership Board is Chaired by an Elected Member of the Council and is a partnership of organisations including the Police, Health, Probation, the Voluntary and Community Sector, Elected Members, the Fire Service and many other organisations. Place-based engagement was used to inform the new developing Environment Strategy, utilising many different stakeholder engagement mechanism to ensure inclusive involvement. For example, there was a Public Survey, feedback via local partner organizations through a scoping exercise, Mini Citizens Assembly, Review of existing data (many the existing plans that the strategy seeks to coordinate with have undertaken public surveys / consultation). The Environment Strategy will be a new top tier strategy that will dictate how the council does its business and provides services and so the place-based method is crucial in its development. Throughout the development of the Adaptation workstream to embed climate risk consideration and monitoring into existing risk management processes there will be a focus on managing interdependencies and cascading risk throughout other organisations which have an impact on the climate risks for Kirklees. Therefore, identifying these risks effectively will allow us to prioritise vulnerable zones that are at a high risk to ensure that climate action is distributed in a fair and equitable manner. The Energy and Climate Change team also regularly presents and updates the council's Inclusion and Diversity hub, which is approached as a check and challenge for proposed climate action plans and top-tier strategies to ensure that inclusion and diversity are considered for a just transition to reach Kirklees Council Climate Ready and Net Zero Targets.

These are defined as: -Shaped by people: All residents and businesses within Kirklees are allies, with rights and responsibilities to deliver this strategy for Kirklees, working inclusively to ensure all aspects of Kirklees society are represented. - Fair: Achieve a just and equal transition to our Net Zero and Climate Ready future, highlighting co-benefits to be realised. We have gathered data on indicators such as fuel poverty and deprivation and are using this data to inform action development. Furthermore, Kirklees will adopt a comprehensive Monitoring and Evaluation process for all actions implemented - utilising both data and stakeholder-led feedback and analysis on the success and failure of these actions. This will ensure that the actions are ever evolving, ensuring they are maximising the benefits and learning from the negative, unintended consequences or 'maladaptation' that may arise. As a council we monitor the risks that each area face, for example, fuel poverty, digital exclusions, flood risk. We use local information and national data to highlight areas of risk and to ensure equitable and inclusive distribution of climate action. For example, the authority is aware of areas which are at a greater risk of digital exclusion, which may not be able to access online advice surrounding climate change, therefore other place-based approaches may be required.

Climate action supports sustainable local development, enhances quality of life, stimulates investment and innovation, creates jobs, and strengthens stakeholder participation and cooperation.

Dundee City Council has already advanced a range of initiatives that deliver these co-benefits. Efforts to promote active travel, improve energy efficiency in buildings, and support the circular economy contribute to healthier lifestyles, reduced energy costs, and more efficient use of resources. Partnerships such as the Michelin Scotland Innovation Parc (MSIP) showcase how collaboration between public, private, and academic sectors can drive green innovation, attract investment, and position Dundee as a hub for sustainable technological development.

Community engagement is central to this approach. The Dundee Climate Fund empowers residents to participate in designing and leading climate solutions, fostering pride, local ownership, and skills development while demonstrating inclusive and participatory decision-making.

Environmental and ecological benefits are also evident. Projects such as sand dune restoration at Broughty Ferry and the creation of wildflower meadows improve biodiversity, protect local habitats, and enhance greenspace across the city.

Finally, Dundee's climate adaptation measures, including flood management and investment in resilient infrastructure, reduce long-term risks and costs associated with extreme weather events. Together, these actions ensure Dundee is better prepared for the future while delivering wide-ranging social, economic, and environmental gains.

Dundee City Council ensures the equitable and inclusive distribution of climate action through community-led funding, inclusive planning, and place-based strategies that embed fairness at the heart of the city's net zero transition.

A cornerstone of this approach is the Dundee Climate Action Fund, Scotland's first council-led green participatory budgeting initiative. The Fund empowers residents to allocate funding to local climate projects, enabling communities to directly shape climate action in their neighbourhoods and ensuring benefits are spread across diverse sectors and groups.

The Council's Net Zero Transition Plan 2024-2030 further reinforces climate equity by embedding community-led and place-based approaches, ensuring that resilience measures and clean energy initiatives reach all demographics. The Dundee Climate Action Plan, co-designed with public, private, and community organisations, also reflects this collaborative and inclusive ethos.

Equitable distribution is actively monitored through the city's governance and engagement structures, such as the Sustainable Dundee partnership and the Dundee Climate Leadership Group, as well as through a suite of tools, projects, and events. These include the Sustainable Dundee website, the publicly accessible City Emissions Dashboard (powered by ClimateView), the Sustainable Dundee Map, and events such as Earth Hour, Scottish Climate Week, and Clean Air Day.

The City Emissions Dashboard is a key transparency tool that allows residents to explore emission sources, targets, and reduction pathways across different sectors. It illustrates the shifts and actions needed to reach net zero and enables citizens to measure the projected impact of policies and initiatives through interactive visuals. Citizens are encouraged to engage, ask questions, and provide feedback on climate actions, reinforcing accountability and inclusivity in decision-making.

Through these combined efforts, Dundee is embedding equity, participation, and transparency across its climate governance framework, ensuring that all communities can contribute to and benefit from the transition to a sustainable future.
column19:
Dundee City Council is taking a range of actions to ensure the equitable and inclusive distribution of climate action across the city. A key initiative is the Dundee Climate Fund, launched in 2022 with a total of £750,000 to support community-led climate projects. Based on the Community Choices participatory budgeting model, the Fund allows residents to directly decide how resources are allocated to deliver on the city's Climate Action Plan. This democratic process ensures every citizen has the opportunity to vote on projects, creating a fair and transparent approach to local climate investment. Funded projects include food growing initiatives, energy efficiency upgrades, and community resilience programmes, many of which are led by grassroots organisations. More details on funded projects are available here: https://www.sustainabledundee.co.uk/projects/dundee-climate-fund

The Dundee Climate Action Plan, co-developed by Dundee City Council with public, private and third-sector partners, embeds equity by ensuring actions address the needs of all communities. Alongside this, the Dundee Climate Leadership Group provides city-wide leadership on the net zero challenge, bringing together major organisations and community representatives to inspire shared ownership of climate action. The group, along with the Sustainable Dundee Network, plays a guidance and advisory role on behalf of communities, including marginalised groups, helping to shape and challenge local government decision-making. More details on membership and governance are available here: https://www.sustainabledundee.co.uk/about-us/dundee-climate-leadership-group

Through these structures, Dundee combines community-led funding, participatory governance, and cross-sector collaboration to ensure climate action is distributed inclusively and benefits all residents

- Identification of Vulnerable Groups
 Socioeconomic Profiling: 
Rzeszów identifies vulnerable populations such as low-income households, elderly people, people with disabilities, and marginalized communities who are more likely to be impacted by climate change and less able to adapt to its effects.

 
Targeted Policy Measures: 
Climate actions, like improving energy efficiency, reducing energy costs, or increasing access to renewable energy, are designed to directly benefit those with fewer resources. For example, Rzeszów may offer subsidies or incentives for low-income families to install renewable energy systems or improve home insulation.

 Rzeszów prioritize the creation of green spaces in underserved areas to ensure that all residents, regardless of income or location, can benefit from healthier, cooler environments, and enhanced air quality.

- Public Consultations
Stakeholder Involvement: The city involves local organizations, NGOs, and advocacy groups that represent vulnerable populations to ensure that climate actions are designed and implemented inclusively.

 EU Funds and Programs: As part of its climate action strategy, Rzeszów may align its initiatives with national and EU frameworks aimed at promoting social equity, such as the Just Transition Mechanism. This ensures that resources for climate action are allocated in a way that reduces inequalities.
 National Climate and Energy Policies: The city also follows national policies that focus on energy poverty and inclusion, ensuring that Rzeszów's local actions are in line with broader social equity goals.

Rzeszów uses a combination of socioeconomic analysis, targeted climate actions, public engagement, and monitoring to ensure that the distribution of climate benefits is equitable and inclusive. The city's climate strategies are designed to ensure that the most vulnerable populations are not left behind and that all residents can share in the environmental, economic, and social benefits of climate action.
column19:
The city of Rzeszów is actively working toward equitable and inclusive climate action through initiatives that involve citizens in decision-making processes and promote sustainable development. Here are some key measures:

Rzeszów Climate Panel
The city organized a citizens' climate panel, engaging 60 randomly selected residents to represent diverse social groups. The panel developed 51 recommendations, including improving energy efficiency, expanding cycling infrastructure, encouraging the use of public transport, and establishing Park & Ride facilities. These initiatives aim to balance environmental sustainability with social inclusion, ensuring all community members benefit from the actions. The panel's methodology is recognized as a model of good practice in Poland.

Participation in the NetZeroCities Project
Rzeszów is part of the EU's “100 Climate-Neutral and Smart Cities by 2030” initiative. This program provides funding for climate-related projects, enabling the city to implement measures such as pocket parks and low-emission housing. These projects enhance inclusivity by making sustainable infrastructure accessible to a broader population.
Green Investments
A notable example is the creation of a pocket park on Jagiellońska Street. This project, co-funded by the EU, includes green spaces with diverse vegetation, benches, insect hotels, and eco-friendly lighting. Such initiatives aim to support biodiversity while ensuring access to green spaces for all residents. [This year, several such parks have already been created, and that's not all].

Through participatory mechanisms and green projects, Rzeszów integrates sustainability with social equity, aiming to improve the quality of life for all its inhabitants.

The city of Rzeszów actively pursues grants from national and international programs in the areas of transport, health, infrastructure, and the environment, including the Interreg Next PL-UA program, which provides environmental education for residents. Investment projects, such as the revitalization of city park, are also underway. These activities are co-financed by EU funds.

In the LIFE project 'Podkarpackie - Live and Breathe,' Rzeszów is one of five pilot cities implementing innovative solutions, including pocket parks, wildflower meadows, and energy management systems. Implementation tasks at the city level are handled by the City Hall's Climate and Environment Department, and residents gain access to air and energy advisors who support them in replacing heat sources, thermal modernization of buildings, installing renewable energy sources, and obtaining energy certificates.

Physical and mental health is positively affected by nature and high quality fresh water. The health benefits coming from urban green areas and urban rivers and lakes
cannot be underestimated. Protecting the city's green spaces will contribute to a healthier community, for ecosystem services such as protection of heat waves, as well as
protecting biodiveristy and ensuring the utterly important pollination. Urban spaces can also be used for pedagogical purposes in school and pre-school acitivies; teaching children to respect and value nature is an important step for future sustainability. Urban green areas unites constructed areas and builds trust among people which is the very base for democracy. Green spaces and urban water encourages recreation and inner peace. Trees work both for noise cancelling, for cooling and for cleaning the air
from traffic pollution. In addition water has a cooling effect in cities.
Heat is a risk for creating violence, so cooling is also important for a safe city. Solna has secured access to green urban spaces for citizens with disabilities.
The city of Solna has a strategic plan for expanding bicycle infrastructure. This has multiple benefits; it promotes equality (more people can afford a bicycle than a car),
public safety (less traffic if bicycles are increasing on behalf of cars), health since cycle instead of driving signifies a healthier lifestyle, less air pollution, less crowded local
roads. The city has a specific strategy for securing safe roads to schools, as children's safety is a priority.
The city has a mission that one can reach its destination anywhere in the city by foot, bicycle or public transportation, hence that the car is not really needed within the city boundary.
Strategic planning of energy supply provides security through long-term and stable electricity and supply. Almost all households in the city are connected to district heating.
Both electricity and district heating production are almost completely fossil-free.
Well-planned energy supply reduces the risk of high prices and thus contributes to equality - ensuring that everyone can afford electricity and heat (or cooling in the future).
The functioning and reasonable prices of electricity and heat are also important for schools and children's education, for companies and their business opportunities and ability to offer jobs. Fossil-free electricity is a competitive advantage for companies and in many cases a requirement from their customers. Fossil free energy for mobility will contribute to better personal and goods' transports which will contribute to stable economy, health and equality.
The city has a well-used strategy for storm water planing and management that provides robust guidance in city planning. The pro-active work within climate adaptation is key for safety, health and resilient infrastructure planning.
Areas exposed to heat waves have been pointed out and measures are being planned. This to protect health especially for elderly and children.
All that we do on land, impacts the health of our streams, lakes, and oceans. Therefore, in all our planning, we take care of stormwater before runoff for example in
sedimentation ponds, green roofs ore rain gardens. Where there is a lack of water in the streams, we often try to combine stormwater treatment with wetland restauration.
Other ecological restoration projects include rebuilding fish communities and restore previous barriers for fish and fauna.
How the city and the citizens consume and treat their waste is important to climate. The waste plan has a five missions that all promotes to sustainability and at the same time make waste management easier for all: 1. Easy to use and
accessible systems 2. Waste prevention (promoting re-use, refurbishment, sharing, alternative to consumtpion et c) 3. Circulation of material 4. Food waste 5. Reduce littering
In the city Master plan, green and blue corridors and the protection of biodiversity is core. The plan emphasizes equality and integration by identifying areas for expansions of housing and work places close to public transport and describe how to remove physical barriers. Accessiblity for all including children is addressed.
The city has an ongoing dialogue with private sector establishing their business in Solna on all these matters including directives for exploiters and a network for business engagement.

column16:
Los beneficios derivados de la acción climática en la comuna se manifiestan en tres dimensiones principales: económica, ambiental y social.
1. Dimensión económica:
Muchas de las acciones impulsadas han sido posibles gracias a la movilización de recursos externos, tanto nacionales como internacionales, que permiten financiar iniciativas locales de alto impacto. Estas medidas incorporan el principio de eficiencia, lo que se traduce en un uso óptimo de los recursos, disminución de gastos y generación de ahorros que pueden ser reinvertidos en otras áreas de gestión municipal. Asimismo, las acciones climáticas otorgan un valor agregado a proyectos y programas, potenciando el comercio y la economía local con un enfoque sostenible. Ejemplos concretos son los millones de pesos obtenidos a partir de alianzas para la acción climática local y los recursos ahorrados mediante medidas de eficiencia hídrica y energética.
2. Dimensión ambiental:
Las iniciativas buscan resguardar el patrimonio natural de la comuna, asegurando la conservación de los bienes, servicios y funciones ecosistémicas. Estas acciones no solo promueven el equilibrio entre los componentes bióticos y abióticos, sino que también reconocen el valor intrínseco de los ecosistemas más allá de su utilidad para las personas. En este sentido, se protege la biodiversidad genética, los paisajes, los hábitats, los suelos, los ciclos hídricos y las cuencas, generando un impacto positivo en la resiliencia del territorio. Un ejemplo destacado es el trabajo realizado en la cuenca de la Quebrada de Macul para la protección de la biodiversidad local.
3. Dimensión social:
Los proyectos desarrollados fortalecen el bienestar y la calidad de vida de la comunidad. Esto se logra a través de la provisión de bienes y servicios ecosistémicos que inciden en la salud física y mental, la creación de espacios de esparcimiento, la percepción de seguridad y la disponibilidad de agua de calidad. Además, las acciones climáticas fomentan la integración social y el fortalecimiento del tejido comunitario, garantizando una distribución equitativa de los beneficios y el acceso a nuevas oportunidades. Aspectos como la dignificación laboral, la participación ciudadana, la equidad de género (incipiente), la justicia climática y la inclusión son parte central de este enfoque. Particularmente, las medidas de adaptación y resiliencia se orientan a reducir vulnerabilidades, evitando que se profundicen las desigualdades y mejorando la capacidad de respuesta de las comunidades más expuestas. Un ejemplo concreto es el Programa de Reciclaje Inclusivo, que dignifica la labor de los recicladores y recicladoras de base, mejorando sus ingresos y condiciones de trabajo.

La manera en que la jurisdicción cuantifica la distribución equitativa e inclusiva de la acción climática depende de la naturaleza de cada programa, pero en general se basa en tres dimensiones: diseño inclusivo, retroalimentación comunitaria y medición mediante indicadores sociales y territoriales. 
1. Diseño inclusivo: los planes y proyectos se desarrollan priorizando a comunidades vulnerables y grupos históricamente desfavorecidos de la comuna, con el objetivo de reducir brechas, mejorar el acceso a oportunidades y elevar la calidad de vida. La Dirección de Medio Ambiente lidera este proceso, mediante un equipo técnico que asegura la creación, ejecución y seguimiento de iniciativas con criterios de impacto, replicabilidad y escalabilidad. Asimismo, se promueve la transparencia y la inclusión mediante compromisos como el Acuerdo de Escazú, la incorporación de la perspectiva de género y el reconocimiento de pueblos originarios. Un ejemplo es el Parque Centro Ceremonial de Pueblos Originarios, que integra y visibiliza, dentro y fuera de la comuna, la cultura indígenas.
2. Retroalimentación comunitaria y mecanismos de ajuste: cada programa mantiene un contacto directo con el público objetivo para el cual se diseñó, lo que permite obtener retroalimentación continua a través de instancias presenciales, atención telefónica y redes sociales. Estos mecanismos de comunicación facilitan identificar necesidades y ajustar servicios en tiempo real, garantizando que los beneficios lleguen de manera justa y equitativa a toda la comunidad, especialmente a grupos en situación de vulnerabilidad. 
3. Medición y cuantificación del impacto: la municipalidad utiliza registros y planillas de seguimiento con indicadores que permiten evaluar equidad e inclusión. Entre ellos destaca; (a) nivel de satisfacción de los usuarios (as), (b) cobertura territorial y social alcanzada, (c) características socio-demográficas de la población beneficiaria, (d) participación diferenciada de mujeres, jóvenes, adultos mayores y pueblos originarios. 
Estos indicadores se cruzan con información social y territorial, lo que permite identificar brechas, valorar resultados y tomar medidas correctivas para asegurar una distribución equitativa de impacto. 
En síntesis, mediante un diseño participativo, retroalimentación permanente y medición de indicadores sociales y territoriales, el municipio puede cuantificar y garantizar que las acciones climáticas se distribuyan de manera equitativa e inclusiva, fortaleciendo la justicia climática y la resiliencia comunitaria.
column19:
Gran parte de los compromisos de acción climática local, bajo principios de justicia climática y distribución equitativa, se encuentran institucionalizados en instrumentos de planificación estratégica comunal, tales como el Plan de Desarrollo Comunal (PLADECO), el Plan Local de Cambio Climático, la Estrategia Energética Local y la Estrategia Hídrica, entre otros. Estos instrumentos cuentan con mecanismos de seguimiento y evaluación anual, coordinados tanto por la Dirección de Medio Ambiente como por otras direcciones municipales pertinentes. Asimismo, la comuna de Peñalolén ha suscrito compromisos internacionales (incluido el reporte en CDP) que refuerzan la obligación de revisar y reportar avances de manera sistemática.
En relación con la equidad e inclusión en la acción climática, destacan diversas líneas de acción dentro de la jurisdicción:
- Infraestructura verde y acceso equitativo a la naturaleza: Se desarrollan análisis espaciales en las posibles áreas de influencia mediante herramientas de Sistemas de Información Geográfica (SIG) para evaluar la distribución y accesibilidad de áreas verdes en la comuna, considerando la cobertura efectiva de beneficiarios(as) directos e indirectos. Este enfoque permite priorizar la creación y mantención de infraestructuras verdes en territorios con mayor déficit, garantizando un acceso equitativo. Un ejemplo emblemático es el Parque Peñalolén (20 ha), diseñado como espacio de encuentro para comunidades con limitada infraestructura verde. Asimismo, el Parque Natural Quebrada de Macul, con acceso gratuito a los senderos de montaña, recibe más de 220 mil visitas anuales y cuenta con un programa de visitas guiadas inclusivas, dirigidas especialmente a grupos vulnerables (niños(as), mujeres, adultos(as) mayores y hogares de bajos ingresos).
- Gestión de residuos con equidad territorial: La planificación de los servicios de manejo de residuos se realiza en función de criterios de vulnerabilidad socio-territorial, lo que asegura un acceso equitativos a puntos verdes, composteras domiciliarias y recolección domiciliaria diferenciada. Adicionalmente, se promueve la inclusión socioeconómica mediante la incorporación de recicladores(as) de base en la gestión, lo que fortalece su empleabilidad, ingresos y calidad de vida.
- Salud pública y bienestar animal: La estrategia zoonótica municipal asegura acceso universal a servicios veterinarios gratuitos o de bajo costo, a través de clínicas fijas y un veterinario móvil, priorizando sectores de alta vulnerabilidad. Estas acciones contribuyen tanto al bienestar animal y a la tenencia responsable, como a la salud comunitaria y el control de plagas y vectores.
- Transición energética justa: Los programas de eficiencia energética, energías renovables y eficiencia hídrica están orientados a hogares de menores ingresos, identificados a través del Registro Social de Hogares. De esta manera, se facilita el acceso a tecnologías de mayor costo y se fortalecen capacidades comunitarias para enfrentar alzas tarifarias y mejorar la resiliencia energética.

column16: In 2016, cost of energy to the Bridgewater community was $89 million and it is projected to rise to $206 million per year in the BAU by 2050 as the population increases, energy prices increase, carbon pricing comes into force and as a result of inflation at 2% per year. Energy costs in 2050 can fall to $56 million per year by investing in the Energy Shift (a pathway proposed in the Community Energy Investment Plan) , a decrease of 81%. As a result, the community can save over $2 billion in energy costs in the 32 year period between 2018 and 2050, and GHG emissions will be 80% lower than they were in 2011. Nearly all of the 20 plus actions contained in the Energy Shift generate financial returns and represent investment opportunities for the municipality, businesses and utilities. With the Energy Shift, total energy consumption is reduced by 37%, or almost 1 million GJ per year- for comparison by 2050. Cumulative savings between 2018 and 2050 are 16 million GJ. In addition, an average of 115 person-years of employment would be added to the economy per year, with a cumulative total of over 3,700 person-years of employment created by 2050. Municipalities have a long history of addressing challenges to improve the quality of life of citizens, as the Town of Bridgewater has demonstrated by its early investments in an electrical grid. The transition to a low carbon economy represents an incredible opportunity to stimulate economic development, improve quality of life, improve public health outcomes, reduce poverty, reduce air pollution and GHG emissions, and generate new employment opportunities. (information sourced from the 2018 Community Energy Investment Plan).\n\nBy early 2025, the Town will update the Community Energy Investment Plan to assess further opportunities related to the transition to a net zero community by 2050.

Asimismo, en el marco de la implementación del Plan de Acción Comunal de Cambio Climático (PACCC), estas acciones representan una oportunidad estratégica para escalar programas de economía circular, educación ambiental y participación ciudadana, promoviendo una comuna más resiliente, consciente y comprometida con el medio ambiente.

column18: En la comuna de Punta Arenas, la distribución equitativa e inclusiva de la acción climática se cuantifica a través de la división del territorio en unidades vecinales, que constituyen la mínima segmentación del territorio habitado. Esta estructura permite identificar, medir y monitorear de manera precisa cómo se distribuyen los beneficios de las iniciativas climáticas entre los distintos sectores de la comuna, asegurando que ninguna población quede excluida de los programas y acciones implementadas.\n\nEn el marco del Plan de Acción Comunal de Cambio Climático (PACCC), esta metodología se aplica para evaluar la cobertura y alcance de proyectos como la gestión de residuos, la educación ambiental, la implementación de infraestructura sostenible y las actividades de participación ciudadana. De este modo, la planificación y ejecución de la acción climática no solo se orienta a maximizar los impactos ambientales, sino también a promover la inclusión social y la equidad territorial, garantizando que los beneficios lleguen a todos los habitantes de la comuna, independientemente de su ubicación o condición socioeconómica.
column19:
Para garantizar la distribución equitativa e inclusiva de la acción climática en la comuna, se ha conformado un equipo de trabajo municipal especializado en acción climática, dependiente de la Comisión de Cambio Climático Municipal. Este equipo tiene la responsabilidad de coordinar, supervisar y ejecutar las iniciativas climáticas, asegurando que se implementen de manera transversal en todas las áreas de la comuna.

Como parte de sus funciones, el equipo genera cartografía base de impactos climáticos, desagregada a nivel de unidad vecinal, lo que permite evaluar con precisión tanto la superficie territorial como la población afectada, garantizando que las acciones lleguen de manera equitativa a todos los sectores. Esta información se utiliza para priorizar intervenciones y focalizar recursos en zonas más vulnerables, asegurando que la implementación del PACCC sea inclusiva y efectiva.

Además, la integración de estas acciones con otros instrumentos de planificación territorial, como el Plan Regulador Comunal, permite que los criterios de adaptación y mitigación al cambio climático se incorporen en la planificación urbana, el ordenamiento del territorio y la infraestructura comunal, fortaleciendo la sostenibilidad y la resiliencia en toda la comuna.

De manera complementaria, se vinculan estas acciones con programas educativos, jornadas de participación ciudadana y proyectos comunitarios (como el Eco-Canje y los puntos limpios), asegurando que los beneficios de la acción climática no solo sean ambientales, sino también sociales y comunitarios, promoviendo la inclusión y la equidad en todas las intervenciones municipales.
