-Programa Maipú regenera su tierra: Capacitación a vecinas y vecinos en lombricompostaje, entrega herramientas para que las personas puedan habilitar la compostera en sus casas. Esta acción permite reducir los residuos orgánicos en las viviendas y generar tierra de compost. 
- Programa de educación ambiental en establecimientos educacionales, este va destinado a toda la comunidad educativa incluye apoderados, docentes y asistentes de la educación). Siguiendo una pauta de actividades anuales, se capacita a la comunidad en materia de eficiencia energética, recursos hídricos, biodiversidad y gestión de residuos. Si bien el público objetivo son las y los estudiantes, el establecimiento es una oportunidad de abarcar la familia que está detrás de cada estudiante, promoviendo acciones desde las áreas mencionadas en los hogares. 
- Programa de recuperación de espacios: A partir de espacios destinados a la disposición ilegal de grandes cantidades de basura, se convoca a las organizaciones y vecinos/as que viven cercanos a estos, generando un plan de acción para el control del microbasural. Buscando el apoyo de las y los vecinos en el monitoreo y la resignificación de los espacios. Lo cual promueve la participación de la ciudadanía, releva la importancia del cuidado de los espacios comunes y finaliza con plantación de árboles y/o plantas ornamentales. Mejorando la apariencia del barrio, fortaleciendo la comunidad y genera alianzas entre el municipio y la ciudadanía.
-Programa de arbolado urbano: Monitoreo y atención de denuncias del estado fitosanitario de los árboles en la comuna. Planifica las reforestaciones y educa a la población respecto a los beneficios sociales y ambientales de los árboles. Así mismo, se educa respecto al riego adecuado, cómo hacer bien una poda y el buen mantenimiento del suelo. El cuidado del arbolado urbano permite reducir las olas de calor en la comuna y prevenir la caída de ramas durante los temporales, lo cual repercute directamente en la salud y seguridad de la población. 
-Operativo 'Adios Cachureos': Busca que las personas acerquen sus residuos voluminosos a containers del municipio, con el fin de evitar la disposición ilegal de estos en los microbasurales. Estos operativos se realizan cada fin de semana y va rotando entre todos los barrios de la comuna. Los desechos de metal y material aprovechable es apartado por los recicladores de base, quienes posteriormente lo venden, evitando que estos vayan al relleno sanitario y generando un nuevo ingreso para las y los recicladores.

Key metrics are the number of participants in programs and initiative, where investments have been made in the City, and how much has been invested. column19: The City's core sustainability program for 2022, the Energy Assistance Solar Savings Initiative (EASSI) was developed and is being implemented through an equity and inclusivity lens. EASSI assists nonprofits and community organizations to complete energy efficiency and solar projects. The Office of Sustainability sought stakeholder input beginning in early program design stages. Community partners IFF and CDFI Friendly South Bend help with program design and implementation. In its core programmatic structure, EASSI considers equity and practical considerations in order to best serve South Bend's nonprofits and community organizations. There is close communication and outreach for the program through stakeholders, partners, and various communication channels and networks that promote the program. EASSI applies an equity lens through its selection criteria for applicants to the program, considering the CDC Social Vulnerability Index and the geographic distribution of applicants. Organizations served by the EASSI program, in turn, provide a wide range of services in the community, ranging from the local county fairgrounds to social service agencies. By targeting energy savings initiatives to the buildings that serve South Bend, EASSI makes it possible for organizations to reallocate funds from energy bills to direct services to residents. The City is also embedding sustainability in grant programs for small businesses that also consider equity. For example the Vibrant Places program, is a matching grant program that provides funding for qualifying exterior improvements to commercial, mixed use, and industrial buildings located in eligible commercial corridors where historically there has been less investment. The program program provides grants Citywide but provides a higher matching grant and higher maximum grant amount for businesses that reside eligible commercial corridors. The City launched Upskill SB, a pilot workforce development program for job seekers, professionals, and recent high school or college graduates to earn industry-level job certifications. By offering a wide range of training options and reimbursing certification costs, Upskill SB aims to develop highly skilled workers in South Bend and retain high quality jobs in the region. Through Upskill SB, the City reimburses 100% of exam costs and at least 50% of any training costs, with additional financial aid available for qualifying participants. Those who do not have access to a computer or broadband internet are also eligible for technology reimbursements. UpSkill SB included targeted outreach to individuals and organizations that would benefit from financial aid. UpSkill SB's application process also considered various factors to ensure equitable participation, such as demographics, income, educational levels. With Upskill SB's launch, six participants in the pilot participated in 32 hours of online training from the Midwest Renewable Energy Association (MREA) for the NABCEP PV Associate Credential. Upskill SB was renewed in 2023, two individuals were pursuing NABCEP certification, and one individual is seeking LEED certification. 16 realtors participated in the NAR Green Designation. The City is collaborating with South Bend's Engagement and Economic Empowerment team on a cross-pollination projects, mostly focused on job creation and green, affordable housing development in neighborhoods impacted by historically racist and classist policies and practices. The City designed and implemented an accessible Climate Action Survey paired with a Climate Action Ambassador program. The climate action survey aimed to collect feedback from community members to guide current City efforts and updates to the climate action plan. The Climate Action Ambassadors program recruited different community members to lead and host climate action survey sessions. Each ambassador hosted a session where they sought to have at least 15 community members participate in the survey session. Ambassadors were provided a stipend and ambassadors and survey respondents were paid for their time to complete the survey. The City in 2023 created a Community Electric Vehicle Charging Infrastructure Plan that will help South Bend prepare for the expected increase in EVs in the community, pursue and prioritize funding for public EV charging stations, and proactively address inequities in access to EV charging. Specifically, it will consider the city's role in solutions for residents that cannot add private EV charging at home. One aim of the plan is to identify and prioritize sites that will improve charging access in areas with a high proportion of low-income households, neighborhoods with a concentration of households without access to private electrical service due to lack of off-street parking or private garage or parking facilities, and near multi-unit dwellings that do not provide charging access for tenants.

column16: The Southeast Florida Regional Climate Change Compact is a decade-old partnership between Broward, Miami-Dade, Monroe, and Palm Beach counties, to work collaboratively to reduce regional greenhouse gas emissions, implement adaptation strategies, and build climate resilience within their own communities and across the Southeast Florida region. The Business Case for Resilience in Southeast Florida: https://southeastfloridaclimatecompact.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/The-Business-Case-for-Resilience-in-Southeast-Florida_reduced.pdf \nThis summary report was created by ULI. Technical support for this study was provided by AECOM's Sustainable Economics Practice and is presented in The Business Case for Resilience in Southeast Florida, a technical report prepared for the Urban Land Institute and Southeast Florida Regional Climate Change Compact. Findings from the technical report are distilled here in addition to supplemental content and narrative provided by ULI. The project has been supported by a coalition of local partners, including Broward, Miami-Dade, Monroe, and Palm Beach counties; the Florida Department of Environmental Protection; the Beacon Council Foundation; Broward Workshop; Community Foundation of Broward; Greater Fort Lauderdale Chamber of Commerce; and Greater Miami Chamber of Commerce. The Southeast Florida region is a bustling hub for business, tourism, and culture that faces a unique set of coastal hazards and economic challenges. This study identifies opportunities associated with resilient investment in the face of climate risks to the region due to more frequent flooding and sea-level rise. There is a clear shared interest among all stakeholders to take action. To advance economic development and climate resilience throughout the region, the Compact counties will need to continue to push forward with a coordinated effort among public and private sectors and identify funding for investment in climate adaptation at the building and community scales. Together, local governments and the business community have an opportunity to build critical physical and social infrastructure that will protect the region's robust economy. Investing in these processes now will not only reduce vulnerabilities, but also grow the economy of Southeast Florida in the years to come. Reducing Climate Risk and Creating Economic Opportunity https://southeastfloridaclimatecompact.org/wp-content/uploads/2016/04/CompactResourceDocWksp9Final.pdf \nThis publication (Reducing Climate Risk and Creating Economic Opportunity) of the Southeast Florida Regional Climate Change Compact (The Compact) is based on the findings of the Regional Climate Action Plan (RCAP) Workshop #9 held at Florida International University's Florida Climate Institute on April 28, 2016. This well-attended workshop sparked dialogue among local leaders in government, risk management, finance, technology, building and development, and academia, and focused on risk reduction, regional economics, and coordinated leadership. The concepts that emerged from the workshop and are presented in this paper address the financial, economic, and physical challenges - as well as the significant opportunities - in Southeast Florida's changing climate. Wider opportunities/benefits of climate action:- The Municipal Bond Market - Government Funding Streams - Traditional Municipal Bonds - Catastrophe Bonds - Green Bonds - The Residential Mortgage Market - The Florida PACE Program: PACE is a relatively new State of Florida program through which homeowners can get special assessments from investing in energy efficient improvements in the home. The rationale for PACE is to provide a uniform program that achieves economies of scale and creates markets with little or no cost to local government treasuries. Miami-Dade County expects to join this program soon. At present, qualifying improvements are limited to energy efficiency, renewable energy and wind resistance improvements, and do not include adaptation measures for flooding.- Bricks and Mortar: Real estate developers - together with builders of public infrastructure - are manufacturing our built environment of the future. Whether our communities have lasting value and physical and economic resilience depends on what is produced by the building sector, on the provision of coherent standards and guidelines for construction, and on new design standards for managing water intrusion. Incorporating sea level rise forecasts into long range building and land development standards will assure a more sound future, as will an evolution among the building community towards meeting a market demand for resilient structures and design that will only grow over time.

Cupertino's climate actions deliver six key co-benefits beyond emissions reductions:

(1) Public Health & Safety: Cleaner air reduces respiratory illnesses while active transportation infrastructure creates more livable neighborhoods. The City's 30% tree canopy coverage and 5.15 miles of separated bike lanes directly support healthier communities.

(2) Economic Development: Climate action drives job creation in clean energy sectors and delivers cost savings through lower utility bills. Municipal facilities now operate on 100% renewable electricity, demonstrating financial benefits of clean energy transitions.

(3) Resilience & Adaptation: Infrastructure improvements increase community ability to withstand extreme heat and other climate hazards. The City's public Hazard Awareness Dashboard and participation in regional climate preparedness planning strengthen community resilience.

(4) Ecosystem Services: Actions improve local creek water quality, reduce bay pollution, and support biodiversity through native species emphasis in the updated approved tree list. The 302 trees distributed to residents in 2024 enhance carbon sequestration while cooling neighborhoods.

(5) Housing & Development: Climate-aligned development policies create pathways for affordable housing while supporting environmental goals. The new building energy reach code (adopted September 2024) ensures future development contributes to emissions targets.

(6) Innovation & Education: Programs like Cooper's Clean Air Quest VR experience (700+ users in three months) demonstrate climate education innovation, while the live utility data portal launched January 2025 increases community awareness of energy consumption patterns.

Cupertino measures equitable climate action distribution through three approaches:

(1) Program Access Metrics: The City tracks participation rates across different community segments, including language accessibility through translation services and stipend programs that compensate community participants for engagement time.

(2) Geographic Distribution: Climate investments are mapped to ensure benefits reach all neighborhoods. The microtransit expansion supported by the $8.5 million CalSTA grant specifically improves mobility access for underserved areas, with estimated 30.29 MTCO₂e mitigated in the first year.

(3) Burden Assessment: The City evaluates potential displacement risks and cost impacts of climate policies, particularly for low-income households. The Multi-Jurisdictional Hazard Mitigation Plan participation helps identify communities most vulnerable to climate impacts, ensuring adaptation resources target highest-need areas.

In addition to the screening criteria, actions included in the plan were reviewed for equity impacts using the paleBLUEdot Equity Assessment Tool. The tool provided CAP Team members with a framework that reviewed each subject action against three equity considerations. Actions were then re-crafted based on the findings of the CAP Team members.

The equity assessment considerations used were:
• What are the potential positive impacts/ benefits/access opportunities created by this action? Who will benefit?
• What are the potential negative impacts/ consequences/ barriers created by this action? Who will be affected by these?
• Are there other equity factors to consider? (inclusive language, supportive services needed, etc.

Climate change disproportionately impacts La Crosse's most vulnerable community members, including low-income and disadvantaged populations, marginalized ethnic groups, racial minorities, the elderly, the very young, and those facing challenges to their health. At the same time, innovative climate action can be a powerful avenue toward reducing inequality, sparking economic growth, and expanding income opportunities.

Therefore, the strategies and actions throughout this climate action plan have been developed to simultaneously address the threat of climate change while seeking out the benefits and opportunities created by climate action for reducing inequality. As the impacts of climate change increase, so does the need to implement effective strategies and actions that ensure equity and empowerment for all in La Crosse.

La cuantificación de la distribución equitativa de la acción climática se realiza mediante indicadores de efectividad de los programas incluidos en el Plan de Acción Climática (PLAC), así como a través de las metas de transparencia establecidas por el municipio. Estos indicadores son fundamentales para evaluar tanto el impacto como la equidad de las iniciativas implementadas.

A continuación, se presentan algunos ejemplos de estos indicadores:

Cantidad de focos LED entregados a la población: Este indicador mide el número de focos eficientes distribuidos, contribuyendo así a la reducción del consumo energético y mejorando la calidad de vida de los ciudadanos, especialmente en comunidades vulnerables.
Cantidad de paneles solares instalados en espacios públicos: Este dato refleja el esfuerzo del municipio por promover el uso de energías renovables y asegurar su acceso equitativo en diferentes áreas de la comunidad.
Kilómetros de ciclovías construidas: Este indicador evalúa la infraestructura de movilidad sostenible, garantizando que todos los ciudadanos, independientemente de su ubicación, tengan acceso a alternativas de transporte ecológicas.
Número de beneficiarios del programa Ecocanje: Este programa permite a los ciudadanos canjear residuos reciclables por pasajes en colectivos, fomentando la participación activa de la comunidad en la gestión de residuos y facilitando el acceso al transporte público.
Índice de caminabilidad: Este índice incluye categorías relacionadas con el arbolado y la sombra, promoviendo entornos urbanos más amigables para los peatones.
Cantidad de beneficiarios en programas de huerta urbana: Este indicador refleja el compromiso del municipio con la agricultura urbana y la seguridad alimentaria.
 Cantidad de participantes en capacitaciones de educación ambiental y cobertura de escuelas: Este dato muestra el alcance de las iniciativas educativas en materia ambiental.
Cantidad de espacios verdes públicos: Se evalúa el estado y el relevamiento de la vegetación en estos espacios, esenciales para la salud ambiental y el bienestar de la comunidad.
Mapas de vulnerabilidad social: Se elaboran mapas que consideran aspectos como servicios, infraestructura y vulnerabilidad ante riesgos climáticos, permitiendo una mejor planificación y respuesta ante emergencias.

A través de estos indicadores, la jurisdicción puede monitorear y ajustar sus políticas y programas para garantizar que la acción climática sea verdaderamente equitativa e inclusiva, beneficiando a todos los sectores de la población.
column19:
La Municipalidad de Godoy Cruz está comprometida con la promoción de una distribución equitativa e inclusiva de la acción climática a través de diversas iniciativas diseñadas para atender las necesidades de todas las comunidades. Un componente clave en este esfuerzo es el uso de datos abiertos sobre información climática en el Observatorio Territorial, que permite identificar y visualizar múltiples capas geoespaciales. Estas capas incluyen información sobre amenazas aluvionales, acceso a redes y servicios, distribución de barrios populares y mapas de vulnerabilidad social. Esto facilita la identificación de las áreas más afectadas y permite dirigir recursos y esfuerzos donde más se necesitan.
Entre las acciones concretas implementadas, se destacan los solmáforos en espacios públicos, que indican el riesgo de radiación UV, contribuyendo a la concienciación sobre la salud de todos los ciudadanos, especialmente aquellos en comunidades vulnerables que pueden tener menos acceso a información sobre salud ambiental. Además, la instalación de cargadores solares y paneles solares en diversas instalaciones, como escuelas y plazas, no solo promueve el uso de energías renovables, sino que también asegura que las comunidades desfavorecidas tengan acceso a recursos energéticos sostenibles.
El programa Godoy Cruz Ilumina es otro ejemplo de cómo se busca una distribución equitativa, ya que se entregan focos LED puerta a puerta, priorizando a los hogares en situación socioeconómica vulnerable. Esto no solo mejora la eficiencia energética, sino que también reduce la carga económica sobre estas familias, permitiéndoles ahorrar en sus facturas de electricidad.
La creación de ciclovías y estaciones multimodales, fomenta la movilidad sostenible, ofreciendo alternativas de transporte accesibles para todos, mientras que la implementación de espacios verdes en áreas urbanas ayuda a mitigar el efecto de la isla de calor, beneficiando especialmente a las comunidades que suelen carecer de acceso a espacios recreativos y naturales.
La jurisdicción también trabaja de manera directa con las comunidades más vulnerables a través de la Secretaría de Desarrollo Humano. Este enfoque es crucial para las comunidades situadas en el sector oeste del departamento, donde se identifican mayores riesgos de inundación y falta de servicios. En respuesta a esta situación, se proyecta la implementación de un Plan de Reacondicionamiento de Techos contra Tormentas Severas, que tiene como objetivo mejorar las condiciones habitacionales de los hogares en situación socioeconómica vulnerable. Este plan busca reducir su exposición a eventos climáticos extremos y fortalecer su resiliencia, asegurando que estas comunidades sean atendidas de manera prioritaria.
Asimismo, en el marco de los programas habitacionales municipales, las viviendas construidas para familias que residen en barrios vulnerables incorporan panelería solar, lo que mejora la eficiencia energética y asegura el acceso a energía incluso en situaciones de emergencia climática. Esta medida refuerza el compromiso del municipio con un desarrollo urbano sostenible y equitativo.
Finalmente, el Departamento de Protección Civil y Gestión del Riesgo coordina acciones preventivas, de respuesta y capacitación comunitaria en todo el territorio de Godoy Cruz. Su labor es fundamental para fortalecer la preparación ante desastres y garantizar una gestión inclusiva del riesgo, integrando a todos los sectores de la sociedad en la construcción de una comunidad más resiliente.

column16: Catbalogan City recognizes that climate action produces benefits far beyond disaster risk reduction. On the environmental side, projects such as mangrove rehabilitation, watershed protection, and reforestation directly strengthen biodiversity and create natural buffers against floods, storm surges, and soil erosion. These measures safeguard both ecosystems and the communities that rely on them. Socially, investments in drainage systems, slope protection, and resettlement programs have improved public safety and health, reducing exposure to flooding and waterborne diseases. At the same time, climate action has supported inclusive governance, with platforms like the Kalibungan Katbalogan Agenda providing opportunities for citizens, especially vulnerable groups to participate in the local decision-making process. Economically, the city sees green growth as a major co-benefit through programs such as eco-tourism linked to coastal resources, sustainable fisheries, and climate-resilient agriculture are generating new jobs and enhancing food security. To ensure that these actions are equitable and inclusive, the City quantifies impacts through systematic data collection and community engagement processes.

1. Community Needs Assessment
- Vulnerability mapping is conducted to identify neighborhoods most at risk from flooding, sea-level rise, and extreme heat.
- Household-level surveys capture disaggregated data by gender, age, and income to highlight groups with the highest exposure and lowest adaptive capacity.

2. Participatory Monitoring
- Community members in flood-prone and coastal areas track benefits such as reduced flood duration, increased mangrove cover, and improved access to clean water.
- Fisherfolk cooperatives and women's groups provide feedback on livelihood diversification programs.

3. Quantitative Indicators Used
- Percentage (%) reduction of households affected by seasonal flooding in frontline communities.
- Percentage (%) increase in household income among fisherfolk benefiting from mangrove rehabilitation and eco-tourism.
- Number of women and youth involved in climate-resilient livelihood initiatives.
- Access rate to adaptation infrastructure (e.g., drainage, shelters, early warning systems) compared between vulnerable areas and citywide averages.
column19:
The Probolinggo City has taken steps to ensure equitable and inclusive climate actions. Below are two examples with evidence:

1. Mangrove Ecosystem Restoration at Permata Beach (since 2022, ongoing)
- Description: Community-led mangrove rehabilitation covering degraded coastal areas to reduce coastal erosion, enhance carbon sequestration, and protect fisheries.
- Equity and Inclusion: The program involves frontline fishing communities, women's groups, and local schools in planting and monitoring activities. This ensures the benefits of coastal protection and improved fisheries are directly experienced by those most vulnerable to climate change.
- Evidence: Annual monitoring reports by the City's Environmental Agency show more than 25,000 mangroves planted by 2024 with participation from over 1,000 local residents, 40% of whom are women and youth.

2. Flood Reduction and River/Drainage Clean-up Campaign (2021-present)
- Description: Regular community-based cleaning and dredging of urban rivers and drainage systems to reduce flood risk.
- Equity and Inclusion: Activities are designed with neighborhood associations, youth groups, and informal settlement residents, who are the most exposed to flood risks. This ensures fair distribution of benefits, with vulnerable communities gaining reduced disaster losses and improved health outcomes.
- Evidence: City Disaster Management Agency reports indicate a 30% reduction in flood-prone points between 2021-2024, with active participation from over 50 community-based organizations.

column16: We recognize that we co-exist and share our climate with many other communities in South Florida. To engage with the wider opportunities, benefits, solutions, and threats related to climate change, Miami-Dade County has long been a member of the South Florida Regional Climate Change Compact. Recognizing the vulnerability of Southeast Florida to the impacts of climate change and following a successful summit on the topic in October of 2009, Monroe, Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach Counties entered into a Regional Climate Change Compact to collaborate on climate change issues. The Compact focuses on joint advocacy of policies and legislation at the local, state and national level as well as collaboration to develop a Regional Climate Action Plan. Implementation of the Compact is occurring through a Staff Steering Committee representing each of the Compact Counties, the South Florida Water Management District and two municipalities. The Compact continues to move forward with regional climate change mitigation and adaptation activities including: finalizing the third edition (3.0) of the SE Fl Regional Climate Change Action Plan (also known as RCAP) and engage partners on implementation; organizing regular summits; developing and sharing regional tools and knowledge; and conducting semi-regular regional greenhouse gas emissions inventories. Miami-Dade County is a key contributor of these activities. While we consider and prioritize many of the qualitative benefits, we continue to work on analysis and reporting to better understand the quantitative impacts of Miami-Dade's climate action with respect to wider opportunities/benefits beyond our County's physical boundaries/jurisdiction. Miami-Dade County is one of the top consumers from our state utility, Florida Power and Light, and we are continuing to actively partner with them to advance efficiency, resilience and sustainability initiatives not just in our community, but state-wide.

Sebagai yurisdiksi yang berkomitmen terhadap aksi iklim, Pemerintah Kota Bandar Lampung secara aktif menilai berbagai peluang dan manfaat lingkungan, sosial, dan ekonomi yang lebih luas dari implementasi kebijakan iklim. Proses penilaian ini dilakukan melalui integrasi analisis manfaat ganda ke dalam dokumen perencanaan strategis seperti KLHS, RPJMD, dan dokumen sektoral yang terkait dengan transportasi, energi, tata ruang, dan lingkungan hidup.

Dari sisi lingkungan, aksi iklim seperti penghijauan kota, pengelolaan air secara berkelanjutan, dan pemanfaatan energi terbarukan telah memberikan manfaat nyata berupa penurunan emisi GRK, perbaikan kualitas udara, pengurangan efek pulau panas perkotaan, serta peningkatan ketahanan terhadap bencana iklim seperti banjir dan kekeringan.

Secara sosial, program adaptasi iklim telah membuka peluang bagi peningkatan kesadaran masyarakat, partisipasi komunitas dalam ketahanan lingkungan, serta perbaikan akses terhadap layanan dasar seperti air bersih dan sanitasi. Aksi ini juga turut memperkuat inklusi sosial, terutama bagi kelompok rentan seperti perempuan, anak-anak, dan masyarakat miskin yang paling terdampak oleh perubahan iklim.

Dari sisi ekonomi, aksi iklim mendorong penciptaan lapangan kerja baru di sektor hijau, seperti pengelolaan sampah berbasis ekonomi sirkular, pembangunan infrastruktur hijau, serta pengembangan UMKM berbasis energi bersih dan pertanian berketahanan iklim. Selain itu, kebijakan ini juga membuka peluang pembiayaan dari mitra pembangunan, CSR perusahaan, dan skema inovatif seperti green budgeting dan pembiayaan berkelanjutan.

Penilaian manfaat ini dilakukan secara berkelanjutan melalui koordinasi lintas OPD, pemanfaatan data pembangunan daerah, serta evaluasi berkala terhadap dampak kebijakan. Aksi iklim yang dilakukan Pemerintah Kota Pontianak membawa manfaat strategis bagi pembangunan berkelanjutan. Melalui pembangunan infrastruktur hijau seperti drainase, tanggul, dan ruang terbuka hijau, kota ini tidak hanya berupaya menekan risiko banjir dan polusi, tetapi juga meningkatkan kualitas hidup masyarakat. Infrastruktur hijau berfungsi sebagai penopang daya tahan kota terhadap iklim ekstrem, sekaligus investasi jangka panjang untuk kesehatan lingkungan dan sosial.

Di sektor pengelolaan sampah, kebijakan larangan kantong plastik sekali pakai sejak awal 2025 serta rencana pembangunan TPS3R dan pusat pengelolaan sampah terpadu (PPSP) memperlihatkan langkah konkret menuju ekonomi sirkular. Dengan mendorong pengolahan sampah dari sumber, Pontianak mampu mengurangi beban TPA, menekan emisi gas rumah kaca, dan membuka peluang ekonomi baru dari daur ulang maupun pemanfaatan sampah organik. Hal ini memberi manfaat langsung bagi kebersihan kota sekaligus mendorong kesadaran masyarakat untuk mengubah perilaku sehari-hari.

Manfaat aksi iklim juga terlihat dari dukungan pembiayaan besar, baik dari pusat maupun lembaga internasional. Pembangunan SPALD-T senilai Rp1,5 triliun dari ADB, serta revitalisasi TPA Batulayang dengan dana Rp260 miliar dari pemerintah pusat dan Rp205 miliar dari Bank Dunia, menunjukkan pengakuan bahwa Pontianak serius dalam transisi menuju kota rendah karbon. Pendanaan ini tidak hanya memperkuat kapasitas infrastruktur, tetapi juga mengurangi beban fiskal daerah dalam menghadapi tantangan iklim.

Lebih jauh, manfaat aksi iklim juga mencakup penguatan teknologi dan sistem informasi. Kehadiran aplikasi SIPPohon yang memuat data seluruh pohon di kota berikut potensi serapan karbon, serta aplikasi Si Gita Jas Berkerah untuk pengelolaan sampah digital, menjadi bukti bahwa Pontianak mulai memanfaatkan data dan inovasi digital dalam tata kelola lingkungan. Walau masih tahap awal, inisiatif ini membuka peluang bagi carbon accounting dan potensi kerja sama pendanaan berbasis karbon di masa depan.

Namun, manfaat terbesar dari seluruh aksi iklim ini terletak pada tumbuhnya kesadaran kolektif masyarakat terhadap ancaman perubahan iklim. Gotong royong lingkungan, partisipasi komunitas dalam bank sampah, hingga adaptasi warga terhadap larangan plastik membuktikan bahwa keberhasilan aksi iklim tidak hanya diukur dari kebijakan dan proyek, tetapi juga dari perubahan perilaku bersama. Kesadaran inilah yang menjadikan Pontianak bukan hanya membangun ketahanan fisik, tetapi juga ketahanan sosial, menuju kota berwawasan lingkungan yang humanis.

Pemkot Pontianak mengukur aksi iklim yang adil dan inklusif, misalnya melalui kombinasi indikator risiko dan ketahanan, partisipasi masyarakat, kebijakan sampah dari sumber, serta pembiayaan kolaboratif agar beban tidak jatuh pada kelompok paling rentan. Dengan cara ini, aksi iklim tidak hanya dilihat dari penurunan emisi, tetapi juga dari seberapa jauh manfaatnya dirasakan oleh seluruh warga kota. Penjelasannya sebagai berikut:

1. Menggunakan Indikator Ketahanan dan Risiko

Pemkot Pontianak tidak hanya mengukur emisi gas rumah kaca, tetapi juga menggunakan Indeks Risiko Bencana (IRB) dan Indeks Ketahanan Daerah. Indikator ini mencerminkan seberapa rawan wilayah tertentu terhadap banjir atau bencana, serta bagaimana kapasitas adaptasi masyarakatnya. Dengan cara ini, kebijakan tidak hanya berfokus pada kota secara agregat, tetapi juga pada wilayah dan kelompok yang paling rentan.

2. Mendorong Partisipasi Masyarakat

Prinsip inklusivitas dijalankan dengan melibatkan masyarakat dalam aksi lingkungan, mulai dari bank sampah, gotong royong pembersihan drainase, hingga aplikasi Si Gita Jas Berkerah untuk melaporkan dan memantau sampah. Dengan partisipasi ini, aksi iklim tidak menjadi program top-down saja, tetapi memberi ruang bagi warga—termasuk kelompok rentan—untuk ikut berkontribusi dan merasakan manfaat langsung.

3. Pengelolaan Sampah dari Sumber

Kebijakan seperti larangan kantong plastik sekali pakai dan pembangunan TPS3R diarahkan agar semua lapisan masyarakat dapat mengurangi sampah dari rumah tangga. Ini mengukur keadilan karena setiap warga diberi peran setara dalam pengurangan emisi dari sampah, bukan hanya dibebankan pada pengelola kota.

4. Kolaborasi Multisektoral dan Dukungan Eksternal

Pendanaan dari pusat (TPA Batulayang Rp260 miliar) dan lembaga internasional (SPALD-T Rp1,5 triliun dari ADB, Rp205 miliar dari Bank Dunia untuk pabrik sampah) menunjukkan bahwa aksi iklim di Pontianak tidak membebani APBD semata. Skema ini juga memastikan bahwa kelompok masyarakat miskin kota tidak menanggung beban biaya transisi, melainkan justru menjadi penerima manfaat dari infrastruktur yang lebih sehat dan ramah lingkungan.
column19:
Aksi iklim yang adil dan inklusif di Pontianak sudah termuat dalam Ranwal RPJMD Kota Pontianak 2025-2029 dengan beberapa poin, antara lain:

1. Integrasi Sosial-Ekonomi dalam Aksi Lingkungan

RPJMD tidak hanya berbicara soal infrastruktur hijau, tetapi juga secara eksplisit memasukkan sasaran pembangunan keluarga berkualitas, kesetaraan gender, dan masyarakat inklusif. Indikator seperti indeks pembangunan keluarga (IPK), indeks ketimpangan gender (IKG), serta capaian anggaran responsif gender (ARG) menjadi tolok ukur sejak tahun 2025 hingga 2030. Ini menunjukkan bahwa kebijakan lingkungan di Pontianak dirancang agar manfaatnya bisa dirasakan setara oleh semua kelompok.

2. Kolaborasi Multisektoral dan Pemberdayaan Masyarakat

Di dalam Ranwal RPJMD 2025-2029 dituliskan bahwa sejak tahun 2027, Pontianak mempercepat implementasi infrastruktur hijau, resiliensi terhadap bencana, transportasi publik, dan energi baru terbarukan. Upaya ini disertai dengan strategi pemberdayaan masyarakat lokal, penguatan peran swasta, serta konservasi ekosistem yang memperhitungkan aspek sosial, ekonomi, dan lingkungan. Hal ini menjadi dasar bahwa keberlanjutan tidak hanya teknis, tapi juga berkeadilan.

3. Fasilitas Dasar dan Akses Layanan Publik yang Merata

Pada misi pembangunan kota berwawasan lingkungan dan humanis, ditetapkan bahwa infrastruktur dasar seperti air bersih, drainase, pengelolaan sampah, hingga akses internet cepat akan diprioritaskan sepanjang periode 2025-2029. Tujuannya adalah agar setiap warga, tanpa kecuali, dapat mengakses layanan publik yang bersih, aman, dan modern.

Semua ini menegaskan bahwa keberlanjutan di Pontianak diarahkan bukan hanya untuk menekan emisi, tetapi juga untuk menjamin manfaatnya dirasakan secara adil oleh seluruh lapisan masyarakat.

Di bidang ekonomi, transisi menuju energi bersih dan efisiensi energi menciptakan peluang investasi hijau, lapangan kerja baru, serta pengembangan industri ramah lingkungan. Di bidang sosial, aksi iklim memperkuat ketahanan masyarakat terhadap bencana, melindungi kelompok rentan, dan meningkatkan kualitas kesehatan melalui berkurangnya polusi udara dan penyakit berbasis lingkungan. Di bidang lingkungan, program penghijauan, rehabilitasi mangrove, dan peningkatan ruang terbuka hijau tidak hanya menyerap emisi, tetapi juga melindungi pesisir dari abrasi, menjaga keanekaragaman hayati, serta meningkatkan kualitas tata ruang kota. Di bidang tata kelola, kolaborasi lintas sektor memperkuat kapasitas kelembagaan, membuka akses ke pendanaan iklim nasional maupun internasional, serta meningkatkan reputasi kota sebagai wilayah yang berkomitmen pada pembangunan rendah karbon. Dengan demikian, aksi iklim dipandang tidak hanya sebagai upaya mitigasi risiko, tetapi juga sebagai katalis untuk pertumbuhan ekonomi hijau, peningkatan kesejahteraan masyarakat, dan perlindungan ekosistem jangka panjang.\n

Ketiga, dalam proses perencanaan partisipatif, masukan dari komunitas lokal dan kelompok rentan dihimpun untuk memastikan suara mereka terwakili dalam dokumen RAD-GRK maupun KLHS. From the perspective of BAPPEDA, ensuring equitable and inclusive distribution of climate action is a key part of our regional development planning. We quantify and monitor this through the following approaches:

Disaggregated Targeting in Planning Documents
Climate-related programs in the Regional Development Plan (RPJMD and RKPD) are designed with specific targets for vulnerable groups—such as low-income communities, women, Indigenous peoples, and rural populations. Indicators are disaggregated by gender, income level, and geographic location to monitor equitable reach.

Use of Social Vulnerability and Climate Risk Maps
We integrate climate risk mapping with socio-economic vulnerability data to identify priority areas and populations most affected by climate change. This ensures climate interventions are directed where they are most needed.

Participatory Planning and Public Consultation
BAPPEDA conducts community consultations, public hearings, and stakeholder engagement processes that include marginalized groups, ensuring their needs and perspectives are reflected in climate-related decision-making.

Climate Budget Tagging (CBT) with Equity Focus
Through climate budget tagging mechanisms, we track how climate-related expenditures benefit vulnerable populations. This helps ensure funding is not only climate-smart but also socially just.

Monitoring & Evaluation with Equity Indicators
Our monitoring and evaluation (M&E) frameworks include indicators that track access to benefits of climate action (e.g. access to renewable energy, resilience infrastructure, training programs) among disadvantaged groups.

These tools enable us to embed equity and inclusivity in climate action while aligning with broader goals of just transition and sustainable regional development.
column19:
Targeted Program Design for Vulnerable Communities
Climate adaptation and mitigation programs are specifically designed to reach vulnerable groups, including low-income families, rural communities, women-headed households, and Indigenous populations. For example, our community-based climate resilience program (CBCR) includes participatory mapping and planning at the village level.

Integration in Regional Planning Documents
We have integrated climate justice principles into key planning documents such as the RPJMD, RKPD, and Spatial Plans (RTRW). These documents include equity-focused targets and indicators, such as the number of underserved households receiving green infrastructure benefits or access to clean energy.

Capacity Building and Participatory Forums
We conduct regular multi-stakeholder consultation forums (Musrenbang) at village, sub-district, and district levels, ensuring meaningful participation from marginalized groups in climate-related planning and budgeting processes.

Climate Budget Tagging with Pro-Poor Focus
Our financial planning includes climate budget tagging (CBT) that tracks allocations directed at vulnerable groups. This data helps to monitor how climate-related expenditures are distributed across socio-economic categories.

Pilot Projects in High-Risk Areas
We have implemented pilot projects in climate-vulnerable areas (e.g., flood-prone or drought-affected regions), focusing on community-based adaptation, nature-based solutions, and green jobs creation—ensuring benefits reach those most impacted.

Data-Driven Decision Making
We use social vulnerability and climate exposure maps to identify priority areas. These tools are critical in guiding resource allocation toward communities most at risk.

These actions reflect our commitment to inclusive development and ensuring that no one is left behind in the transition toward a climate-resilient future.

column19: To successfully implement the Climate Action Plan (CAP), economic and equity factors must be taken into consideration. Low-income, minority, and other communities of concern are expected to be most impacted by future climate changes. Therefore, the City's CAP includes the consideration of socially equitable climate adaptation, equitable implementation of mitigation measures, and a focus on green jobs. The City continues to address equity through existing housing programs and planning for future housing. Ongoing programs include the City's Housing Choice Voucher Program (Section 8 rental assistance) and Community Development Block Grant Program (CDBG). Since 1995 the City of Encinitas Housing Authority (EHA) has operated a Section 8 Rental Assistance Program. The Section 8 Program offers financial rental assistance to low-income Encinitas households through a voucher-based program. The program is very popular with an ongoing wait list. Additionally, the City has managed a CDBG program since 2011. The CDBG program facilitates the administration of federal funding for housing related projects to create a suitable living environment, to provide decent housing, or to create economic opportunities for low-to-moderate income households and communities. The City's Housing Element identifies existing and projected housing needs in order to preserve, improve and develop housing for all economic segments of the community, in addition to demonstrating how the City will accommodate its fair share of regional housing. The City's Housing Element identifies existing and projected housing needs in order to preserve, improve and develop housing for all economic segments of the community, in addition to demonstrating how the City will accommodate its fair share of regional housing. Underserved and underrepresented communities often do not have the same level as participation in planning processes. Thus, the City has worked to engage community members of diverse backgrounds by attending various city-wide events to promote climate action plan related opportunities. In 2024, staff attended 16 community events. Events attended by City sustainability staff included the Spring Egg Hunt, Cyclovia, Spring and Holiday Street Fairs, Dia de los Muertos, Small Business Resource Fair, Zero Waste Fair, and farmers' markets. Policies created to advance the deployment of renewable energy generation at residential, and commercial buildings in Encinitas directly support the creation of green jobs. Every year in Encinitas, hundreds of solar PV systems are installed at homes and businesses, both voluntarily or as a result of Encinitas green building regulations. Of the solar installed, a majority of installers are locally based companies. According to California Public Utilities Commission data, of the 2684 kW solar PV systems installed in Encinitas in 2024, 223 were installed by companies based in San Diego County. Solar PV systems installed by San Diego County based companies directly support our local green economy and create green jobs.

column18: Boulder County strives to include metrics and indicators in mapping studies and other programs to track our inclusive distribution of climate action. column19: The following list includes a summary of highlights that our jurisdiction has completed to increase inclusive/equitable climate action into programs; please note this does not include all equity actions. (1) Created the Community Forestry Corp which empowers underrepresented youth in tree stewardship roles (2) Applicants with a lower Average Moderate Income (AMI) are scored higher in Soil Health Initiative grant applications (3) the Built environment team has a Small Business Equity Program that predominantly serves businesses owned by People of Color. This program provides sizeable rebates for energy efficiency renovations as well as on-site advising, (4) we have been collaborating on a regional scale with other municipalities, non-profits, and utilities to promote electric vehicles equitably. This includes determining which communities to address first, what type of charging infrastructure we need, and what barriers we as a government entity face in meeting the needs of our residents, (5) helping to fund a community-led group that is focused on climate justice and how to ensure that government efforts in the community are equitable. Using the framework of co-creation, this collaboration shifts power to the community, providing effective and impactful projects and policies are enacted, (6) creation of a vulnerability map using climate projections and current social vulnerability data to help us locate which portions of our jurisdiction need the most focus when facing climate change, (7) creation of a full-time Climate Equity Specialist position to coordinate community engagement efforts and internal equity capacity building, (8) creation of the Climate Policy Action Leadership Collaborative, CPAL. This space will introduce policies being considered and answer questions to eight diverse community leaders participating, and (8) partnering with local Latinx media partners (Radio and Press), both partners highlight key topics relevant to community and climate equity, (10) creating a OSCAR departmentwide strategy that 40% of OSCAR's operating budget is directed to Justice 40 communities with the goal of racial equity and climate justice outcomes, (11) creation of a Climate Equity Fund that directly resources individuals and communities historically excluded from formal climate solutions work through community capacity building and inclusive climate action, (12) planning equity-centered community engagement for several programs to co-create sustainability solutions with underserved community members, and (13) launched Growing Shade, an urban forestry expansion program providing free trees on residential properties in disproportionately impacted communities as defined by Colorado's EnviroScreen Tool.

column16: Short term: Community Solar for New Mexico State was passed in April, 2021. Since this time, the focus in the County's SLDC has created codes that are specific to increasing access for community solar developers throughout the County. Community Solar ordinance amendments were approved by the Board of County Commissioners after the public hearing process July 12, 2022. The County was approved for one Community Solar project in 2023 and going forward is now able to take advantage of the limited opportunities (200 MW cap throughout the State) for promoting more community solar development within the County boundaries, with few barriers or restrictions, while promoting projects on brown fields and/or on unusable land. As part of our Climate Action Plan we committed to pursuing six categories of broader benefits while reducing emissions. These benefits are:
•	Addressing social and economic injustices associated with the fossil fuel economy
•	Increased health benefits associated with lower emissions
•	Increased economic benefits in terms of lower operating costs, less imported energy and family-supporting jobs in the clean energy economy
•	Increased ecosystem benefits associated with less pollution, including improved air and water quality, enhanced wildlife habitats and increased biodiversity
•	Reduced rural-urban tensions (in Wisconsin, like many purple states, there has been increased tension between rural farming communities and urban centers)
•	Increased climate resiliency and ability to adapt to changes already baked into our local climate

Increasingly Dane County recognizes that many of our environmental efforts have important co-benefits. For example, our efforts to purchase land that can be transitioned back into prairie is often driven first by the desire to mitigate flooding and protect water quality but the effort also delivers natural carbon sequestration benefits. Similarly, a solar array on rural land delivers clean electricity while creating family-sustaining local construction jobs and also reducing phosphorous runoff associated with applying fertilizers to the land. In 2022 Dane County's Department of Land & Water Resources established an Ecosystem Benefits Team to help quantify the multiple benefits associated with various projects.

These environmental impacts also directly translate to public health benefits. For example, better air quality reduces risk for respiratory disease, flood protection reduces risk to property damage and human endangerment during storm events, and more access to open space allows for more opportunities to recreate outdoors, which improves physical and mental well-being.

Perhaps most important for us is the equity opportunity. There are substantial inequalities baked into the fossil fuel economy. Transitioning to a clean energy economy creates an opportunity to ensure that equity is infused into our system, so that everyone has access to clean energy job opportunities and the other economic, environmental and health benefits associated with a clean energy economy. In particular, one such opportunity is to grow the green economy workforce, with a focus on recruiting underserved populations to fill these emerging needs in this sector.

Dane County monitors a variety of equity metrics across its many departments and functions. Specific to climate action, Dane County uses various environmental justice tools to monitor climate impacts (including air quality, flooding and high heat) on different populations. We are also partnering with academic and community-based groups to increase equitable and inclusive access to the benefits associated with climate action. This includes monitoring participation levels in various energy efficiency and clean energy opportunities across various environmental justice communities.

One example of Dane County's commitment to equitable climate action is through the Tree Canopy Collaborative. The focus of this work is to maintain, protect, and expand tree canopy across Dane County, with an emphasis on underserved areas. Priority areas for tree planting events and outreach are within socially vulnerable areas, given the disproportionate impact heat health and air quality can impact these residents.

In late 2022 the Dane County Office of Energy & Climate Change began convening a group of leaders of community-based organizations to better understand environmental justice impacts and priorities in our diverse communities. Motivated in part by new federal funding opportunities under the Infrastructure and Inflation Reduction bills, the convenings aim to increase collaboration across different communities and to give Dane County staff increased insight into the nuances of equitable and inclusive climate action locally.
column19:
Dane County is actively collaborating with local municipalities and a variety of environmental justice groups to assess disparities associated with our current systems. Specifically we are working with the Capital Area Regional Planning Commission, University of Wisconsin-Madison researchers, and various community groups to map the intersection of both climate resilience factors like tree canopy and disparities like energy burden to maps of environmental justice communities. This enables us to target our efforts so that the communities who have suffered disproportionately are prioritized for new opportunities.

We are also working with stakeholder groups to co-create new initiatives that will better serve environmental justice communities. These efforts include our Sustainable Leadership Collaborative (SLC) and a community engagement project in partnership with UW-Madison researchers. The SLC is a partnership of cities, towns, municipalities, and school districts to facilitate climate-oriented collaboration. The UW-Madison research will pilot a process for engaging BIPOC communities in climate action decisions (see https://univercity.wisc.edu/2023/01/23/uw-madison-research-team-partners-with-dane-county-organizations-to-host-environmental-justice-discussions/ for details).

In late 2022 the Dane County Office of Energy & Climate Change began convening a group of leaders of community-based organizations to better understand environmental justice impacts and priorities in our diverse communities. Motivated in part by new federal funding opportunities under the Infrastructure and Inflation Reduction bills, the convenings aim to increase collaboration across different communities and to give Dane County staff increased insight into the nuances of equitable and inclusive climate action locally. Through these discussions we have identified two priority issues for local groups--energy affordability in housing and access to fresh food. We have also collaborated on one major grant proposal and started discussions on additional joint grant applications.

One such joint grant application Dane County led was a $15 million proposal to develop electric car charging across the county in areas of economic need. This collaborative proposal emphasizes the need to ensure charging options exist for all residents, with the knowledge that market forces will not likely move quickly enough to install chargers in lower income areas without a current demonstrated need. However, in order for residents in multi-family homes to make the switch to electric vehicles, these charging opportunities need to exist in the community. If received, this funding will allow Dane County to help these residents make the transition.

Antalya Metropolitan Municipality has created a comprehensive approach to climate actions that includes Mitigation, Adaptation, and SDGs that generates co-benefits to the economy, society, and environment. Antalya's journey began in 2013 with its Sustainable Energy Action Plan (SEAP), which was updated in 2021, and became the Sustainable Energy and Climate Action Plan (SECAP) in 2022. These plans followed the EU Covenant of Mayors methodology and serve as action plans as we aim to build a low-carbon climate-resilient Antalya. The institution and protection of climate change at the highest level is also reflected in the establishment of the Climate Change and Zero Waste Department in Antalya Municipal Council in 2022 which was the first municipal department dedicated to climate change for any municipality in Türkiye. In the same year, Antalya became the first municipality in Türkiye and by TSE to achieve the 'Climate Friendly Organization Certificate', for energy efficiency and renewable energy usage.
There are various opportunities that stem from climate actions and initiatives from an economic perspective, such as the cost reductions to energy consumption in municipal buildings from efficiency measures reducing operating expenses, freeing up, improving other community services proceeding from available resources to access other community services. Investments made in solar energy plants among 18, biogas facilities about 4 & already underway to waste heat-to-energy (WHR) project at 1 will increase local energy generation, reducing dependency on external resources. Green projects such as energy-efficient public transport and waste valorization projects enhance local supply chains, create more job opportunities, and additional market opportunities for various sectors including clean technology and environmental services.
The social benefits included from our climate actions were similarly impressive and there are unquantifiable social benefits. For example, climate adaptation measures such as flood protection, heatwave responses (our CLIMAAX project), and fire amelioration processes increase community safety and reduce the health hazards from climate change. The raising awareness campaigns, school education programs, and collaborative public participation events build on environmental education (our Environmental Education and Innovation Center) and empower citizens to create climate actions in their own lives. Through our 'Solar School' project where unemployed youth or NEET youth (Not in Employment, Education or Training) received technical and theoretical trainings on installing solar panels and creating a specialized labor force that will be employable when there is demand for skilled workers in the renewable energy sector. Our urban agricultural projects create examples of food and water securities to support locals when there is ever-increasing demands from
 growing global population and tourism industry.
Furthermore, environmental co-benefits produced are more significant than originally anticipated including improved air quality from low-impact commuting and vehicles that rely on fossil fuels and improvements made to managing waste from recyclable waste and composting. The implementation of techniques to preserve important coastal and marine ecosystems such as sea water quality and assistance with ghost net removals affected by maritime service fishing. Our projects to create reforestation opportunities, and green space development projects provide multiple benefits, including carbon storage, improving microclimates and urban biodiversity, partially reducing urban heat island effects.
Governance and recognition also really matter in solidifying these benefits in a connected and engaged community. Antalya's approach to climate action, integrated planning can be supported through national frameworks such as Türkiye Climate Law (2025), local framework Climate Change Action Plan Regulation (YİDEP) (Antalya is one of the pilot municipalities), as well as undertake participation in subnational, national, and international affiliated networks (EU Covenant of Mayors, ICLEI, MedCities, etc.) where there are opportunities for knowledge exchanges, and additional financial and technical resources are brought into the city. Recognition through success from addressing the agendas of international municipal awards for environment initiatives and whereby Antalya collectively has won 24 environmental awards' at local, national, and global levels to validate our approach and establish a form of accountability to intentionally improve.

column18:
Antalya Metropolitan Municipality approaches equitable and inclusive climate action through the guiding framework of its Sustainable Energy and Climate Action Plan (SECAP). The plan explicitly recognizes that climate measures must not only deliver environmental benefits, but also strengthen social resilience, support livelihoods, and ensure that vulnerable groups are not left behind in the transition to a low-carbon, climate-resilient future.
To operationalize this vision, the municipality integrates equity considerations into climate action design and implementation, prioritizing sectors and communities with higher vulnerability to climate risks such as drought, extreme heat, flooding, and rural economic instability. Examples include:
Solar School Program - Provides theoretical and hands-on photovoltaic system installation training to young people who are neither in education nor employment (NEET), creating direct pathways to jobs in the renewable energy sector.
Women's Cooperatives Support Program - Strengthens women's economic participation through targeted support in production, branding, marketing, and cooperative management, enabling women to benefit from green economy opportunities.
Beğişsusuzu Climate-Resilient Irrigation Project - Upgrades rural irrigation from waste water treatment infrastructure to secure water availability for smallholder farmers, increasing productivity and resilience against climate-induced drought.
Beekeeping Support & Training - Promotes sustainable beekeeping practices that protect biodiversity, enhance pollination, and diversify rural incomes.
Eco-Friendly Farmer Card - Encourages climate-positive agricultural practices by rewarding farmers who collect and recycle agricultural waste, allowing them to redeem points for economic incentives.
Smart (Digital) Agriculture System - Enables greenhouse owners to monitor temperature, humidity, and frost risk in real time via a remote system, triggering SMS and email alerts for rapid response, thus protecting yields and reducing losses.
Climate Change Unit Representatives - An internal governance innovation where designated representatives from different municipal departments contribute to climate planning and monitoring, ensuring interdepartmental collaboration and sector-specific inclusion.
These programs deliver multiple co-benefits: reducing greenhouse gas emissions, enhancing adaptive capacity, improving public health, creating green jobs, empowering women, and supporting rural development. While the municipality does not yet systematically collect fully disaggregated beneficiary data by gender, age, or income for every project, equity outcomes are tracked through project-specific reporting, beneficiary counts, and integration into municipal performance reports such as the Annual Activity Report. The Local Equality Action Plan provides an additional policy backdrop to identify priority groups and guide equitable distribution in project design.
By embedding inclusion and fairness into climate planning, and by implementing initiatives that directly link environmental goals with social and economic gains, Antalya Metropolitan Municipality works to ensure that the low-carbon transition is both just and widely beneficial across the community.
column19:
Antalya Metropolitan Municipality actively pursues equity and inclusion in climate action decisions, with public involvement through structured forms of participation, which are institutionalized, and decision-making that is inclusive. 
 A critical part of public involvement is the Environmental Board (Çevre Kurulu) which was created by municipal council decision, in 2020, and is the only body like it in Türkiye. The board consists of many stakeholders - municipal departments, public institutions, universities, professional chambers, NGOs, neighborhood representatives, and groups of citizens, to give input, review and have oversight on policies with environmental or climate associations. The Environmental Board is a permanent committee, and provides a mechanism to ensure diverse community perspectives, including voices from those most impacted by climate change, that gets incorporated into decision-making within the context of actions related to the implementation of the SECAP, coast of Antalya, waste reduction, renewable energy, and restoring ecosystems. 
While the SECAP was being developed, a robust stakeholder process was completed. Workshops took place both internally with units of the municipality, and externally with other stakeholders, to determine priority areas for actions and projects related to mitigating climate change (greenhouse gases) and adapting to climate change. For instance: 
● The first mitigation workshop (March 17, 2021) drew from city wide stakeholders around assessing sources of local emissions, and determining highlighted opportunities for local emissions (GHG) reductions. 
● An adaptation workshop assessed climate risks and vulnerabilities, with contributions from the national Provincial Disaster Risk Reduction Plan (IRAP), the Environmental Plan (2019), and the Transport Master plan (2016), and feedback from the community. 
● While COVID-19 was a challenge, some sessions (Antalya IRAP, Transportation Master Plan) were considered online using Microsoft Teams for accessibility and continuity. 
Events targeting the public can enhance inclusive participation and shared knowledge. For example, the Antalya Climate Change summit (February 2, 2024) held municipal leaders, academics, NGOs, youth, and the private sector in a venue to share solutions to climate adaptation and mitigation. The Antalya International Science Forum - ANISF (2023-2024) was a space for scientists, and citizens to discuss innovation around, coastal resilience, wildfire prevention and sustainable agriculture.
As well as in planning, inclusive participation is also evident in the implementation of projects. Strong examples from 'We Promised to our Nature' books (2019-2023, and 2024 editions) and the 2024 Activity Report are as follows: 
●Eco-Friendly Farmer Card: Registered farmers are government endorsed to adopt more sustainable practices by collecting waste with the card, earning point equivalents on agricultural inputs. (e.g fertilizer) sustainably from waste collection more easily, market access to renewable conversion - carbon credits etc. 
●Smart (Digital) Agriculture systems: Farmers record greenhouse conditions remotely, which is reducing water use, avoiding potential crop loss and supporting climate adaptation for rural producers.
●Women's cooperatives and rural income for women's sustainability in climate change impacts: Providing trainings, ensuring market access and access to a variety of income sources. 
●Rural beekeeping and biodiversity support focusing on rural livelihoods, sustaining increased pollinator populations. 
●Creation of unit role representatives for climate change, within different municipal departments, but for the purpose of coordinating climate actions across departments. 
Through these formal mechanisms, the municipality ensures that climate action benefits - i.e from improved resilience (storms, floods etc.) and emissions mitigation reducing harm to future livelihoods, and social and economic co-benefits across sectors and communities. Using a mix of formal governance mechanisms, and participatory processes for projects, is also the surety decision-making remains non-partisan, transparent, inclusive, and centered in local needs.

The wider opportunities and benefits of climate action identified by İzmir include access to financial support from international funds and EU programs, which enables the implementation of ambitious projects. Climate action also enhances the city's international profile, positioning İzmir as a leading actor in sustainability and resilience. In addition, participation in global initiatives fosters networking and the creation of new alliances, opening pathways for innovation and knowledge exchange.

These opportunities have been further reinforced through İzmir's active role in the EU Mission on Climate-Neutral and Smart Cities. İzmir joined the Mission in 2022, prepared and signed its Climate City Contract in 2023, and in 2024 was officially awarded the EU Mission Label. This recognition provides continuous access to technical assistance, capacity-building and innovative financing mechanisms. The city has also launched or applied for several EU-funded projects, such as CRIZ-ERS (Horizon Europe CLIMAAX call), CRIZ-CoRe (Pathways2Resilience program), GCC-SYNERGY (NetZeroCities Pilot Cities Programme), and CARDIMED (Mediterranean Climate Resilience Demonstration), each contributing to knowledge transfer, nature-based solutions, digital innovation, and investment planning. Moreover, the adoption of Türkiye's Climate Law in 2025 reinforces the role of municipalities, offering İzmir a stronger mandate to lead local climate action and resilience strategies.

İzmir has already gained tangible benefits from its climate action efforts. The city's participation in the EU Mission on Climate-Neutral and Smart Cities has provided access to technical expertise, international visibility and funding opportunities, culminating in the official Mission Label granted in 2024. İzmir is also part of the EU Mission on Adaptation to Climate Change, through which municipal staff benefited from MIP4Adapt technical assistance and training, strengthening local capacities for resilience planning.

Under these frameworks, İzmir secured significant EU-funded projects:

CRIZ-ERS (Horizon Europe - CLIMAAX call): €145,000 to conduct detailed climate risk and vulnerability assessments at city and neighborhood scale.

GCC-SYNERGY (NetZeroCities Pilot Cities Programme): €598,062 to deploy digital solutions for decarbonization of electricity consumption.

CARDIMED (Horizon Europe - Mediterranean Climate Resilience Demonstration): €405,125 to implement nature-based solutions in the Gediz Delta.

CRIZ-CoRe (Pathways2Resilience): a €210,000 proposal under evaluation to prepare İzmir's baseline assessment, climate resilience strategy, action plan and investment plan.

At the local level, the İzmir Climate Citizens' Assembly (2024-2025) has enhanced participatory governance by directly involving residents in shaping climate and resilience policies, thereby strengthening trust, awareness and collective ownership of climate solutions. Finally, the entry into force of Türkiye's Climate Law in 2025 provides municipalities, including İzmir, with a clearer mandate to prepare and implement climate action plans, creating a stronger legal basis for advancing resilience and decarbonization efforts.

These are only selected some examples among a broader portfolio of EU-funded, national and local projects, which collectively demonstrate how İzmir leverages climate action to achieve financial, social and environmental benefits.

Dessa forma, a jurisdição não apenas supervisiona os riscos relacionados às mudanças do clima, mas também se posiciona de maneira proativa, identificando oportunidades estratégicas para transformar os desafios climáticos em benefícios socioeconômicos, ambientais e institucionais.

O Município da Maia pretende refletir o princípio da equidade na resposta transformadora à crise climática.
A quantificação da ação climática foi prevista aquando do planeamento estratégico do Plano para a Energia Sustentável da Maia 2030 (PAES) e do Plano Municipal de Adaptação às Alterações Climáticas (PMAAC). Estes planos incluem várias medidas de mitigação e adaptação às alterações climáticas, respetivamente, sendo que cada uma delas tem prevista uma metodologia de implementação e uma metodologia de monitorização articulada com indicadores de realização. Cada medida está igualmente enquadrada em vários setores estratégicos nomeadamente: Ordenamento do território, Agricultura, Floresta e Biodiversidade, Recursos Hídricos, Saúde e Segurança de Pessoas e Bens, Energia e Edificado, assegurando assim a equitabilidade e inclusão das mesmas. 
As alterações climáticas têm o potencial de aumentar a desigualdade social, afetando de forma desproporcional as comunidades mais vulneráveis. Por este motivo, o Município considera fundamental atuar sobre as vulnerabilidades de maior risco, com uma atuação transversal a toda a população, mas que de forma indireta garante a proteção das populações mais vulneráveis sujeitas a maior risco. 
Desde logo, o primeiro Objetivo Estratégico do PMAAC alude aos territórios mais vulneráveis e às populações residentes: “Reduzir a exposição aos riscos climáticos - reduzir a vulnerabilidade climática dos setores estratégicos e dos territórios mais vulneráveis aumentando a capacidade de resposta para lidar com o agravamento dos riscos climáticos; “
A atenção aos territórios e populações vulneráveis é, igualmente, realçada no Objetivo Estratégico 5 - “Promover a monitorização - assegurar um acompanhamento regular da evolução climática do concelho, dos impactes das alterações climáticas e da evolução da capacidade adaptativa dos atores, setores e territórios vulneráveis.“
Não menos importante, as medidas projetadas para adaptar o território às alterações climáticas cobrem todo o território do Concelho, atendendo às circunstâncias e necessidades de cada povoação. O único tipo de discriminação verificada é positiva, nos territórios mais vulneráveis e faixas populacionais mais fragilizadas como doentes crónicos, idosos e crianças.
No que toca à componente de mitigação, que consta no PAES do município, são apresentadas ações para diversos setores, tais como os edifícios residenciais, os edifícios de serviços, indústria e resíduos, incluindo assim uma preocupação por abranger toda a população, especialmente a mais vulnerável no que toca, por exemplo, à temática da diminuição do consumo energético através da reabilitação de edifícios e ao acesso abrangente a energia limpa através da produção de energia renovável.
A monitorização destas ações desenvolve-se maioritariamente com recurso a informação sobre a utilização de energia e emissões de GEE, bem como ao nível da implementação de ações e medidas. As bases de informação para a realização da sua monitorização são essencialmente de fontes estatísticas, disponibilizadas publicamente, complementadas com informação de base local, sempre que seja possível recolher essa informação junto de diferentes atores, tendo em atenção o respeito pela privacidade da sua informação.
column19:
Um dos exemplos do princípio da equidade do Município da Maia na resposta às alterações climáticas e, especificamente, na atenção dada às populações mais expostas aos fenómenos extremos é o “Projeto de intervenção no Parque Fluvial de Alvura - um exemplo de adaptação às Alterações Climáticas”, em que se pretendeu adaptar esta zona mais vulnerável do território do Concelho da Maia aos fenómenos extremos e reduzir os riscos associados a fenómenos de cheias e de inundações, aumentando a resiliência do ecossistema identificado, bem como das espécies e habitats existentes aos efeitos das alterações climáticas, através da recuperação e consolidação de galerias ripícolas, a criação de refúgios e corredores ecológicos para espécies vulneráveis, aplicando soluções estruturais de base natural, integrando boas práticas de adaptação, com caráter demonstrativo e de replicabilidade. Considerou-se absolutamente imprescindível desenvolver ações concretas passíveis de reduzir a sensibilidade e exposição de uma das zonas mais inundáveis do Concelho ao clima (atual ou projetado), permitindo, se possível, aproveitar eventuais oportunidades emergentes, nomeadamente: limpeza do leito do rio, Plano de Abates/Controlo de Invasoras e consolidação da galeria ripícola.
Outro exemplo é a proposta de criação de uma pérgola viva, traduzindo-se numa solução estrutural de base natural com um caráter inovador e demonstrativo de um novo paradigma de construção de estruturas que dão resposta à crise climática e passam conceitos essenciais para o futuro.
No que toca à vertente da Mitigação, para apoiar diretamente os cidadãos a implementar medidas de eficiência energética nas suas habitações e melhorar as suas condições de habitabilidade, Maia disponibiliza, um balcão único (one-stop-shop) digital e físico denominado Maia Energy Hub. Este balcão, desenvolvido no âmbito do projeto Porto Energy ElevatoR (PEER), financiado pelo programa Horizonte 2020 e coordenado pela Agência de Energia do Porto, compreende o aconselhamento acerca de soluções de eficiência energética e de energias renováveis, legislação aplicável, identificação de oportunidades e apoio a candidaturas para financiamento. É um exemplo concreto da atuação do Município da Maia em prol da garantia da equidade e inclusividade nas políticas em prol do clima. 
Para além disto, o projeto de regeneração urbana e reabilitação dos edifícios do Bairro do Sobreiro na Maia é outro exemplo de promoção de uma ação climática equitativa. Neste caso, é expectado o incremento de elementos de isolamento térmico em fogos de habitações sociais de forma a promover a eficiência energética e, consequentemente, a mitigação da pobreza energética entre as populações mais vulneráveis.
