column16: A jurisdição identificou como um dos seus objetivos \'reduzir a vulnerabilidade aos eventos climáticos extremos e aumentar a capacidade adaptativa do município\', bem como tomar partido de potenciais oportunidades, isto é: criar orientações para dar resposta ao número máximo de eventos extremos que possam vir a afetar o território municipal (a médio e longo prazo), minorando os impactos previstos e beneficiando de eventuais oportunidades, através do desenvolvimento de um conhecimento integrado das características físicas, socioeconómicas e organizacionais do município. O Plano Municipal de Ação Climática de Loulé consubstancia a abordagem local de resposta aos desafios decorrentes das alterações climáticas, que se pretende, por um lado, norteadora da ação municipal (direta e indireta) de mitigação das emissões de GEE e de adaptação ao clima atual e futuro, e, por outro, mobilizadora de transformações na comunidade, nas instituições e na economia locais, no sentido da sua progressiva adaptação e descarbonização. Ou seja, o município de Loulé considera e reconhece a adaptação às Alterações Climáticas como uma oportunidade para o desenvolvimento e implementação de políticas e iniciativas promotoras de um território mais sustentável. A ação climática local permite e tem vindo a permitir obter uma vasta gama de benefícios mais amplos, com melhora significativamente a qualidade de vida da população, nomeadamente melhorias na saúde pública, na economia e na segurança alimentar e hídrica. As medidas de adaptação implementadas têm igualmente contribuído para a diminuição da poluição do ar e da água, enquanto práticas agrícolas, florestais e industriais mais sustentáveis promovem e aumentam a qualidade e a resiliência ambiental. Economicamente, a transição para energias renováveis e o aumento da eficiência energética cria empregos verdes, impulsiona a inovação tecnológica, reduz custos energéticos e a reduz a dependência de combustíveis fósseis. Além disso, a gestão aprimorada dos recursos hídricos e a agricultura sustentável garantem a disponibilidade de alimentos e água, essencial para a segurança alimentar e hídrica. A ação e adaptação climática promovem ainda a resiliência das infraestruturas, um planeamento urbano mais sustentável, bem como opções de mobilidade sustentável e a criação de mais espaços verdes, protegendo a biodiversidade e os ecossistemas. Ao mesmo tempo, promove a justiça climática, beneficiando comunidades vulneráveis e aumentando a equidade social. As cooperações institucionais e intersectoriais também têm sido favorecidas e fortalecidas através da ação climática municipal. A consciencialização e educação ambiental promovem estilos de vida mais sustentáveis e saudáveis.

column19: São vários os projetos e medidas/ações que o município de Loulé tem em curso que permitem uma distribuição equitativa e inclusiva da ação climática, dos quais se podem destacar: apoio a medidas de eficiência energética e de energias renováveis na habitação, BALCÃO MUNICIPAL LOULÉ ENERGIA (que disponibiliza aos munícipes um serviço de apoio e aconselhamento sobre eficiência energética e energias renováveis, incluindo aconselhamento na otimização da fatura energética, identificação de oportunidades e soluções de eficiência energética e energias renováveis e informação de apoio à elaboração de candidaturas a programas de financiamento), e o BALCÃO MUNICIPAL DE ENERGIA MÓVEL (viatura elétrica p/funcionamento do balcão móvel que permitirá a expansão do serviço a localidades fora dos centros urbanos, promovendo assim uma maior equidade territorial e providenciando apoio técnico para a prestação de serviços mais especializados aos utentes) a AGENDA DE SUSTENTABILIDADE - FLORESTA, BIODIVERSIDADE E DESENVOLVIMENTO RURAL DO CONCELHO DE LOULÉ 2020-2025 (que define uma estratégia ampla para o interior do território e que passa pela concretização de projetos estruturantes que permitam dar uma projeção temporal e mobiliza os atores do território para novos modelos de intervenção e valorização), a COMUNIDADE ENERGÉTICA ESCOLAR (projeto que visa a produção de energia renovável nas escolas do município, sobretudo para autoconsumo e incluindo uma componente pedagógica, que abrange atualmente 35 escolas do concelho e tendo uma potência instalada de cerca de 934 kWp, permitindo uma produção superior a 1530 MWh por ano e evitando a emissão anual de cerca de 390 t de CO2), o projeto de AUTOCONSUMO COLETIVO DE ALTE, o PROGRAMA DE APOIO AO DESENVOLVIMENTO SOCIAL DE LOULÉ (no âmbito do qual foram apoiadas cerca de 20 Instituições Particulares de Solidariedade Social (IPSS) na implementação de medidas de eficiência energética e na instalação de centrais solares fotovoltaicas, totalizando uma potência instalada de 340 kWp, e permitindo a produção renovável de 560 MWh por ano, reduzindo a fatura energética destas instalações com um carácter social ciclável, o município de Loulé tem apostado no desenvolvimento e implementação de projetos de requalificação urbana e remodelação do espaço público, integrando soluções de infraestrutura de rede ciclável, como pistas cicláveis, passeios partilhados, ciclovias uni e bidirecionais e parqueamento de bicicletas, que contribuem para a dinamização e promoção da utilização da bicicleta nas All eight CAP Priorities will deliver mitigation and adaptation outcomes, as well as significant co-benefits: https://www.bradford.gov.uk/media/bm3ps2mc/cbmdcclimateactionplan.pdf

1. In Travel & Transport, for example, improvements to public transport provision (for example, West Yorkshire's integrated transport network known as the Weaver Network), low emission vehicles and active travel infrastructure, along with mode shift behavioural initiatives and campaigns will improve air quality, reduce congestion and reduce noise pollution. 

This leads to better wellbeing, physical and mental health, and economic benefits. Less traffic and clean air supports social cohesion by freeing up public space and improves road safety. This encourages less tension, more physically active communities (for example, from the district's Low Traffic Neighbourhoods, Play Streets and School Streets) and fewer traffic related accidents. 

Improved access to employment opportunities from an affordable, inclusive and integrated transport network improves social mobility, economic inclusion and enhances mental health. A strong sense of citizenship, purpose and contribution to society results in wealthier and healthier neighbourhoods.

The remaining priority areas of the CAP have identified the following wider opportunities and co-benefits:

 2. Diversifying and localising greener and renewable energy sources such as Bradford's Low Carbon Hydrogen facility, Bradford Energy Network and Anaerobic Digestion-generated bio-gas will stimulate investment in infrastructure and technology, leading to job creation, new educational and upskilling opportunities. 
This will also enhance energy security and resilience for businesses, leading to lower operational costs throughout the supply chain and greater competitive advantage. 'Clean, green, ethical and innovative' businesses attract employees, investment and a loyal customer base.
As well as supporting circular economy principles, reducing emissions and minimising waste, digestate from Bradford's potential Anaerobic Digestion facility will improve soil health and reduce the need for nitrogen-based fertilisers and chemical pesticides across the district's growers and farming communities.

3. Through Industrial Decarbonisation and a shift towards a more sustainable and inclusive economy, businesses become more resilient, both operationally and economically. Bradford's decarbonisation partnership approach within the manufacturing sector (known as Bradford Manufacturing Futures Ltd) supports collaborative action, peer learning and knowledge exchange within industrial and geographical sectors. This leads to reduced operational costs, competitive advantage, and a future-proofed business.

4. Retrofit upgrade plans and schemes to tackle thermal inefficiency in Bradford's ageing housing stock will generate significant co-benefits, such as lower household energy bills which lead to reduced levels of fuel poverty and better indoor air quality. Houses will become more climate resilient from extreme weather patterns, leading to less mental and physical stress associated with draughty, cold and expensive to run houses. For example, in thermally comfortable homes, children's enhanced mental and physical health will result in enhanced educational attainment levels, leading to greater social and economic inclusion, and reduced health and social care costs. Additional co-benefits include upskilling, job creation and reduced pressure on the electricity grid.

 5. Community climate action in itself generates positive co-benefits. Communities that are empowered to drive forward projects that have been endorsed and supported by Bradford Council will reap the benefits of social cohesion and improved physical and mental wellbeing. Examples of inclusive community based climate action includes litter picking, tree planting, Clean Air Schools Programme, community gardens within faith or educational settings, nature friendly allotments etc. Activities with young people can lead to upskilling, green careers
citizenship roles, and social and economic resilience.

6. Land and nature-based climate action not only improves biodiversity, flood resilience, soil health and carbon capture, but also leads to improved mental and physical wellbeing through social cohesion, community engagement, job creation and improved access to nature. Examples include the city centre pedestrianisation improvements, Trees for Every Child scheme, designation of the Bradford Pennine Gateway National Nature Reserve and restoration of Ilkley Moor.

Through our ongoing collaborative work with key partners such as University of York - 'Made in Common', internationally recognised research programme, Born in Bradford, and Bradford's Health Determinants Research Collaborations (HDRC), we will be able to quantify and understand the impacts of climate change and climate action across all demographics. 

In collaboration with WYCA, a further event, 'Inclusive Retrofit: Sharing Solutions Workshop' will be hosted in Bradford in November 2025. Key stakeholders/actors will come together to discuss and quantify the challenges of retrofit across the housing sector. This will inform policy, priority action and service delivery for the West Yorkshire region.

Our detailed knowledge and experience of marginalised and vulnerable communities, particularly through the Clean Air Zone programme and air quality modelling, will enable us to leverage and use existing metrics and KPIs to measure future impacts and distribution of climate action. 

We will use existing KPIs from adopted Council strategies to measure progress. Additionally we will use government and publicly available datasets to measure climate action performance.

Examples include:
-Achievement of clean air targets across all parts of the district.
-WYCA's Transport Strategy, the emerging Local Transport Plan and Bradford's future Transport Strategy and mode shift targets, patronage data, trip data, target kms by mode etc.
-Socioeconomic data from the district's Growth & Economic Strategy will indicate shifts in fuel poverty and employment data. 
-Energy consumption data for both fossil fuels and renewables, including green hydrogen and biomethane. This will be measured for residential, commercial and industrial sectors. 
-Internal Council carbon accounting to reduce Scope 3 emissions as part of a sustainable procurement strategy to localise and decarbonise the supply chain.
-Tree and woodland cover as identified within the White Rose Forest strategy to meet target number of households living close to accessible woodland.
-Anaerobic Digestion processing rates.
-Recycling rates to be more in line with national average performance levels.
-Number of designated local nature reserves across the district.
-EPC data to ensure that a minimum of Band C is achieved for social housing.

Facilitating carbon literacy training for Elected Members. Officers and Area Coordinators ensure they are equipped with the skills and understanding of climate change to support their communities to be climate resilient. Climate change impacts differ significantly depending on level of social/economic deprivation, well-being, and geographical location so it is imperative that public facing officers and Councillors understand how to empower their communities around climate action. 

This ensures an inclusive approach to policy making. Examples include Allotment Policy, the Local Plan, Sustainable Food Strategy, Housing Strategy etc, along with strategic infrastructure projects such as Mass Transit and Southern Gateway and City Village which aim to provide accessible and affordable amenities such as sustainable transport, low carbon housing, green spaces and nature, education and employment opportunities.
 
The Council's inclusive, accessible and jargon-free public consultation process for new policies and strategies uses different communication platforms, channels and networks to ensure engagement with all communities within the district. This was adopted for the Climate Action Plan public consultation phase to include different participating groups at different venues and locations.

For example, to ensure inclusion within active travel policy, barriers across the different active travel modes need to be mapped out. This includes assessing pavement obstructions, widths, surfacing, segregated lanes, greenways, dropped curbs etc to enable car-free, seamless journeys for walking, wheeling and all forms of cycling (adapted bikes, cargo bikes etc). 

Through the equity principle, the CAP aims to ensure that all groups and people, especially those who have been historically or are currently 
marginalised or underrepresented, achieve parity in relevant policies, processes, and outcomes. Achieving equity does not always mean having equal access to something, but rather evaluating the needs of each group or person and providing the relevant tools and support that may be needed to ensure that the same outcomes can be achieved from these unequal starting points.

The Sixth Assessment Report by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) highlights the importance of equity and inclusion in climate action - “Actions that prioritise equity, climate justice, social justice and inclusion lead to more sustainable outcomes, co-benefits, reduce trade-offs, support transformative change and advance climate resilient development.” It is recognised that “Adaptation responses are immediately needed to reduce rising climate risks, especially for the most vulnerable. Equity, inclusion and just transitions are key to progress on adaptation and deeper societal ambitions for accelerated mitigation.”

Within transport, for example, we will work with Bradford's Active Travel Hubs to ensure that infrastructure improvements are not just focused on more affluent areas. Communities not currently part of typical cycling culture due to socioeconomic barriers such as culture or poor infrastructure, may require cycle training.

Bradford Council is part of WYCA's new Weaver Network for integrated transport across West Yorkshire, its new franchising model for buses and regional implementation of low-emission buses. These strategic actions will make public transport physically, practically and financially more accessible to everyone.

The outcomes of homes retrofit schemes, particularly those targeted at social housing and low-income households, will help residents achieve parity in terms of access to educational, social and economic opportunities. 

As a trusted source, ongoing educational campaigns will help to remove information barriers around climate action in homes, travel choices, green careers etc.

column16: There are a wide range of opportunities to take action on climate change, and these actions can deliver a range of wider benefits for local communities. Some of the key benefits of climate action include: Improved air quality, reduced energy bills, job creation, improved public health, increased resilience and improved quality of life. : Reducing greenhouse gas emissions can help to improve air quality, which can lead to a range of health benefits, such as reduced respiratory problems and improved heart health. This can in turn reduce health inequalities and lessen the demand on the NHS and social care. Reduced energy bills: Taking steps to make homes and businesses more energy efficient can help to reduce energy bills, which can save residents money and make businesses more competitive. Created jobs: Investing in renewable energy and other green technologies can create new jobs and boost the local economy. This has been showcased through Cornwall's Green Industrial Revolution which will provide opportunities for new jobs and skills with the development of Cornwall's Geo-thermal, floating off-shore wind and other renewable energy programmes. Recent examples of activity in Cornwall such as retrofitting homes have proven there are positive impacts on the extensive supply chains involving a large number of SME's, which make up the core of the local economy. Improved public health: Climate change is already having a negative impact on public health, and taking action to reduce emissions can help to protect people from the health risks associated with climate change, such as heat waves, air pollution, and flooding. Increased resilience: Climate change is making extreme weather events more common, and taking action to build resilience to these events can help to protect communities and property from damage. Improved quality of life: Taking action on climate change can help to improve the quality of life for local residents by making their communities more sustainable, healthier, and more resilient. In addition to these direct benefits, climate action can also help to build a more sustainable and equitable future for all. The benefits are identified and included within the use of the Cornwall Development and Decision Wheel at the planning stages of new projects as well as within our social value policies within Sustainable Procurement.

column19: We are working to become a carbon neutral council and combat climate change, making changes to how we work to reduce the greenhouse gases and carbon emissions that we produce. As a Council we also have a duty to ensure fair treatment and access to opportunities for all Cornwall's residents and are prioritising actions that we undertake to support those who need it most. Cornwall Council launched the Cornwall Development and Decision Wheel in 2021 to help us make decisions that, wherever possible, seek to combat climate change and do not disadvantage Cornwall's residents. Our decision wheel is based on Kate Raworth's Doughnut Economics model. The wheel helps to show us how decisions and projects will affect planet and people. If the wheel shows at an early stage that the decision/project will have a negative effect on planet or people, we can look at mitigations or how we might redesign it.\n \nThe wheel is used for the majority of decisions we make as a council. This ensures that we use the wheel to make decisions that place planet and people at the heart of everything we do. The decision wheel consists of an environmental and social wheel and an equality and inclusion wheel. The inner part of the environmental and social wheel focusses on social and economic issues for example prosperity and housing. The outer part of the wheel focusses on environmental issues for example greenhouse gas emissions and biodiversity. The equality and inclusion wheel focuses on protected characteristics and other important communities/areas. The decision wheel has introduced a new way of thinking for the Council. It is helping us to connect how we live, and how we can use money better for us and the environment. By looking at a set of completed wheels we can see how we are changing and improving the services we provide. Decision wheels are an important part of our journey to becoming a carbon neutral council and help officers consider whether more detailed carbon assessments are required.

En CORCLIMA, representando a la Municipalidad de Monteverde, la equidad y la inclusión son ejes fundamentales de la acción climática.
Para asegurarnos de que cada esfuerzo climático llegue de forma justa a distintos sectores de la comunidad, hemos integrado:
1. Hay una participación diversa en las distintas iniciativas o acciones que se planifican.
2. Distribución de los beneficios en los proyectos (Ruta Eléctrica Monteverde)
3. CORCLIMA elabora materiales divulgativos en lenguaje sencillo y realiza charlas abiertas a toda la comunidad, midiendo la asistencia y retroalimentación recibida.
4. Se cuantifica el alcance de publicaciones en redes sociales y la participación en espacios públicos, con el fin de verificar que la información no quede en grupos técnicos cerrados.
column19:
Ejemplos de proyectos:
Construcción de varios kilómetros de aceras en distintos barrios de la comunidad cada año para que toda la población pueda acceder a espacios seguros, fomentando la caminabilidad. 

En el desarrollo de talleres, charlas, consultas participativas, encuestas a la comunidad se toman en cuenta la totalidad de los sectores que representa la zona: mujeres, jóvenes, personas trabajadoras del turismo, personas con limitaciones en su movilidad, productores rurales, líderes comunales y población estudiantil, etc.

En la Ruta Eléctrica Monteverde, se cuantifica cuántos cargadores están en negocios pequeños y medianos, cuántos en espacios comunitarios y/o empresas privadas, para asegurar acceso equitativo de los visitantes en las distintas empresas locales.

column18: Quantification of co- benefits from climate emergency related activities is not easily monitored and it is exceptional that the authority would include detailed statements in decision making processes. The authority does however recognise that there are some general assumptions made for the health benefits of improved green space. Additionally, there are more detailed public health data sources which can be used to analyse and determine the outcomes of active travel. These examples of co- benefits, and many more, are well documented however the authority does not have the current capacity undertake comprehensive monitoring. The authority has started to map climate vulnerability in the borough and link it to potential health outcomes. This will help facilitate a just transition when considering climate action. The Net Zero Action Plan and Climate Adaptation Plans have both undergone equality impact assessments to ensure our climate action considers and includes all characteristics of people
column19: The authority is clear that fairness in the transition towards a low carbon future for our businesses and residents is paramount across the borough. The principles of a just and fair transition fall into two main themes: 1. those of adaptation to a future physical climate change with, for example an increase trends towards events of unprecedent weather extremes 2. the adaptation to a transformed economy where the demands for greener services and products will become the norm. In this is the fundamental aspects of skills and training towards that future. A holistic plan is required to ensure stakeholders of the borough are a core part of the process and not excluded from opportunities within the borough and also recognising there is a regional role to be undertaken - the newly elected mayor for North Tyneside sits on the cabinet for the North East Combined Authority and leads the portfolio for the Green Energy Revolution, overseeing Energy, Net Zero, and Environment and Coast. Transitioning towards a greener economy is something that is a coordinated and joint approach is required. This will be challenging in the context of a changing climate specifically in the areas of economic development where new technologies and the associated skills supersede the tried/tested, and existing status quo. Additionally, climate change impacts and adaptation actions will have unequal effects. For many climate impacts, it is the most vulnerable within our communities that will be most affected and have the least ability to adjust. The authority has started to map climate vulnerability in the borough and link it to potential health outcomes. This work has informed a JSNA for climate change (https://my.northtyneside.gov.uk/sites/default/files/web-page-related-files/JSNA%20Climate%20Change%20%28March%202025%29%20V2.pdf). Simple changes are also important, such as making our Net Zero Action Plan more accessible on the NTC website and ensuring it is written in plain and simple English. This will help facilitate a just transition when considering climate action.

The WMCA operates with the Inclusive Growth Framework as a core model for work in the region. This means that all projects, including climate action delivery, have inclusive growth principles embedded in the project from the beginning. As a result, climate action is developed with the following aspects as fundamentals and the equity and inclusion of these projects are measured against inclusive growth. The inclusive growth fundamentals include: climate and environment, inclusive economy, power and participation, affordable and safe spaces, connected communities, education and learning, health and wellbeing and equality.
As a result of this approach, climate action is focused on simultaneously delivering across these wider outcomes, ensuring equitable and inclusive distribution and accountability across these metrics. More about the inclusive growth work at the WMCA can be found here: https://www.wmca.org.uk/what-we-do/inclusive-growth/ 
Additionally, each major project in the WMCA is required to develop a Health and Equity Impact Assessment, ensuring that equalities and inclusivity are included in all climate actions. Furthermore, the Environment and Net Zero data dashboard (covered in more detail elsewhere) allows for spatial data to assess success of climate actions across the region, mapping against indices of multiple deprivation- for example community projects to improve green space are mapped, showing areas of further need . The Dashboard also includes a Climate Risk and Vulnerability map, which allows for projects to be focused on areas with the highest climate risks, as is being done in the WM-Adapt neighbourhood projects (more elsewhere).
column19:
A key principle of WM2041 and the 5YP is to ensure that we 'change our economy without leaving anyone behind' and 'decouple prosperity from the consumption of energy and resources'. Combined with working with the Inclusive Growth Framework as a core model for work in the region, this ensures that climate action is equitable and inclusive. 
Since 2022 the WMCA has also ran a 'Greener Together' Citizens Panel, to deliberate and provide actions for the WMCA to take on environment and energy. The panel has created participatory and deliberative processes to allow citizens to influence climate-related issues. With a representative selection of citizens from across the region (selected through a sortition process), the Citizens Panel ensures that climate action includes the perspectives of a broad range of people, helping to deliver equitable and inclusive action. 
An example of an action to ensure equitable and inclusive distribution of climate action is around the retrofit programme, which is now being funded through the 'Building Retrofit Pilot', with an integrated settlement from government allowing greater flexibility on how the money is spent. The retrofit programme is focusing on abating fuel poverty in all homes, in particular social housing. As a result, the programme is improving living standards and tackling fuel poverty for thousands of low-income private and social households, with up to 14,000 of the oldest and coldest homes in the region to be upgraded to make them warmer and cheaper to run.
In August 2025 the WMCA launched the Community Environment Network, building on four years of grant-funding for community groups to target environment interventions in some of the most deprived areas in the West Midlands; for example, Community Green Grants was awarded by a panel based on data and metrics related to deprivation and green space access, with grants largely going to more deprived communities with limited access to green space. The Network will grow a network of community-based organisations delivering projects involving the environment, providing support to a diverse range of communities to deliver climate action across the region. 
The WMCA is working with the University of Birmingham to deliver a UKRI-funded West Midlands-Adapt project which includes significant public engagement via the deployment of community researchers in the delivery of ward-level world cafes. World café workshops are designed to engage with representative groups of residents at the hyper-local, ward level to understand their lived experiences of severe weather. The location of these workshops are based on overall Climate Risk & Vulnerability Assessment (CRVA) scores. The WMCA's CRVA includes several socio-economic layers that indicate vulnerability to climate impacts. This is used to demonstrate with disproportionate impact of climate hazards on protected groups. The vulnerability factors include different types of deprivation, English as a second language and limited disposable income.

The City of Ligao formulated the Local Climate Change Action Plan (LCCAP) is designed to align with and further the development goals of Ligao City as outlined in the Comprehensive Land Use Plan (CLUP) and the Comprehensive Development Plan (CDP). The LCCAP aims to integrate climate change adaptation and mitigation into the broader development strategy of Ligao City, thereby ensuring that growth is sustainable, inclusive, and resilient. In particular, the Climate Change Council/LCCAP TWG aligns the plan's overall goal to the LGU's vision: 
“Ligao City: a Premier Government center for the Province of Albay, a vibrant hub for agriculture, trade, commerce, industry, technical-vocational education, and a tourism and pilgrimage destination where a morally upright and resilient people live in an eco-friendly, technologically-advanced, highly organized, clean and safe environment with a progressive economy and a responsive, innovative and accountable leadership”
The overarching development goal of Ligao City is to increase community and institutional resilience while preserving the environment, assuring economic growth, food security in the face of climate change challenges. 
In pursuit of this overall goal, Ligao City is committed to implementing sustainable and innovative initiatives that foster social inclusivity and enhance the overall well-being of its residents. The city aims to create a thriving and vibrant community that not only adapts to climate change but also actively contributes to mitigating its impact.
The objectives of the LCCAP are to provide actionable climate change adaptation and mitigation strategies that support the achievement of the city's development goals. These objectives are formulated to address the technical findings and implications identified for each affected barangay and decision area.

Peluang dan manfaat yang lebih luas dari tindakan iklim di bidang lingkungan, ekonomi, dan sosial antara lain:

Lingkungan
1. Mengurangi perubahan iklim: Mengurangi emisi gas rumah kaca dan memperlambat perubahan iklim.
2. Melestarikan keanekaragaman hayati: Melindungi ekosistem dan keanekaragaman hayati.
3. Meningkatkan kualitas udara dan air: Mengurangi polusi udara dan air, meningkatkan kesehatan masyarakat.

Ekonomi
1. Meningkatkan efisiensi energi: Mengurangi biaya energi dan meningkatkan efisiensi.
2. Menciptakan lapangan kerja baru: Industri hijau dan teknologi ramah lingkungan menciptakan lapangan kerja baru.
3. Meningkatkan pertumbuhan ekonomi: Tindakan iklim dapat meningkatkan pertumbuhan ekonomi dengan menciptakan peluang baru.

Sosial
1. Meningkatkan kesehatan masyarakat: Mengurangi polusi udara dan air, meningkatkan kesehatan masyarakat.
2. Meningkatkan kesadaran masyarakat: Meningkatkan kesadaran masyarakat tentang pentingnya lingkungan dan perubahan iklim.
3. Meningkatkan keadilan sosial: Tindakan iklim dapat membantu mengurangi kesenjangan sosial dan ekonomi.

Manfaat Lainnya
1. Meningkatkan ketahanan pangan: Tindakan iklim dapat membantu meningkatkan ketahanan pangan dan mengurangi kerentanan terhadap perubahan iklim.
2. Meningkatkan kualitas hidup: Tindakan iklim dapat membantu meningkatkan kualitas hidup masyarakat dengan menciptakan lingkungan yang lebih sehat dan berkelanjutan.
3. Meningkatkan reputasi dan citra: Perusahaan dan negara yang melakukan tindakan iklim dapat meningkatkan reputasi dan citra mereka.

Dengan demikian, tindakan iklim memiliki banyak peluang dan manfaat yang lebih luas di bidang lingkungan, ekonomi, dan sosial.

Pemerintah dapat mengukur distribusi tindakan iklim yang adil dan inklusif dengan beberapa cara:
- Mengintegrasikan strategi perkotaan dalam Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC): Pemerintah perlu memastikan bahwa NDC memprioritaskan kebutuhan masyarakat miskin perkotaan dan komunitas rentan dalam perencanaan iklim.
- Prioritas pada adaptasi dan keadilan iklim: Pemerintah harus memprioritaskan adaptasi dan keadilan iklim dalam kebijakan perubahan iklim, bukan hanya fokus pada mitigasi dan proyek investasi besar.
- Pengakuan atas solusi berbasis komunitas: Pemerintah perlu mendukung inovasi rendah karbon dan solusi komunitas yang hemat biaya sebagai strategi mitigasi dan adaptasi.
- Desentralisasi aksi iklim: Pemerintah harus memberikan dukungan keuangan dan teknis untuk meningkatkan kapasitas kota dalam aksi iklim yang terdesentralisasi.
- Pastikan akses pendanaan untuk komunitas lokal: Pemerintah perlu memberikan pendanaan langsung bagi inisiatif komunitas di kota untuk meningkatkan ketahanan terhadap iklim ekstrem.
- Dokumentasi kerugian dan kerusakan: Pemerintah harus mengalokasikan dana untuk 'loss and damage' bagi komunitas terdampak, memastikan dukungan langsung bagi masyarakat miskin yang terkena dampak bencana.

Dalam mengukur distribusi tindakan iklim yang adil dan inklusif, pemerintah juga perlu memantau dan mengevaluasi kebijakan perubahan iklim secara teratur untuk memastikan bahwa kebijakan tersebut efektif dan adil bagi semua lapisan masyarakat.

column19: 도봉구는 2021년 4월 22일, 가정에서부터 마을, 학교, 직장에 이르기까지 모든 생활에서 실천 의지를 반영한 「도봉구민 탄소중립 실천 헌장」를 제정하고, 이를 구민과 공유하고 실천 의지를 다짐하는 '2050 탄소중립 실천 범구민 결의대회'를 온·오프라인으로 개최하였다. 또한, 누구나 생활 속에서 쉽게 실천할 수 있는 사항들과 관련 정보를 '녹색' △건물 △수송 △에너지 △순환 △숲 △생활 △교육 등 7대 전략별로 수록한 매뉴얼인 『도봉구민 탄소중립 실천 요령』(부제: Green Life, 내가 그린 Green Dobong!)를 제작하고, 지역사회의 통·반장, 각급 학교, 위원회, 신규 전입 세대 등에 배포하여 탄소중립 실천을 지원하고 있다. 아울러, '내가 실천하는 10대 온실가스 줄이기' 방안(▲친환경보일러를 설치하고 냉·난방 온도 준수하기(여름 26℃ 이상, 겨울 20℃ 이하), ▲친환경 운전하고 자가용 대신 1주일에 한 번 대중교통 이용하기, ▲우리 집에 미니태양광 설치하기, ▲먹을 만큼만 밥하기(전기밥솥 보온시간 3시간 줄이기), ▲에너지효율이 높은 TV, 전기밥솥 사용하기, ▲1회용 비닐봉투 대신 장바구니 사용하기, ▲음식물 쓰레기 20% 줄이기, ▲사용하지 않는 TV, 세탁기, 전기밥솥, 전자레인지, 가습기의 플러그 뽑기, ▲재활용이 가능한 유리병, 캔 등 분리배출하기, ▲에코마일리지 가입하고 친환경상품 사용하기) 중 2가지 이상을 선택하여 실천을 약속하는 '도봉구민 온실가스 1인 4톤 줄이기 실천 약속 캠페인'을 2021년 4월 론칭하여 지역사회에 실천문화를 확산시키고 있으며, 2024년말까지 주민40,879명이 참여하여 연간 온실가스 41,912톤 감축을 약속하였다. 또한, 도봉구는 스스로 생활 속 탄소중립을 실천하고, 가족·친구·이웃 10명에게 실천운동을 전파하는 탄소중립 촉진자인 '도봉구 제로씨(Zero-C)'를 2050년까지 3만 명을 양성하는 것을 목표로 하고 있다. 2024년 말 현재 3,777명의 도봉구 제로씨가 양성․배출되어 도봉구 곳곳에서 구민의 탄소중립 실천을 촉진하는 데 기여하고 있다. '도봉구 제로씨(Zero-C)' 양성교육은 2023년 12월 외부 전문기관의 용역을 통해 교육프로그램을 리뉴얼하고, 환경부에 우수 환경교육프로그램으로 지정 받았다 또한, 도봉구는 일상생활 속에서 탄소중립 실천을 강력히 유인하고 촉진할 수 있는 체감형 도구가 필요하다고 판단하고, 약 1년8개월의 준비과정과 구 예산 1억 7천만원을 투자하여 창의적이고 독창적인 도봉형 기후행동보상제도인 '탄소공(Zero)감(減)마일리지를 2023년 4월부터 시행하고 있다. 탄소공감마일리지는 웹 접속이나 앱 설치 후 인증 절차를 진행하면 누구나 이용이 가능하며, 마일리지 적립과 사용은 정회원인 도봉구민과 도봉구 생활권자만 가능하다. 현재 실천 항목은 총 47개 항목을 기본으로 하고, 필요에 따라 새로운 탄소중립 정책을 즉시 반영할 수 있도록 확장이 가능하다. 1마일리지는 1원에 상당 하며, 실천 항목의 난이도, 참여 주기, 자부담 등을 고려하여 차등 적립되고 1인당 연간 최대 8만 마일리지까지 적립이 가능하다. 마일리지 사용은 지역경제 활성화를 위해 도봉사랑상품권으로 교환 사용하고, 이에 필요한 재원은 공공 태양광 발전사업으로 조성한 도봉구 기후대응기금을 활용하고 있다. 탄소공감마일리지는 2024년 말 현재 회원수 10,166명, 참여회수 1,762,983회, 온실가스 감축 3,213톤, 12,195만 마일리지를 적립하고 있다.

column19:
Mitigation refers to activities that reduce greenhouse gas emissions and protect, enhance, or restore carbon sinks. In other words, mitigation actions aim to slow down climate change by reducing the amount of greenhouse gases released into the atmosphere.

Adaptation, on the other hand, involves adjusting to actual or expected climate change and its effects. It includes actions to prevent or minimize potential damage, as well as taking advantage of opportunities that may arise.

The mitigation and adaptation goals are listed below in five categories:

I. Buildings, Stationary Energy Consumption and Energy Production Sectors and Horizontal Issues

Strategic Goals
Ensuring energy efficiency in buildings and promoting the use of renewable energy
Implementing emission-reducing measures in new urban development
Increasing capacity for energy efficiency and greenhouse gas reduction
Investing in energy-efficient green infrastructure systems
II. Transportation Sector

Strategic Goals
Encouraging the use of public transportation and reducing energy consumption and emissions from transportation
Promoting the use of alternative fuels in public transportation systems
Increasing the number of safe pedestrian areas and promoting the use of bicycles and other non-motorized vehicles
Supporting the transition to zero-emission vehicles in traffic and increasing traffic efficiency
III. Industry Sector

Strategic Goals
Improving processes through resource efficiency applications in industry
IV. Water, Wastewater, Land Management, Biodiversity and Disaster Management

Strategic Goals
Promoting the reduction of water use, on-site reuse, and recycling of water
Protecting water resources
Strengthening the stormwater network
Transitioning to renewable energy in wastewater treatment
Ensuring water efficiency in agriculture
V. Waste Sector and Human Health

Strategic Goals
Effective implementation of the zero waste system
Making the collection and transportation of household waste energy efficient
VI. Agriculture and Livestock Sector

Strategic Goals
Improving agricultural, livestock, and forestry processes

PKC's climate action plan outlines a number of actions that co-benefit environmental, social and economic benefits.

Opportunities and co-benefits have been developed have been identified for every theme of our climate action plans.

Nature and land use: Afforestation and Peatland restoration for example, can provide multiple benefits to biodiversity, flood mitigation and carbon savings. Certain areas across Perth and Kinross have an increased flooding risk which can be mitigated by peatland restoration. This will have a direct economic impact on communities that are economically impacted by floods over the years. In addition, actions to create a resilient Perth and Kinross will have many benefits like reduced risk of disruption to infrastructure, improved economic and social resilience, healthier ecosystems, and improved water quality. 

Energy: The Council published its Local Heat and Energy Efficiency Strategy that focuses on the decarbonisation of Perth and Kinross's building stock. The strategy had two main drivers of addressing climate change and reducing fuel poverty and identified priority zones for action areas which would make positive contributions to both objectives. It also recognised the wider health and wellbeing benefit to residents and the economic opportunity to the area this transformation to the housing stock could bring. 

Transport: the Council's Mobility strategy (approved Oct 2024) recognises several co-benefits including addressing fuel poverty, air quality, health and well being and road safety. 

Business and Circular Economy: The Council recognises the huge potential value of green growth to the Perth and Kinross economy and opportunity this brings. Circular economy can also help residents and businesses address cost of living pressures (e.g. tool libraries, food share schemes, etc).

column18: A Climate Change Risk and Opportunity Assessment (CCROA) was undertaken to identify risks and opportunities across Perth and Kinross. Once all risks were identified, a high-level assessment of the potential risks, their impacts, the likelihood of the risks occurring, and the response needed by the council was undertaken. The impacts include: financial impact, social impact, health impact and environmental impact. The outcomes of the assessment have been reflected in the Council's updated Climate Action Plan and include measures to ensure equitable and inclusive distribution of climate action, taking into consideration vulnerable communities. The Action Plan is reviewed annually, taking into account the CCROA's findings (the CCROA will be reviewed every 5 years in accordance with Scotland's National Adaptation Plan). Additionally, Tackling Climate Change is one of the top priorities within the Council's Corporate Plan alongside tackling poverty and protecting vulnerable communities. The Climate Action Plan is therefore interlinked and contributes to the Corporate Plan's objectives in relation to making Perth and Kinross a sustainable and equal place for our communities.\n\nThe Council has developed an Impact and Value Assessment (IVA) tool that has been designed to screen every Council project, strategy or proposal against statutory and non-statutory environmental, social and economic requirements. The questionnaire has been designed to give a robust screening of proposals, with sections covering strategic and resource implications, and impact assessment for Climate change, Equality & Fairness, Child Rights & Wellbeing, Sustainable Procurement & Supply, and Strategic Environmental Assessment. Once the IVA form is submitted, documents are automatically emailed based on answers given in relation to: Strategic and Resource Implications, and Impact Assessments.
column19: Ensuring climate action is fair and benefits all is one of the key principles of the Climate Change Strategy. In order to ensure inclusive/equitable climate action, Perth & Kinross Council has committed to develop and deliver an annual climate change engagement plan for residents and a wide range of stakeholders across Perth and Kinross. A Climate Change Commission has now been developed which and acts as an independent active leadership and support network for cross-sector collaboration and action on climate change. The Commission members come from a variety of backgrounds from across Perth and Kinross and are experts in various sectors. This allows them to engage and inspire collective ownership and a shared commitment to reaching net zero. The Commission also plays a vital role in promoting a climate resilient future which is also fair and ensures that no one is left behind during the transition to a more sustainable future. A Climate Change Working Group was formed by our Community Planning Partnership (CPP) Board in February 2022. The CPP partners include a range of public and other agencies mandated to ensure a real and sustainable reduction in inequalities is achieved and that communities are central to the process. The CPP's latest Local Outcome Improvement Plan identified Climate Change as a golden thread and the action plan was reviewed through a climate change lens. The Council works with external partners to ensure a fair and equal transition to net zero such as providing funding to two organisations to deliver free energy advice services across Perth and Kinross. The scope of this funding is to reduce the number of households living in fuel poverty in the local authority area while also reducing emissions by providing energy efficiency advice and promoting the use of renewable energy measures.

Nowon-gu is promoting various initiatives to ensure a just transition toward carbon neutrality while simultaneously generating socio-economic co-benefits.

(Expanding Climate Accessibility and Collecting Citizen Feedback)
Nowon-gu is prioritizing housing improvement projects for climate-vulnerable groups and plans to publish and distribute the “Nowon-gu Carbon Neutrality Brief” ten times (with one issue completed and the second in preparation), which provides local greenhouse gas emission statistics. In addition, the district has published and distributed the “Nowon-gu Carbon Neutrality Citizen Guidebook”—a citizen-friendly version of the legally mandated Carbon Neutrality Basic Plan—to enhance public access to climate-related information and enable residents to understand and monitor Nowon-gu's mitigation policies. Furthermore, public forums are being operated to ensure that residents' opinions are reflected in the policy-making process.

(Just transition)
The district plans to transform traditional automobile repair streets into EV-centered cultural streets, while also providing training programs to help workers acquire the necessary skills to shift toward low-carbon industries.

(Carbon-neutral job creation)
Nowon-gu plans to identify and support social enterprises that promote the use of reusable containers to create jobs, and to establish an electric vehicle-specialized street to provide a foundation for young people to start businesses in green industries.

(Support for energy-vulnerable households)
Support programs include energy vouchers, residential energy efficiency renovation project, replacement of conventional boilers with eco-friendly models, and LED lighting retrofits. These initiatives aim to improve quality of life while simultaneously advancing carbon neutrality.

(Promotion of eco-friendly mobility)
Nowon-gu is expanding electric vehicle (EV) charging infrastructure and fostering a bicycle-friendly city, with the expectation of achieving greenhouse gas (GHG) reductions in the transport sector.

1. Nowon-gu adopted the “Basic Plan for Carbon Neutrality and Green Growth” in 2025 to strengthen implementation of GHG reduction policies and ensure policy sustainability. A clear division of responsibilities among implementing bodies and an integrated management system have been established.

Monitoring & Evaluation: Implementation is assessed through a self-evaluation system, in line with the Ministry of Environment's “Guidelines for the Establishment and Monitoring of Local Government Basic Plans on Carbon Neutrality and Green Growth” (May 2023). The process consists of four stages: planning, monitoring, reporting, and reflection of improvement measures. Results are reported to the district council by the end of December each year, pursuant to Article 78 of the Enforcement Decree of the Framework Act on Carbon Neutrality and Green Growth.

Indicators:

- Quantitative projects are evaluated through transparent calculations of GHG reductions, achievement rates against reduction targets, and budget execution rates.

- Qualitative projects, which are expected to contribute to GHG reductions but are difficult to quantify, are evaluated using implementation records, budget execution rates, and descriptions of measurable social impacts.

Continuous Improvement: Identified shortcomings and areas for improvement are addressed through corrective action plans, which are incorporated into the final evaluation report and reflected in subsequent year projects.

2. Nowon-gu has established the Climate Change Adaptation Plan (2021-2025) to address risks and vulnerabilities caused by climate change, while contributing to the improvement of adaptive capacity and resilience. and has introduced an evaluation framework to enhance the effectiveness of implementation.

Monitoring & Evaluation: Annual self-evaluations are conducted through a four-step process: establishing an evaluation plan, conducting interim reviews, assessing projects and preparing results, and reflecting findings for improvement.

Indicators: Evaluation criteria include alignment with adaptation objectives, scientific basis, overlap with similar measures, potential for scaling-up, implementation completeness, and efforts in coordination and outreach.

- Quantitative indicators measure achievement rates against targets and budget execution levels.

- Qualitative indicators assess effort levels relative to targets and budget execution.

Continuous Improvement: Corrective action plans are developed for underperforming or problematic areas identified in self-evaluations and are integrated into subsequent year projects.

1. Energy-vulnerable household housing improvement
Nowon-gu plans to implement various programs to reduce the energy burden and improve the living environment of climate-vulnerable groups. Measures include providing energy vouchers to low-income households, supporting energy-efficiency retrofitting for semi-basement and aging homes, replacing outdated boilers with eco-friendly models, and installing LED lighting free of charge for vulnerable households. In addition, the “Safe Home Repair Project” and the “Hope Home Repair Project” will be carried out to enhance housing safety, improve insulation, windows, and waterproofing, and strengthen resilience against climate-related disasters such as flooding and heat waves.

2. Strengthening access to education and information
Nowon-gu has published the Nowon-gu Carbon Neutrality Citizen Guidebook to ensure that residents have easy access to information on carbon neutrality policies, and will continue to regularly distribute the Nowon-gu Carbon Neutrality Brief to share local greenhouse gas emissions data. Furthermore, public forums are being operated to ensure that citizens' opinions are reflected in the policy-making process.

3. Support for job creation and industrial transition
Nowon-gu plans to provide training and education programs for workers in vulnerable sectors such as internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicle repair, and to transform traditional auto repair streets into EV-specialized districts to create new job opportunities for youth and small business owners. At the same time, the district will identify and support social enterprises that promote the use of reusable containers and resource circulation, thereby creating green jobs.

4. Health and livelihood support
To protect vulnerable groups during heat waves, Nowon-gu is operating cooling shelters and installing “Healing Fridges” in parks and walking trails to provide free drinking water. In addition, the district is operating an air quality alert system to deliver timely health information to sensitive groups, including children and the elderly, helping them respond appropriately to air pollution events.

Tepebaşı Municipality quantifies the equitable and inclusive distribution of climate action through a set of measurable indicators embedded in its Sustainable Energy and Climate Action Plan (SECAP) monitoring framework. These indicators are designed to capture both the environmental impact of actions and the fairness of their distribution across demographic and geographic groups. 

Participation rates in climate education programmes, such as zero waste trainings, compost workshops, and children's environmental assemblies, are disaggregated by age, gender, and neighbourhood to assess inclusivity. 
In sustainable mobility initiatives, metrics such as the length of pedestrian and cycling routes accessible within a 10-minute walk from residential areas are used to measure equitable access. 

For nature-based solutions, the number and area of new parks or rehabilitated green spaces are mapped and cross-referenced with socio-economic data to confirm that underserved districts benefit proportionately. 

These quantitative assessments are complemented by qualitative feedback collected through public consultations, workshops, and surveys, which provide insight into whether climate actions are perceived as accessible, relevant, and beneficial by all community segments. 

Furthermore, Tepebaşı Municipality aligns its efforts with national social inclusion policies and international frameworks by embedding principles of climate justice and inclusive governance into climate action strategies. As part of ongoing efforts, the municipality continues to explore data-driven approaches for evaluating how benefits are distributed and how the most climate-vulnerable groups are supported.

The results of these evaluations are publicly reported in the Annual Activity Report, allowing for transparency and continuous adjustment of strategies to maximise both equity and climate impact.
column19: As stated in the Tepebaşı Municipality 2024 Annual Activity Report, the municipality implements a comprehensive and multi-dimensional climate action programme designed to ensure that the social, economic, and environmental benefits of sustainability measures are distributed equitably and inclusively. This approach is firmly embedded in the Municipality's strategic vision as a signatory of the Covenant of Mayors and an active ICLEI member, and is reflected comprehensively in the Sustainable Energy and Climate Action Plan (SECAP), which is based on detailed risk and vulnerability assessments covering health, housing, water, agriculture, and transport sectors, developed through participatory workshops, stakeholder engagement sessions, and the use of disaggregated spatial data to identify priority intervention areas. In line with the principle of equity and inclusion, green spaces and parks have been created in locations with limited access to greenery and where vulnerable populations reside, with 8 new parks (totaling 19,201 m²) built and 16 parks (totaling 40,653 m²) renovated in 2024, along with upgraded irrigation and lighting systems; over 80,000 seedlings have been produced in municipal nurseries and distributed to hobby gardens, enabling 374 citizens to engage in nature-focused volunteer activities. Climate awareness and education activities have been carried out extensively, with five Children's Environmental Assembly meetings, 36 zero waste trainings, 12 compost trainings, and 60 climate change awareness activities, complemented by applied workshops such as the “Paper Recycling Cenrter (formerly Su Kurusu Application Centre),” which repurposed waste paper into 14,643 handmade sheets reused by the municipality; these efforts also included international collaboration with the Berlin Treptow-Köpenick Municipality. The municipality has supported local and sustainable agriculture through women's producer markets, strengthening both environmental and socio-economic resilience. Post-implementation monitoring integrates equality indicators—such as per capita green space access, renewable energy capacity distribution, energy savings in social facilities, and the coverage of education programmes—into the evaluation framework, ensuring transparent assessment of whether benefits are shared equitably across demographic and geographic segments. These environmental and climate actions are reinforced by an inclusivity-focused institutional culture supported through partnerships with local NGOs, professional chambers, and academic institutions, ensuring that climate-related facilities and services—from children's ecology and art centres to community houses and senior cafés—are accessible in multiple neighbourhoods, including peripheral and disadvantaged areas, rather than being concentrated in central or affluent districts. By aligning municipal climate strategies with both national social inclusion policies and international sustainability frameworks, Tepebaşı Municipality ensures that its environmental initiatives—whether in renewable energy, green space provision, sustainable mobility, waste management, or climate education—not only contribute to emission reduction and resilience building, but also actively reduce inequality, strengthen social cohesion, and engage residents in the green transition while ensuring they benefit from it.

column19: Whitby's CERP Phase 1: Resilience integrated an engagement process that involved the public in decision-making aspects and used input from key internal and external interested or affected groups. Engagement was guided by the project engagement plan, which aimed to ensure that interested and affected groups were given opportunities to inform and provide feedback to create the best possible Whitby CERP and support its implementation. CERP included the use of surveys and ISeeChange (ISC), an online climate engagement platform that enables community members to share their experiences of climate and social vulnerability through photos and narratives. Results obtained through engagement with community members suggested that engagement support should be expanded to improve engagement outcomes, particularly for equity- denied groups in the Town. It was recommended to integrate equity throughout the plan and work alongside vulnerable communities (i.e. integrate equity into implementation of climate actions to ensure that inequity is not further exacerbated by climate change). Integrating equity into the implementation of climate actions is essential to ensure that equity-denied and vulnerable communities are not left out. Also, working closely with various vulnerable groups at every stage is key to enhancing understanding of how community residents use or access community services, particularly during an emergency. La Municipalidad de Cerro Navia ha identificado varias oportunidades y beneficios significativos asociados a generar acciones ante el cambio climático, asociado a las dimensiones ambientales, sociales y económicas:
Beneficios ambientales:
Reducción de emisiones de gases de efecto invernadero (GEI) mediante proyectos de eficiencia energética, reconversión de luminarias a LED y promoción de energías renovables en equipamientos comunitarios.
Fortalecimiento de la biodiversidad y mejora de los servicios ecosistémicos a través de la creación de corredores verdes, arborización urbana y recuperación de suelos degradados.
Mitigación de islas de calor y mejora de la calidad del aire mediante la expansión de áreas y la infraestructura verdes en espacios públicos.
Beneficios sociales:
Incremento de la resiliencia climática, de los vecinos(as), especialmente a los grupos más vulnerables como adultos mayores, niños y familias de bajos ingresos, frente a eventos extremos como olas de calor, inundaciones o sequías.
Fortalecimiento del desarrollo humano y la participación ciudadana mediante educación ambiental en escuelas, programas de sensibilización comunitaria y participación ciudadana en la planificación climática.
Creación de refugios climáticos y espacios comunitarios seguros que contribuyen a la protección de la salud y bienestar de la población.
Beneficios económicos:
Reducción de costos operativos a largo plazo mediante eficiencia energética en edificios y equipamientos municipales.
Generación de oportunidades de empleo verde, vinculadas a la instalación de energías renovables, arborización, infraestructura verde y mantenimiento de sumideros de carbono.
Potencial para atraer financiamiento externo y fondos estatales, al alinearse con estrategias nacionales de carbono neutralidad y planes de acción climática (PACCC, Estrategia Energética Local).

La Municipalidad de Cerro Navia cuantifica la distribución equitativa e inclusiva de la acción climática a través de un enfoque combinado de datos cuantitativos y participación comunitaria.
Se hace uso de datos censales y diagnósticos territoriales: se utilizan estadísticas sociodemográficas (Censo, catastros municipales y levantamientos de infraestructura crítica) para identificar las necesidades territoriales y focalizar las acciones en sectores con mayor vulnerabilidad climática y social.
En este sentido, la planificación se hace basándose en las necesidades locales: tanto el Plan de Acción Comunal de Cambio Climático (PACCC) como la Estrategia Energética Local (EEL) incorporan la información levantada con los vecinos a partir de cartografías participativas, talleres de participación, entre otros, lo que permite diseñar medidas cuantificadas en función de las brechas detectadas (ejemplo: déficit de áreas verdes, infraestructura escolar sustentable, acceso a energías renovables).
Es de ello que, dentro de las medidas, se consideran indicadores de equidad e inclusividad en su implementación. En ejemplo, una vez que se empiecen a implementar las medidas se generaran insumos tales como: N° de refugios climáticos instalados en zonas críticas por islas de calor, priorizando áreas con mayor vulnerabilidad, % de escuelas con mejoras de infraestructura sustentable, (Ha) de áreas verdes creadas o rehabilitadas, Participación ciudadana en talleres y consultas comunitarias, como indicador de inclusión social, entre otros.
Otros compromisos apuestan a robustecer la cuantificación mediante metas verificables como implementar ERNC en un 30% de los hogares vulnerables al 2028, la creación de una red de cuidados climáticos para adultos mayores y el aislamiento térmico de viviendas sociales en barrios vulnerables, entre otros.
En síntesis, aunque la cuantificación de la equidad aún es incipiente, Cerro Navia ya combina análisis de vulnerabilidad, indicadores de cobertura, participación comunitaria y planificación estratégica, avanzando hacia un modelo de gestión climática progresivamente más sistemático, medible e inclusivo.
column19:
Dentro de las acciones específicas que se han realizado para garantizar la distribución equitativa e inclusiva de los recursos para la acción climática, se encuentran:
Plan de Acción Comunal de Cambio Climático (PACCC): incorpora criterios de vulnerabilidad territorial y social, priorizando a comunidades más expuestas a olas de calor, inundaciones y déficit de áreas verdes.
Estrategia Energética Local (EEL): establece metas concretas como facilitar el acceso a energías renovables no convencionales (ERNC, con énfasis en barrios de mayor precariedad energética.
Refugios climáticos y áreas verdes: se busca priorizar zonas críticas por islas de calor donde se proyecta instalar refugios climáticos y aumentar áreas verdes, asegurando que los beneficios lleguen a los sectores con menor acceso a espacios públicos y mayor densidad poblacional.
Participación ciudadana: a través de talleres comunitarios y cartografías participativas, los vecinos han definido prioridades locales, lo que asegura que las medidas respondan a las necesidades reales de los grupos más afectados.
Programas de inclusión social: se encuentran en desarrollo iniciativas como la red de cuidados climáticos para adultos mayores, el aislamiento térmico de viviendas sociales y la incorporación de infraestructura sustentable en escuelas, todas orientadas a reducir brechas de vulnerabilidad.
Monitoreo de indicadores de equidad: se proyecta registrar métricas como número de refugios climáticos instalados, % de escuelas con mejoras sustentables, hectáreas de áreas verdes creadas o rehabilitadas y participación comunitaria efectiva, entre otros que funcionarán como evidencia del avance en equidad.

column19: A large proportion of our spending on decarbonising the built environment is targeted towards households more likely to be on lower incomes and vulnerable to climate risks. This includes council housing tenants; 85% of all residents in receipt of housing benefit in Hammersmith & Fulham live in the social rented sector, and the three Lower Super Output Areas with the lowest average incomes are on the council's Edward Woods, White City and Clem Attlee estates. 106m, the majority of the council's budget committed to climate action, is assigned to making council housing energy efficient. This scheme has been superseded by H&F Healthy Homes, a dedicated fuel poverty service offering free support to help residents save money on energy bills and keep their homes warm, including energy saving advice and information, free home visits and assessments, and help accessing financial support for home improvements, such as assistance with completing grant applications.\n\nBeyond financial relief, H&F Healthy Homes aims to deliver long-term health and wellbeing benefits. By improving energy efficiency and effective heating/cooling, the service helps reduce the risk of preventative health related illnesses, damp and mould -conditions that disproportionately affect energy inefficient homes. Ultimately, the programme seeks to create healthier, more comfortable living environments whilst reducing energy bills.

The Electric Mobility Strategy notes the benefits of shifting from internal combustion engine vehicles towards EVs is a complementary priority in order to reduce emissions and achieve the identified carbon reduction targets. The Integrated Mobility Plan recognizes the benefits of shifting the focus to planning for sustainable transportation options (i.e. active transportation and transit) instead of a car centric city - economically responsible by refraining from expanding road right-of-ways to increase capacity, saving costs; improving safety and equity for all residents; and improving air quality and reduction of greenhouse gas emissions. The feasibility study completed for the City's home energy efficiency program, Better Homes Burlington, recognized that supporting homeowners improve energy efficiency can in particular assist those homeowners facing energy poverty by reducing energy costs. Lastly, the work completed for the City's climate adaptation plan, Climate Resilient Burlington, will help ensure climate resiliency and reduce risk and vulnerability to residents and businesses to prepare for flooding, improve biodiversity, ensure an effective economy, and reducing the urban heat island, among other co-benefits.

column18: This is an area of continuous improvement. The Burlington Climate Plan going to Council in October 2025 includes a section on climate equity, to recognize that while every resident of Burlington will be impacted by climate change, not every resident will be impacted equally. This updated plan contains several action items that include an equity lens. A risk and vulnerability assessment was completed to support the development and implementation of Climate Resilient Burlington, helping to identify vulnerable communities within the City. Vulnerable populations can have higher risks associated with the increasing risks of a changing climate (ie. heat alerts and flooding events). The City along with Halton Region has initiatives to assist property owners to improve flood resilience as well as ensure we have park amenities to assist with cooling during heat events, such as spray pads and water features, as well as cooling centres currently identified as our public libraries. An emerging area that the City will be monitoring is indoor temperatures during warmer weather. In Ontario, there is legislation to ensure heat is provided in rental accommodation during colder temperatures but there is no corresponding legislation to ensure moderating warmer summer temperatures. With respect to mitigation of greenhouse gas emissions, consideration will also be given to assisting low-income households with improving energy efficiency of their dwelling and reducing their carbon footprint. Some programs already exist in Ontario to provide assistance, but the City will be working with partners to consider how we can amplify and support these programs.
column19: American Forest's Tree Equity Score methodology was used to explore tree equity in Burlington as part of the Urban Forest Master Plan project which was approved by City Council in 2024. This created a priority index where highest priority areas have a greater proportion of populations that are vulnerable to heat and higher surface temperatures indicating a higher need for the cooling benefits of tree canopy. Areas with a high priority index, combined with areas of low tree canopy, were used to create a Tree Equity Score to inform the Master Plan update. The tree equity mapping offers insights into the relationship between canopy distribution and social need. Urban forest equity is one of the topics covered on the story map about the City of Burlington Urban Forest Master Plan (https://storymaps.arcgis.com/stories/41c887d86e6643c689b449a0b7a571cb) and in the State of the Urban Forest Report (August 2022) and is available from the Urban Forest Master Plan project page at getinvolvedburlington.ca/ufmp. The City also offers tree giveaways twice a year, and a Street-Side Tree Planting Program in an effort to bring more trees to neighbourhoods. Residents can call the City and note their interest in the program. A member of the City's forestry team will assess the site and if criteria is met (space, proximity to road, etc.), then scheduling will be determined. After the 2024 flood, the City provided a $1000 grant was offered to residents impacted by the flood to help with insurance deductibles, etc. if they were not eligible to receive the $1000 grant from Halton Region (only covers sewer backup). Sakarya Metropolitan Municipality takes a holistic approach to combating and adapting to climate change, not only with the goal of carbon reduction but also through environmental sustainability, social welfare, and economic development opportunities. In this context, in 2018, it became a party to the European Union's Covenant of Mayors, committing to more systematic and transparent planning of climate action at the local level. In line with this commitment, the city's Sustainable Energy and Climate Action Plan (SECAP) and Climate Change Adaptation Action Plan constitute the municipality's long-term strategic roadmaps.

Environmental Opportunities:

Climate action aims to achieve environmental benefits such as protecting natural resources, improving water and air quality, and sustainable management of biodiversity. Reducing waste, expanding recycling, and closing the raw material cycle within the scope of Zero Waste Management contribute to both reducing carbon emissions and alleviating pressure on nature. Green infrastructure investments offer multifaceted benefits, such as reducing the urban heat island effect, increasing carbon sinks, and managing rainwater. Ecological corridors within the city, the protection of natural habitats, and the creation of climate-resilient green spaces support the vitality of urban nature.

Social Opportunities:

The social dimension of climate action becomes evident in the protection of vulnerable groups, climate justice, improving quality of life, and public awareness. Creating a disaster-resilient city will ensure that low-income groups and the elderly, in particular, are less affected by climate-related risks. Energy efficiency projects aimed at reducing energy poverty reduce energy costs in disadvantaged households and support social equality. Education programs, climate awareness programs in schools, and public awareness activities encourage individuals to develop sustainable lifestyles.

Furthermore, nature-compatible transportation systems and the expansion of walkable and bicycle-accessible living spaces offer opportunities to improve public health by supporting active living. Increasing urban aesthetics and comfort also contribute to strengthening the connection people form with the city.

Economic Opportunities:

Climate action serves as a lever for Sakarya's sustainable economic transformation. In line with the principle of green growth, businesses based on environmentally friendly technologies are developing; The potential of renewable energy sources like solar and biomass attracts new investments. Projects such as the renovation of public buildings for energy efficiency and the conversion of street lighting to LEDs provide long-term financial savings. Circular economy practices such as waste-derived fuel (RDF), composting, and energy recovery make it possible to use municipal resources more efficiently.

Furthermore, the transition to green building and green transportation standards creates jobs and encourages local entrepreneurship. Digital monitoring systems and data-based decision-making infrastructures aimed at reducing carbon footprints increase the efficiency of urban services and add value to administrative capacity. Support for projects developed in this context in Sakarya with numerous national and international funding and grant sources directly contributes to the local economy.

Conclusion:

Sakarya Metropolitan Municipality considers climate action not only an environmental responsibility but also a tool for sustainable development. The impacts of climate change are taken into account in urban planning processes, and these opportunities are evaluated with a multi-stakeholder approach across a wide range of areas, from infrastructure investments and social policy to economic strategies and disaster management. Thus, environmental resilience, social inclusiveness and economic dynamism are sought to be achieved together through climate action.

Sakarya Metropolitan Municipality (SBB) plans and implements climate action with an approach that is equitable, inclusive, and considers the needs of vulnerable groups. To this end, data-based analyses and monitoring studies are conducted to identify the groups most affected by climate change and ensure the socially equitable distribution of climate action.

In this context, SBB prepared a district-level Vulnerability and Risk Analysis Report for Sakarya province. This analysis assessed numerous parameters, including socioeconomic indicators, disaster risk, elderly population density, the presence of migrants, and access to infrastructure services, to determine each district's vulnerability to climate change. This study identified the districts to be prioritized in climate action planning and contributed to the direction of public investments in line with the principle of social justice.

SBB's climate strategies are being shaped within the framework of the Climate Change Adaptation Strategy Document, developed in accordance with this analysis.

Sakarya Metropolitan Municipality implements the following methods to monitor and evaluate the impact of climate action on social equity and inclusion:

District-level spatial monitoring: This analyzes the districts where climate projects and investments are concentrated and whether they align with districts where vulnerable groups live.

Integration of socio-demographic data: Vulnerability indicators such as age, income, disability, and immigration are assessed in project areas.

Participatory processes: While developing climate action plans, public opinion surveys, stakeholder workshops, and focus group discussions with target groups are conducted, gathering the views of vulnerable communities.

Investment distribution analysis: The balanced distribution of infrastructure and adaptation investments made within the scope of climate action is monitored across districts, and priority areas in need are supported.

Furthermore, our municipality integrates adaptation measures targeting these groups, particularly women, the elderly, children, migrants, and individuals with disabilities, into its policies and action plans. For example, by combining social support programs with energy efficiency efforts, living conditions are improved in low-income households.

As a result, SBB systematically utilizes tools such as district-level vulnerability analyses, spatial data management, and participatory decision-making processes to ensure equitable and inclusive climate action, aiming to integrate the fight against climate change with social justice.
column19:
Sakarya Metropolitan Municipality prioritizes the principles of equity and inclusiveness when planning its climate action and takes concrete steps to ensure that low-income and vulnerable groups, in particular, benefit equitably from these actions.

A key initiative implemented in this context is prioritizing citizens with low social welfare during the transition from solid fuels to natural gas. This transition, implemented to improve air quality, reduce carbon emissions, and prevent health risks, identified economically disadvantaged neighborhoods and households as priority areas. This not only supports the right to access clean and safe energy sources but also upholds social justice in the energy transition process.

In this initiative:

District-based income and air quality data were evaluated together.

Natural gas infrastructure projects were accelerated in areas where citizens benefiting from social support services are concentrated.

Energy conversion costs and the transition process were streamlined among households.

This approach aims not only to achieve environmental goals but also to increase equality in health, energy rights, and quality of life.

Sakarya Metropolitan Municipality sees it as a fundamental principle that climate action should be implemented in a way that leaves no one behind and is committed to continuing to prioritize vulnerable groups in future projects.
