The Metropolitan Council's climate actions can help mitigate the current impacts that stem from past planning practices. A focus on equity and environmental justice within Imagine 2050, the Climate Action Work Plan, the Comprehensive Climate Action Plan, and more, seeks to ensure the conscious distribution of the costs and benefits associated with climate actions. 

Improving air quality and better ecosystem health has ripple effects throughout the region. The World Bank found that air pollution costs the U.S. economy over $790 billion per year or approximately 5% of our GDP in economic welfare losses. Improving air quality would mean improving the economic productivity of the region. It can also result in more equitable health outcomes, as communities that experience health impacts like increased asthma rates due to pollution exposure would benefit from cleaner air. Improving air quality involves addressing pollutants from two angles: reducing pollution at the source and promoting vegetation-rich landscapes that can remove existing pollution from the air. These landscapes, such as urban forests, can foster human health benefits valued at over $6.8 billion USD nationally. 

Within the 2025 Comprehensive Economic Development Strategy update, a SWOT (strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats) analysis was conducted to determine the key factors shaping the Twin Cities new climate economy. The external opportunities that influence the new climate economy found within that analysis are listed below: 

• University of Minnesota has many researchers working on innovation in different components and areas of the new climate economy, which could benefit from bringing them together to discuss their potential contributions. 

• Hydrogen and ammonia are opportunities for decarbonization by serving as clean fuels and energy carriers. 

• Educate small business service providers (e.g., nonprofits and CDFIs) on opportunities in the new climate economy to share with their clients. 

• Identify innovative strategies, particularly opportunities for businesses owned by people of color. 

• Work with existing companies that are looking to expand in the Twin Cities. 

• Understand how the workforce needs to upskill or reskill to be able to fill climate-related positions. 

• Promote renewable energy incubators. 

• Public-private partnerships opportunities are critical to future growth. Businesses can solve problems but need government certainty. 

• Attract more of the supplier and related functions of the clean energy cluster, for example manufacturing and headquarters that could bring jobs to the region. 

• Work with businesses that support climate-smart practices. 

• Promote reforestation and afforestation. 

• Assist local governments in siting utility-related clean energy projects.

The operationally-based Climate Action Work Plan engaged in an environmental justice assessment of all plan actions in order to amend the actions to reflect the 17 EJ principles outlined by the Delegates to the First National People of Color Environmental Leadership Summit held on October 24-27, 1991, in Washington DC. 

The regional development guide, Imagine 2050, includes an explicit environmental justice commitment that cuts through all of the climate commitments across the Plan. The commitment is the following: Acknowledge and remedy historic and ongoing environmental injustices to provide environmental benefits for all. The plan also includes an Environmental Justice and Equity Framework which centers these principles across the Plan policies and actions. 

One example of the equitable and inclusive distribution of climate action is through our tools provision to local governments. The award-winning Growing Shade tool centers environmental justice and equity in tree planting protection, enhancement and maintenance. The Council engaged early with neighborhood-level tree advocates to create a tool with equity and environmental justice at its heart. Users can use prioritization variables in the tool to ensure that tree planting benefits communities that need those benefits the most, which creates efficiencies in local climate action, while meeting environmental justice goals. 

In 2025 the Metropolitan Council ran a Community Tree Planting Grant from $2 million of funds awarded by the State of Minnesota. As part of the grant process, communities with overburdened neighborhoods, and areas experiencing extreme heat were prioritized.

La revisión del Plan Local de Acción Climática (PLAC) es el resultado de un 'proceso participativo y técnico'. El plan busca situar a la 'población local en el centro del proceso'.
Prioridad a los Grupos Vulnerables: Un principio fundamental del plan es que las políticas de adaptación y mitigación 'deberán priorizar las necesidades de los grupos sociales en condiciones de mayor vulnerabilidad al Cambio Climático'.
Identificación de Vulnerabilidad: La jurisdicción identifica la vulnerabilidad social utilizando el 'Índice de Vulnerabilidad Social' (IVS) y datos del 'Registro Nacional de Barrios Populares' (RENABAP). Estas medidas se trabajan en conjunto con la Secretaria de Hábitat y Ordenamiento Urbano.
Proyectos con Participación Comunitaria: El documento menciona diversas acciones que involucran a la comunidad:
La reforestación en el 'Cañadón Nomeolvides' se lleva a cabo con 'participación de los vecinos del lugar'.
Se promueve el uso de la bicicleta como medio de transporte alternativo a través de diferentes acciones de publicidad y prensa para incentivar el uso de la bicicleta.
Construcción Colectiva: El plan enfatiza que el futuro de Ushuaia es una 'construcción colectiva' y se invita a los residentes a 'apropiarse de este Plan, a conocerlo, a participar en su implementación y a ser parte activa de esta transformación'
column19:
Acciones Específicas en Barrios Vulnerables
Se están llevando a cabo o se han planificado las siguientes acciones, enfocadas en los Proyectos Específicos con Enfoque Comunitario, donde la equidad se manifiesta en proyectos concretos. Por ejemplo, se mencionan acciones como el desarrollo de infraestructura de servicios básicos (agua y cloacas) y la reubicación de asentamientos en zonas más seguras. Además, la reforestación en el 'Cañadón Nomeolvides' se llevara cabo con la participación directa de los vecinos, convirtiendo un proyecto ambiental en una iniciativa de construcción comunitaria.
En relación a la Justicia Climática y Equidad de Género, la jurisdicción también reconoce la importancia de la justicia climática, que va más allá de la simple distribución de proyectos. Programas pensados para las mujeres por una justicia climática que buscan construir redes de trabajo con mujeres de estas comunidades para desarrollar políticas públicas que mitiguen el impacto de la crisis climática, reconociendo que ciertos grupos enfrentan una vulnerabilidad desproporcionada.
En síntesis, la distribución equitativa de la acción climática en Ushuaia no se limita a la mera implementación de proyectos, sino que se basa en un enfoque integral que identifica a las comunidades más vulnerables, las involucra en el diseño de soluciones y ejecuta acciones que abordan sus necesidades específicas de manera inclusiva.

column16: Ormoc City has identified wider opportunities and benefits from climate action that extend beyond social and economic gains. On the people side, initiatives such as the circular economy program provide green jobs and CSO grants for community-driven solutions, while Project TRANSFORM equips MSMEs with financial literacy to strengthen their disaster preparedness and recovery. At the same time, the city recognizes that climate action also allows the environment to heal. Through Project TRANSFORM, a comprehensive biodiversity assessment was conducted, highlighting the value of protecting local ecosystems and guiding nature-based solutions such as mangrove rehabilitation, watershed conservation, and urban greening. These environmental co-benefits improve carbon sequestration, enhance ecosystem services, and build long-term resilience. Together, these opportunities demonstrate that climate action in Ormoc not only safeguards communities but also restores the natural environment that sustains them.

column18: Ormoc City quantifies the equitable and inclusive distribution of climate action through the combined use of the Climate and Disaster Risk Assessment (CDRA) and the Community-Based Monitoring System (CBMS), which together identify hazard-prone areas and map out socioeconomic vulnerabilities down to the household level. This ensures that climate investments are prioritized for the most at-risk and underserved communities, including the 35 flood-prone barangays. Beyond geographic and socioeconomic targeting, the city also measures inclusivity by tracking participation across different social groups. For example, youth organizations in Ormoc have been capacitated on climate action, the SDGs, and disaster risk reduction and management (DRRM), empowering them to actively contribute to resilience-building efforts and sustainable development planning. Alongside MSMEs supported through Project TRANSFORM, and CSOs receiving grants for community-led projects, the engagement of the youth demonstrates that climate action benefits are widely shared, multi-generational, and socially inclusive.
column19:
The 2024 Climate and Disaster Risk Assessment (CDRA) and the 2024 Community-Based Monitoring System (CBMS) allow the city to map hazard exposure alongside poverty and vulnerability indicators, helping prioritize the most hazard-prone barangays for climate investments like flood control, drainage systems, and nature-based solutions.

Inclusivity is also advanced through the engagement and capacity building of diverse groups. Youth organizations are trained on climate action, SDGs, and DRRM, while MSMEs are supported under Project TRANSFORM with financial literacy and training on the development of Business Continuity Plans (BCPs) to strengthen resilience against disasters.

In addition, CSO grants are leveraged to drive community-led climate solutions, particularly in advancing the circular economy. These initiatives focus on plastic reduction, behavioral change campaigns, and formalizing the informal sector by supporting enterprises like the repair economy, which extends product life cycles, reduces waste, and creates sustainable green jobs.

The equity is safeguarded through budget allocations, such as the mandated Local DRRM Fund, which increasingly prioritizes preparedness, prevention, and adaptation rather than just response.

Evaluación de Oportunidades y Beneficios de la Acción Climática en Ambato

Análisis Climático Detallado: Se ha realizado un diagnóstico climático que incluye la variabilidad de temperatura y precipitación en las últimas décadas. Aunque no se presenta una evaluación cuantitativa de beneficios específicos, el análisis proporciona información clave para identificar zonas vulnerables y planificar acciones de adaptación y mitigación.

Integración en la Planificación Territorial: El PDOT 2050 y el PUGS 2033 incorporan consideraciones climáticas en el ordenamiento del territorio, promoviendo el uso sostenible del suelo y la resiliencia frente a fenómenos climáticos extremos. Esto implica reconocer los beneficios de la acción climática en la reducción de riesgos y la mejora de la calidad de vida urbana y rural.

Participación Ciudadana y Gobernanza Climática: La actualización del PDOT 2050 se ha llevado a cabo con la participación de diversos sectores de la comunidad, lo que permite identificar oportunidades locales para la acción climática y fortalecer la gobernanza climática a nivel cantonal.

Compromiso con la Acción Climática: La participación de Ambato en foros nacionales e internacionales sobre cambio climático refleja un compromiso con la sostenibilidad ambiental y la mitigación de los impactos del cambio climático. Esto también implica reconocer los beneficios de la acción climática en términos de desarrollo sostenible y bienestar comunitario.

Aunque no se dispone de una evaluación cuantitativa específica de los beneficios de la acción climática en Ambato, los documentos de planificación y las iniciativas en curso indican un reconocimiento de las oportunidades que ofrece la acción climática para mejorar la resiliencia, la sostenibilidad y la calidad de vida en el cantón.

This stability indicates that while some efforts to manage and mitigate emissions may be taking hold, there is still significant work to be done to achieve meaningful reductions. It is critical for us to analyze the factors contributing to this steady level, identify opportunities for improvement, and implement more effective strategies to enhance sustainability. Engaging the community in awareness initiatives, investing in renewable energy sources, and encouraging energy-efficient practices are crucial steps towards significantly reducing our carbon footprint and fostering a more sustainable future.

column16: WCC's opportunities around climate change adaptation are an indicator of the council's adaptive capacity. The City Plan: As the central document setting out where development will be located in the city and the planning and design standards that will be required, the City Plan presents a central opportunity to lead the resilient transition of the environment. The Council is effective at engaging with residents through targeted consultation activities, running communication and awareness campaigns, and reaching people face to face through existing community groups and community facilities (e.g. libraries, community centres, schools, etc.). Campaigns can be run to raise awareness of risks and impacts in advance of, or during, extreme weather events as a way of increasing preparedness and social resilience.Westminster is home to many academic and research organisations, and the council is well networked with the private sector, national agencies and local government groups (e.g. London Councils, Local Government Association) as well as neighbouring authorities and organisations (e.g. Camden Council, Royal Borough of Kensington and Chelsea). There are opportunities for collaboration on adaptation interventions, particularly where the potential impacts of climate events transcend administrative boundaries. As a centre of national importance, Westminster is well positioned to advocate for improvements to national policy on climate-related issues, particularly in relation to areas of very high risk for the city, and areas where existing national policies fall short (e.g. climate resilience measures for cultural heritage buildings and conservation areas).

column18: Through the Westminster Local Energy Action Plan, we are providing pathways for the decarbonisation of energy systems in Westminster through domestic fabric improvements, heat pumps, communal heating, solar PV installations, electric vehicles infrastructure etc. We have also published the Climate Adaptation and Resilience Plan in 2024, an ambition set out in WCC's Climate Emergency Action Plan. The Climate Adaptation and Resilience Plan (CARP) aims to safeguard Westminster from climate risks and extreme weather events. This Climate Risk and Vulnerability Assessment is the key preliminary step to the CARP, forming the evidence base of the key climate risks facing the city, both at present and in the future. The Climate Risk and Vulnerability Assessment identifies the likelihood of future climate hazards and their potential impacts across Westminster, including on lives, livelihoods, health and wellbeing, ecosystems and species, economic, social, and cultural assets, services, industries, and infrastructure. 1. Conservación de la biodiversidad
La JIAN destina recursos significativos al monitoreo del águila real, incluyendo la evaluación de su territorio, anidación y presas.

Este tipo de acción permite generar información científica valiosa para la gestión de ecosistemas, lo que constituye un beneficio directo de la acción climática, ya que la conservación de especies ayuda a la resiliencia ecológica ante cambios climáticos.

2. Gestión integral del territorio
Los talleres de capacitación jurídica ambiental para servidores públicos municipales buscan fortalecer capacidades institucionales frente a riesgos climáticos, como contaminación, deforestación o degradación del suelo.

Esto permite identificar oportunidades para integrar la adaptación y mitigación del cambio climático en los planes de desarrollo municipal, promoviendo decisiones más sostenibles y eficientes.

3. Cultura ambiental para el desarrollo sostenible
La promoción de la cultura del agua y campañas de educación ambiental evidencia un enfoque en beneficios sociales y económicos de la acción climática:
Reducción de riesgos por escasez hídrica.
Conciencia ciudadana que promueve ahorro de recursos y prácticas sostenibles.

4. Fortalecimiento institucional y eficiencia operativa
La inversión en energía, transporte y equipamiento refleja un interés en la operación eficiente de la institución

5. Síntesis
La JIAN evalúa oportunidades y beneficios climáticos principalmente en tres dimensiones:
Ambiental: Conservación de especies, ecosistemas y recursos hídricos.
Social: Educación ambiental y cultura del agua, fortaleciendo resiliencia comunitaria.
Institucional: Mejora en la gestión y operación de proyectos, optimización de recursos y fortalecimiento normativo.

Ya, Kabupaten Sumbawa telah menilai sebagian peluang dan manfaat yang lebih luas dari beberapa aksi iklim yang dilaksanakan. Dalam beberapa program adaptasi dan mitigasi, pemerintah daerah melakukan penilaian terhadap dampak lingkungan, sosial, dan ekonomi yang muncul sebagai manfaat tambahan dari aksi iklim tersebut.
Sebagai contoh, rehabilitasi daerah aliran sungai, penghijauan lahan kritis, dan penanaman mangrove tidak hanya dipandang sebagai upaya mengurangi risiko banjir dan abrasi, tetapi juga dinilai memberikan manfaat tambahan berupa peningkatan kualitas air, perlindungan habitat perikanan, dan dukungan terhadap mata pencaharian masyarakat pesisir. Demikian pula, pembangunan infrastruktur pengelolaan air seperti embung, jaringan irigasi adaptif, serta pemanenan air hujan dinilai menghasilkan peluang sosial dan ekonomi, termasuk stabilitas produksi pertanian, pengurangan kerugian akibat kekeringan, dan peningkatan ketahanan desa.
Selain itu, pemerintah daerah juga menilai peluang ekonomi baru yang muncul dari aksi iklim tertentu, seperti potensi ekowisata berbasis konservasi, pengembangan pertanian berkelanjutan, dan penciptaan lapangan kerja lokal dalam kegiatan restorasi lingkungan. Penilaian manfaat ini biasanya dilakukan melalui proses perencanaan Bappeda, evaluasi program perangkat daerah, serta diskusi lintas sektor dalam penyusunan RKPD.
Meskipun demikian, penilaian manfaat yang lebih luas belum dilakukan untuk semua jenis aksi iklim, tetapi telah diterapkan secara konsisten pada beberapa program prioritas yang berkaitan dengan pengelolaan air, pengurangan risiko bencana, perlindungan ekosistem, dan penguatan ketahanan masyarakat.

Kabupaten Sumbawa mengukur distribusi aksi iklim yang adil dan inklusif melalui pendekatan evaluasi yang menggabungkan analisis kerentanan sosial, pemerataan manfaat program, serta monitoring partisipasi kelompok rentan dalam perencanaan dan pelaksanaan kegiatan. Pendekatan ini bertujuan memastikan bahwa manfaat aksi iklim tidak hanya dirasakan oleh kelompok tertentu, tetapi terbagi secara merata kepada masyarakat yang paling membutuhkan.

Pertama, pemerintah daerah melakukan pemetaan kerentanan sosial dan spasial untuk mengidentifikasi kelompok dan wilayah dengan risiko tertinggi, seperti desa rawan kekeringan, daerah pesisir yang terpapar abrasi, rumah tangga berpendapatan rendah, kelompok perempuan, lansia, dan masyarakat dengan akses terbatas terhadap layanan dasar. Hasil pemetaan ini digunakan untuk menentukan prioritas lokasi intervensi dan memastikan bahwa program adaptasi menjangkau kelompok yang paling rentan.

Kedua, distribusi manfaat aksi iklim dinilai melalui indikator pelayanan dan akses, misalnya peningkatan akses air bersih, stabilitas produksi pertanian bagi petani kecil, perlindungan pesisir bagi masyarakat nelayan, serta peningkatan kapasitas desa dalam mitigasi dan adaptasi. Pemerintah Kabupaten melakukan evaluasi dampak sosial secara berkala untuk memastikan manfaat program dapat dirasakan oleh kelompok sasaran yang lebih luas.

Ketiga, Kabupaten Sumbawa memastikan inklusivitas melalui mekanisme partisipasi masyarakat. Proses perencanaan program adaptasi—mulai dari musrenbang desa hingga konsultasi publik—melibatkan perempuan, pemuda, kelompok adat lokal, dan masyarakat miskin agar suara mereka masuk dalam prioritas aksi iklim. Tingkat keterlibatan kelompok rentan menjadi salah satu indikator penilaian keadilan distribusi manfaat.

Keempat, perangkat daerah seperti Bappeda, DLH, Dinas Pertanian, Dinas Sosial, dan BPBD melakukan monitoring berbasis data untuk mengukur sejauh mana program iklim memberikan manfaat merata kepada masyarakat. Data yang dihasilkan mencakup jumlah penerima manfaat, perubahan kondisi sosial-ekonomi, dan tingkat penurunan kerentanan di kelompok tertentu.

Secara keseluruhan, Kabupaten Sumbawa mengukur distribusi aksi iklim yang adil dan inklusif melalui kombinasi:

pemetaan kerentanan,

penilaian pemerataan manfaat,

partisipasi masyarakat yang luas, dan

monitoring berbasis data lintas sektor.

Pendekatan ini memastikan bahwa kebijakan dan program iklim dapat meningkatkan ketahanan seluruh masyarakat, terutama mereka yang paling rentan terhadap dampak perubahan iklim.
column19:
Bukti dan Rincian Tindakan Kabupaten Sumbawa untuk Menjamin Distribusi Aksi Iklim yang Adil dan Inklusif
Kabupaten Sumbawa telah mengambil beberapa langkah konkret untuk memastikan bahwa aksi iklim didistribusikan secara adil dan inklusif, dengan fokus pada kelompok masyarakat yang paling rentan terhadap dampak perubahan iklim. Berikut bukti dan rincian tindakan yang sedang dan telah dilakukan:

1. Pemetaan Kerentanan Sosial, Ekologi, dan Spasial
Pemerintah Kabupaten Sumbawa telah melakukan pemetaan wilayah rawan kekeringan, banjir, abrasi pesisir, serta identifikasi kelompok berpendapatan rendah, petani kecil, nelayan, dan desa terpencil.
Bukti tindakan:
•	Penetapan desa-desa prioritas intervensi pada wilayah DAS kritis dan kawasan rawan kekeringan.
•	Integrasi hasil pemetaan kerentanan ke dalam RKPD dan usulan desa (Musrenbang).

2. Prioritas Pendanaan untuk Desa dan Kelompok Rentan
Aksi iklim diarahkan terlebih dahulu ke wilayah yang paling membutuhkan. Dana APBD, Dana Desa, serta bantuan provinsi diarahkan ke program adaptasi bagi masyarakat rentan.
Bukti tindakan:
•	Program pipanisasi air bersih dan sumur bor untuk desa sangat terdampak kekeringan.
•	Bantuan sarana pertanian tahan iklim (benih tahan kering, pompanisasi) khusus untuk petani skala kecil.
•	Rehabilitasi mangrove dan perlindungan pesisir untuk desa nelayan terdampak abrasi.

3. Mekanisme Perencanaan Partisipatif dan Inklusif
Pemerintah daerah memastikan bahwa masyarakat, terutama kelompok rentan, berpartisipasi dalam proses penentuan prioritas aksi iklim.
Bukti tindakan:
•	Keterlibatan perempuan, pemuda, dan kelompok masyarakat adat dalam Musrenbang Desa dan Kecamatan.
•	Konsultasi publik untuk program adaptasi pesisir dan konservasi DAS.
•	Forum multipihak (OPD, desa, masyarakat, akademisi, dan kelompok rentan) dalam penyusunan dokumen lingkungan dan kebencanaan.

4. Implementasi Program Aksi Iklim yang Menyasar Komunitas Rentan
Kabupaten Sumbawa menjalankan berbagai program yang manfaatnya dirasakan langsung oleh masyarakat yang paling terdampak perubahan iklim.
Bukti tindakan:
•	Program embung, sumur resapan, dan irigasi mikro di wilayah rawan kekeringan.
•	Sistem peringatan dini (EWS) dan pelatihan kesiapsiagaan untuk desa rawan banjir/longsor.
•	Restorasi lahan kritis di daerah hulu untuk melindungi komunitas hilir dari banjir dan kekurangan air.

5. Monitoring Distribusi Manfaat secara Terukur
Monitoring dilakukan melalui pelaporan OPD, survei lapangan, dan evaluasi program untuk memastikan manfaat aksi iklim diterima secara merata.
Bukti tindakan:
•	Data jumlah penerima manfaat program air bersih, irigasi, rehabilitasi pesisir, dan bantuan pertanian.
•	Laporan evaluasi dampak sosial (jumlah desa tangguh bencana, peningkatan akses air, stabilitas produksi pangan).
•	Indikator partisipasi kelompok rentan dalam perencanaan dan pelaksanaan program.

6. Kolaborasi dengan Provinsi, Nasional, dan Mitra Pembangunan
Kerja sama dengan lembaga eksternal membantu memperkuat akses masyarakat rentan terhadap manfaat aksi iklim.
Bukti tindakan:
•	Program rehabilitasi mangrove berbasis masyarakat bekerja sama dengan provinsi/NGO.
•	Pelatihan adaptasi pertanian dan manajemen risiko bencana bekerja sama dengan BPBD, PKK, dan lembaga pendidikan lokal.
•	Program penguatan kapasitas desa dalam penyusunan rencana adaptasi berbasis masyarakat.

Oportunidades de financiamiento e innovación: La participación en programas como Cities Forward, Reinventing Cities y Youth Climate Action Fund ha abierto nuevas oportunidades de colaboración técnica y captación de recursos para proyectos climáticos transformadores.

Sin embargo, durante 2024 se han utilizado indicadores territoriales y poblacionales indirectos que permiten orientar acciones con criterios de justicia climática.

Algunos ejemplos incluyen:

La plantación de árboles y recuperación de espacios públicos priorizó sectores con déficit de áreas verdes y mayor densidad poblacional, de acuerdo con mapas comunales de inequidad territorial.

El diseño participativo de proyectos como el Parque Costanera, la Plaza Miraflores o el Plan Maestro del Agua ha incluido procesos abiertos con representación comunitaria, asegurando inclusión en la toma de decisiones.

Si bien aún no se cuenta con un sistema integral de monitoreo cuantitativo de equidad, el municipio está avanzando en la sistematización de datos territoriales y sociodemográficos, lo cual permitirá en el futuro próximo medir de manera más precisa la distribución de los beneficios de la acción climática.
column19:
La Municipalidad de Renca ha implementado durante 2024 diversas iniciativas que garantizan una distribución equitativa e inclusiva de los beneficios climáticos, especialmente orientadas a sectores históricamente marginados y con menor acceso a infraestructura ambiental:

Priorización territorial en áreas verdes: La plantación de 350 árboles y la recuperación de 44 espacios públicos degradados se enfocaron en macrozonas con bajos índices de vegetación y alta densidad poblacional, atendiendo a brechas históricas de acceso a naturaleza urbana.

Participación comunitaria inclusiva: Procesos participativos como el diseño del Parque Costanera, la Plaza Miraflores y el Plan Maestro del Agua para los Cerros de Renca incluyeron juntas de vecinos, organizaciones territoriales, comités ambientales y escolares, promoviendo una toma de decisiones compartida con enfoque territorial y generacional.

Educación ambiental en sectores vulnerables: Se ejecutaron campañas y actividades educativas en jardines infantiles, escuelas municipales y centros comunitarios, fortaleciendo la conciencia climática desde la infancia y en sectores con menor acceso a formación ambiental.

Estas acciones reflejan el compromiso de la comuna con una transición justa, garantizando que los beneficios ambientales lleguen a toda la población y que las decisiones se construyan desde la participación activa y representativa.

column16: Through a resilience framework based on people (health and equity), places (built infrastructure and natural environment), and prosperity (economic resilience), the region has worked to gain an understanding of the impacts of short-term shocks and long-term stressors like climate change and the opportunities the region has to reduce risk and vulnerability and our carbon footprint and increase sustainable actions. As a result, the R2C works to incorporate and provide holistic approaches that provide effective and efficient governance and use of funding. \nUnderstanding risk alongside the identified high impact actions (HIA), which include grid decarbonization, a reduction in vehicle miles traveled, an increase in alt fuels and electric vehicle deployment, an increase in solar photovoltaic deployment, and an increase in residential and commercial building energy efficiency, allows identification of co-benefits and an increase in collective action and impact. These actions have been established to focus our region to reduce its emissions 40% by 2030 and net zero by 2050. These have guided efforts to plan and implement projects and strategies to support these actions that are not only essential to mitigate climate change impacts but also to bolster resilience, improve public health, and reduce costs of energy, among other benefits and opportunities alike. The R2C has continued working with regional partners to address these actions, formulate strategies, and seek opportunities that will help propel these activity shifts/ HIA and other climate actions. Furthermore, through climate action, the R2C will work to mitigate climate-related hazards and vulnerabilities, such as extreme heat and its impacts on health, infrastructure, and economy; exacerbated weather-related impacts on the affordable housing stock; coastal and inland flooding; and other hazards and vulnerabilities that are and will continue to be identified through various regional assessments. The R2C and partner Emergency Management directors from across the region recently completed a regionwide risk assessment with standardized and consistent climate and asset datasets, identified climate sensitive hazards as well as incorporated health data to illustrate impacts currently existing that have traditionally not been considered for significant mitigation. This work includes a definition of risk based on region-specific threats, vulnerabilities, and severity of consequences, which considers climate sensitivity. The region-wide risk assessment details standardized and consistent hazards, climate sensitivities, social vulnerabilities, and asset datasets that can be operationalized in each state-required vulnerability assessment throughout the region. In addition, the R2C will complete a regional integrated climate action plan for release February 2026 that will establish pathways toward the 40% and net zero emissions reduction target which include direct emission mitigation strategies, alongside mitigation efforts for risk reduction, and a climate-informed conservation strategy that will support local governments with their efforts and policies toward these ends. The benefits analysis in the climate action plan will include an evaluation of how GHG reduction efforts also impact air pollutants, assessing the potential reduction of co-pollutants in the region and translating that into health and economic benefits to apply a \'people first\' focus to our analysis.

Through R2C committee work, common vulnerabilities were identified through three systems to include people, places and economic resilience. The commonalities were labeled the region's 'drivers of vulnerability' and then related indicators and metrics were agreed upon. These indicators exceed the 15 identified by the CDC and provide a locally driven picture of vulnerability throughout the region. 
To operationalize these indicators, several pathways were undertaken: one with the Central Florida Foundation, the Orlando Economic Partnership who frame their social data in people, places, and prosperity, and with the University of Central Florida. Work with our academic partners commenced to incorporate additional indicators into a SOVi model that would assist in spatially organizing and understanding risk that includes these indicators, as well as climate sensitivities and local Department of Health data. With the completed regional risk and vulnerability assessment, the R2C is now able to formulate mitigation and emissions-reducing action with a people-focused baseline understanding and analysis of regional vulnerability. Moving forward, this assessment will help the R2C appropriately identify, implement, and track climate action and relating co-benefits. 
While the risk assessment was being conducted, the R2C engaged with frontline communities to draft a heat hazard strategy map. The communities' words formed the goals, strategies, and actions they would like to see implemented across the region. 
In addition, as the regional integrated Climate Action Plan is being drafted, the R2C continues to engage with the region's disadvantaged communities through community-based organizations who were selected by committee review to gather insights on community members' priorities and needs and collect feedback on drafted strategies and actions, associated co-benefits, and best path to implementation.
column19: Through the R2C's advisory committees' work in building an understanding of the region by assessing and defining vulnerabilities within all community aspects (people, places, and prosperity/economic system), correlating and interconnected sets of indicators of vulnerable communities were identified and named \'drivers of vulnerability.\' Some of the most consistent correlating drivers include safe and affordable housing; safe open spaces; health care access; food access and security; access to energy and clean water; economic mobility; and safe, clean, reliable, and affordable transportation. In addition to focusing on management and response to shocks and stressors, building adaptive capacities through robust, integrated processes to address these \'drivers\' will lead toward transformative change and decrease vulnerability overall in the region, especially in those communities that are most disadvantaged and vulnerable. These drivers are discussed and adopted in the R2C Strategic Resilience Action Plan. Guided by this document and encouraged to further increase equity and resilience in the region, the R2C has worked through the committees to adopt and implement a people-focused approach to all collaborative efforts and has consequently developed an Equity Guide to direct and support municipalities and counties across the region to create people-centered, action-oriented, and inclusive and equitable resilience programs, policies, and decision-making processes that consider local socioeconomic conditions including inequities to ensure all can participate and prosper. In addition, the R2C has worked on a regional risk assessment, which has incorporated risks in the affordable housing stock and highlighted those coastal and inland areas at most risk from flooding. Moreover, regional areas that are and will be most vulnerable to climate-related risks based on climate identified hazards, social vulnerabilities and population characteristics, among other factors, have been defined. In this comprehensive approach, jurisdictions will have the ability to deploy appropriate and limited resources and meet the communities where they are instead of where the jurisdiction is at. To complement this work and better address findings, the R2C will work with regional partners to incorporate the community and all relevant stakeholders in project identification for adaptation and mitigation processes.

New Glasgow quantifies equity in climate action by using qualitative and demographic indicators drawn from existing municipal plans and engagement processes:

Identification of priority populations.
The Town's Equity & Anti-Racism Strategy (2025-2028) and the Community Climate Action Plan identify groups more exposed to climate impacts (e.g., seniors, renters, low-income households, people without access to private cooling/heating, and equity-deserving communities).

Geographic and facility-based assessment.
Through the Resiliency Hub initiative, the Town maps which neighbourhoods have reliable access to safe community spaces during extreme weather events. This provides a practical measure of physical access to resilience services.

Representation metrics.
Inclusion is quantified through the presence of youth representatives on the Climate Change Steering Committee and through tracking participation diversity in public engagement sessions, workshops, and surveys.

Program reach and service distribution.
When implementing programs funded through climate or adaptation grants, the Town records which facilities, neighbourhoods, and community groups benefit, creating a distributional map of who receives services.
column19:
New Glasgow is actively embedding equity considerations into the design and delivery of climate initiatives:

Equity & Anti-Racism Plan (2025-2028)
The Town has formally adopted this plan, which guides staff to assess how policies and programs—including climate action—affect marginalized or under-represented community members.

Resiliency Hubs as community-first infrastructure
The Town is scaling a model that uses existing community centres as climate-resilience spaces, with a deliberate focus on neighbourhoods that may lack private cooling/heating, backup power, or social supports. This ensures climate-response services are physically and socially accessible.

Youth and community representation
The Climate Change Steering Committee includes youth members, increasing generational representation and ensuring climate strategies reflect different lived experiences.

Inclusive engagement practices
Public engagement for climate planning (e.g., workshops, surveys, pop-ups at community events) intentionally targets a broad demographic range, improving the likelihood that climate programs reflect community diversity.

Partnerships with local and regional organizations
The Town collaborates with groups that work directly with vulnerable or underserved populations, ensuring climate programs are informed by frontline social service knowledge.

Grant-funded climate programs with equity requirements
Recent provincial funding specifically supports equity-centred implementation of the community climate plan. This creates structured requirements for the Town to identify impacts on vulnerable groups and to prioritize actions that improve climate resilience for those residents.

En nuestra organización, el Plan de Acción Comunal de Cambio Climático (PACCC) desarrollado entre 2024 y 2025 nos ha proporcionado una comprensión profunda de las oportunidades de nuestro territorio frente a la crisis climática.

Gracias a este plan, hemos identificado áreas clave donde podemos generar un impacto significativo, tales como:

Conservación de espacios naturales estratégicos: Proteger y gestionar de forma sostenible los ecosistemas que son vitales para la biodiversidad y el bienestar de nuestra comunidad.

Planes y estrategias ambientales: Desarrollar hojas de ruta concretas para mitigar los efectos del cambio climático y fortalecer la resiliencia de nuestro entorno.

Educación con un nuevo enfoque: Crear programas educativos y de sensibilización que no solo informen, sino que también empoderen a la comunidad para ser agentes de cambio.

Rediseño de proyectos: Ajustar los proyectos que están en etapa de planificación para que sean más sostenibles y estén alineados con nuestros objetivos climáticos.

De la oportunidad a la acción: 
Ahora que hemos identificado estas oportunidades, nuestro siguiente objetivo es transformarlas en acciones concretas. Para lograrlo, nos enfocaremos en:

Integrar el cambio climático en la planificación: Asegurarnos de que todos los nuevos proyectos consideren el riesgo climático y las oportunidades de adaptación desde su concepción.

Formar alianzas estratégicas: Colaborar con otras organizaciones, instituciones y la comunidad para amplificar nuestros esfuerzos y recursos.

Medir nuestro impacto: Establecer indicadores claros para evaluar el progreso de nuestras acciones y asegurar que estamos generando un cambio real y medible.

La Municipalidad de Quilicura puede garantizar la equidad en la entrega de beneficios a través de la implementación de mecanismos específicos, diseñados para abordar las desigualdades preexistentes. Estos mecanismos son la forma en que el diagnóstico participativo se transforma en beneficios tangibles para los vecinos.

Asignación de recursos basada en vulnerabilidad: Los fondos para proyectos de mitigación y adaptación no se distribuyen de manera uniforme, sino que se priorizan las zonas que, según el diagnóstico participativo, son más vulnerables a los impactos del cambio climático. Por ejemplo, si un sector de Quilicura sufre más por el calor extremo, se priorizará la creación de refugios climáticos (áreas con sombra, fuentes de agua, techos verdes) en esa zona.

Programas de subsidios y apoyo técnico: La municipalidad puede ofrecer subsidios directos a familias de bajos ingresos para implementar medidas de eficiencia energética en sus hogares, como la instalación de paneles solares o la mejora del aislamiento térmico. Además, se puede brindar capacitación técnica gratuita para que los vecinos aprendan a mantener estos sistemas, garantizando que el beneficio perdure en el tiempo.

Infraestructura verde inclusiva: Al planificar nuevos parques o remodelar áreas existentes, se considera la accesibilidad universal. Esto significa que los beneficios de la infraestructura verde (reducción de la temperatura, mejora de la calidad del aire) son accesibles para todos, incluyendo a personas mayores o con movilidad reducida. Se pueden crear senderos accesibles, bancas estratégicamente ubicadas para el descanso y señalización clara.

Beneficios Entregados a la Comunidad
Los beneficios de estas políticas se manifiestan en múltiples niveles, mejorando la calidad de vida de todos los habitantes de Quilicura de forma directa.

Beneficios económicos: La reducción en las facturas de energía gracias a la eficiencia energética, la creación de nuevos empleos verdes en la instalación y mantenimiento de tecnologías sostenibles, y la revalorización de las propiedades en áreas con más infraestructura verde.

Beneficios de salud: La disminución de enfermedades respiratorias debido a la mejor calidad del aire, la reducción del estrés por el acceso a espacios naturales y la mitigación de los riesgos por golpes de calor en los meses de verano.

Beneficios sociales: Fortalecimiento del tejido comunitario a través de la colaboración en proyectos locales, mayor cohesión social al sentir que las políticas responden a las necesidades reales de cada barrio y el empoderamiento de los vecinos como guardianes de su propio entorno.

To ensure that this plays out in the years that follow publication, the National Park will put resource into monitoring the impacts of this plan, reporting on them, and advocating for further action where the data shows us the plan is not being effective.

A series of indicators have been selected as the best metrics for understanding and tracking change in the 
National Park in relation to the Doughnut Economics:
• Ecological ceiling (Planetary Boundaries) 
• Social foundation (Sustainable Development Goals), and 
• The 'safe and just space' in the middle of the ring which reflects ecological and human wellbeing in the 
unique context of Bannau Brycheiniog National Park. 
The indicators have been chosen because they represent the best direct metric or proxy, and because it is 
envisaged that data will be available to track change over a long timescale. 

Timescales 
Several different timescales are important in considering the sustainable future of the National Park. 
Ongoing: Updates on the BBNPA website and other platforms, and that of partners, sharing information about actions and outcomes, celebrating successes, and highlighting opportunities and challenges. 
1 year: Annual Doughnut Economics assessment 'health check' of the National Park, and annual assessment of progress in achieving the missions. 
4 years: State of the Park Report 2027 The State of the Park report is an important synthesis of all the data being gathered in relation to the doughnut. It is an important moment to reflect on the key issues facing the Park in order to inform the review of Y Bannau. 
5 years: The duration of Y Bannau: The Future management plan. Used to focus near-term action towards achieving the missions. 
2030 and 2035: The timescales to achieve the nature and water missions and the climate mission respectively. 
25 years: The medium-term vision for the National Park. 
50 years: Long-term change horizon. Used to track long-term sustainability as indicated by Doughnut Economics metrics.

Public Health: Improved housing energy efficiency reduces fuel poverty and health risks; active travel promotes healthier lifestyles and eases pressure on healthcare.

Access to Nature: Initiatives like Biodiversity Net Gain and woodland planting enhance wellbeing and support thriving ecosystems.

Air Quality: Transitioning to electric vehicles and cleaner transport reduces harmful emissions, improving compliance with air quality regulations.

Economic Growth: Embracing low-carbon technologies and natural capital fosters clean growth, local supply chains, skills development, and community-owned enterprises.

Community Resilience: Climate action builds stronger, more adaptive communities, reduces energy costs, and supports local solutions like community assets and greenspace access.

Energy Security: Reducing energy use and increasing renewables lowers costs and strengthens public sector resilience.

Environmental Protection: Enhancing greenspaces improves air quality, reduces flood risk, and supports rural vitality aligned with the council's Rural Commission and task force goals.

A key principle for North Yorkshire Council is ensuring equality of opportunity. We want to enable equal access to the low carbon economy so that every person, business, and community is able to take climate responsible action. At a global scale we want to ensure our climate actions do not inadvertently impact negatively on other geographical areas. 

North Yorkshire Council use Equality Impact Assessments (EIA's) to ensure statutory protected characteristics are considered as well as people living in rural areas, people with lower socioeconomic status, and unpaid carers are. As a part of the Council's duty to provide equitable and inclusive distribution of intervention, high level objectives are set which are regularly monitored and reported through the performance framework. To ensure the needs of North Yorkshire's communities are met, the Council commits to carry out effective community engagement, foster good community relations, encourage participation in public life by all North Yorkshire communities and address local inequalities. Equitability and inclusivity distribution data is quantified through the Council's equality objectives, where the objectives align to the Council Plan, and are embedded into the performance framework. They are monitored and reported through quarterly performance reporting to Management Board and Executive Additionally regular directorate equality-based meetings take place across the Council which link with the Corporate Equality Diversity and Inclusion (EDI) Group.

The Council's Climate Change Strategy emphasises collaboration with public, private, voluntary, and community partners, ensuring inclusive and equitable climate action. The Council engages residents through initiatives like the Let's Talk campaigns, which include surveys, virtual briefings, and in-person events across the county—targeting diverse groups including young people.

To support informed decision-making, the Council uses data and behavioural insights to guide investment and avoid stranded assets, such as through the Local Area Energy Plan. Flexibility is key to adapting to evolving legislation, technology, and evidence.

Area Committees of elected councillors (broadly aligned with parliamentary constituencies), help reflect local needs and voices. Feedback from Let's Talk Climate was analysed at Area Committee level to understand community-specific concerns.

The Council is developing cross-sector wrap-around groups to coordinate climate efforts in areas like education, public health, woodland, and energy infrastructure. Funding from the UK Shared Prosperity Fund is distributed equitably, with applications reviewed to ensure fair representation across North Yorkshire's diverse communities.

£1.2m funding has been secured from the York and North Yorkshire mayoral Combined Authority to develop 32 Town Investment plans, for settlements across the jurisdiction and there are clear opportunities to integrate climate actions.

The Powys Well-being Plan, has been developed to provide a long term vision of well-being in Powys. Intersectional and cross-cutting impacts and opportunities were considered in developing the Well-being Plan.

To deliver our well-being objectives, we will need to undertake a series of steps. A step is a 
delivery mechanism, which may include a project, work focus, or board that helps us to make 
progress against our objectives. Three priorities have been identified as the most important focus 
to help achieve the Well-being Objectives:
● Responding to the Climate Emergency
● Taking a whole systems approach to healthy weight
● Shaping the future by improving our understanding of what matters to the people of Powys through evidence and insight

The areas of work are interconnected and will contribute to achieving all three well-being 
objectives

● Take our fair share of the action to decarbonise, in line with the 2025 Paris Agreement
● Scale up carbon sequestration - increasing the space for nature to absorb carbon
● Adapt to climate impacts - improving the resilience of people and nature to cope with 
climate impacts that are unavoidable

The Public Services Board (PSB) is a statutory strategic partnership established under the Wellbeing of Future Generations (Wales) Act 2015. The Act requires key local organisations in Powys to work together and take a more co-ordinated and long-term approach to the issues that really matter to the people of the county. 

In doing so, the PSB must assess the state of well-being locally every five year Powys PSB produces a Well-being Plan. A Well-being Plan is a document agreed by the Public Services Board (PSB) to agree what objectives and steps they will be undertaking to improve the well-being of the people of Powys.

This 

The last Future Generations Report was published in 2020. In setting its local objectives the PSB 
must also consider the latest Future Generations Report as prepared by the Commissioner, which 
provides an assessment of the improvements public bodies should make in order to set and meet well-being objectives in accordance with the sustainable development principle. This plan also 
considers how the objectives set contribute towards the well-being goals outlined below:

1. A prosperous Wales: An innovative, productive, and low carbon society which recognises the 
limits of the global environment and therefore uses resources efficiently and proportionately 
(including acting on climate change); and that develops a skilled and well-educated population 
in an economy which generates wealth and provides employment opportunities, allowing 
people to take advantage of the wealth generated through securing decent work.

2. A resilient Wales: A nation which maintains and enhances a biodiverse natural environment 
with healthy functioning ecosystems that support social, economic, and ecological resilience 
and the capacity to adapt to change (for example, climate change).

3. A healthier Wales: A society in which people's physical and mental well-being is maximised 
and in which the choices and behaviours that benefit future health are understood.
4. A more equal Wales: A society which enables people to fulfil their potential no matter what 
their background or circumstances (including their socio-economic factors).

5. A Wales of cohesive communities: Attractive, viable, safe and well-connected communities.

6. A Wales of vibrant culture and thriving Welsh language: A society which promotes and 
protects culture, heritage and the Welsh language, and encourages people to participate in the arts, and sports and recreation.

7. A globally responsible Wales: A nation which, when doing anything to improve the 
economic, social, environmental and cultural well-being of Wales, takes account of whether 
doing such a thing may make a positive contribution to global well-being.

To help us know whether we are making progress towards achieving the well-being goals, Welsh Ministers ('Ministers') must set national indicators.

An indicator (*As SET OUT HERE https://www.gov.wales/well-being-future-generations-act-essentials-html#60668): 

must be expressed as a value or characteristic that can be measured quantitatively or qualitatively measured against a particular outcome
may be measured over such a period of time as the Welsh Ministers deem appropriate
may be measureable in relation to Wales or any part of Wales.

Powys PSB will work towards joining the United Nations' Race to Zero. This global initiative 
supports public bodies and organisations to take action aligned to the Paris Agreement, and to 
build a fairer, more resilient future.
Powys PSB's work will be shaped by the five membership criteria of Race to Zero:
Pledge: to take concrete action toward or beyond a fair share of the 50% global greenhouse 
gas reduction needed by 2030, and to reach net zero by 2050 at the latest.
The fair share decarbonisation target will be based on expert advice and will include embodied 
emissions in the goods consumed in Powys, not just emissions produced directly in the county.
Plan: within 12 months develop an evidence-based emissions reduction plan in line with 
the pledge.
A set of research and analysis will be developed to understand the biggest climate interventions 
needed across Powys that will also bring well-being benefits for this and future generations of 
people, and for nature recovery. This action planning will involve engagement with local 
communities, businesses and third sector organisations to ensure actions are tailored to local 
needs. A pipeline of funding-ready projects will be developed with partners.
Proceed: take immediate action towards meeting the pledge.
Powys PSB will work in partnership across the county to scale up climate action, and to attract 
investment in the projects needed.
Publish: commit to report data and actions in relation to meeting the pledge, publicly and at 
least annually - feeding into the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change
Global Climate Action Portal.
Powys PSB will make public the analysis, plans, and delivery record to maximise transparency, 
accountability and public confidence.
Persuade: align lobbying and advocacy activities with net zero by proactively supporting 
climate policies consistent with the Race to Zero criteria.
Powys PSB will work with people, businesses, and organisations across the county and wider to 
make the case for a zero-carbon nature-friendly Powys that supports local well-being and a strong 
local economy.

There are a range of ways it will particularly embed the principle of sustainable development, equitable and inclusive action including: 

Long-term: Developing a Powys-wide evidence-based climate action plan across sectors 
will enable an understanding of the future threats and opportunities posed by climate change and the transition to a net zero economy. In particular it will:

- enable strategic support to accelerate the development of the net zero 
goods and services needed in Powys in a way that benefits local 
people
● enable strategic planning and support for a just transition
● catalyse investment in the low carbon infrastructure, projects, 
organisations and practices needed in Powys
● inform how the nature and climate emergencies can be addressed 
together in a way that maximises nature recovery and supports 
people's well-being 

Integration: Having a planned approach will enable work to be shaped in a way that 
contributes to achieving all the well-being Goals. Synergies will be actively identified and maximised between the three PSB well-being Steps, and the wider work of PSB organisations.

Involement: Having a planned approach will enable high quality engagement with a 
diverse range of stakeholders and communities. This will enable plans to be 
informed and tailored to meet the needs of local communities including in 
particular people with protected characteristics and those facing socio-economic disadvantage.

Collaboration: A Climate Well-being Working Group has been set up to facilitate collaboration between Powys PSB members. It will also engage with wider statutory bodies and other stakeholders.

Prevention: Developing a Powys-wide climate risk assessment will enable a medium and 
long-term understanding of the anticipated impact of the climate crisis on the well-being of people and nature. This will inform plans to reduce and manage risk.

Opportunities and benefits of climate action extend from environment and society to economy and health. 
Climate action strengthens the resilience of people, systems and infrastructure to severe climate incidents, such as flooding, extreme heat, drought etc. It protects public health through climate mitigations actions, such as reducing greenhouse gas emissions, improving air quality and increasing green spaces. It reduces long term economic costs for municipal authorities and households through supporting renewable energy sources and energy upgrades of public and private buildings. It promotes social cohesion through the protection of vulnerable groups who lack in general the access to funding to implement climate adaptation and mitigation measures. Through awareness raising campaigns people become more aware of the challenges and they develop a more responsible and participatory attitude. Furthermore, through the adoption of smart technologies and systems to address climate challenges, legitimacy and public acceptance of public and municipal authorities is strengthened.

The projects that are implemented or planned on the field of environment (plantings, green spaces preservation, pocket parks etc.) are covering the entire municipal territory. 
Ilion Municipality runs a municipal health center at a central location of Ilion (Agios Nikolaos district) which conducts free of charge preventive health care exams to address vulnerable population needs. The Social Service Department of Ilion Municipality also conducts regularly a series of preventive examinations addressed to minors in primary and secondary education premises.
Ilion Municipality also runs 8 Open Care Centers for the Elderly (K.A.P.H.), covering geographically the entire municipal territory.

Athienou Municipality recognizes that climate action generates not only environmental gains but also significant social and economic opportunities for the community. Our approach to sustainability emphasizes co-benefits that strengthen resilience, support inclusive growth, and improve the overall quality of life for our residents. The Municipality systematically considers the wider impacts of climate initiatives during planning and implementation, ensuring that every environmental measure contributes to social well-being and economic vitality.
Through initiatives such as improving energy efficiency in municipal buildings, promoting renewable energy adoption, and developing sustainable mobility options, Athienou directly contributes to reducing greenhouse gas emissions and improving air quality. Tree planting campaigns, the creation of shaded areas in public parks, and the protection of natural habitats enhance biodiversity, mitigate the urban heat island effect, and reduce flood risks during extreme weather. Waste management programs, including recycling and awareness-raising campaigns, not only reduce landfill use but also cultivate a culture of responsibility among citizens. These measures support both ecosystem protection and public health by ensuring cleaner air, safer streets, and a healthier living environment.
Climate action in Athienou is designed to reinforce social cohesion and inclusiveness. Public spaces, such as the Konstantineio Municipal Park, are increasingly used for activities that combine environmental awareness with cultural and recreational value. For example, the recent “Yoga in the Park” event, organized in collaboration with the Embassy of India, brought together Athienou residents and migrant workers, demonstrating how climate-conscious activities can foster intercultural dialogue and mutual respect. The promotion of cycling and walking infrastructure encourages active lifestyles, strengthens community interaction, and improves accessibility for children, elderly citizens, and vulnerable groups. Furthermore, educational programs in schools introduce children to sustainable practices—such as recycling, energy saving, and respect for nature—empowering the next generation to be proactive climate leaders.
Investments in sustainable infrastructure, energy-saving technologies, and renewable energy not only reduce long-term municipal expenses but also create opportunities for local businesses and skilled workers. Energy efficiency projects in municipal buildings decrease operational costs, freeing resources for essential community services. Supporting local agriculture through sustainable practices strengthens food security, provides stable income for farmers, and highlights Athienou's position as a center of traditional yet environmentally responsible food production. These measures enhance the Municipality's competitiveness in agrotourism, attracting visitors who are increasingly interested in authentic and sustainable experiences. By branding itself as a green and climate-conscious community, Athienou increases its attractiveness for tourism, partnerships, and investment.
As a town with rich cultural heritage, Athienou integrates climate initiatives into cultural life. Traditional festivals and local events increasingly incorporate environmental elements, raising awareness while preserving local identity. Such integration helps residents view climate action not as a distant obligation but as a natural extension of everyday life and culture. By linking heritage and sustainability, the Municipality demonstrates that protecting the environment also protects traditions, landscapes, and community values.
Climate action is also seen as a tool for long-term resilience and future-proofing. By embedding sustainability criteria into local planning and decision-making, Athienou ensures that policies, infrastructure, and community services align with sustainable development goals. The Municipality engages with local schools, organizations, and cultural groups to ensure broad participation, creating a sense of shared ownership of climate initiatives. This participatory approach not only increases effectiveness but also ensures that benefits are widely distributed. Importantly, Athienou views climate action as an opportunity to position itself as a forward-looking rural municipality that combines tradition with innovation, serving as a model for other towns of similar size and context.

Athienou Municipality recognizes that equitable and inclusive distribution of climate action benefits is essential to building a fair and resilient community. Although we are a small jurisdiction, we take deliberate steps to monitor, evaluate, and ensure that opportunities created by climate initiatives reach all groups in our society. Our approach combines both quantitative and qualitative methods of assessment.
Participation in climate-related programs and activities is systematically monitored. For public awareness events such as tree-planting campaigns, recycling initiatives, and community activities in municipal parks, the Municipality records the number of participants, while also noting demographic diversity (age, gender, background). For example, school-based sustainability programs ensure that all children in public schools are reached equally, and records of school participation help confirm equitable coverage. The Municipality also tracks participation in cultural-environmental activities such as “Yoga in the Park,” which brought together both local residents and migrant workers, thereby demonstrating inclusivity in practice.
When developing or upgrading public spaces—such as shaded areas in Konstantineio Municipal Park or improvements to pedestrian and cycling infrastructure—the Municipality applies accessibility standards to guarantee that elderly citizens, children, and persons with disabilities can benefit equally. The presence of ramps, seating, shaded paths, and safe crossings is measured and documented as part of project evaluation. By quantifying physical accessibility, Athienou ensures that environmental improvements do not disproportionately benefit only certain groups.
In the agricultural sector, the Municipality supports sustainable farming practices that benefit both large and small producers. To quantify inclusiveness, participation in training sessions and adoption of environmentally friendly methods are monitored across different scales of farms. This ensures that the economic opportunities of the green transition—such as reduced costs, new market potential, and agrotourism—are not concentrated only among larger enterprises but shared more widely.
Beyond numerical data, Athienou uses community engagement as a tool to assess equitable distribution. Consultations with residents, feedback from schools, and collaboration with cultural and migrant associations provide valuable insights into whether climate actions are experienced as inclusive. Feedback is reviewed after events and programs, and this information is used to adapt future initiatives so that they better reflect the needs of underrepresented groups.
Another measure of equity is the principle of free access to municipal climate programs. By offering initiatives without cost, the Municipality eliminates financial barriers and ensures that low-income families can participate equally. Attendance rates are tracked to confirm broad community involvement, including groups that might otherwise be excluded.
Through a combination of monitoring participation, measuring accessibility, tracking economic benefits, and engaging directly with citizens, Athienou Municipality quantifies the equitable and inclusive distribution of climate action. While our methods are practical and adapted to our size, they provide a clear picture of how benefits are shared and where improvements may be needed. By embedding these practices into planning and evaluation, Athienou demonstrates its commitment to fairness, inclusion, and the principle that climate action must serve all members of the community equally.

Athienou Municipality ensures equitable and inclusive distribution of climate action benefits through practical and community-oriented measures.

Free and open access: All municipal climate-related programs, such as recycling campaigns, tree planting, and awareness events, are free of charge and open to everyone. The “Yoga in the Park” event (September 2024), organized with the Embassy of India, is a clear example of inclusivity, as it brought together residents and migrant workers in a green, healthy activity.

Equal access for children: Environmental education programs are delivered across all schools in Athienou. Activities such as recycling competitions, tree planting, and energy-saving campaigns ensure that every child, regardless of background, benefits from climate awareness.

Accessibility in public spaces: Green infrastructure projects, like upgrades in Konstantineio Municipal Park, include shaded areas, ramps, and safe pedestrian routes, so that elderly citizens, families, and persons with disabilities can equally enjoy climate-friendly spaces.

Support for local farmers: Training and awareness sessions on sustainable agriculture are open to small-scale farmers, ensuring that economic opportunities from the green transition are not concentrated only among larger enterprises.

Community engagement: The Municipality works with cultural associations and migrant groups to encourage broad participation in campaigns, ensuring that underrepresented voices are included in climate action planning.

Through these actions, Athienou demonstrates that environmental, social, and economic benefits of climate initiatives are distributed fairly and inclusively, strengthening both resilience and community cohesion.

Climate change has evolved from being merely an environmental threat to becoming a multidimensional crisis with profound economic, social, governance, and urban implications. Local policies developed in response to this crisis, when aligned with global goals, not only reduce carbon emissions but also make significant contributions to the construction of more inclusive, resilient, and livable cities. In this context, the Sustainable Energy and Climate Action Plan (SECAP), prepared by the Municipality of Çorlu and committed to under the Covenant of Mayors, not only includes emission reduction targets in the fight against climate change, but also brings with it multifaceted opportunities such as economic revitalization, environmental improvement, social awareness, transparency in governance, and resilient urbanization. These action plans, shaped by the SECAP document, enable sustainable development to be achieved at the local level by turning the threats posed by the climate crisis into opportunities. 

Climate actions developed in line with this goal are part of a long-term sustainability vision and improve the quality of life of city residents, supporting them in living in a healthy and safe environment. Sustainable urban transformation practices bring various benefits, including not only emission reduction but also resilience to disasters, social inclusiveness, and economic flexibility. 

However, in rapidly growing, industrial cities such as Çorlu, climate change adaptation efforts are critically important. These adaptation efforts encompass many different components, from infrastructure planning to land use policies, increasing green spaces to urban water management. For example, green roofs and vertical gardens are being promoted to reduce the urban heat island effect, and permeable surfaces are being increased to allow rainwater to naturally seep into the ground. These practices offer numerous benefits from both a climatic and environmental perspective, while also contributing to urban aesthetics. 

Climate actions also initiate a long-term learning process in terms of social awareness and behavioral change. Environmental education provided in educational institutions, public service announcements, neighborhood-based awareness campaigns, and workshops are raising the level of awareness of the city's residents regarding the climate crisis. Children and young people, in particular, are seen as the most important actors in this process and are being raised to become environmentally friendly individuals of the future.
In conclusion, the climate actions planned and implemented by the Çorlu Municipality within its jurisdiction aim not only to reduce current risks but also to build a sustainable and resilient urban structure for the future. Thanks to this comprehensive approach, the fight against climate change is being addressed at the local level in an effective, holistic, and transformative framework, with social, economic, environmental, and governance benefits being achieved simultaneously. Thus, Çorlu is taking firm steps toward becoming not only one of today's livable cities but also one of tomorrow's.

Üsküdar Municipality carries out comprehensive projects in social, economic and environmental areas in order to support equal and fair participation of vulnerable groups (women, children, disabled, elderly and disadvantaged groups) in social life within the framework of climate justice approach. Entrepreneurship trainings and producer markets were organised for women's participation in economic life, and approximately 370 women benefited directly. Through academies, sports schools and environmental assemblies for children, more than 2,300 children were provided with education, cultural and environmental awareness. In order to strengthen the social cohesion of people with disabilities, 550 people were reached through the Barrier-Free Life Centre and sports activities. Social activities and health screenings were organised for the elderly, and direct support was provided to 1,500 elderly people. In addition, more than 5,500 people were reached through social assistance projects, psychosocial support services and awareness seminars. These activities contribute to reducing social inequalities, empowering vulnerable groups and supporting the social dimension of climate justice. 
In order to create a disaster-resilient city, Disaster Management Directorate was established within Üsküdar Municipality and disaster preparedness activities were initiated rapidly. Site assessments for 270 areas were made and evacuation and assembly areas were reviewed. Disaster Resilient Üsküdar Panel was organised with the participation of 400 people and urban search and rescue training of 7 AFAD volunteers was completed. In addition, 3,000 people were directly reached through disaster awareness trainings given in schools and municipality buildings. These activities increase urban resilience and contribute to reducing disaster risks.
Important steps were also taken in the field of health and social support. Free HPV vaccination was initiated for socioeconomically disadvantaged individuals between the ages of 9-26, reaching 400 people. Market shopping support of 5,000 TL was provided for pensioners in need, and 1,970 pensioners were supported. More than 100,000 healthy and affordable meals were served at the City Restaurants opened for the first time in Üsküdar's history. Within the scope of early childhood education, the first kindergarten was opened within the municipality, and the foundation of a new kindergarten with a capacity of 60 students was laid in İcadiye Neighbourhood. This nursery will also include a Women's Support Centre and a Child Support Centre.
All these studies show that Üsküdar Municipality realises a vision of a city that is both resilient to climate change and socially inclusive and fair. Thus, it both contributes to our carbon neutral targets and prevents vulnerable groups from being disproportionately affected by climate change.

Broader Opportunities and Benefits of Climate Action Identified by Quang Binh

Quang Binh, with its coastal location and rich ecosystems, has recognized numerous opportunities and benefits beyond mitigating climate risks through targeted climate action strategies. These benefits focus on sustainable economic development, resource conservation, and improving community well-being. Below is a detailed overview:

1. Economic Opportunities from Emission Reduction and Green Transition





Implementing the methane emission reduction plan by 2030 in the livestock sector delivers clear economic benefits by optimizing costs and allocating effective reduction measures at the district level. This not only supports the national goal of reducing methane emissions by 12.39% but also fosters sustainable livestock production models, enhancing productivity and reducing long-term costs for farmers. Additionally, transitioning to ecological agriculture (e.g., raising herbal chickens under forest canopies) opens markets for high-value, eco-friendly products, boosting local incomes and establishing green supply chains.

2. Sustainable Tourism Development and Biodiversity Conservation





Quang Binh is adapting to climate change in the tourism sector by protecting natural heritage sites like Phong Nha - Ke Bang National Park. Climate action measures help preserve ecosystems, attracting international tourists interested in green tourism, thereby increasing revenue from entrance fees, accommodation services, and local products. Broader benefits include biodiversity conservation, supporting community projects like mangrove reforestation, positioning Quang Binh as a national model for climate-focused tourism.

3. Enhanced Community Resilience and Public Health





Climate action is critical for mitigating the impacts of natural disasters such as floods and droughts, safeguarding crops and water resources. This brings significant social benefits, including improved food security for over 200,000 coastal households, reduced disaster recovery costs, and enhanced public health by lowering air pollution from livestock activities. Awareness campaigns on climate change, particularly through women's organizations, promote community engagement, create new green jobs, and strengthen social cohesion.

4. Attracting Investment and International Cooperation





By integrating climate action into local development, Quang Binh creates opportunities to attract foreign investment in renewable energy and low-carbon agriculture, supporting Vietnam's net-zero emissions target by 2050. Benefits include access to international funding for adaptation projects, such as early warning systems for natural disasters, which can yield returns up to 10 times the initial investment while driving regional economic growth.

In short, Quang Binh views climate action not only as a responsibility but also as a catalyst for comprehensive development, transitioning from traditional economies to green models, delivering long-term benefits for the environment, economy, and people.
